Energy stocks shine as vaccines fuel oil.headline: Energy stocks shine as vaccines fuel oil rally
Energy stocks shine as vaccines fuel oil.text:
Next week's meeting of the world's largest oil producers to consider extending supply cuts will be key to whether Australian energy stocks can build on their 30 per cent rally this month.

The gathering of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in Vienna comes as oil prices have been lifted by positive progress on a vaccine, boosting hopes that international travel could restart in 2021.

Over the last four weeks, the price of Brent crude has risen 27.4 per cent to $US47.72 ($64.67) a barrel by late Friday and US crude has climbed 25.2 per cent to $US44.83, the highest levels since March.

The commodity market tailwinds have pushed the S&P/ASX 200 Energy Index 29.8 per cent above its close at the end of October as the re-open trade carried equities sharply higher across the board. Among the local oil and gas producers, since the start of November, Beach Energy shares surged 49.6 per cent to $1.77, Santos shares rose 32.1 per cent to $6.25 and Oil Search shares climbed 42 per cent to close at $3.65 on Friday.

However, oil prices eased on Friday for the first time in a week after UK biotechnology company AstraZeneca released new details of its vaccine trial results, weighing on confidence in its efficacy and, therefore, the hopes of wide-spread inoculation delivering a return to unencumbered energy demand.

Supply-side factors also loom over the market as petrostates jostle with the ongoing uncertainties thrown up by the pandemic and worsening budgetary press

Travel stocks take off on vaccine rollou.headline: Travel stocks take off on vaccine rollout
Travel stocks take off on vaccine rollou.text:
Investors are betting that the vaccine rollout has paved the way for a resumption of travel, putting pressure on states and territories to commit to keeping borders open to stoke confidence.

Three of the five best performers among the S&P/ASX 200 yesterday were travel companies. Webjet rose 8.9 per cent, Corporate Travel Management gained 8.2 per cent and Flight Centre rose 7.1 per cent.

Karen Jorritsma, head of equities at RBC Capital Markets in Australia, said the jumps were attributable to the rollout, which investors saw as a sign of a return to normality. "I think it's sort of a hope trade," she said. News p4

Why investors don't believe the RBA on i.headline: Why investors don't believe the RBA on interest rates
Why investors don't believe the RBA on i.text:
Monetary policy Nursing multibillion-dollar losses after being wrong-footed on bond yields, investors no longer trust the RBA's interest rate guidance.

The Reserve Bank of Australia insists that interest rates are likely to be anchored near zero until around 2024, but money markets are pricing in about four cash rate increases totalling 1 per cent next year.

There has rarely, if ever, in Australia's financial history been such a disconnect between the RBA and bond markets.

Why the dichotomy?

A differing view on the outlook for inflation and wages is only part of the reason. Another factor is that sections of the investment community have lost confidence in the RBA's word.

The RBA's messy exit from yield curve targeting this month inflicted huge losses on some institutional investors who had backed the central bank's easy money policies.

Global hedge funds, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds and life insurers had bet that the RBA would keep its pledge to pin the April 2024 bond yield at 0.1 per cent, or at least limit their losses if the policy was changed.

But stronger than expected inflation arrived and bond yields spiked wildly, causing the RBA to abandon the peg. Shocked investors discovered the central bank no longer had their back.

Nursing multibillion-dollar losses on their carry trades after being wrong-footed, these investors and traders now feel battered, bruised and betrayed by the central bank.

sentiment_pool.headline: Transpacific extends CEO's term
sentiment_pool.intro: Waste handler Transpacific Industries has given chief executive Bob Boucher a new four-year contract with millions of dollars of remuneration incentives linked to strategic goals.
sentiment_pool.text:
Waste handler Transpacific Industries has given chief executive Bob Boucher a new four-year contract with millions of dollars of remuneration incentives linked to strategic goals.

Transpacific chairman Martin Hudson said the board considers Mr Boucher's four-point strategy to grow revenue, boost productivity, make tuck-in acquisitions and improve landfill capacity, is "vital to the success of the turnaround of Transpacific".

"Bob was given a clear mandate to fix the balance sheet, reshape the ­senior management team and start to address our legacy operational issues, all of which he has done inside 12 months," Mr Hudson said.

In the wake of the global financial crisis, Transpacific was left with a huge debt burden and a series of poorly integrated businesses.

It had been losing market share and was not able to focus properly on long-term strategic goals.

Mr Boucher, an industry veteran from the United States, was appointed in late 2013 to lead a turnaround of the company. He tidied up the balance sheet by selling Transpacific's New Zealand business to China's Beijing Capital Group for $892 million in 2014.

The company has been struggling against weak industrial waste markets and its hydrocarbons business – which sells recycled waste oils – is now under pressure due to the oil price collapse. F­leet impact

sentiment_pool.headline: Auditors failing to meet standards on violations
sentiment_pool.intro: In reference to "ASIC to crackdown on miners' dodgy overseas assets" (AFR, January 13), ASIC does not face "a fine line" in cracking down on the quality of disclosure by speculative listings with operations primarily overseas in emerging economies.
sentiment_pool.text:
In reference to "ASIC to crackdown on miners' dodgy overseas assets" (AFR, January 13), ASIC does not face "a fine line" in cracking down on the quality of disclosure by speculative listings with operations primarily overseas in emerging economies.

The alleged accounting fraud by Sino-Forest Corporation, previously listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange, is only one recent example of clear violations of basic reporting requirements.

Regulators in the US and Canada have documented several similar cases of fraudulent accounting schemes including overstated assets, non-existent sales, or failure to disclose relationships to related parties.

Cases have also typically noted the failure of auditors to meet generally accepted auditing standards with respect to collecting evidence regarding overseas operations.

Neil Fargher

ANU College of Business & Economics

Canberra, ACT

sentiment_pool.intro: If Prime Minister Tony Abbott delivers on his pledge to be Australia's infrastructure prime minister, construction materials and building products giant Boral could have all three of its key markets firing at once.

If Prime Minister Tony Abbott delivers on his pledge to be Australia's infrastructure prime minister, construction materials and building products giant Boral could have all three of its key markets firing at once.

Boral's Australian earnings could surge with new home construction hitting record highs and billions worth of new infrastructure projects on the horizon.

At the same time the housing recovery in the United States is moving Boral's US business back into profitability and the company's new joint venture with USG Corp is plugging USG's plasterboard technology into fast growing Asian markets.Recent record

sentiment_pool.headline: AML breaks new ground in Myanmar
sentiment_pool.intro: Years of patience and understanding the culture of Myanmar has paid off for Aaron Masters.
sentiment_pool.text:
Years of patience and understanding the culture of Myanmar has paid off for Aaron Masters.

Aaron Masters was working on mining projects at the small fishing port of Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh when he stuck his nose into the neighbour's backyard.

It was 2006 and the Australian had set eyes on Myanmar's mineral-rich coastlines – stretches of old beach sands that contain high-grade concentrations of rutile, ­ilmenite, zircon and monazite.

The trouble then was Myanmar had little contact with the outside world, which meant there were virtually no Western businesses operating in the country.

Thus he began an eight-year crusade to convince the Myanmar government, through the era of the military junta and the volatile times of a new civilian government, to allow him to explore and mine the sands.

In 2012, it paid off.

The Myanmar government granted him the rights to explore the coastlines of the state of Mon and Rakhine, on the edge of the Andaman Sea.

In September last year, Masters's unlisted mining company, Singapore-based Asia Mining Limited, signed three feasibility study and mining licence agreements with the Myanmar government.

"AML is the first foreign company to sign a feasibility agreement direct with the ­government," Masters says.

"No doubt, there have been agreements signed in the past in terms of mining. But they have all been done under a local JV structure agreement."

sentiment_pool.headline: Regional Express grabs Skytrans routes
sentiment_pool.intro: Regional Express is poised for another major expansion in Queensland after rival regional airline Skytrans ceased all of its operations on Friday as a result of financial difficulties.
sentiment_pool.text:
Regional Express is poised for another major expansion in Queensland after rival regional airline Skytrans ceased all of its operations on Friday as a result of financial difficulties.

Rex said it intended to fly all of the Cape York routes that were abandoned by Skytrans. Rex said it expected to begin limited operations within six weeks, pending clearances from the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). Rex also plans to mobilise additional aircraft and crew to undertake a full service within three to four months, after conducting a feasibility analysis.

"Rex is fully aware of the critical importance of air services to some of the very isolated communities in the Cape, especially during the wet season," Rex chief operating officer Neville Howell said. "In the meantime Rex will request permission from CASA and Skytrans to perform emergency charter substitution services so that the communities will not be completely cut off for weeks."

Six remote towns, including Aurukun and Coen, have been left without air services from Skytrans's closure.

Cairns-based Skytrans, which had operated for 25 years, was until recently the dominant independent regional airline in Queensland. But in October, the state government awarded Sydney-based Rex three regulated routes that had previously been operated by Skytrans. Rex took over those routes on Thursday, the day before Skytrans decided to shut down.

sentiment_pool.headline: Qantas out of the clouds
sentiment_pool.intro: A year ago, the ailing national carrier was struggling with headwinds of competition, oil prices and industrial action. Now it's back in the black. There are several reasons for this dramatic reversal, writes Jamie Freed.
sentiment_pool.text:
A year ago, the ailing national carrier was struggling with headwinds of competition, oil prices and industrial action. Now it's back in the black. There are several reasons for this dramatic reversal, writes Jamie Freed.

It has only been a year since Prime Minister Tony Abbott ruled out the prospect of a federal bailout for the then-ailing national carrier, Qantas Airways. At that time, the airline was making headlines for all the wrong reasons, including plans to sack 5000 staff over a three-year period as it dealt with a triple-whammy from high fuel prices, a domestic fight with Virgin Australia Holdings and an influx of capacity from international rivals.

"We are facing some of the toughest conditions Qantas has ever seen," chief executive Alan Joyce said last February.

Fast forward 12 months, and Qantas is now firmly back in the black, reporting a $367 million underlying profit before tax in the first half. To the delight of investors, the share price has more than doubled to trade at the highest levels since 2010 and there are smiles all around at the airline's Mascot headquarters near Sydney Airport.

"I'm very happy for Qantas employees and Qantas customers as a consequence of these results," Joyce said on Thursday.

UBS has forecast Qantas could report underlying earnings of $1 billion for the full year.

These are the five key factors behind the airline's quick turnaround.

sentiment_pool.headline: MYOB IPO placed in the $750m-$800m range
sentiment_pool.intro: There will be added interest when MYOB chief executive Tim Reed fronts noteholders on Thursday, for what is likely to be his last profit result as an unlisted company chief executive.
sentiment_pool.text:
There will be added interest when MYOB chief executive Tim Reed fronts noteholders on Thursday, for what is likely to be his last profit result as an unlisted company chief executive.

Reed is expected to reveal record revenue of about $280 million in the year to December 31 and earnings of about $140 million. But noteholders are likely to look past the headline numbers and ask what MYOB's listing plans mean for their investment.

MYOB's main shareholder, Bain Capital, is expected to push the button on a $750 million to $800 million initial public offering in late March, with the release of pre-marketing materials

The raising is expected to have Bain maintain about a 60 per cent stake in the company and value MYOB at $2.5 billion to $3 billion.

It would also imply a mid-20s price-to-earnings multiple, in line with listed peers such as Carsales.com and REA Group.

The timetable would have MYOB hit the ASX boards in early May after a back-end initial public offering aimed at domestic and offshore investors.

Noteholders are expected to be offered shares as part of the float. Healthscope ran a similar structure for its noteholders as part of its listing last year.

sentiment_pool.intro: Japan Post may lose some of Toll Holdings' contracts before completing its $6.5 billion takeover of the Australian group if change of control clauses in key businesses are triggered, creating business opportunities for logistics rivals.
sentiment_pool.text:
Japan Post may lose some of Toll Holdings' contracts before completing its $6.5 billion takeover of the Australian group if change of control clauses in key businesses are triggered, creating business opportunities for logistics rivals.

Toll is required to disclose change of control clauses in contracts with more than $40 million in annual revenues to Japan Post, and help negotiate the transition of contracts to the Japanese group.

But analysts have cautioned that some Toll customers could be concerned by the proposed change in ownership, with UBS identifying Toll's $300 million contract handling logistics for the Singapore Ministry of Defence as "the greatest risk".

Toll may also be forced to sell businesses in New Zealand to secure its sale to Japan Post if the proposed deal does not receive regulatory approval under the country's Overseas Investment Office.

Toll's board is confident the deal will receive approval from Australia's Foreign Investment Review Board but Toll's domestic competitors, which include trucking group Linfox as well as Australia Post and express delivery group TNT, could raise objections, analysts said.

"Australia Post and TNT are likely to be unimpressed by a state-owned enterprise entering the Australian express freight market, which is already facing overcapacity and a number of structural issues," said UBS analyst Simon Mitchell.

sentiment_pool.headline: Australia to miss oil fall 'free kick'
sentiment_pool.intro: The collapse in oil prices will leave Australia slightly worse off even though the nation is a net oil importer, research from Barclays shows.
sentiment_pool.text:
The collapse in oil prices will leave Australia slightly worse off even though the nation is a net oil importer, research from Barclays shows.

Because Australia is a gas exporter - and the price of gas is linked to the price of oil - Australia would miss out on the "free kick" that plummeting oil and petrol prices had given to many economies around the world, the paper said.

At present, oil net imports were 1.7 per cent of gross domestic product (imports of 2.6 per cent of GDP less exports of 0.9 per cent), while gas exports were 1.2 per cent of GDP, Barclays said.

The prediction comes as Citigroup downgraded its oil forecast for the second time this year, and warned that West Texas Intermediate Crude, which currently trades at around $US52 a barrel, could fall to the $US20 range "for a while" before rebounding. Citi expects WTI to average $US54 a barrel across the year.

Because oil imports outstrip gas exports, Australia is benefiting from the plunge in oil prices. This is especially the case as gas prices have held up. It usually takes three to six months for gas prices to follow oil prices.

However, the plunge in oil prices has come as Australia is expecting a surge in gas production and exports.

The expected plunge in gas prices, Barclays said, would mean the forecast revenue from this surge would take a hit. "[Currently] falling oil and gas prices have little effect on the terms of trade as a lower net import bill for oil broadly offsets lower gas export earnings,"

The boom in new housing, with record amounts of homes being approved, is expected to boost the earnings of Australia's listed residential developers and add shine to their forecasts.

Developer Villa World has already upgraded its full-year guidance on the back of a stronger market and sales momentum.

Moelis analyst Simon Scott said that despite price growth slowing a little, "we believe the key to residential developer profits is the amount of volume they put through.

"Providing unemployment doesn't blow out substantially, with interest rates where they are, we expect the developers to do well.

"Perth is clearly coming off the most. NSW is probably the strongest now and Queensland has the most potential upside. Victoria is grinding higher."

sentiment_pool.subhead: Resources Steps taken mean there is no immediate threat, says S&P
sentiment_pool.intro: Santos is in no immediate danger of a further cut to its credit rating despite last month's downgrading of crude oil prices, Standard & Poor's has declared.
sentiment_pool.text:
Santos is in no immediate danger of a further cut to its credit rating despite last month's downgrading of crude oil prices, Standard & Poor's has declared.

Investor sentiment around Santos, one of the worst hit by the plunge in oil prices, has been harmed by speculation that its investment-grade credit rating of BBB is at risk.

But S&P senior director Craig Parker said moves Santos had already taken to cut spending and add $1 billion of debt funding has put it on the way to achieving the financial ratios it needs for its negative outlook to be removed."We don't see any immediate threat to the Santos rating," Mr Parker said.

He said S&P will be looking for evidence Santos was going to continue towards a crucial 30 per cent ratio between funds from operations and debt in fiscal 2016.

S&P last month cut its oil price assumptions for the third time in two months and is assuming Brent averages $US55 a barrel this year, rising to $US65 in 2016 and $80 longer term.

On Tuesday, oil prices staged a mini-recovery, jumping 7 per cent, but they slipped again on Wednesday.

S&P reaffirmed its BBB+ rating on Woodside, saying that even if oil prices stay depressed, it should maintain important financial ratios as it beds down its $US3.75 billion ($4.8 billion) acquisition of Apache's LNG interests.

sentiment_pool.intro: Perpetual chief executive Geoff Lloyd is confident he can avoid a repeat of what happened three years ago when the blue-chip wealth management company lost its last pedigree stockpicker. That transition did not go so well.
sentiment_pool.text:
Perpetual chief executive Geoff Lloyd is confident he can avoid a repeat of what happened three years ago when the blue-chip wealth management company lost its last pedigree stockpicker. That transition did not go so well.

Billions of dollars of funds followed John Sevior out the door when he took a sabbatical and never returned. The same thing happened when Peter Morgan left the role years earlier.

The departure of a star fund manager is something that anyone running a prominent fund management outfit dreads.

It is a business which relies heavily on the performance and reputation of a handful of high-profile individuals. It is inevitable that the best and brightest eventually move on, usually to set up their own boutique fund.

Matt Williams joined a list of the country's most high-profile fund managers when he announced plans to step down at Perpetual's head of equities on Monday. He follows in the footsteps of Anton Tagliaferro, John Murray, Peter Morgan and John Sevior, who all held the job over the past two decades.

Like his predecessors Williams, 47, is relatively young and is expected to resurface in mid-2016 when the non-compete clauses expire. For now, he will take a break and is not saying what his next step will be.

sentiment_pool.headline: Partnership leads way on emissions
sentiment_pool.intro: Topping out at 217 metres tall, Lend Lease's new office towers at Barangaroo will illuminate a new corner of the city.
sentiment_pool.text:
Topping out at 217 metres tall, Lend Lease's new office towers at Barangaroo will illuminate a new corner of the city.

But a decision to save on energy costs means the lights installed in the towers are likely to glow for 18 years before a single globe needs changing.

Lend Lease is a signatory of the City of Sydney Council-led initiative called the Better Building Partnership, in which big landlords and property managers making up about half the commercial space in the city are targeting a 70 per cent reduction in carbon emissions by 2030.

Established in 2006, with signatories including Dexus Property Group, Charter Hall, GPT, Investa and others, the scheme is ahead of schedule to reach its reduction target.

The partnership has already cut emissions by 35 per cent since 2006. Members have reduced energy bills by $30 million a year since the partnership started, and prevented 113,000 tonnes of carbon emissions from being released in the atmosphere in the past year alone.

"It's a pretty remarkable outcome for a city which is continuing to grow in density and in occupation," Green Building Council of Australia chief operating officer Robin Mellon said.

"Most initiatives like this are slow to kick off, but what the City of Sydney tried to do was build scale very quickly through strong partnerships."

City of Sydney lord mayor Clover Moore agreed.

The fund also played a role in convincing James Packer to fork out $330 million for a 9.35 per cent stake in Zillow in 2013. It may be only a matter of time until the likes of Packer and some of Caledonia's other high-profile contacts start piling into Auto Trader. sentiment_pool.intro: South32 begins life with a management talking about the patience and prudence needed to establish a sustainable level of stakeholder confidence in its doubtless buoyant future.

But, at first glance, you have to wonder whether the faithful pilgrims of South32 will be given breathing space enough to establish mining's newest mid-tier colony. Put bluntly, South32 will be born a giant with an undergeared balance sheet and a target on its back.

That debt figure is less than half the best outcome anticipated by the market and leaves the business geared at a pretty inviting 5 per cent. sentiment_pool.headline: NSW electricity privatisation will fail
sentiment_pool.intro: The pro-privatisation article on NSW electricity networks ("NSW's biggest power users support privatisation", AFR, March 5) talks up lower costs by comparison with Victoria's privately owned network, but is wrong because it fails to look at the bigger picture.
sentiment_pool.text:
The pro-privatisation article on NSW electricity networks ("NSW's biggest power users support privatisation", AFR, March 5) talks up lower costs by comparison with Victoria's privately owned network, but is wrong because it fails to look at the bigger picture.

The electricity network businesses are in a death spiral. NSW wants to sell its network off while it can but because of the huge financial risks posed by battery storage technologies, no one would buy it without massive sweeteners and guaranteed returns. That means no innovation and artificially inflated, locked-in, high prices and power bills for decades. Privatisation would be a disaster.

The existing networks have refused to see the energy revolution coming because they are raking in the profits from overinvestment in poles and wires, which they have been allowed to do by the regulator under the fatally flawed National Electricity Market rules. By refusing to reform the NEM, state and federal governments have been overtaken by technology.

Affordable battery storage is rapidly coming down the cost curve. As networks keep increasing charges, it will soon be cheaper to leave the grid, resulting in higher costs for a shrinking customer base, which in turn will push more off the grid.

The electricity networks, if sold off, will not generate profits for state governments into the future, nor will there be lower electricity prices.

Senator Christine Milne

Canberra, ACT

sentiment_pool.text:
Multinational tech giant Google can add another site to its long list of options for its new Sydney headquarters: the heritage-listed White Bay Power Station within the Bays Precinct.

"It is anticipated that a range of proponents will respond. The draft Transformation Plan will be presented to government in April 2015 for their consideration and release for public engagement, commencing with the Sydneysiders Summit in May 2015."

UrbanGrowth is not due to present its draft plan for the Bays Precinct until after the state election. Plans have been unveiled to turn White Bay and the nearby Glebe Island into a new waterfront commercial and residential precinct. But any decision on Google's part is lying with global headquarters in the United States after options for sites were presented to management in January. The company declined to comment when contacted. A decision is still said to be a long way off.

sentiment_pool.intro: Total SA has been appointed to run the Papua New Guinea Elk-Antelope gas venture, setting the French oil major up as a direct rival to US giant ExxonMobil.
sentiment_pool.text:
Total SA has been appointed to run the Papua New Guinea Elk-Antelope gas venture, setting the French oil major up as a direct rival to US giant ExxonMobil.

The move, which follows the resolution last month of a dispute over Total's entry into Elk-Antelope, is expected to accelerate development towards a new LNG export project in Papua New Guinea, separate from Exxon's $US19 billion ($24.3 billion) PNG LNG venture, which started export shipments last May.

Oil Search, which owns stakes in both PNG and Elk-Antelope, had disputed the right of its Elk-Antelope partner InterOil to bring Total into the PRL 15 permit holding the gas fields, which some say could be the biggest gas discovery in Asia in the past decade.

Oil Search managing director Peter Botten said on Monday the election of Total, an experienced LNG operator, to run the PRL15 venture "will help facilitate the completion of appraisal and the timely development of the world-class Elk-Antelope fields."

Bernstein Research analyst Neil Beveridge said that with Total in charge, Elk-Antelope was more likely to move forward "in a timely and efficient way", which was positive for both InterOil and Oil Search. Oil Search shares still slid 0.5 per cent to $8.12.

Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance is expected to shake up the commercial insurance market as it seeks to lure large corporate clients after opening the doors of its Sydney office on Monday.

The new Australian boss of Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance, Chris Colahan, says BHSI will be "playing in the large corporate segment" of Australia's insurance market, which is dominated by players such as Insurance Australia Group, Suncorp Group, and QBE Insurance Group.

"We're targeting across Australia and to start with, as of today, we're launching in property, casualty, financial lines and marine cargo insurance in Australia," he told Fairfax Media.

"In the US we have other lines as well - healthcare, surety, home owners insurance and travel. We'll get into that if it makes sense to do so in the future," Mr Colahan said.

The entry of the Warren Buffett-linked BHSI will worry some of Australia's biggest commercial insurers amid a tough market peppered with increasing competition. Ross Curran, insurance analyst at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said the brand alone "will open every broker door in the country".

"They [the brokers] would want Berkshire on their panel, because it's such a respected name globally," he said.

"It poses a problem for the domestic [insurers]," he said.

sentiment_pool.text:
When you get it right, investing can be a simple business: understand a company, buy the shares, sit, watch and wait.

But then there's trading. And when it comes to trading there's only one thing everyone wants to know about: the no-brainer, the sure-fire win.

Of course, it's never that easy, but getting that one, single trade where you can make a killing, and swiftly, is always handy.

There's been a few well-known trades over the years and the latest one comes courtesy of Bill Gross, the former head of bonds giant Pimco, who is now plying his trade as a bond guru at Janus Capital.

This week he took to Twitter to say selling the 10-year benchmark German Bund was "the short of a lifetime" and "better than the pound in '93".

But there is a catch. He makes it clear you can't put the trade on until the European Central Bank ends its program of printing money. And there's no sign of that just yet.

The other point to make is selling the pound was a great trade in 1992, not 1993. But he is referring to one of the all-time great moves by any investor when George Soros made his name by taking on the Bank of England. Soros brought the bank to its knees when he made more than $US1 billion by almost demolishing the monetary system of Great Britain in a single day.

sentiment_pool.text:
A flurry of lodges and chalets have changed hands at Perisher, in the NSW Snowy Mountains, for more than $6 million, as buyers rush to seal deals in time for winter.

The Stables apartments in Perisher have sold for almost $5 million in a deal that settled in late March.

The upmarket timber-and-granite apartment complex, which includes a dining room and 21 stylish one- and two-bedroom apartments laid out over two levels and a mezzanine, is a short walk from the base of the mountain and is regarded as some of the most stylish accommodation in the region.

A group of individual owners had bought the apartments, which were likely to be let as holiday accommodation over the winter, agent Michelle Stynes, of Forbes Stynes Real Estate, said. "The new owners are very excited that Vail has purchased Perisher," she said. "All the new owners are putting money back into the apartments with renovations and refurbishments."

While owners are attracted to the region in search of a weekender in a ski resort, Vail's $177-million purchase of Perisher has also boosted confidence in the return profile of the investment.

A number of other deals are expected to close in time for winter.

The nearby Barrakee Ski Lodge has sold for about $1.5 million. The lodge, which is near the bottom of the North Perisher T-Bar and Interceptor chairlift, has 25 bedrooms and 50 bed licenses, which equates to council rates of about $86,000 a year. sentiment_pool.headline: NAB fine won't stop UK exit
sentiment_pool.intro: National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Thorburn said a $40 million fine imposed on its British Clydesdale Bank over mis-selling will not delay his plans to sell the lender.
sentiment_pool.text:
National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Thorburn said a $40 million fine imposed on its British Clydesdale Bank over mis-selling will not delay his plans to sell the lender.

Britain's Financial Conduct Authority dished out the fine as it highlighted serious failings in Clydesdale between 2011 and 2013 in relation to how it handled complaints about payment-protection insurance, which was widely mis-sold. The fine was the highest on record in Britain relating to PPI.

Clydesdale may now have to review up to 93,000 customer complaints that may have been mishandled.

Mr Thorburn on Wednesday said the fine, announced on Tuesday night, was a "very disappointing" outcome and the bank would review the penalties handed out to staff involved in the incidents identified by the FCA.

But it has not prompted the bank to set aside extra provisions for customer redress for PPI and he does not expect it to delay plans to sell Clydesdale.

NAB set aside an extra $756 million for customer redress relating to payment-protection insurance in its latest full-year results last year and Mr Thorburn said the fine had not increased this number.

"There's nothing here that's causing us to change that but of course this is an ongoing situation that we flagged then," he said.

Uncertainty over potential costs from compensation for mis-selling has been cited as one challenge Mr Thorburn needs to address in order to sell Clydesdale.

So convinced were equity traders and investors that the Reserve Bank was about to cut rates again at its April policy meeting on Tuesday that they drove up the S&P/ASX 200 index more than 1 per cent in the first hour of trading that morning.

The exuberance defied futures pricing, which had the market opening lower, or flat at best.

sentiment_pool.intro: The Australian equities market looks overvalued and even a small rise in global interest rates could make it look "incredibly expensive". That's the message from the UK-based product director of Invesco's multi-asset team Georgina Taylor.
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian equities market looks overvalued and even a small rise in global interest rates could make it look "incredibly expensive". That's the message from the UK-based product director of Invesco's multi-asset team Georgina Taylor.

"Equities have done OK, but it does look very expensive versus broader global equities," she said.

Ms Taylor, who was in Melbourne last week to meet superannuation fund managers and retail investors, said yields were likely to remain low in bonds and cash, with global growth and inflation stuck in low gear. There is likely to be little change globally in economic growth and very low inflation had driven yields lower in bond and cash markets.

The US Federal Reserve was likely to raise interest rates within the next year, but there was little inflation in the system and economic growth was not strong enough to significantly raise rates, she said.

But Ms Taylor was concerned about the impact of even a small interest rate rise given the way investors have relentlessly hunted yield. Investors had been buying fixed income-like equities and credit as though it posed no risk, she said.

"Any equity that's paying out a bit of a dividend, suddenly that's a risk-free investment apparently because you've got some yields and that looks great versus what you would get with government bonds," she said.

Investors are returning to the large-format retail sector, with the Waurn Ponds Plaza in Geelong in regional Victoria selling to a private Melbourne investor for $18.2 million on a yield of 8.5 per cent.

Recent centre sales include Australian retail entrepreneur Brett Blundy's BB Retail Capital acquiring the Wendouree Homemaker Centre in Ballarat from Australian Unity for $27.1 million, and Sydney-based private equity group Altis Property Partners paying $40.5 million for the Lake Haven Home MegaCentre on the NSW Central Coast.

Mr Taylor said JLL Research indicated the average midpoint yield for large-format retail assets in Victoria compressed by 50 basis points to 8.75 per cent in the year to December 2014. All the predictions for 21st-century motoring were for flying cars, electric cars, solar cars, even nuclear cars. No-one predicted that by 2015 there would be more conventional, petrol-powered, 12-cylinder engines being sold than ever before.

BMW will sell you one. Same for Rolls-Royce and Bentley. Ferrari too, of course. Plus Lamborghini and Aston-Martin. Toyota produces a V12 for its Japan-only Century limousine.

GSK's consumer brands include Sensodyne toothpaste, the malted-milk drink Horlicks, and Nicorette nicotine replacement product. Last year it filed a regulatory application for the world's first malaria vaccine. But the majority of its GSK's sales (about 60 per cent) come from its pharmaceutical operations, which includes HIV and respiratory products in which GSK claims a 33 per cent share of a $US29 billion global market.

By its own account 2014 was a mixed year for the company.

The problem is GSK's most popular product, the Advair asthma drug, is ex-growth and will be an ongoing drag on earnings this year.

sentiment_pool.intro: A surge in Chinese visitors has helped kick-start the tourism sector as Australians also decide to holiday at home rather than head overseas.
sentiment_pool.text:
A surge in Chinese visitors has helped kick-start the tourism sector as Australians also decide to holiday at home rather than head overseas.

With the Australian dollar falling from historic highs, Australia is re-emerging as an attractive destination for both international and domestic travellers, helping the tourism sector record some of the strongest growth since before the global downturn.

Queensland is moving to capitalise on the China tourism boom, announcing on Tuesday that Jetstar would introduce the first direct flights from China to the Gold Coast in September.

The agreement will see Jetstar operate two flights a week from Wuhan to the Gold Coast, providing seats for up to 35,000 additional travellers a year.

Next week, the tourism industry will host 300 Chinese travel agents on Hamilton Island to help them deliver package holidays to the nation's rising and affluent middle class.

Tourism Australia chief executive John O'Sullivan said the industry was moving to capitalise on the Chinese market, which contributes the second-largest visitor numbers to Australia and the biggest spenders.

He said tourism would be one of the key drivers of the nation's economy while the resources sector was in the doldrums.

"As you see some sections of the economy go through some really big corrections ... we're seeing that the services economy, particularly tourism, is starting to come to the fore," Mr O'Sullivan told The Australian Financial Review.

Westpac Banking Corp will raise an additional $2 billion of capital via its dividend reinvestment plan and has left open the prospect of additional equity raisings in the face of growing regulatory pressure to increase bank equity buffers.

With the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision also indicating that capital levels for big banks will rise as floors are put under their risk models, Westpac on Monday reported a decline in the group's common equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio to 8.76 per cent, down 21 basis points from the level at the end of September. Part of this fall was due to changes to Westpac's mortgage default risk model, which lifted the average risk weightings for mortgages from 14 per cent to 16 per cent. The biggest-ever boom is benefiting the mid-range market.

Since the housing market recovered in the wake of the global financial crisis, prices in the top quarter of suburbs by ranked price, have risen less than those in the middle 50 per cent. In Melbourne, the top quartile gained 44 per cent while the mid-market rose almost 53 per cent. In Brisbane, where overall growth has been much more subdued, the top quartile rose 8.8 per cent compared with 11.7 per cent in the middle two quartiles.

sentiment_pool.intro: The postal workers' union has called on Communications Minister Malcolm Turnbull to sack Australia Post boss Ahmed Fahour after the government-owned business said it will spend up to $150 million slashing almost 2000 jobs in response to a diving volume of letters.

The postal workers' union has called on Communications Minister Malcolm Turnbull to sack Australia Post boss Ahmed Fahour after the government-owned business said it will spend up to $150 million slashing almost 2000 jobs in response to a diving volume of letters.

The company said on Friday that losses in its mail delivery business were approaching $500 million this financial year, taking losses to more than $1.5 billion over the past five years, and it will report its first full-year loss in more than 30 years in 2014-15.

It is understood that 1900 jobs will be axed from the postal service provider over the next three years through a voluntary redundancy program. There will be no forced redundancies.

Australia Post employs 36,000 people, about 23,000 of whom work in the troubled mail services business.

"We have reached the tipping point that we have been warning about where, without reform, the business becomes unsustainable," Mr Fahour said in a statement.

"We welcomed the federal government's decision to support reform so we can manage the mail service losses, meet the changing needs of our customers and continue to invest in growing parts of our business such as parcels and trusted services."

Despite assurances there would be no forced redundancies, the Communications, Electrical and Plumbing Union said it was "extremely disappointed" by the announcement and called on Australia Post to fully reveal the details of the job cuts.

sentiment_pool.headline: Asian inflation gap to raise profits
sentiment_pool.intro: London | The gap between consumer and producer price inflation across emerging Asia has risen to its highest level since 2009. The greater uncertainty is exactly what this means.
sentiment_pool.text:
London | The gap between consumer and producer price inflation across emerging Asia has risen to its highest level since 2009. The greater uncertainty is exactly what this means.

Baring Asset Management is convinced that this inflation gap is likely to herald rising profit margins for Asian manufacturers, which are seeing the cost of their inputs tumble even as the price they can charge for their products continues to rise, albeit modestly.

However some other commentators are less convinced that the story is as simple as that.

Data compiled by Barings suggest the Asia ex-Japan region is experiencing producer price deflation of around 5 per cent, the fastest rate of price falls since the global financial crisis.

While consumer price inflation is also trending downwards, it is still solidly positive. As a result, the gap between the two, at around 7 percentage points, is at its widest since 2009. Given this gap turned negative in both 2010 and 2011, the reading is striking. Just what conclusions to draw from it, though, are less clear-cut.

Barings describes the CPI-PPI gap as its "profit margin proxy" for manufacturers, on the basis that it measures the differential between the rates of inflation for their inputs and their outputs.

"Commodity price falls are good for manufacturers, if your product price is not going down as fast as your commodities," says HyungJin Lee, head of Asian equities at Barings.

Brisbane-based PanAust has the Frieda River mine project in Papua New Guinea and two operating mines in Laos.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX mines Kingsgate disclosure
sentiment_pool.intro: The Australian Securities Exchange is investigating goldminer Kingsgate Consolidated after a shareholder questioned the company's compliance with disclosure rules.
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian Securities Exchange is investigating goldminer Kingsgate Consolidated after a shareholder questioned the company's compliance with disclosure rules.

It's understood the ASX has confirmed it is investigating the matter identified in a letter from BRW Young Rich Lister Sean Tomlinson. Tomlinson, who owns about 2 per cent of Kingsgate, wrote to the goldminer's board and the ASX about a range of issues including Kingsgate's proposed Thai spin-off.

If the ASX finds a breach, it would be required to refer the matter to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission who would have to decide whether to pursue criminal or other regulatory action. The ASX may also pursue its own action if a breach is found, which could be made public.

Tomlinson believes Kingsgate should update the market about the proposed Akara Resources float on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET), first flagged in 2007. The company has spent about $12.5 million plus further expenses on the proposal, while the miner's market value has plunged to $181 million from $1.35 billion in 2011.

Kingsgate said last week it was in had complied with its obligations under Listing Rule 3.1. The miner's chairman Ross Smyth-Kirk has told Street Talk the Akara IPO expenses were largely made up of consultancy and legal fees.

sentiment_pool.headline: Activists lean on AGL to hasten its exit from coal
sentiment_pool.intro: AGL Energy is facing mounting pressure to speed up its transition away from coal, with activist shareholders demanding the country's largest electricity supplier comes up with a plan to maintain profits in a low-carbon world.
sentiment_pool.text:
AGL Energy is facing mounting pressure to speed up its transition away from coal, with activist shareholders demanding the country's largest electricity supplier comes up with a plan to maintain profits in a low-carbon world.

Shareholders will vote at their annual meeting on September 30 on the special resolution, which is supported by several ethical financial advisers as well as pressure groups Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility (ACCR), GetUp! and Asset Owners Disclosure Project (AODP).

They believe AGL's commitment to exit coal-fired generation by 2050 is too long-dated and see a serious risk for investors in the company dragging its feet.

"The danger for Australia now being a reactor to what's going on elsewhere in the world means that companies like AGL need to proactively diversify much faster than they are currently planning," Julian Poulter, chief executive of AODP, said from London.

"AGL needs to get ahead of that and understand that just having the government in the back pocket is no long-term solution to managing your risk."

The AGL shareholder resolution is part of a wider campaign being waged by ACCR and GetUp! against the three largest electricity suppliers, with Origin Energy potentially facing a similar move. Slater & Gordon has seen its agreement with British insurance broker Swinton Group terminated just months after the ASX-listed law firm's $1.3 billion acquisition of Quindell's professional services division.

The Slater & Gordon announcement is light on detail and the company says its affect will not be material but given the "current circumstances" chose to disclose the agreement termination, which comes into effect in October 2015.

A reason for the termination of the agreement was not given. A Slater & Gordon spokeswoman said the company was bound by a confidentiality agreement.

sentiment_pool.headline: How Echo won Brisbane's crown

After a four-year roller-coaster ride, the victory over James Packer is sweet, write Michael Smith and Perry Williams.

It was a nail-biting moment for Matt Bekier as he paced the floor of his office in Sydney's The Star casino on Monday afternoon.

Below, the sun was setting over Darling Harbour and the construction crews working on James Packer's new casino tower across the water were packing up for the night.

Bekier knew journalists had been called to the Queensland government's Executive Building in Brisbane for the long-awaited decision on its $2 billion-plus Queen's Wharf project.

It was the moment the Echo Entertainment chief executive and a project team of almost 100 had been working towards for 18 months. But with only minutes to go before the official announcement there had still been no tip-off they had won.

Worse still, there was a rumour Crown boss James Packer, who was bidding against Echo, was flying back to Australia. Had his last-minute campaign to steal the prize from Echo worked?

Then the phone rang.

With general counsel and company secretary Paula Martin by his side, a tense Bekier finally broke into a smile: Echo had won.

While the odds favoured Echo from the beginning, the sense of relief was palpable.

Many cars on the market already had driverless car features, such as automated parking and Mr Waldron believed it would take less than three years for driverless cars to be roaming the streets in Australia, and another 10 years before car companies were mass producing vehicles without steering wheels. "The major issue from our point of view is building credibility while we showcase the potential," Mr Waldron said.

ARRB would launch a campaign for further industry and government support for driverless car technology and tests. The SA government had been actively engaged for months.

Myer's financial year ends next week and it reports full-year results in September. Umbers is unlikely to show his hand until the new recruits have had a chance to get their hands dirty.

"We've got a fair amount of cash, but we're not going to part with it quickly.

"Our sense is for the year, the market's been fully valued," he said.

The LIC's underperformance can also be traced back to the large number of call options exercised during the year. Djerriwarrh invests in Australian equities with a focus on stocks where there is an active options market.

sentiment_pool.headline: Mine closures tipped as iron ore prices drop

sentiment_pool.text:
Fund managers have questioned whether Australia's second and third-tier iron miners can sustain the massive cost cuts made in the past 12 months, as iron ore's latest plunge below $US50 ($67.60) a tonne raises questions about who will survive.

Tim Schroeders, resources fund manager at Melbourne-based Pengana Capital, said the market needed to be cynical about how much of the cost cutting would stick, and warned some miners were reducing the lives of their mines as they scrambled to slash.

"The sustainability of the current cost environment has to be called into question," he said. "Shortcuts are taken. When you are trying to artificially lower your costs for a short period, in two years' time some of your reserves won't be able to be mined because you've changed your mine plan. Some of the efficiencies stay around, but you have to be a bit cynical about how much is going to stick five years out."

The sector had enjoyed a few months of slight relief as iron ore clung to the $US60 mark, but the pressure is again mounting on Australia's juniors. This has allowed many of the smaller miners to reduce their break-even prices - at which they are neither losing nor making money - from $US60-plus to about $US50.

But iron ore has staged a steep decline since Thursday last week to crash below $US50 a tonne overnight Tuesday. It has fallen about 22 per cent from its recent peak in June.

The offer values Vision's shares at 88¢ each, 31 per cent more than its closing price on Friday.

Both companies were placed in a trading halt on Monday, prior to the takeover offer being announced to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The merged group will have a market capitalisation of about $255 million and a pro forma financial year 2015 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $32.3 million.

The bear became a household item when Chinese celebrity Zhang Xinyu posted a picture of her with the bear on social media, Ms Zhou said.

"Two years ago, nobody knew about the product from Tasmania but a celebrity introduced it on social media and now everyone wants to buy it."

Australian SMEs needed to gear up their efforts to reach Chinese customers, she said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Buffett fan goes with the strong cash flow
sentiment_pool.intro: Investment - Perpetual's global portfolio is fond of healthy balance sheets.
sentiment_pool.text:
Investment - Perpetual's global portfolio is fond of healthy balance sheets.

A lot of kids would have been happy to pick up the pocket money and think of something else to do with their life - but not Perpetual Investments portfolio manager for global equities Garry Laurence.

So intrigued was he with the way his family's printing business was run that the young Garry looked beyond his after-school and weekend work putting pages together to the nuts and bolts of balance sheets, suppliers, customers and market trends.

When his father, sensing the ramifications of the digital revolution, sold the company and bought a software venture, Laurence ran his slide ruler over that one, too. His love of the minutiae of cash flow, interest coverage, leverage and profit margins was born - as was his suspicion of cyclical industries.

And both have endured. Today, Perpetual's 34-year-old strategist travels the world, talking to senior executives from some of the best-known companies on the planet while weighing up geopolitical concerns, market trends and capital flows. At home, he also helped set up his wife's online fitness business, and never tires of getting to know the DNA of companies.

With about $670 million under management in the company's Global Share Fund, Laurence and his team have a portfolio crammed with some of the biggest corporate names in the United States, along with stocks from China, Japan and Europe. sentiment_pool.intro: Financial services giants AMP and Westpac are exploring the possibility of automating back office and finance functions - some of which have been offshored to low cost centres in Asia - using software systems.
sentiment_pool.text:
Financial services giants AMP and Westpac are exploring the possibility of automating back office and finance functions - some of which have been offshored to low cost centres in Asia - using software systems.

It heralds the beginning of a trend that is expected to affect white-collar jobs in much the same way that machines displaced blue-collar workers on assembly lines.

It comes after ANZ Bank revealed to The Australian Financial Review that it had been refining over the last 12 months a program in the emerging field of robotics process automation which will change the composition of its workforce.

AMP said it was "not looking to automate to replace roles". Rather its aim is to "automate small, time-consuming processes, such as data entry" and free up employees to "focus on higher-value tasks that add real value to the customer".

"Robotics process automation is actually solving a 20th century workload problem," a Westpac spokesman said. But in reality someone, somewhere in the world is currently performing these low-level tasks manually. And soon, they won't be.

Software is taking a bigger share of the corporate-finance workload. As it does the finance profession is bracing for a wave of technology-driven change greater than that bought about by outsourcing and offshoring over the last decade.

"The benefits of this technology is just coming in so there will be another wave of change over the next 12 months," Chartered Accountants ANZ head of education Jason Dale said.

If Treasurer Scott Morrison is looking for ideas to revive the tax reform process, he need go no further than this week's AFR Tax Reform Summit.

It's early days and there is still disagreement about how best to tweak taxes to boost innovation, investment and jobs.

But the contours of a grand bargain to lighten the burden on wealth and job creation by shifting it towards consumption took shape at the Tax Summit, which was sponsored by KPMG.

It would involve raising the GST rate to 15 per cent, possibly broadening the base, curbing superannuation and negative gearing tax breaks for the rich, and maybe reinstating the carbon tax or a broad-based land tax.

The proceeds - $50 billion or more - would be allocated among compensation for poor households, income and company tax cuts, deficit repair, state spending and other items.

Morrison and Treasury secretary John Fraser backed the push. Fraser told AFR Weekend that the idea that boosting rewards for being innovative and entrepreneurial would create more jobs was "an obvious point to me".

Morrison said he wanted a tax mix to drive growth rather than grow revenue by hiking taxes.

When it was created in the 1990s, ATP was a way to link three universities into business, commercialising cutting-edge research and development and giving shape to Australia's "Clever Country" ambitions.

Today, its success is patchy at best. On the northern side of the 14-hectare site are the heritage-listed buildings, including the old locomotive workshop with a working smithy. There's the government technology research body NICTA, which is being crunched into the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO). Other buildings are spread out, populated by random tenants like the NSW Roads and Maritime Service, and disconnected by empty plots of land used as car parks. The only cafes are of the staff cafeteria ilk, there is no nightlife or weekend activity, and the connection to Redfern Railway Station needs upgrading, as does the station itself.

But to his surprise and that of other Arnold Schwarzenegger fans that day, he was instead handed a ticket to the Chinese patriotic war movie, The Hundred Regiments Offensive.

He didn't have to go and see the movie about the Communist Party's 1940 military assault on the Japanese army but he did have to take the ticket.

According to photographs and videos posted on China's main social media websites, moviegoers were handed bogus tickets to ensure a strong showing for the patriotic film before Beijing's grand military parade in early September. This reportedly followed a list of specific sales targets being handed to cinemas by the central government's propaganda department.

The scam, which was first flagged in the Hollywood Reporter, came to light just as the government announced China's box office takings so far this year have already surpassed the total for 2014. By the end of last week, ticket sales had topped 30 billion yuan ($6.7 billion), up 48.5 per cent on the year.

Actually, their history is tarnished by deep bigotry. From the 1800s, the labour movement fought against non-white arrivals to Australia. Skilled or unskilled, unions opposed them, fearing competition from Asian and Islander workers on lower pay and longer hours and from the likes of Japanese deep-sea divers possessing superior expertise.

The White Australia policy was enacted in 1901 by the new Commonwealth government, a Protectionist/Labor coalition. It didn't expressly ban non-white migrants. sentiment_pool.text:

Like many baby boomers, retired Canberra public servant Ian Giles has profited handsomely by investing in real estate over the past few years. But unlike compatriots who have ploughed their cash into the booming Sydney and Melbourne property markets, Giles bet on the United States.

The decision may seem ironic, given the imploding US housing market was at the epicentre of the global financial crisis that brought the world economy to its knees in 2008. But the combination of crashing US house prices from 2007 to 2011 and a soaring Australian dollar between 2011 and 2013, presented a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for one of the greatest ever property plays by Australians.

"I could see the potential of investing in US property because you knew it was going to come back," Giles says. "The Australian dollar was also getting near parity."

Giles, 66, invested more than 20 per cent of his self-managed superannuation fund in a US residential property fund set up by local financial planning firm Dixon Advisory in 2011. He is not alone. Thousands of local retail and institutional investors have jumped into US property in recent years.

The $117 billion Future Fund, Australian Super and REST Industry Super have all stepped up their exposure to US property. Sydney-based Spire Capital has co-invested in apartments and office buildings on behalf of its wealthy clients and institutions.

The sustained price growth that has generated concerns about a socially damaging lack of access to home ownership for locals is having a similar effect on foreign investors, many of whom are limited to similar budgets, real estate agency PRD Nationwide says.

The Australian dollar's 29 per cent decline against the yuan over the past three years has made real estate cheaper for investors, but the report makes clear that not even this has been sufficient to keep the majority of Chinese investors in the game in Sydney, where prices are significantly overvalued, investment bank UBS said last week.

The report knocks the widely held but inaccurate notion about the wealth of investors from China.

Separate research from Sydney academics has already made it clear that Chinese investments, which make up only 2 per cent of the $270 billion residential market in Australia, have no effect on housing prices.

sentiment_pool.headline: New country, same problem as Brookes battles landlords
sentiment_pool.intro: The former chief executive of Myer, Bernie Brookes, has borrowed part of the turnaround template used early in his stint running the Australian department store chain for big restructuring plans at South Africa's largest non-food retailer, Edcon.
sentiment_pool.text:
The former chief executive of Myer, Bernie Brookes, has borrowed part of the turnaround template used early in his stint running the Australian department store chain for big restructuring plans at South Africa's largest non-food retailer, Edcon.

Mr Brookes says the power of landlords is a big challenge, as it was at Myer. In his new role as Edcon chief executive for about 10 weeks, he says his fix-it strategy there is a back-to-basics approach, including stocking more private label products and making sure the nine retail brands in the sprawling Edgars empire are more accountable.

"It is about the basics, including aligning the divisions to have responsibility and autonomy for their profit and loss," Mr Brookes told Fairfax Media.

Mr Brookes says the global mining slowdown is having a big impact on South African consumers, with unemployment rates at 25 per cent. There are many similarities in the retail sector to Australia: "the power of landlords, the climate and spending patterns, the over-reliance on promotions and the impact of unemployment".

He intends to ramp up the amount of fast-fashion private label clothing in core Edgars stores and to wind back some of the international brands, because some are being spurned by customers. Edcon runs 1527 stores based mainly in South Africa. It also trades in other African countries including Zimbabwe, Namibia, Botswana and Mozambique. There are nine main retail brands.

sentiment_pool.intro: Suncorp Group chief executive Michael Cameron insists that lifting insurance premiums and reining in costs will insulate the insurance and banking group from a repeat of the profit downgrade that sent its shares plunging on Monday.
sentiment_pool.text:
Suncorp Group chief executive Michael Cameron insists that lifting insurance premiums and reining in costs will insulate the insurance and banking group from a repeat of the profit downgrade that sent its shares plunging on Monday.

Mr Cameron, the former GPT Group boss who took the reins from from Patrick Snowball on October 1, blamed the pre-Christmas profit warning on higher claims and higher costs due to a lower Australian dollar.

He warned the group's insurance trading ratio (ITR) would fall to 10 per cent for the six months to December. The 10 per cent ITR target, a key measure of insurance profitability, is a sharp decline from the 14.7 per cent posted for the year to June 30.

Mr Cameron, who was previously a non-executive director of Suncorp, said the company was hit by higher-than-anticipated large losses in commercial insurance, a $75 million increase in natural hazards allowance, increased claims in compulsory third-party insurance in NSW and lower investment yields.

The insurer has been raising the prices of its policies, but the changes would take time to flow through the balance sheet, Mr Cameron said.

"This operational issue that we're working through needs to be dealt with, but we have plans in place and I'm comfortable that the actions that we're taking will pull the claims cost back to a point where we can continue with the great levels that we delivered in the past," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Tech talent war makes grass at home greener
sentiment_pool.intro: A talent war in Silicon Valley has sparked a software engineer shortage and driven up wages to near unaffordable levels for start-ups, nudging Australian expat entrepreneurs to consider expanding their businesses back home.
sentiment_pool.text:
A talent war in Silicon Valley has sparked a software engineer shortage and driven up wages to near unaffordable levels for start-ups, nudging Australian expat entrepreneurs to consider expanding their businesses back home.

Members of the so-called Aussie Silicon Valley "mafia", estimated at about 20,000 people, say if the Turnbull government's innovation policy hits the right note it could prove crucial in accelerating the shift Down Under of the two key ingredients for success: high-quality tech skills and venture capital.

Originally hailing from Sydney, San Francisco-based serial entrepreneur Ryan Junee, founder of Wearable Intelligence, which is backed by Google, said the competition for talent had reached "crazy extremes".

"It has become impossible to hire good talent here, even if you have lots of money to throw at the problem which start-ups rarely do," he said.

"I think it's a competitive advantage to hire your engineering team outside of San Francisco, and Australia is a good choice to do that, with the only downside being the time zone difference."

Developing the local tech industry by increasing the amount of talent and capital available to start-ups may encourage entrepreneurs to set up regional offices in Australia or return for lifestyle reasons.

Michael Overell, co-founder of online marketplace for contractors RecruitLoop recently relocated his chief technology officer from San Francisco to Sydney to set up a product development team.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX surges by 1.9pc as bargain buyers pounce
sentiment_pool.intro: Australian shares rallied strongly despite falls on Wall Street, fresh lows in iron ore, disappointing Chinese economic data and the Reserve Bank keeping rates on hold.
sentiment_pool.text:
Australian shares rallied strongly despite falls on Wall Street, fresh lows in iron ore, disappointing Chinese economic data and the Reserve Bank keeping rates on hold.

The market was up from the outset, recording strong early gains that lasted until the end of the session. The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index surged close to 100 points, or by 1.9 per cent, to 5266.1, while the broader All Ordinaries put on 1.8 per cent to 5312.6.

"We've recovered all the losses for the past month," said Commsec market analyst Steven Daghlian. This was despite the fact that "there were no major drivers from Wall Street and there were no big changes to the commentary in the Reserve Bank statement".

Mr Daghlian said it was the blue-chips who led the market higher.

"BHP is up over 3 per cent today so that certainly [helped]. There were a few standout stocks today but really it was the banks who were lifting things the most, up more than 2 per cent as a sector."

IG Market analyst Angus Nicholson called the session "a fine display of bottom picking". "Dick Smith bounced back today after losing more than 50 per cent the previous day on their financial year 2016 earnings warning. Metcash also saw strong gains as its recent earnings update seemed to show that the worst was over and that hopefully it was only up from here. Both consumer discretionary and staples gained more than 2 per cent."

sentiment_pool.headline: Will central bankers ride to the rescue?
sentiment_pool.intro: Will the world's major central banks step in to rescue slumping global equity markets?
sentiment_pool.text:
Will the world's major central banks step in to rescue slumping global equity markets?

The hope of a fresh round of monetary stimulus has been the greatest source of comfort for despondent investors, as the wave of selling swept through markets from Wall Street to Tokyo, causing the world's major bourses to drop almost 10 per cent in less than three weeks.

Not surprisingly, they reacted jubilantly when European Central Bank (ECB) president Mario Draghi signalled on Thursday his institution could launch a fresh round of monetary stimulus as soon as March. The ECB, he said, would not surrender to "these global factors" - referring to the tumbling oil price and the slowdown in the Chinese economy, concerns, which have both dragged global markets lower. Instead, he said, the central bank has "the power, the willingness, the determination to act" in order to reach its inflation target of just below 2 per cent.

Draghi's words were just what the market wanted to hear. Earlier this week, billionaire investor Ray Dalio, founder of the world's largest hedge fund Bridgewater, argued that the US central bank should reinstate its aggressive bond-buying program - known as quantitative easing (QE) - in the wake of hefty market declines.

sentiment_pool.headline: Investors right to worry about China's slowdown
sentiment_pool.intro: Global markets are continuing to fret about the slowing Chinese economy, despite the release on Tuesday of figures showing China's economy expanded by 6.9 per cent in 2015 - in line with Beijing's official target of "about 7 per cent".
sentiment_pool.text:
Global markets are continuing to fret about the slowing Chinese economy, despite the release on Tuesday of figures showing China's economy expanded by 6.9 per cent in 2015 - in line with Beijing's official target of "about 7 per cent".

It's easy to dismiss investor fears as a short-term and irrational obsession that will probably disappear over time. After all, the fact that the Chinese economy can no longer keep up the breathtaking growth rates seen in the past is hardly news. And investors have long realised that Chinese sharemarkets are highly speculative and volatile.

The real problem is that China's slowdown coincides with the end of the massive stimulus programs that were embraced by the world's large central banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

China's response to the financial crisis is also relevant because the huge stimulus program launched in 2008 to support growth is now showing up in severe overcapacity in many industries, which is putting downward pressure on prices, and squeezing corporate profits.

Even worse, Beijing's problems are coming at a time when the outlook for global growth remains weak, debt levels remain elevated and global liquidity is no longer expanding.

sentiment_pool.headline: The creeping menace of Asian Islamism
sentiment_pool.intro: The first self-styled Islamic state of the postwar era was established not in the Arab world but in south Asia, in Pakistan. It was followed by Mauritania in west Africa, Iran and then Pakistan's neighbour, Afghanistan.
sentiment_pool.text:
The first self-styled Islamic state of the postwar era was established not in the Arab world but in south Asia, in Pakistan. It was followed by Mauritania in west Africa, Iran and then Pakistan's neighbour, Afghanistan.

While the world frets over the spread of violent Islamist extremism through the Middle East, most recently under the banner of IS, there is a tendency to forget the menace of violence and creeping religious bigotry among the vast Muslim populations of Asia. It is in Asia, after all, that most Muslims live.

In Asia, as in Europe and the Middle East, IS is a popular brand among young Islamist militants. But the puritanical and bloodthirsty Sunni ideology it represents has been extending its influence there for decades under the guidance of other groups and governments, including al-Qaeda, Saudi Arabia and a plethora of local organisations.

Many Westerners - because their own troops have been fighting and dying there in the recent past - are aware of the savagery of the civil war in Afghanistan between the ultra-conservative Taliban and the government in Kabul.

But how many recall that Sunni extremists in Bangladesh have in the past few months hacked to death liberal writers and attacked foreigners, police officers, Shiite Muslims, Hindus and Christians? sentiment_pool.headline: Ensuring super will last your life
sentiment_pool.intro: Adelaide retiree Barry Barber isn't limiting how much he draws down on his superannuation to leave a pot of gold for his kids - rather he fears how long he will live.
sentiment_pool.text:
Adelaide retiree Barry Barber isn't limiting how much he draws down on his superannuation to leave a pot of gold for his kids - rather he fears how long he will live.

The 69-year-old former financial planner stopped working two and a half years ago and said it was always a goal that he would retire and not qualify for an aged pension.

Unfortunately, he said, due to a number of factors including the global financial crisis, he wasn't able to do so.

Mr Barber said his current superannuation fund was in accumulation mode and he opted to draw down just a little more than 5 per cent a year, which he uses on day-to-day living expenses.

He said at this stage he has a good lifestyle, holidaying overseas every second year and locally on alternate years.

However, he expects as he ages his body and mind won't be as active, so he expects to draw down less money.

"My attitude is a little different to many people - I think I will live for a long time," Mr Barber said.

However, he insisted he wasn't stockpiling money to leave his children a large inheritance. "My main goal is to make sure I'm financially secure for as long as I live," he said.

"But I don't have enough money to keep it sitting in a bank account accumulating interest of 3.5 per cent."

Financial adviser Mark Draper from Gem Capital said if retirees knew when they were going to die, running down the capital would be an acceptable strategy.

sentiment_pool.headline: Further rate cut waits on growth outlook
sentiment_pool.intro: Market bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates again this year have strengthened slightly amid this week's market upheaval, although most economists are likely to stick to their "on-hold" forecasts unless domestic conditions deteriorate quickly.
sentiment_pool.text:
Market bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates again this year have strengthened slightly amid this week's market upheaval, although most economists are likely to stick to their "on-hold" forecasts unless domestic conditions deteriorate quickly.

However, at least one economist has warned that low energy costs, deflationary pressures and the risks of further market contagion from China will weigh heavily on the bank's final decision and commentary at its first meeting of the year, on February 2.

"This is all something that the market should be pricing in a bit more," said HSBC's chief economist for Australia Paul Bloxham.

According to latest interest rate futures pricing from Citigroup, the chances of a cut to the cash rate, to 1.75 per cent, at next month's RBA board meeting have edged up from 12 per cent to 16 per cent this week.

The odds of a reduction in March are now 28 per cent, compared with 24 per cent on Monday, while for April they've moved from 36 per cent to 44 per cent.

None of this suggests further monetary easing any time soon, says Citi's head of G10 rates trading in Australia Sylvie Renaud-Calmel.

"There's been a little bit of a rise in the chance of a cut by the RBA in the next few months," she said on Thursday. The scalps are lining up for Australia's hedge fund clique.

High on confidence after calling the demises of Vocation, Dick Smith Holdings, Slater & Gordon and - to a lesser extent - Woolworths, the hedge fund set is looking for its next target.

One contender is small-cap darling-turned-top-200 growth stock Corporate Travel Management.

This time last year, barely a bad word was spoken about the corporate travel agent. Its shares had rocketed from $2 to $12 in only 2½ years, making plenty of money for its early backers and chief executive Jamie Pherous.

But hedge funds are asking whether the phenomenal acquisition-led growth story is coming to an end. The sceptics have been crawling all over Corporate Travel's acquisition accounting and cash flow statement - and will be watching closely when the company presents first-half results on Friday.

The doubters - who now hold 6 per cent of the company's shares as short - reckon corporate travel is a scale game. The bigger a player like Corporate Travel Management gets, the better the terms from its suppliers such as the major airlines and hotel owners.

Corporate Travel's roll-up strategy provides two benefits: an instant earnings arbitrage with its own stock trading at 26-times forecast June 2016 profit and those better terms from suppliers. Both benefits provide substantial one-off wins for shareholders.

sentiment_pool.intro: It's been nearly a year now since the market furore over the shock appointment of former magazine editor and publicist Deborah Thomas as chief executive of listed property and entertainment group Ardent Leisure.
sentiment_pool.text:
It's been nearly a year now since the market furore over the shock appointment of former magazine editor and publicist Deborah Thomas as chief executive of listed property and entertainment group Ardent Leisure.

The morning of that announcement, and for no other apparent reason, Ardent shares fell 28 per cent, shredding more than $300 million of $1.1 billion shareholder value. Under both Thomas and her predecessor Greg Shaw, Ardent has trumpeted a growth story around its Main Event video arcades in the United States, of which there will be 35 by June next year. But Street Talk can reveal a key group of listed and unlisted infrastructure players would like the sales to go further. It's understood they are running the ruler over a bunch of Origin's power stations and power transmission and distribution assets, seeking to drum up a few more deals.

Frischknecht points to startling progress on the cost front over the past few years for utility-scale solar projects.

In 2012-13 in the ACT's 40 megawatt reverse auction scheme for 40 megawatts of large-scale solar, costs at the successful projects were about $180 per MWh.
