One of Australia's leading architects has designed a house that shows how to spread natural light through small homes.

Andrew Maynard has built a double-storey extension on the back of a small Melbourne terrace, with a staircase and floors made of perforated steel that spread light throughout the four-bedroom dwelling.

Mr Maynard, who specialises in designing in small spaces and whose Tower House won last year's top national award for residential renovations, has created storage space in the 154-square metre Middle Park home by raising the floor in the living area at the back of the house. The raised floor provides 12 cubic metres of space into which belongings - such as toys - can be swept and covered over at short notice.

The design comes at a crucial time in the debate over housing in Victoria. Victoria, which approved more than 34,000 new apartments in the year to November, is playing catch-up to NSW, where the SEPP65 guidelines have influenced apartment design for over a decade. Planning Minister Richard Wynne will in the second quarter of this year publish draft design guidelines for apartments, with finalised rules in place in the second half.

Revisions to SEPP65 in NSW last year made it harder for councils to reject developer plans based on size of rooms and the prospect of new guidelines is generating debate in Victoria. Finally, there are the re-sellers such as Vocus Communications - owner of Dodo - which largely buys and resells Telstra's broadband services for the slimmest profit margins of all.

"Over the past year, we've really increased the scale of our operation in Australia because we had demand from some of our large investor clients to bring the GIP focus and approach to Australia in a bigger way," GIP Australia managing partner Rob Stewart said.

The fund, which has secured more than $1 billion in commitments from potential co-investors on top of the $2.75 billion directly invested, closed its first round of investment a month ago.

GIP, which employs operational and financial specialists, targets returns of between 15 and 20 per cent. It does not disclose returns but is understood to have met or exceeded these targets for its global funds.

The group, which opened its first Australian office in Sydney in 2008, focuses on transport and energy investments, and previously owned a stake of almost 27 per cent in the Port of Brisbane before selling it to Canadian pension fund Caisse de Depot et Placement du Quebec for $1.4 billion in 2013.

sentiment_pool.headline: Pipelines on the nose as ethical investors divest
sentiment_pool.intro: Coal, weapons and gambling have long been among the no-go sectors for ethical investors: they are now being joined by gas pipelines.

Coal, weapons and gambling have long been among the no-go sectors for ethical investors: they are now being joined by gas pipelines.

Australian Ethical Investment, admittedly one of the hardliners in the field, has divested from DUET Group this year, since at the end of 2015 adding gas pipelines to the sectors it avoids. The local leader in pipelines, APA Group, had already been dropped last year after its $6 billion purchase of the pipeline that carries coal seam gas to BG Group's LNG export plant in Gladstone, which meant the stock breached the investment company's ban on unconventional gas investments.

As head of ethics research Dr Stuart Palmer says, it's not just the pipeline, it's what it carries.

Australian Ethical's exclusion of coal seam gas caused it to divest from Origin Energy in 2011, then Energy Developments, the now DUET-owned company that uses CSG for power generation. Divestments in the overseas portfolio will follow later this year, with holdings in Britain National Grid PLC, Japan's Osaka Gas and Tokyo Gas, and the US's New Jersey Resources Corporation all to be sold.

The expansion of the $1.4 billion fund's sector exclusions to include conventional gas and pipelines is driven by the absolute priority the group puts on tackling climate change. Michael Cameron has been in the top seat of Suncorp Group for five months and he is blunt about his biggest priority as CEO: solving the company's expensive claims dilemma.

The $15.3 billion bancassurer issued a shock profit warning in December after Mr Cameron raised the alarm on the group's working claims costs.

Billions of dollars in natural disaster claims coupled with policy price cuts that failed to fuel large customer numbers growth dealt heavy blows to the company's bottom line.

The group's underlying insurance trading ratio (UITR) - a key indicator of an insurer's profitability - fell from 14.8 per cent in 2015 to 10.1 per cent during the first half of fiscal 2016, below the 12 per cent target introduced by former Suncorp boss Patrick Snowball.

Plunging investment returns due to rocky markets were another stumbling block, after Suncorp booked $270 million less in investment earnings compared with 2015.

sentiment_pool.headline: Housing rents may fall this year, says analyst
sentiment_pool.intro: Residential rents are growing at their weakest rate since 1996 and are set to start falling - on a national basis - as the housing boom floods the market with new properties.
sentiment_pool.text:
Residential rents are growing at their weakest rate since 1996 and are set to start falling - on a national basis - as the housing boom floods the market with new properties.

Rents show no growth over the past 12 months, as a combined average for houses and units in all capitals, according to CoreLogic RP Data figures released on Monday. Over the past year, house rents fell 0.2 per cent while unit rents increased by 1.3 per cent.

"With construction activity set to peak over the next 24 months, and with many new properties still to settle, there is a real possibility that rental rates will fall over the coming months," analyst Cameron Kusher said.

Rents picked up slightly in February for both units and houses, but the increases were likely due to a seasonal lift in rents that are typical the first months of the year.

Rents in Sydney picked up 1.5 per cent in the past year and in Melbourne by 2.2 per cent. Canberra rents gained 1.6 per cent and Hobart's rental market was flat.

Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth and Darwin all experienced declining rents in the past 12 months to February, with Perth and Darwin experiencing some of their largest annual falls on record.

"Based on our expectations, landlords have little scope to lift rental rates while for renters, it potentially means more surety in securing accommodation and the potential to upgrade into a higher level of accommodation for a similar cost," Mr Kusher said.

Troubled transport group McAleese has flagged a potential equity raising, after it suspended trading in its shares and deferred the release of its interim financial results.

"The company is in discussions with its lenders in relation to a number of alternative recapitalisation proposals, including with external providers of new capital, which would involve those parties acquiring the company's existing debt and the potential issuance of new equity," McAleese said.

McAleese, which is being advised by Moelis & Company, expects to update investors by March 7. The company has already warned investors it will take up to $55 million in write-downs against the carrying value of its assets in the first half.

McAleese's stock has slumped since its initial public offering two years ago because of a fatal accident involving one of its Cootes tankers, and a series of poor decisions that has left the company heavily exposed to the resources slump.

The stock, which floated at $1.47 a share, closed at 5.8¢ on Friday.

McAleese needs to restructure its debt to avoid breaching financial covenants. The company was carrying $170 million of net debt at the end of fiscal 2015.

Chief executive Mark Rowsthorn has a vested interest in a successful restructuring because he owns 31 per cent of the transport group. Keith Price, a founder shareholder and former executive, owns 6 per cent.

sentiment_pool.headline: ResMed shares hit as profit falls to $US88m
sentiment_pool.intro: ResMed chief executive Mick Farrell said the medical device maker is only one mile into a marathon in its push to integrate data and cloud technology with healthcare.
sentiment_pool.text:
ResMed chief executive Mick Farrell said the medical device maker is only one mile into a marathon in its push to integrate data and cloud technology with healthcare.

In February the $10.6 billion ResMed inked a deal to acquire health information technology group Brightree for $US800 million in a clear signal of strategic intent.

Mr Farrell said the deal, which closed on April 4, is "doubling down on connected care".

"This is maybe then end of mile one on a marathon run ... we're transforming the business of healthcare with what we're doing. There's well over 1 million connected medical devices out there and it is growing every day with more than 900 a day signing onto [ResMed app] myAir," he said.

"I think it is going to explode and it is driven by patients. They are downloading and tracking on Fitbits and Apple watches and tracking their sleep on myAir. We are seeing a big pull to that and we want to not only be part of it, we want to lead it."

On Wednesday ResMed, which sells masks and air-flow generators to treat respiratory problems such as sleep apnoea, reported a disappointing third quarter result. The 3 per cent fall in third quarter profit to $US88.5 million ($116 million) fell short of analyst expectations, with weaker margins affecting the result.

The San Diego-based company said revenue for the three months to March 31 rose 7 per cent to $US453.9 million, which represents a 9 per cent increase excluding currency movements.

sentiment_pool.headline: Domestic airfares fall as demand starts to dip
sentiment_pool.intro: The average price of domestic airfares fell by 5.77 per cent in the first quarter of the calendar year, after having risen by 8 to 9 per cent last year when demand was stronger.
sentiment_pool.text:
The average price of domestic airfares fell by 5.77 per cent in the first quarter of the calendar year, after having risen by 8 to 9 per cent last year when demand was stronger.

"We are now seeing cheap fares available right up to five and three days prior to departure," said Virginia Fitzpatrick, the general manager of Flight Centre Travel Group's consulting arm, 4th Dimension.

Her comments came as 4th Dimension and CAPA released their latest Australian aviation and airfare analysis report. It found that the decision by Qantas and Virgin Australia to limit capacity additions last year had paid off in the form of higher airfares.

The cost of the average one-way fare rose by 9.4 per cent to $147.10 for leisure travellers, while fares for corporate travellers rose by 8.1 per cent to $176.20, in part because they tended to book closer to the travel date.

The cost increases differed by route, with fares from Sydney to Perth rising by just 3.5 per cent but Sydney to Canberra up by 22 per cent. On average, Qantas airfares rose by 7.4 per cent while Virgin's were up by 12.5 per cent from a lower base.

However, the pricing trend is reversing this year, as evidenced by Qantas' warning on Monday it would add less capacity than expected in the current half due to softness in demand related to the upcoming election and a drop in consumer confidence.

Beefing up the protection of whistleblowers will dramatically improve bank culture, says Jordan Thomas, a pre-eminent lawyer and former regulator in the US, where authorities are taking more aggressive action against banks that retaliate against staff who identify misconduct.

As the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) writes this week to 30,000 companies to encourage their participation in a survey of employee attitudes to whistleblower protection, Mr Thomas, a former assistant director at the US Securities Exchange Commission (SEC), said whistleblowers were ‘‘a powerful engine for law enforcement’’ in the US because of their inside knowledge of scandals.

Mr Thomas, a partner at Washington law firm Labaton Sucharow, where he represents many whistleblowers, says it is still common for US banks and other companies to retaliate against employees who speak up against bad conduct – and this is now being targeted by the SEC as a matter of priority.

‘‘Retaliation is a very real problem and the US is aggressively policing that part of the equation,’’ Mr Thomas said during a visit to Sydney to conduct a lecture for business students at the University of Wollongong.

‘‘Regulators are beginning to investigate and charge companies for whistleblower retaliation, and that provides a public vindication and makes the next whistleblower more confident to come forward.’’

Energy infrastructure owner DUET Group has made it clear it is not done yet with acquisitions, after striking a $205 million deal to buy out Alcoa from their jointly owned gas pipeline in Western Australia.

The purchase of Alcoa's 20 per cent stake in the Dampier-Bunbury pipeline, WA's key gas transmission line, had been anticipated in the market as DUET had made no secret of its appetite to move to full ownership of its operating assets.

It will be funded by about $230 million in fresh equity from an institutional placement and share purchase plan priced at $2.20, a 3.5 discount to Wednesday's close of DUET securities.

Details of the raising were first revealed by Street Talk on Thursday morning.

Chief executive David Bartholomew said the move would further simplify DUET's structure, given that now it would own 100 per cent of four of its five operating businesses.

He said in February that DUET was on the lookout for acquisitions again after wrapping up the purchase of Energy Developments Ltd. Sources had suggested that Alcoa's stake in the WA pipeline was a potential target. DUET is also thought to have examined other assets on the market, including TransAlta Australia's stake in the Fortescue River Gas Pipeline in WA.

Alcoa, which was the initial cornerstone customer for the Dampier pipeline, is to maintain access to about 30 per cent of the transmission capacity of the line, which feeds its three alumina refineries in WA.

It's understood PEP's pursuit is spearheaded by the firm's Tony Duthie and David Brown, and they are preparing to buy it with a shell company named Australasian Foods.

Patties biggest shareholders include The Myer Family Company and the company's founders, the Rijs family, according to its most recent annual report.

The company is expected to report about $30 million earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for the year to June 30, 2016.

Accused insider trader Oliver Curtis bought and sold contracts of difference aggressively to make tens of thousands of dollars in a matter of one afternoon, a court heard.

On the sixth day of his trial, Mr Curtis appeared solemn as the taped conversation with his broker CMC Markets from 2007 and 2008 was played to the jury.

Mr Curtis was a 21-year-old university dropout at the time, but he was making tens and thousands of dollars by trading CFDs in large volumes, pushing his broker to "slam any bid", "just grab everything you can" and short sell certain shares "as many as possible".

The conversation reveals Mr Curtis describing a $67,000 windfall as a "good little afternoon". In another, he made $24,000 one afternoon which, in the broker's words, would see him "in good stead for the weekend".

Mr Curtis, 30, has pleaded not guilty to a charge of conspiring with his then best friend John Hartman to make $1.4 million.

Prosecutors allege Mr Hartman, who was equities dealer at Orion Asset Management, passed on Orion's trading information to Mr Curtis, who bought contracts of difference immediately before Orion trading.

According to the prosecution, this lasted for 13 months in 2007 and 2008 when the pair made 45 parallel transactions, most of which were profitable.

The freehold of one of Melbourne's best-known Chinatown restaurants, Shark Fin House, is on the market with expectations it could fetch in the range of $15 million.

Not to put too fine a point on it, the sale is expected to generate a feeding frenzy among would-be buyers, with properties in Chinatown rarely changing hands.

That reputation, along with its net rental of $465,000 annually, are being put to the test through a private sale campaign.

The four-storey building at 131 Bourke Street, midway down Melbourne's main Chinatown strip, has a net lettable area of 928 square metres. It sits on a 288 sq m plot. The lease has almost 13 years to run.

"This is one of the most prominent Chinatown retail assets to hit the market in many years and will bring an influx of global interest particularly from China, Singapore and Malaysia," said Colliers International's Oliver Hay, who is handling the property with colleagues Daniel Wolman and David Sia.

The property is held by a group of three local investors, who acquired it in 2012 for $7.5 million on a 5.46 per cent yield.

sentiment_pool.headline: Investors turn on Murray Goulburn, unleash class action
sentiment_pool.intro: Australia's biggest milk producer, Murray Goulburn, and its board are being sued by investors for allegedly misleading investors ahead of its float last year.
sentiment_pool.text:
Australia's biggest milk producer, Murray Goulburn, and its board are being sued by investors for allegedly misleading investors ahead of its float last year.

The class action was filed in the Supreme Court of Victoria just days after it emerged members of the board of the milk producer were allegedly aware it was not meeting its targets months before informing the market.

Investor advocate Mark Elliott - who recently won a class action on behalf of investors in Downer EDI - lodged the claim on behalf of investor John Webster, who will act as "lead plaintiff" in the case on behalf of other investors who join the action.

The class action alleges the company and its directors -- including chairman Phil Tracy and former chief executive Gary Helou -- were aware it "did not have reasonable grounds for making the misleading PDS representations" at the time it embarked on its $500 million pre-float raising.

It is also alleged the company breached its continuous disclosure obligations by not telling the market sooner it would not meet its profit forecasts, including as early as at its October annual general meeting.

A spokeswoman for Murray Goulburn said the company did not consider it had any issues with its continuous disclosure regime or the statements made in its product disclosure statements.

She said the company was limited in what it could say because it was yet to be served with the claim.

sentiment_pool.headline: Start-ups may face $20m bar for ASX listing
sentiment_pool.intro: Early-stage companies with a market value of under $20 million and less than $5 million in net tangible assets will be restricted from listing on the ASX if proposed changes to listing rules are implemented.

Early-stage companies with a market value of under $20 million and less than $5 million in net tangible assets will be restricted from listing on the ASX if proposed changes to listing rules are implemented.

The increase in the market capitalisation threshold is a jump of $10 million from the current cap, and the net tangible assets test would be raised by $2 million from its current $3 million threshold, if the changes are implemented.

The slated changes, first reported by The Australian Financial Review this week, should mollify the concerns of some start-ups which expressed concern that the ASX might have been considering implementing a revenue threshold.

ASX chief compliance officer Kevin Lewis said the aim of the changes was to "maintain and enhance" the standards for listing.

"[The proposed changes] go to the issue of if a company is too small to list. Some of the thresholds have been in place for quite some time," he said.

"It also addresses the question of why some stocks are listing. If they're coming with a very small float [in terms of the percentage of the company being listed], then there's no apparent reason to access capital markets."

But chief executive of ASX-listed automotive technology company Connexion Media, George Parthimos, said one of the "biggest automotive software deals in Australian history" would not have happened if the ASX's proposed admission requirements had applied when the Melbourne-based business reverse-listed in August 2014.

sentiment_pool.headline: RBA gives ANZ an $80m profit boost
sentiment_pool.intro: ANZ Bank will reap an estimated $80 million by only passing on part of Tuesday's reduction in official interest rates, and Suncorp is following its lead by also cutting home loan rates by a smaller amount than the Reserve Bank.
sentiment_pool.text:
ANZ Bank will reap an estimated $80 million by only passing on part of Tuesday's reduction in official interest rates, and Suncorp is following its lead by also cutting home loan rates by a smaller amount than the Reserve Bank.

In contrast to big four rivals Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and Westpac, which are cutting home loans by the official reduction of 0.25 percentage points, ANZ is cutting mortgage rates by 0.19 percentage points.

ANZ has some $243 billion in home loans, making it the country's third largest home lender, so even 0.06 percentage points translates to tens of millions of dollars for the bank.

Investment analyst at Watermark Funds Management Omkar Joshi estimated ANZ would save itself about $115 million in a year, or $80 million after tax, by only passing on part of the cut in official interest rates to mortgage customers.

"They've saved around $80 million they would have lost otherwise if they had passed it on like the other banks," Mr Joshi said.

That is slightly more than 1 per cent of its full-year profits, which are estimated to be about $7 billion.

However, ANZ's general manager of corporate communications, Paul Edwards, said that keeping part of the RBA's cut would not make up for an increase in the bank's cost of funding, which has risen as credit markets have become more cautious towards lending to banks.

sentiment_pool.headline: Tegel Group spreads wings and flies on Australian debut
sentiment_pool.intro: New Zealand is no longer known for its lamb chops after the country's biggest chicken producer flew onto the ASX.
sentiment_pool.text:
New Zealand is no longer known for its lamb chops after the country's biggest chicken producer flew onto the ASX.

Shares in Tegel Group soared as high as 10 per cent when it made its dual listing on the NZX and ASX on Tuesday before easing back to close with a 5.2 per cent gain at $NZ1.63 ($1.51).

Tegel chairman James Ogden said the company had global ambitions as the world eats more chicken.

Global poultry consumption has soared in the past 25 years, rising 55 per cent. This compares with beef and sheep meat slumping 11.7 and 39 per cent respectively, OECD figures show.

Mr Ogden hoped Tegel's exports would account for 25 per cent of its overall sales within the next five years as it capitalised on this trend.

It already sells chicken meat to Australia, United Arab Emirates and Hong Kong, and plans to expand to other Asian countries such as Japan and Singapore and elsewhere in the Middle East. sentiment_pool.headline: Reform needed to boost women's super
sentiment_pool.intro: Liberal Senators Sean Edwards and Dean Smith have broken party ranks to back superannuation tax reform, improved parental leave, and other measures to reduce the number of women retiring in poverty.
sentiment_pool.text:
Liberal Senators Sean Edwards and Dean Smith have broken party ranks to back superannuation tax reform, improved parental leave, and other measures to reduce the number of women retiring in poverty.

On average Australian women retire with half as much super as men. As previously flagged, the final report from a Senate Inquiry into women's economic security in retirement released on Friday found the single biggest driver of the super gender gap is women's lower average lifetime earnings.

It also found the super gender gap is forecast to narrow very little over the next 40 years. This is due to a continued over representation of women in low-paid, casual or part-time jobs, and their increased likelihood of taking a career break to care for children. "It is pretty clear that people who take time out of the workforce to meet family caring responsibilities, and those people are overwhelmingly women, are at an inordinate disadvantage when it comes to enjoying a comfortable retirement," Mr Edwards said. "There is no quick fix but it is important to try and address some of the very challenging long-term structural issues."

Alongside Mr Edwards and Mr Smith other Senators that signed off on the 19-point package of suggested reforms were Labor's Jenny McAllister, Chris Ketter and Sam Dastyari, the Greens' Larissa Waters, and independent Nick Xenophon.

sentiment_pool.intro: Starwood has taken its Australian development pipeline to 12 hotels and more than 3000 rooms after revealing it will open a new $80 million Four Points by Sheraton hotel in Parramatta by the end of 2018.

Starwood has taken its Australian development pipeline to 12 hotels and more than 3000 rooms after revealing it will open a new $80 million Four Points by Sheraton hotel in Parramatta by the end of 2018.

The 271-room Four Points by Sheraton Parramatta at 89 George Street will be developed by JL Parramatta Pty Ltd, owned by Chinese entrepreneur Jian Zhao.

It is the third new Australian hotel announced by New York-listed Starwood in three weeks, all of them in partnership with Asian-based developers.

Starwood's Pacific director of acquisitions and development Andrew Taylor told The Australian Financial Review about 80 per cent of investor appetite for new hotels was from Asia, with the recent Brexit decision having a positive impact on the local market given the uncertainty in Europe and Britain.

"Investors like the value proposition presented in Australia and New Zealand. It's a flight to safety to come to these markets," Mr Taylor said.

He added that hotel development in Australia was "stacking up better than ever" due to stable occupancy rates and rising room rates.

"There has always been a concern around construction costs, but they have levelled out now," he said.

The Parramatta hotel, which is going through the planning process, will sit on a 1353 square metre site acquired by JL Parramatta last September for $9.5 million. Construction is due to begin early next year and take about 24 months.

The value of rural property transactions around Australia has leapt to $17.5 billion in the 12 months to February, up 17 per cent on last year's high with the value of transactions up in every state as low interest rates and healthy commodity prices drive deals.

Landmark Harcourts' general manager Mark Brooke said that as the value of agricultural exports continued to rise, especially in the meat sector, more property transactions were taking place. "This is reflected in the continuing increase in value of agricultural holdings in states such as Queensland," he said.

The big jump in Queensland is also yet to reflect recent sales such as the Macquarie Group-run Paraway Pastoral's $148 million purchase of two cattle stations owned by the Western Grazing Company and Queensland Investment Corporation's purchase of an 80 per cent stake in the $519 million cattle station operator North Australian Pastoral Company.

sentiment_pool.intro: With the Tatts merger seemingly dead and buried and Western Australia's TAB sale stalled, Tabcorp is now looking across the Tasman for its next potential deal.

With the Tatts merger seemingly dead and buried and Western Australia's TAB sale stalled, Tabcorp is now looking across the Tasman for its next potential deal.

Well-placed sources told Street Talk the Australian wagering giant may now be looking to launch a takeover bid for the management rights of the fixed odds business of New Zealand's state-owned TAB.

While the Kiwi wagering operator is not officially on the block, Tabcorp wants to position itself in the box seat as the logical buyer should the John Key-led National government push ahead with another tranche of asset sales and privatise its TAB network.

Tabcorp's vast experience, particularly in the surging fixed odds part of the business, could make it a strong partner for a business which is well run but ripe for innovation.

The wagering giant has been broadcasting New Zealand racing since 2001, and there's been a co-mingling relationship - where all bets are consolidated in the same pool - between the two sides for nearly a decade.

Sources close to the process say there is also talk the New Zealand Racing Board may be considering product fee deals similar to those in place between corporate bookmakers and Racing Victoria.

There is also understood to be a battle brewing for the New Zealand television racing deal.

Tabcorp's Sky Channel holds the rights but Racing.com - the fast-growing joint venture between Kerry Stokes' Channel Seven and Racing Victoria - has thrown its hat into the ring for the contract.

Despite the new scheme not coming into effect until October 1, the Labor government attached the new tax to its budget legislation which was set to pass state parliament on Friday night.

The property industry had been lobbying the government since Tuesday's budget to withdraw the new foreign property surcharge from the budget bills so they could argue for amendments.

The PCA's Queensland executive director Chris Mountford said the current legislation would capture student accommodation, hotels, motels, retirement villages and aged care.

He said the Victorian government, which in April increased its own transfer duty from 3 per cent to 7 per cent, and amended their legislation to exclude commercial residential premises such as retirement villages, student accommodation and hotels.

sentiment_pool.headline: Sydney house prices slip as 'market takes a pause'
sentiment_pool.intro: Sydney house prices have given up some of their recent strong gains, with prices ticking lower over both the past week and month, figures from CoreLogic RP Data show.
sentiment_pool.text:
Sydney house prices have given up some of their recent strong gains, with prices ticking lower over both the past week and month, figures from CoreLogic RP Data show.

Home values in the NSW capital fell 0.1 per cent last week and are down 0.2 per cent over the past four weeks, the data provider said on Monday. It was the first four-weekly decline in prices since late January and a reverse from the 3.1 per cent monthly gain CoreLogic reported two weeks ago for the month of May.

"I think it's the market taking a pause," said Sydney buyers' agent Rich Harvey. "It's catching its breath. 0.2 per cent is a small number."

Prices have fallen over the past four weeks in each of the five largest cities except Melbourne.

The figures partly reflect the results of a quiet Queen's Birthday long weekend that held half as many auctions as a week earlier. Just 1053 auctions were scheduled over the week to Saturday, down from 2008 last week. Sydney's preliminary clearance rate of 76.3 per cent was based on 337 auctions, compared with 72.9 per cent from 627 a week earlier.

A two-bedroom apartment without a car park in Randwick was passed in at auction on Saturday after a $950,000 vendor bid. The 1/280 Carrington Street unit last sold for $737,000 in December 2011. The stock and its peers have seen some major downgrades by analysts.

However, he saw some concerns with Estia especially around its acquisitions and financing.

"In the last few weeks we have covered our short positions, and now in the last few days have started investing," Mr Ross said. "Regis is our preferred pick, however we are uncertain about Estia.

"They do have some top-notch facilities but there are questions about whether they paid too much and hence questionable goodwill on the balance sheet."

sentiment_pool.headline: Frank Lowy revitalises America's sacred site
sentiment_pool.intro: Nearly 15 years after the devastating terrorist attacks in New York, Frank Lowy is readying for the opening of Westfield's remarkable part of the rebuilt World Trade Centre.
sentiment_pool.text:
Nearly 15 years after the devastating terrorist attacks in New York, Frank Lowy is readying for the opening of Westfield's remarkable part of the rebuilt World Trade Centre.

It's a long way from the 85-year-old's humble beginnings, a shopping centre in Sydney's Blacktown, to Manhattan and this latest achievement in his multibillion-dollar global empire.

Lowy applauds America for rebuilding the 9/11 site into a powerhouse of commerce and business.

"What better response could there be?" he asks in an interview with The Australian Financial Review Magazine. "It shows rather than diminishing us, that act of terror activated us, made us more determined and resilient."

Lowy says Westfield wanted to be part of the spectacular rebirth of the site not just for commercial reasons but for "the pride and satisfaction of the comeback". The project combines the traditional shopping centre rental income with earnings from digital displays, corporate partnerships and events in an innovative model to be rolled out across the Westfield empire.

Amid weak commodity prices, BHP reduced production in all divisions except coking coal in the 2016 financial year, but has forecast increasing production over the next 12 months in iron ore, copper, coking coal and nickel, which is enjoying a price rebound on changes to mining laws in the Philippines.

But the rising tide will not extend to the petroleum division, where a further spending cut will ensure production volumes slide by between 13 and 17 per cent in the 2017 financial year.

While the bulk of the cuts will be in BHP's loss-making US shale division, volumes of conventional oil are also forecast to slide by between 3 per cent and 6 per cent.

BHP measures its company-wide production volumes by standardising each commodity group into "copper equivalent" terms, and the company's output is expected to be roughly flat over the next year in those terms.

Brenton Saunders from BT Investment Management said despite recent efforts by BHP to highlight the latent capacity that exists within its portfolio, there was little sign of growth in the near term.

The cost to the big four banks of a one-notch credit rating downgrade could be as little as about $200 million a year in extra funding costs, and a bigger worry is how far the Reserve Bank of Australia goes with cutting interest rates.

The big four would fall one notch to A-plus from AA-minus if the sovereign rating is downgraded to AA-plus from AAA.

S&P said on Friday if banks raised $7 billion to $8 billion each, they could hold onto a AA-minus status, but that was unlikely in the view of the ratings agency.

The banks already are well-capitalised, and increased regulatory capital levels would pressure return on equity, S&P said.

However, the ratings agency could also see a scenario where compliance with even tougher Swiss regulatory rules sees the banks in a better capitalised position than they are today. Were that to play out, S&P could not rule out keeping the big four on a double-A rating.

That scenario is not that different to the views of equity analysts, who are convinced banks need $20 billion to $30 billion to meet the upcoming Basel IV regime expected to be finalised at the end of this year.

Credit analysts are untroubled by the prospect of the fall one notch to single-A.

"A-plus is still a very strong rating, the ratings downgrade is not a reflection of their standalone credit fundamentals but would be a function of the Commonwealth's modestly lower capacity to support the banks," said Phil Miall, head of credit research and strategy at QIC.

sentiment_pool.headline: Business needs soul-searching
sentiment_pool.intro: One lesson from the weekend election debacle is that business needs to become more proactive about economic reform.
sentiment_pool.text:
One lesson from the weekend election debacle is that business needs to become more proactive about economic reform.

The need for a different approach is obvious from the general acceptance among business leaders that the country is now headed down a path of incremental reform.

All of the large-scale taxation reform that was on the agenda last year, including changes to the goods and services tax with the possible support of the Australian Council of Social Services, is dead in the water.

The most Australia can hope for now is limited changes in health and education, according to Warwick Smith, the former Liberal politician who is now chairman of Greater China for ANZ Banking Group and a director of Seven Group.

Smith, who spoke to Chanticleer from Shanghai, says reforms are necessary if Australia is to continue the remarkable period of economic growth stretching over 25 years.

He is concerned about complacency in relation to Australia's AAA credit rating, which has never been more important given the rapid changes in the global economy.

Smith's concerns were echoed on Tuesday by Peter Nash, chairman of professional services firm KPMG.

Nash is particularly concerned about the rising federal deficit. "The cost of failing to maintain a sustainable fiscal position will be a declining credit rating and higher interest payments on our debts," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Can we keep defying the odds?
sentiment_pool.intro: Australia has had 99 consecutive quarters of growth. The next PM will have his work cut out to keep it up.
sentiment_pool.text:
Australia has had 99 consecutive quarters of growth. The next PM will have his work cut out to keep it up.

Post the Brexit vote, in the shadow of strange tidings from an America at war with itself and on a day when Australia will elect a new government, it might serve us best to look to the future.

This is a valedictory column in the sense this will be my last regular contribution in this space in this newspaper, about which more at the end.

Valedictories can be, well, indulgent, so let's avoid all of that and consider where we might be heading, and what the prospects are for a country that is at risk of squandering its good fortune.

Let's assume - these sorts of predictions are risky on election eve - that Malcolm Turnbull is returned as prime minister with a workable majority. In those circumstances, how might a second Turnbull government, and one elected in its own right, acquit itself in what is certain to be an extremely challenging international economic environment with China slowing and global growth stuttering?

All of this against a background of a country that appears to be having great difficulty facing up to its budgetary circumstances, including an exploding debt to GDP ratio whose trajectory is the steepest in the OECD.

Among the more dispiriting aspects of this interminable election campaign has been the unwillingness of either side to commit to the sort of budget repair that would enable it to withstand inevitable shocks - and shocks there will be.

"The ACCC inquiry, to begin in November, will investigate sharing of risk along the supply chain, supply agreements and contracts, competition, bargaining and trading practices in the industry and the effect of world and retail prices on profitability," Mr Joyce said.

The ACCC would undertake the inquiry under Part VIIA of the Competition and Consumer Act, allowing it to obtain company information.

Mr Joyce said an issues paper would be released and industry groups could make submissions. It would report in late 2017.

Mr Joyce said findings from the inquiry would help establish the Coalition's commodity milk price index, which was an election promise.

sentiment_pool.headline: The crisis in Anglo-American democracy
sentiment_pool.text:
Two of the great political parties in the west - the Republicans in the US and Labour in Britain - are in a state of near collapse. That, in turn, threatens the health of democracy on both sides of the Atlantic.

The crises in the Republican and Labour parties are strikingly similar. In both cases, a leader has emerged from the fringes of politics and taken the party in a different and radical direction. The emergence of Donald Trump and Jeremy Corbyn threaten to destroy the electoral prospects of their two parties - and will sow division and ideological confusion into the future.

Even if Mr Trump and Mr Corbyn never make it into the White House or 10 Downing Street, their ascendancy is also damaging to the wider political system. Well-functioning democracies need a credible opposition to hold the government to account. But in the UK and the US, that basic function is no longer being properly performed.

In Britain, the challenge of negotiating the UK's exit from the EU cries out for an alert and responsible opposition. The government, led by Theresa May, has managed to acquire a reputation for competence, partly because Labour is such a shambles. Yet, although two months have elapsed since Britain voted to leave the EU, there is very little sign that the May government has any idea of how to handle the issue. Simply repeating "Brexit means Brexit" is no substitute for a strategy.

sentiment_pool.headline: What moved the market
sentiment_pool.text:
BHP

Investors drove BHP shares to their highest level since early May, despite the big Australian on Tuesday night posting its biggest loss ever and slashing its dividend. But the loss was a bit lower than feared and analysts liked the miner's efforts to cut costs and lift productivity. It also didn't hurt that iron ore - BHP's biggest cash cow - jumped 3 per cent on Tuesday night to $US62 a tonne.

Wages

Wages rose just 0.5 per cent in the second quarter and 2.1 per cent over the year, the equal-slowest pace on record. Despite the anaemic growth, real wages are still rising due to low inflation. Economists expect wages growth to remain weak over the next year or so, due to significant spare capacity in the labour market keeping overall inflation low.

China

Beijing has taken another step towards opening China's financial markets, unveiling a second channel for foreign investors to buy stocks while also lifting restrictions on asset flows. Regulators approved the launch of a link between Hong Kong and Shenzhen's tech-heavy exchange. It also scrapped quota limits for an earlier scheme linking Hong Kong to the Shanghai bourse. The measures are regarded as a bid to include Chinese shares in global indices.

sentiment_pool.headline: CRACKS SHOWING IN FED ORTHODOXY
sentiment_pool.text:
Economy San Francisco's central banker has called the entire inflation-targeting framework into question, writes Jeanna Smialek

A new economic reality calls for a new approach to central banking.

That's the message a growing number of monetary policy makers are espousing - and it's a point San Francisco Fed president John Williams is making more forcefully than ever. Williams argues in an essay issued yesterday that the level of interest rates that neither stimulates nor slows the economy has fallen. In the new low-natural rate environment, the Fed's policy of targeting low inflation will no longer make sense, he said.

Williams isn't the first to suggest that the economy is mired in a new normal, or to question the way the Fed is dealing with it. St Louis Fed president James Bullard is pessimistic about potential growth and says making long-run economic projections is no longer useful. Chicago's Charles Evans says that the Fed should wait to see inflation hit its 2 per cent goal before lifting rates, rather than hiking early to avoid an inflation overshoot.

Still, Williams's endorsement helps to mainstream the idea that a new normal merits a new framework. He's a prominent researcher who succeeded Janet Yellen in San Francisco and who is seen as a centrist on monetary policy. His comments suggest that a serious discussion is percolating at or near the core of the Federal Open Market Committee about whether the present policy-setting approach is the right one.

sentiment_pool.headline: Santos CEO Gallagher in no rush on sales
sentiment_pool.intro: Santos chief executive Kevin Gallagher has insisted the oil and gas player is under no pressure to sell assets as it claws back into positive cash-flow territory after a horror $US1.1 billion first-half loss.
sentiment_pool.text:
Santos chief executive Kevin Gallagher has insisted the oil and gas player is under no pressure to sell assets as it claws back into positive cash-flow territory after a horror $US1.1 billion first-half loss.

Mr Gallagher, who took over as CEO in February, said Santos had been cash-flow positive for the past three months thanks to the stepped-up cost reduction effort which still had a long way to run.

But Santos would look to continue to reshape its portfolio, potentially by selling down interests or increasing others, he signalled after the first-half earnings report, which saw the bottom line dragged into the red by a hefty write-down on the new liquefied natural gas project in Queensland. The result before write-downs was also in the red, by $US5 million, with the result Santos scrapped its first-half dividend. "The business has been stabilised, that was the first step in the process," said Mr Gallagher, who took the reins three months after Santos was forced to raise $3 billion in new equity to beef up its balance sheet which had been strained by funding for the GLNG project and the collapse in oil prices since mid-2014. "It's early days - there's a lot more we want to achieve from that but I want to emphasis there is no pressure to sell assets and there are no current sales processes."

The comments come after speculation Santos could look to divest its Western Australian or Asian businesses, or could sell some pipelines.

sentiment_pool.headline: OpenAgent raises $12m for home seller service
sentiment_pool.intro: OpenAgent, a start-up that lets home sellers find and compare real estate agents, has raised $12 million, led by the Westpac-backed venture capital firm Reinventure, as it looks to build new features into its platform.
sentiment_pool.text:
OpenAgent, a start-up that lets home sellers find and compare real estate agents, has raised $12 million, led by the Westpac-backed venture capital firm Reinventure, as it looks to build new features into its platform.

Founded by former McKinsey & Company analysts Zoe Pointon and Marta Higuera in 2013, OpenAgent has doubled in size every year and in the past 12 months claims to have helped 10,000 people choose real estate agents.

This latest capital raise brings its total to $20 million. Also participating in the oversubscribed round were Sydney fund Breakthrough Labs and Singapore-based venture capital firm Qualgro.

Ms Higuera said the $12 million would mostly go towards developing new tools, particularly one that will help homeowners value and sell their property. "We figured out that comparing agents was very important, but there are a lot more things that come into the process that technology can help with still," she said.

"One of the hardest things was deciding what to do with the little money we had. There's a lot of things we haven't been able to put into practice because we didn't have the resources."

OpenAgent was the second Australian investment made by Qualgro and the first by Reinventure's new $50 million Fund 2.

In June last year OpenAgent raised $6 million from South Africa-based Hollard Investments.

sentiment_pool.headline: Bankers, lawyers to get busy as merger deals poised to pick up
sentiment_pool.intro: There are tentative signs that mergers and acquisitions in Australia will pick up in the fourth quarter, following a dearth of deals so far this year for bankers and lawyers.
sentiment_pool.text:
There are tentative signs that mergers and acquisitions in Australia will pick up in the fourth quarter, following a dearth of deals so far this year for bankers and lawyers.

A report by technology and dataroom company Intralinks that tracks early-stage mergers and acquisitions (M&A) suggests deal announcements will rise in the last quarter of 2016. The more positive outlook comes despite lingering concerns by bidders around the application of foreign investment rules after binding offers for NSW's electricity network Ausgrid were blocked on Thursday on national security grounds.

Intralinks's Deal Flow Predictor showed activity growing by 6.9 per cent, the first positive reading since at least the fourth quarter of 2014. The findings are backed up by anecdotal evidence from bankers and lawyers.

The report forecasts the volume of future M&A announcements by tracking transactions across the world that are in the preparation stage or have reached the due diligence stage. These early-stage deals are, on average, six months away from public announcement.

The Australian results were in contrast to the broader Asia Pacific market, which is expected to see a decline in the last quarter of 2016 compared to last year. That is due to reduced levels of early-stage M&A activity in South East Asia and South Korea.

sentiment_pool.headline: Gold Coast a clear medal winner for industrial farce
sentiment_pool.intro: Industrial relations The antics of the CFMEU on the Gold Coast Commonwealth Games stadium might make unready Rio look good.
sentiment_pool.text:
Industrial relations The antics of the CFMEU on the Gold Coast Commonwealth Games stadium might make unready Rio look good.

If the Turnbull government was looking for a narrative to sell its stalled industrial relations reforms, the chaos that has plagued the site of the Gold Coast Commonwealth Games stadium offers a near perfect working example.

The stand-off that saw the CFMEU use twice daily "union meetings" to bring work on the $126 million development to a near standstill for weeks highlights every major deficiency of the construction sector's existing regulatory framework.

During Federal Court proceedings against the embattled construction union last week, Justice John Reeves remarked that - "If [head contractor Hansen Yuncken] want to protect themselves, they shouldn't enter into agreements with those clauses." His observation goes to the heart of the problem.

If building firms operated in a truly competitive market, contractors agreeing to restrictive union terms - for instance, rights granting four hours of discretionary union meetings a day - would soon find themselves uncompetitive and, before long, out of work. Yet the reality is that CFMEU enterprise agreements replete with stifling and unproductive work practices enjoy a virtual monopoly over the work sites of major public infrastructure projects.

sentiment_pool.headline: It's separation time - from my house
sentiment_pool.intro: The local coffee shop and perhaps a modest apartment balcony have replaced the appeal of a backyard.
sentiment_pool.text:
The plumber is promising to come back ... again. This time, it's the wall on the other side of the house rather than the pipes in the back garden. It now seems possible to get the washing done by simply holding clothes against the peeling, damp paint rather than loading them into a washing machine - also leaking.

That's as opposed to the outside wall adjoining the neighbour's driveway a few metres distant. This is now listing at an alarming angle, suggesting my neighbour's car will soon join the washing machine in a state of disaster.

The apprentice builder son of a friend comes around as a favour to investigate. His mother tells me later he is too embarrassed to call me because it's too big a job for him to fix and he's not quite sure what to do anyway.

But, she says, he is sure of something. Whatever it is will be very EXPENSIVE.

All around Australia, houses of a certain age are making adults of a certain age realise the time has come for separation - from their once happy(ish) home, preferably, rather than their marriages.

The size of the house has become a burden rather than a delight. All that maintenance so long put off in order to deal with more immediate cash-flow problems has now become a matter of urgent repairs required in almost every nook and cranny.

They are just proposals at the moment (so they are not law) but they will most likely be tabled and introduced to Parliament as a bill. sentiment_pool.headline: Lendlease's next Italian job
sentiment_pool.text:
Global property and construction group Lendlease has taken a step towards the development of a major mixed use project in the Italian city of Milan.

Listed Italian property company Risanamento SpA announced on Tuesday that it had entered "exclusive talks" with Lendlease "over possible cooperation for the joint development" of Santa Giulia.

Santa Giulia is a significant site, suitable for about 300,000 square metres of offices, shops and residences, some 4.5km south-east of the city centre and close to Linate airport - as is Westfield Corporation's Milan project.

On its website, Risanamento said the aim was to create "a modern district, with a wide scope of cultural services ... where efficiency, dynamism and quality of life can co-exist in harmony".

A Lendlease spokeswoman said the group had "agreed an exclusivity period with Risanamento to undertake early stage due diligence" on the project. "It is important to emphasise that we see this opportunity as exploratory at this stage," she said.

Lendlease has worked in Italy for 15 years with a focus on construction, like the recent Excelsior Hotel Gallia in Milan, and on healthcare, like the Brescia pfi hospital phase 1, which is the first completed healthcare private finance initiative in Italy. Lendlease has indicated its intention to increase offshore earnings from 30 to 40 per cent.

Volatility is rising. Stocks and bonds are getting sold off and poor old investors are losing money.

And it's all the fault of those villainous computer-driven hedge funds?

As markets have convulsed, commodity trading advisors (CTAs) and quantitative hedge funds that trade on market trends are once again being singled out for amplifying market moves.

But Anthony Todd, chief executive of the $US6.7 billion London-based quantitative hedge fund Aspect Capital, said those who point the finger at his and other funds for exaggerating market moves showed a "lack of understanding" about how they work.

"[At the beginning of the year] we were getting calls from journalists who were told we were catalysing this collapse in stock markets," Mr Todd said.

He said the way Aspect's models worked meant it had short positions in stock and commodity markets before the January sell-off and that increases in market volatility led them to scale back their trades.

"We were actually buying back our positions. We were providing liquidity to the market and closing off our positions."

"Trend-following" or "momentum" hedge funds use systematic trading strategies to profit from developing trends in major markets. As trend-following hedge funds have grown in size, some commentators have suggested they are crowding each other out as they deploy similar strategies.

sentiment_pool.headline: How onion analogy helps explain the bond crunch
sentiment_pool.text:
It's been a little over a week since a sudden rush of fear hit Wall Street, sending stocks plunging to their worst day since the Brexit decision of late June. Back then the catalyst for the sell-off was clear: an unexpected vote by Britain to leave the EU. After that shock, in what is now time-honoured tradition, central banks rushed in to reassure investors and provide the expected backstop to asset prices.

But in this latest sell-off, rather than the solution to the market's woes, central bankers have been causing them. The usual will-they-won't-they Fed speculation has certainly played its part in upsetting investors.

But beneath that there is deeper unease around whether the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank's extraordinary monetary policies have reached exhaustion point.

One of the main issues vexing central bankers is whether negative rates are doing more harm than good, by hurting banks' profit margins and making it more difficult for them to lend.

If the ECB and BoJ are reconsidering their negative rate policies, then longer bond yields below zero do not look very realistic - and in response investors have scrambled to get out. In recent days yields on a reported $US1 trillion ($1.33 trillion) worth of government and corporate bonds have been shunted back into positive territory.

sentiment_pool.headline: Brexit cost may be less than was initially feared
sentiment_pool.text:
Referendum A small long-term loss may be worst-case scenario.

The United Kingdom's vote to "Brexit" the European Union is on course to become the year's biggest non-event. Beyond a weaker pound and lower UK interest rates, the referendum has not had much of a lasting impact. Financial markets wobbled for a few weeks after the referendum, but have since recovered. Consumer spending remains unmoved. More surprising, investment has remained consistent, despite uncertainty about Britain's future trade relations with the EU. Have the costs of Brexit been overblown?

Not exactly. In fact, Britain may well end up losing the predicted 2-3 per cent of GDP from Brexit. But it is the exit from the single market, not the initial vote to leave, that will bring those losses, and that may happen over a long period. If the exit turns out to be a 10-year process, the losses would be borne gradually over that period, costing Britain about 0.2-0.3 per cent of GDP per year, on average.

This could be very good news for Britain. With a weaker currency, the country will benefit from an increase in export competitiveness that could offset those incremental losses and the transient investment weakness that is likely to arise.

sentiment_pool.headline: Saving the 'smelly soap shop'
sentiment_pool.intro: Cosmetics maker goes from a $5 million-a-year loss to the sweet aroma of success, writes Jessica Gardner.
sentiment_pool.text:
Cosmetics maker goes from a $5 million-a-year loss to the sweet aroma of success, writes Jessica Gardner.

When Peta Granger was asked to come home to Australia and turn around cosmetics maker Lush's worst performing country, the request came with an ultimatum: make it work or the British parent would shut it down.

There wasn't a deadline as such, other than the need for "drastic improvement" each year, but suddenly Granger had a time limit of her own. She was pregnant.

The turnaround was going to be a massive job - Lush was losing $5 million a year in Australia and New Zealand - so Granger offered head office "an out" given her newfound personal circumstances. "They were like 'absolutely not, you just better get a wriggle on'," she tells AFR Weekend. "But it did mean we had to move quite quickly in the first six months."

Shoppers will know Lush from the olfactory overload they get when passing by. Its wooden barrels and shelving is stacked high with sweet smelling bath bombs and soaps. But when Granger joined in January 2011, the air inside Lush had turned putrid.

Sales staff were unhappy, store managers distrusted head office and customers were indifferent.

"We were called anything from 'that cheap soap shop' to 'that expensive soap shop'," she says. "I guess it was overcoming the 'smelly soap shop persona' and letting people know that there was so much more underneath all that."

The representatives of major parties in all Western democracies personify the political class. The perception is that we are the establishment, the elite. We are perceived as self-serving and arrogant. We are the ones who make promises and do not deliver. We do not share in the frustrations of ordinary people.

If we are honest, though, we have to accept some of the blame.

The cynicism is stronger, much stronger, in the outer suburban areas and regional centres. Some of these voters feel they have not been sharing in the extraordinary wealth generated in the knowledge economies right around the world.

sentiment_pool.intro: As Metals X flourishes, Kasbah is doing it tough.

"Business needs to do a much better job of representing itself to the wider community," he said. "We are in an age of populism and soundbites and social media."

He gave the example of the push for a royal commission into the banking sector, following a political and popular backlash against the big four's multibillion-dollar profits.

"I don't think the returns are the problem, it is the headline, the actual sums of money involved. When people see a headline saying '$8 billion profit', the populist reaction is they must be ripping people off," Mr Mullen told The Australian Financial Review and JPMorgan Chanticleer Lunch.

While Groves, 41, is best known for floating online classifieds companies such as IProperty and iCar Asia on the ASX in the past decade, he also likes to personally hedge against his technology holdings.

Alphabet Inc shares on the NASDAQ have risen 14 per cent in the past 12 months and 9 per cent since January 1.

Grove was an accountant at Arthur Andersen in Sydney before striking out on his own with a series of internet investment companies, including iProperty, which was sold to REA Group in a $741 million deal this year.

The sale of 10 non-core pubs - six already divested and four under contracted - will generate $69 million in sales at a 14.6 per cent premium to book value.

According to the 2016 Lantern annual report, the value of its land and buildings was $62.8 million as of June 30 2016. It does not disclose the value of individual pubs.

Lantern CEO John Osborne told The Australian Financial Review the core pubs were expected to exceed the premium achieved for the non-core pubs.

"Our intention is to proceed with the sell- down. Recent sales of pubs support a strong market for these assets," he said.

The coal haulage contract will contain rights, subject to certain limitations, to exclusively haul all coal produced at Glencore's existing mines in the Hunter Valley to the Port of Newcastle and will have minimum guaranteed volumes during the first 18 years, according to Glencore legal advisers King & Wood Mallesons.

Changes to regulatory hurdles to encourage fledgling banks to challenge the dominance of the big four are among the recommendations a parliamentary committee is likely to put to the government.

Committee chairman David Coleman has identified two potential roadblocks to greater competition within the banking sector.

Mr Coleman, a former director of Yellow Brick Road non-bank financial services group, has been quizzing bank chiefs and regulators about barriers to entry for start-ups.

He has strongly hinted he would like to see change.

When Australian Prudential Regulation Authority chief Wayne Byres appeared before the committee last week, Mr Coleman wanted to know how the regulator might respond to changes to the 15 per cent shareholder limit and $50 million capital requirement.

"The Parliament has determined that a shareholding above 15 per cent is 'unacceptable' - that is the wording of the act," Mr Byers said in response.

"I think it has generally served us in quite good stead as a gate. It is not a complete barrier."

Chinese authorities have launched a criminal investigation into staff at Crown Resorts and confirmed they have detained a number of Australians for gambling-related offences.

"Australians are under criminal detention ... for suspected involvement in gambling crimes," China's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement to The Australian Financial Review on Sunday. "At this stage the case is under further investigation."

The Crown staff were detained in a series of overnight raids on Thursday and Friday, as first revealed by the Financial Review, in an apparent crackdown on illegal marketing by offshore casinos.

Australian consular officials in China are expected to receive official notification about the detentions on Monday morning and be allowed to visit the Crown staff by midweek.

It is believed one of the detained men, Jason O'Connor, the head of VIP International at Crown, is being held at the main detention centre in Shanghai.

The Crown staff may have been targeted as part of "Operation Chain Break", launched by Chinese authorities last year in an effort to stop the illicit flow of funds into foreign casinos.

sentiment_pool.headline: We need a supply-side revolution
sentiment_pool.text:
The new RBA governor makes a case for freeing up the economy that Thatcher and Reagan would be proud of.

When the new Reserve Bank governor, Philip Lowe, testified before a parliamentary committee recently, some Labor politicians who love big spending saw an opportunity. They quizzed him on the global failure of low interest rates to boost "aggregate demand" - the sum of all spending in an economy - and raised the case for more government spending to boost it. The new governor, keen to be polite and appear impartial, fell for the trap. While he rejected the relevance of the question for Australia, he went on to muse about global conditions and the general case for government spending on infrastructure.

That was enough for commentators of the left to declare that the new Reserve Bank governor supports more, smarter government spending. Infrastructure is it, they reported him saying, and conveniently left out any reservations about Australia.

In fact, the rest of the governor's testimony was actually a defence of supply-side economics that would have made Reagan and Thatcher proud. Because while the Reserve Bank governor is responsible for managing "aggregate demand" through adjusting interest rates, he is acutely aware that this is not the sole, or even the key, driver of incomes and employment in Australia. Mr Lew negotiated for the famous Trump name to be splashed across the beach-side complex. Under the deal the retail entrepreneur struck with Mr Trump, his daughter Ivanka and son Donald jnr, the real estate celebrity flew to Tokyo to market the units.

On a single auction day in 2006, all of the 465 off-the-plan apartments were pre-sold for $US700 million. Half the buyers were Japanese who paid an average of $US1.5 million, 50 per cent above forecast. Mr Trump nabbed a large fee and had his photo taken with every Japanese buyer.

Mr Lew, who has known Mr Trump for more than two decades, told The Australian Financial Review his experience with Mr Trump was "positive, successful and, very importantly, profitable for all involved".

"He has bred a great culture within both his family and his organisation." Mr Lew said. "I'd be happy to build a hotel with him again."

The world's biggest economy appears poised under Mr Trump to shift from a dependence on the fading power of ultra-low interest rates to kick-starting fiscal stimulus.

Global markets responded to the promise of a policy switch by reversing earlier Trump-related losses, after discounting his trade-protection threats and other geopolitical concerns.

BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto both soared 8.2 per cent, while Fortescue Metals surged 10.7 per cent.

"Trump may implement just some fiscal policy in size," said Adam Donaldson, head of fixed income, rates and research at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. sentiment_pool.text:
Counter culture A key text of the late 1960s generation is being republished in luxury format, writes Mick Brown.

In 1964, when Ken Kesey, author and LSD evangelist, and a group of friends calling themselves the Merry Pranksters, set off across America in a bus daubed in psychedelic colours, they talked of being either on the bus or off the bus. It was a phrase both literal and metaphorical. Not simply were you there physically - bumping and jolting across the great expanse, jagged on drugs and sleeplessness - but were you there, one might say, mystically? Were you attuned to the deeper, collective acid unconscious, "The Great Flow" as they called it, that, so it was believed, would presage a revolution in consciousness and turn the whole world Day-Glo?

Tom Wolfe was not, in any sense, on the bus. Yet in 1968 Wolfe wrote the definitive account of that journey and its aftermath, The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test, that would become one of the key texts of the psychedelic revolution that swept across America in the late '60s. The book is now being republished in abridged form by Taschen in a deluxe edition, featuring extraordinary pictures by the photographers Larry Schiller and Ted Streshinsky, who chronicled Kesey and the California LSD scene when it was in its infancy.

"I think young people today probably look back on that period in the '60s in much the same way as I look back on the 1890s," Wolfe says with a laugh. "But it was a very wild time."

Rio Tinto has spent billions trying to plot a course to production at Simandou that is untainted by corruption or by the excessive complexity that walks hand-in-glove with working in the opaque West African vortex that is Guinea.

Rio's internal confidence in its claim to untainted moral authority stretched, in 2014, to a failed attempt to bring US racketeering, bribery and corruption charges against Brazilian iron ore kings Vale after it formed an alliance with an Israeli billionaire and elements of the Guinean government that allegedly aimed to poach half of Rio's four Simandou tenements.

Guinea removed the northernmost pair of Rio tenements from the company in 2008 and they were then immediately presented to interests associated with the New York resident diamond trader, Benny Steinmetz. He immediately on-sold a share in the leases to Vale, which had only recently withdrawn from an effort to acquire Rio's Guinean giant.

"I scratched my head [at the time]," he said. "It's not necessarily a good idea to have thousands of security holders in small companies, but this achieves a good balance."

Australian Shareholders Association chairman Diana D'Ambra also applauded the move, although it would have liked the ASX to go a step further. "While we would have preferred a 25 per cent free float, we believe 20 per cent is a move in the right direction," she said.

On Wednesday the exchange released its revised changes to the listing rules, after first proposing tightening the restrictions in May.

Overall, the rules have been toned down since May, pleasing members of the start-up community who had been nervous it would block too many early-stage companies from listing.

Under the new listing requirements, companies will need to have either $4 million in net tangible assets or a market capitalisation of $15 million to list. For all companies admitted under the NTA test, they will also need to have $1.5 million of working capital.

A battery technology firm backed by entrepreneur Simon Hackett has developed a better way to make electrodes for lithium ion batteries and is seeking $6 million to build a pilot plant and scale up the process.

Nano-Nouvelle, based near Maroochydore on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, has successfully trialled a nanotechnology process that coats a highly porous polymer sheet with a thin layer of copper to make battery anodes up to 70 per cent lighter than solid copper anodes.

Nanotechnology is science, engineering and technology conducted at a tiny scale - down to the level of atoms and molecules - that enables products and processes to be engineered with much greater precision.

To date, working at this level has been a slow process. But Nana-Nouvelle managed to continuously coat polymer sheeting 100 times faster than existing nanotechnology methods in a trial with British manufacturer Cemco last month.

The copper-coated polymer, Lumafoil, could add 50 per cent to the capacity of lithium ion batteries just as they move into more demanding and critical uses in vehicles, drones, electricity grids and household storage systems.

"It's really a big milestone. We have been working for a long time to make sure it would be manufactured at mass production scale but it's a really big thing to be able to do it roll-to-roll," said Stephanie Moroz, Nano-Nouvelle's chief executive.

sentiment_pool.text:
An agreement by OPEC to reduce oil production has lifted energy stocks and caused a sell-off in global bonds on the expectation that higher oil prices will further fan inflation, picking up on the reflationary wave fuelled by Donald Trump's election victory.

The OPEC deal is the first co-ordinated cut of its kind since 2008 and if its members, including Saudi Arabia and Iraq, follow through on the accord it will mean output falls 1.2 million barrels a day from January 2017. Oil rallied near 10 per cent after the bigger-than-expected deal was struck, to $US49.90 a barrel, the highest level in a month for WTI and $US52.40, the highest in six weeks for Brent.

Australian shares advanced 1.1 per cent to 5500.20 points. Ten-year United States Treasury yields rose to 2.38 per cent from 2.29 per cent and the Australian dollar climbed to US74.11¢.

The reaction in the bond market lends further credence to the view that global yields bottomed earlier this year, building on the bond sell-off that was revived with the election of Mr Trump as United States President last month and began about September with rumblings about the tapering of monetary stimulus.

"The Republican reflation trade, which is what's been surging post the election - it's back to the '80s, it's back to Reagan policies, a large fiscal spending program - it's supportive of the inflation that was likely to come out of that," said Chris Daily, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Tribeca Investment Partner

sentiment_pool.text:
Any good fund manager knows from experience that stock-picking is a humbling pursuit.

The winners one year tend to find themselves among the losers the following year - as the market rewards, and then punishes, them for the stocks they own and the strategies they deploy.

It is this longer-term perspective in which Mercer's annual fund manager league tables should be assessed. One positive is that even though the median fund manager underperformed over the year - tracking 1.4 per cent below the 11.8 per cent market return - fund managers beat the index over three and five years by 1.1 and 1.5 per cent.

The negative, which no doubt will be raised by those who advocate a low-cost passive approach to sharemarket investing, is that the median return in 2016 didn't deviate all that much from the broader index.

Also there's a strong whiff of "survivorship bias" - about 100 funds reported their December-quarter numbers to Mercer compared to 74 reporting performance over five years.

In time, those lagging the index will shut shop. So what can we gauge from the performance of Australia's pro stock-pickers in 2016?

sentiment_pool.headline: Jobs boost adds to rebound
sentiment_pool.text:
The labour market continues to hold ground, sending the jobless rate down to 5.7 per cent in January and raising hopes this year will see the nation pulled into a global economic rebound that will eventually drive up inflation and official interest rates.

Speculation is growing that the Reserve Bank of Australia will be forced to consider later this year increasing the official cash rate for the first time since late 2010, particularly if employment growth gathers pace after employers added 13,500 workers last month. The ABS labour force report on Thursday showed hours worked strengthened in January and a fall in youth unemployment.

The figures came after US Federal Reserve boss Janet Yellen reiterated her expectation that the central bank would look to raise interest rates this year. The world's largest economy is increasingly showing signs of reaching a major turning point, as data over the past few days point to strong retail sales and the biggest annual consumer price index rise - up 2.5 per cent - in almost four years.

Market pricing suggests the chance of a Fed rate increase in March has climbed from 18 per cent to 27 per cent.

Rising borrowing costs in the US would put upward pressure on the US currency, increasing the RBA's scope to raise its interest rate without pushing the Australian dollar too high.

The unexpected fall in January's unemployment rate - which analysts expected to stay steady at 5.8 per cent - saw the dollar stabilise above US77¢, close to its h

sentiment_pool.headline: Former Metcash CEO to chair Retail Apparel
sentiment_pool.text:
Menswear retailer Retail Apparel Group (RAG) has appointed former Metcash chief executive Andrew Reitzer as chairman in another sign its private equity owners are considering an initial public offering rather than a trade sale.

Mr Reitzer, who oversaw a four-fold increase in sales and a $280 million earnings turnaround during his 15-year reign at Metcash, was approached by RAG's 80 per cent shareholder, private equity firm Navis Capital Partners, to join the board in December.

Mr Reitzer accepted the challenge, even though he sits on the boards of four other companies - mobile phone company Amaysim, fleet operator SG Fleet, and two start-ups, optometry group George and Matilda and customer loyalty company Cash Rewards.

"They wanted someone to join them to take the business forward, to see how to develop and grow the business and see what sort of ownership structure would be best suited for the business," Mr Reitzer told The Australian Financial Review.

"It's a fantastic business with a great leadership team and an exceptional culture so I decided to join them. I don't want to just sit there, I only want to do things where I can make a difference.

"Now that the peak [Christmas] trading period is over it's about knuckling down and deciding what they want the future to look like and how do we make it happen," he said.

Mr Reitzer's appointment is another sign that Navis Capital is accelerating plans for an initial public offer which could value RAG at as much as $400 millio

sentiment_pool.headline: A fine view to the pacific
sentiment_pool.text:
Homes with a vista of the ocean are the perfect antidote to stress.

It’s no secret that you’ll pay more for a hotel room with an ocean view, and these days there’s scientific research backing the soundness of that decision.

A recent University of Exeter study found that health outcomes improve, relative to how close one lives to the ocean.

Marine biologist and author Wallace J. Nichols says our brains are hardwired to react positively to water.

In his book Blue Mind, Nichols explores why so many of us are drawn to the ocean. He discovered research that shows proximity to water floods the brain with feel-good hormones such as dopamine and oxytocin, while levels of the stress hormone cortisol drop.

Perhaps in the future there will be a case to be made for claiming back some of the cost of our ocean-view hotel room from our health insurance provider.

For those looking for a more permanent solution, ocean views are on hand year-round in Sydney’s coastal suburbs providing a stress-releasing backdrop after a long day at work. They are also the perfect place for a weekend wind down.

Here’s a selection of just such properties on the market today. These luxurious homes all come with a 24/7 dose of positive hormones thanks to glorious, front-row views over the Pacific Ocean.
