sentiment_pool.headline: Toyota to axe 2600 jobs when car-making stops on October 3
sentiment_pool.text:
Toyota Australia will axe 2600 jobs when it shuts down its car manufacturing plant at Altona in Melbourne's west on October 3.

The carmaker on Tuesday officially announced the specific timetable for the closure which will slice its Australian workforce down to one third of its current 3900 employees. The actual date came almost three years after Toyota originally signalled it would close some time late in 2017.

The Toyota shutdown will come almost three weeks before General Motors Holden ends car manufacturing at its plant at Elizabeth in Adelaide's northern suburbs in what will be the final chapter in Australia's car-manufacturing history.

A former executive chairman of Toyota Australia, John Conomos, who worked for almost 30 years building up Toyota's manufacturing capability, said it was "devastating". "To see it go because of external circumstances is just heartbreaking," he said.

Holden said on January 13 it would cease carmaking at Elizabeth on October 20. That announcement came after Holden first revealed in December 2013 that it was planning to stop carmaking in Australia, at a time when then prime minister Tony Abbott and his treasurer Joe Hockey took a hardline stance on ending billions of taxpayer subsidies which had been paid to car manufacturers over decades.

Ford shut its carmaking plant at Broadmeadows in Melbourne in October 2016 after dwindling sales of its locally made vehicles made its local operations unviable.

sentiment_pool.headline: Protection has hurt sugar sector
sentiment_pool.text:
If government support for an industry is supposed to ensure it ultimately stands on its own feet, sugar growers are one of the nation's greatest and most persistent failures.

Just one year after Federation in 1901, the sugar industry became the first in Australia to win tariff protection because it couldn't compete after the loss of low-wage Melanesian workers it relied on.

Australians have been leant on by the industry ever since - first because the commodity is available more cheaply on global markets, and secondly, through a history of trade barriers, industry "adjustment" packages and, more recently, a trend towards re-regulation in Queensland.

Yet 115 years after its first taste, the industry is more co-dependent on government featherbedding than ever.

With the federal Coalition once again under pressure this week to intervene in a dispute between growers and millers, Wednesday's report by the Productivity Commission into the regulation of agriculture makes for timely reading.

It picks on the sugar industry as a particularly egregious example of the negative effects of too much intervention, caused in this case because of the way the politics of key seats in North Queensland - Capricornia, Hinkler and Dawson - ensures patronage from the Liberal-National Party, which competes for sugar votes against One Nation.

"The sugar industry are the biggest pack of featherbedding bludging rent-seekers ever," says Liberal Democrat senator David Leyonhjelm.

sentiment_pool.headline: Lending interest rates on the rise at smaller banks
sentiment_pool.text:
The boss of Bendigo and Adelaide Bank has warned of the impact of "ultra-competitive mortgage pricing" on lenders struggling to balance demand with rising funding and regulatory costs and pressure on profits.

It comes as some smaller lenders struggle with a surge in borrower applications as the big four raise their investor and owner-occupier rates.

Mike Hirst, managing director of Bendigo and Adelaide Bank, warned rates needed to return to levels that "reflect the current market funding and capital costs".

That comes after Adelaide Bank announced an increase in its deposits for residential investors from 10 per cent to 20 per cent on top of the 25- basis-point increase in costs for investor loans.

Mr Hirst said: "As has been well telegraphed to all Australian authorised deposit-taking institutions, there is an expectation that as lenders, we must manage within the regulator's 10 per cent growth speed limit for investor loans."

Teachers Mutual Bank, Unibank and Firefighters Mutual Bank are also increasing owner-occupier fixed rates from one to five years by 7 basis points. It applies to interest only and principal and interest.

For example, the interest rate on a one-year principal-and-interest loan for an owner occupier will rise from 3.77 per cent to 3.84 per cent.

For five years the rate will rise from 4.54 per cent to 4.61 per cent.

Investor rates for the same borrower will respectively increase to 4.14 per cent and 4.91 per cent over the same terms.

sentiment_pool.headline: Downer should 'walk' from bid
sentiment_pool.text:
Downer EDI chief executive Grant Fenn has insisted the $1.2 billion takeover of Spotless will be "great" for investors despite a 21 per cent slump in the contractor's share price and calls by Allan Gray to "walk away" from the proposed transaction.

"We think this is going to be a great deal for Downer and whilst I watch the short-term reaction to the share price through the bookbuild that hasn't got where we would like, my focus now is absolutely on delivering for shareholders that what we've said we can produce we will," Mr Fenn told AFR Weekend.

"Our systems and processes are applicable across Spotless, we run our business hard, we put accountability into our management team, and we think that's very applicable and it will drive results."

But Allan Gray managing director Simon Mawhinney, who owns stock in Downer but is not a substantial shareholder, described the bid as "disastrous." "We're very upset with this deal, I think it's crazy," Mr Mawhinney said. "They could walk away from this deal, hopefully they do."

The contractor's shares tumbled $1.45 on Friday to close at $5.55 after re-opening for trading, their lowest levels in five months and below the price offered to investors to participate in Downer's $1 billion equity raising.

Institutional investors were offered a 20 per cent discount to the contractor's most recent closing price and were given the opportunity to buy stock as $5.95 per share but only took up about 66 per cent of the shares available to them.

sentiment_pool.headline: Morrison intervenes on risky lending
sentiment_pool.text:
A pending crackdown on bank lending to riskier investor and low-deposit borrowers is being spearheaded by a special regulatory working group set up last week following direct intervention by the Treasurer Scott Morrison.

The group whose members are understood to be made up of officials from the Council of Financial Regulators - ASIC, APRA and the Reserve Bank of Australia - are expected to move on imposing tougher lending rules on the banks imminently.

The Treasurer doesn't normally attend the council's regular schedule of quarterly meetings, which are convened to monitor and manage risks in the financial system, but did so before attending the Group of 20 finance ministers in Germany late last week.

Among the measures being considered are halving the annual speed limit on investor lending growth from the current 10 per cent imposed in 2015. Bank experts are speculating that capital risk weightings for investors with multiple properties will be raised fourfold. Banks will also be required to test the ability of borrowers to repay their loans at interest rates 3 percentage points higher than today, up from 2 percentage points.

"The regulators clearly have their sights set on addressing this issue," Citibank analyst Craig Williams said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Super fund ISPT secures Perth office
sentiment_pool.text:
Industry superannuation property fund ISPT has secured two long-term leases over 20,000sq m of premium-grade office space at its Perth office tower, 100 St Georges Terrace.

Japanese oil and gas company INPEX Corporation has signed a 10-year lease for 13,000sq m which will be fitted out. The new lease will accommodate INPEX's Darwin-based Ichthys LNG project's transition from the construction to production phase. Inpex has also secured non-exclusive roof-top signage rights.

Australian oil and gas company Quadrant Energy has renewed its lease for 7000sq m for another 12 years. As part of the renewal Quadrant will undertake a significant refit of their floors.

The tower at 100 St Georges Terrace is a 19-floor, 31,394sq m building developed by ISPT in 2009. It sits above the Enex100 retail centre.

ISPT has committed another $4.5 million for lobby and on-floor upgrades and new end of trip facilities.

It is understood market incentives were involved in the deals, around the low to mid 40s of the net rent over the term of the leases. While rents on the lease were confidential, St Georges Terrace commands net annual rents in the $500s a square metre.

Sheffield Property's Digby Sutherland and Mark Clapham represented ISPT.

"Both tenants were provided with market-level incentives and ISPT were flexible in the way that the tenants could apply the incentives," Mr Clapham said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Time for the RBA to tighten as well
sentiment_pool.text:
Policy failures elsewhere are now sucking Reserve Bank governor Philip Lowe into a bubble of housing speculation in Sydney and Melbourne that is injecting more risk into a financial system already sitting on a mountain of household debt. There seem to be no easy answers given the continued weakness in household income growth and the soft February job market numbers. But ultra-easy monetary policy has gone beyond propping up the Australian economy to instead threatening to destabilise it. With yesterday's move, US Federal Reserve Board chair Janet Yellen has lifted US interest rates for the second time in three months and plans two more this year as the American economy picks up momentum and fears of deflation fade. China's central bank followed suit yesterday with a sort of reverse currency war response that aimed to prevent its exchange rate from falling against the greenback. Now the global interest rate cycle is turning up, Australia's central bank needs to prepare to start normalising monetary policy as well.

Treasury secretary and Reserve Bank board member John Fraser reckoned Sydney house prices were in a speculative bubble as far back as mid-2015. But, in the belief that lending controls aimed at property investors were biting, the Reserve Bank cut its cash rate twice, in April and August last year, to help the rest of the economy. sentiment_pool.headline: Confident RBA chief sees world in lasting growth phase
sentiment_pool.text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia has been buoyed by hard evidence the global economy has decisively entered a lasting expansionary phase, which will ultimately increase the central bank's scope to reverse official interest rate cuts blamed for the overheating Sydney and Melbourne property markets.

Led by a raft of strong economic data around the world, including gains in industrial production and trade flows, the Reserve Bank is feeling more confident that this year's surge in global sentiment may be the real deal.

Board members left the official cash rate on hold at 1.5 per cent on Tuesday for a sixth straight meeting because of continuing concerns about the lack of full-time employment growth and sluggish wage pressures.

However, the central bank's post-meeting statement reflected a growing sense among policymakers first expressed at the February meeting that the global economy had turned a corner. That in turn, is bolstering the outlook for Australia's economy, which would probably benefit from a widely-anticipated US Federal Reserve rate hike this month, as well as a rise in non-mining business investment at home, long lamented as the "missing link" for future growth.

While the central bank is expected to keep the official cash rate in coming months, the commentary is further evidence that many within the bank are increasingly eyeing the timing of what would be the first rate increase since late 2010.

sentiment_pool.headline: China stays on growth path
sentiment_pool.text:
Beijing | China will use infrastructure spending, private sector investment and business tax cuts to keep the economy growing around 6.5 per cent "or higher" this year as Premier Li Keqiang stressed in a keynote speech that stability was the government's "overriding" priority ahead of November's leadership reshuffle.

In his work report to the country's annual session of parliament on Sunday, Mr Li slightly downgraded the country's growth and money supply targets, signalling the government would do more to tackle problems such as high debt levels and industrial overcapacity.

At the same time, the government will maintain a high level of infrastructure spending to offset the slowdown in housing construction, a move that is expected to shore up demand for commodities like iron ore and coking coal used in producing steel.

The confirmation that China was largely sticking to the economic growth script and putting off any drastic, and potentially destabilising, reforms will be interpreted as good news for Australian exporters of iron ore and coal.

The iron ore price has nearly doubled since June last year to be trading above $US90 a tonne, while coking coal has pulled back sharply from its highs of last year last year, but is still above the depressed levels of 2015.

sentiment_pool.headline: Wary investors seeking shelter from the storm
sentiment_pool.text:
Forget the reflation trade. The new market meme looks set to become the "stealth flight to safety", as a growing number of investors are quietly seeking sanctuary in traditional "safe harbours" such as bonds and gold.

Jeff Gundlach, often dubbed the US "bond king", was one of the first to highlight this new market trend. He predicted the yield on benchmark US 10-year bonds would drop below 2.25 per cent as global investors flocked to safety. (Yields fall as bond prices rise.)

"There is a stealth flight to safety going on. German bond yields are leading the way down," Gundlach told Reuters last week. "Gold is rising. Speculators remain massively short bonds and the market is going to squeeze them out."

Growing risk aversion is a potential negative for the US equity market, which has enjoyed a spectacular rally on hopes US President Donald Trump's policies will boost US economic growth and fuel inflationary pressures.

The S&P 500 has climbed more than 10 per cent since the November election, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has risen more than 13 per cent, on hopes that Trump's fiscal stimulus and tax cuts will boost corporate earnings.

"Stocks are out of sync with the stealth flight to safety. Lots of hope built in," Gundlach noted.

Investors flocked into US bonds last week, pushing the yield on the benchmark 10-year bond down to 2.32 per cent, the lowest level since November.

sentiment_pool.headline: The other Russian-linked president
sentiment_pool.text:
Foreign lawyers are still allowed into Australia under the federal government's same-same-but-different 457 visa, proof that you can never have too much of a good thing, even in an over-lawyered market.

But refugees who may one day become or give birth to lawyers? 

"Australia accepted [my parents] and they came here, as refugees. We would now call them asylum seekers," said Queensland's new Court of Appeal president Walter Sofronoff, QC, in his appointment speech.

Speaking separately with The Australian Financial Review, Justice Sofronoff revealed he felt "a bit foreign" in his early years in the Anglo-Celtic dominated legal community. That has changed since he joined four decades ago.

"Here we are in this wonderful milieu, where all of that is really old history," he said of his beloved bar.

"It is entirely a meritocracy. If you're no good, then you'll be out."

Justice Sofronoff took the top appellate spot earlier this month. His verdict so far? "The whole enterprise is much more tranquil and pleasurable."

His strongly held belief in the rule of law - in short, "fair play" - is rooted in his parents' search for "order" beyond oppressive rule: his father fled Siberia in 1930; his mother, Harbin in China. Together, they fled Japan after World War II, living in a tent city on an island in the Philippines for two years before coming to Australia in 1949.

Russian was the judge's first language, Cantonese his second. English came later, at school.

sentiment_pool.headline: HARRISON'S RISKY 'TRIAL OF THE YEAR'
sentiment_pool.text:
By forcing Seven executives to give evidence, barrister Julian Burnside is deploying a high-risk strategy, writes Aaron Patrick.

Amber Harrison's go-nuclear approach to managing relations with her former lover and her ex-employer has forced important people into difficult decisions, including Seven West Media chairman Kerry Stokes, Sunday Telegraph editor Mick Carroll and NSW Supreme Court judge John Sackar.

Now it is celebrity barrister Julian Burnside's turn. Harrison's allies want Burnside, her lawyer and a human rights champion, to use a court hearing to put embarrassing questions to the Seven West Media hierarchy, which they feel victimised the executive assistant for having an affair with chief executive Tim Worner, who she alleges ignored her after she complained their relationship was damaging her career and mental health.

After the NSW Supreme Court refused to move Seven's gag-order application to the Federal Court, where Harrison is suing the media group under the Fair Work Act, journalist, activist and Harrison supporter Stephen Mayne posted on Twitter: "Today was some win for @sevenwestmedia - now has entire board & management cross-examined by Burnside in Sydney on July 10. Fabulous lads!"

Harrison, who is legally prohibited from discussing Seven publicly, retweeted the post under the words "presented without comment". (Mayne was the first journalist she followed on the social network. Carroll was the second.)

sentiment_pool.headline: Electric, off-road future seen for local carmaking
sentiment_pool.text:
TomCar and the CSIRO are funding a study.

Australia's largest locally owned carmaker has partnered with the CSIRO for a pivot into off-road electric vehicles, a niche both claim could be a lifeline for the industry once Toyota and Holden shutter their factories here in October.

The CSIRO and Melbourne's TomCar, which has designed, made and sold 160 cars since 2011, will each spend $50,000 on a feasibility study it's hoped will turn the TomCar electric and meet demand from mining companies which require zero-emission vehicles.

The customers of TomCars to date have mostly been cattle stations and defence buyers, including the Royal Australian Air Force.

However, mining companies have been helping TomCar design an off-road, zero-emission electric vehicle, according to co-founder and chief executive David Brim.

Underground vehicles used by miners still predominantly have diesel engines - the Toyota Landcruiser used to be a favourite - however, they release emissions that must be ventilated at considerable cost.

Mr Brim wants TomCar to produce nothing but electric cars by the end of 2018, and he hopes the CSIRO can help ready the vehicles for the test they will face in underground mines.

"The TomCar body is already tough enough, its fully welded metal and fibreglass, no plastic. Where we can improve with the switch to electric cars is in the toughness of the battery, and having a smaller motor with more power," Mr Brim said.

sentiment_pool.headline: IAG warns of 'dark web' risks
sentiment_pool.text:
After a week of being bruised and battered over elevated reputation and credit risks, the last thing the bankers attending The Australian Financial Review Banking and Wealth Summit needed was a reminder of the rising operational risks from cyber attacks.

But the straight-shooting chief executive of Insurance Australia Group, Peter Harmer, did not dodge the question when asked what his own firm had found while trawling through the "dark web".

He said IAG had uncovered the personal details of customers belonging to one of the big four banks. The information was being sold online for $25 per customer. That suggests the systems of at least one major financial institution have been breached and customer data stolen.

IAG has informed the institution involved.

Harmer was primed for this conversation about cyber risks at the summit. On Wednesday he had led the IAG board of directors on a tour of the company's cyber security facility in Sydney.

Harmer said any chief executive who believes that they have a secure digital environment is "completely oblivious to the threats that are out there".

"We trawl our systems all the time looking for unusual activity," he said. "We trawl the dark net looking for where our data might be up for sale and it's amazing when you actually see what is being offered for sale.

sentiment_pool.headline: Topshop adds to retail A-REIT woes
sentiment_pool.text:
The collapse of fast fashion retailer Topshop Australia has cast another dark cloud over the retail sector and the under pressure retail A-REITs.

Westfield Corp, Vicinity Centres and Scentre Group are the worst performing A-REITS this year with negative total returns to date of 7.8 per cent, 6.7 per cent and 6.3 per cent respectively compared with a 1 per cent positive return across the S&P/ASX 200 A-REIT Index.

Weak retail sales growth, declining consumer confidence, the imminent arrival of e-commerce giant Amazon in Australia and declining sales at iconic US retailers like Macy's and Nordstroms have swung investor sentiment against the retail property trusts.

In a note following the retail chain collapse, Credit Suisse said while the Topshop stores would continue to trade and pay rent "it won't help sentiment given TopShop & TopMan was one of the first major players to enter Australia and is now placed into administration".

Scentre Group has Topshops in three Westfield malls in Miranda, Chatswood and Bondi Junction while Topshop is a multi-level anchor tenant in Vicinity Centres, Emporium Melbourne in the CBD. The diversified GPT Group has a Topshop in its flagship Highpoint Shopping Centre.

Scentre Group and Vicinity both declined to comment while a spokesman for GPT said: "We have a strong relationship with the Topshop Australia business and will work with the administrators in regard to this site."

sentiment_pool.headline: Mining and quarrying boost Orica
sentiment_pool.text:
Improving conditions in the mining sector have helped explosives maker Orica to post improved profits and dividends, while the company flagged it would challenge ongoing tax audits in Australia and Germany.

Despite generating 5 per cent less revenue in the first half, Orica's underlying profit was 3 per cent better than the previous year at $195.2 million.

An absence of impairments ensured the statutory profit was 31 per cent better than for the same period last year, also at $195.2 million. Shareholders will receive an interim dividend of 23.5¢, with 3¢ of that being franked. Last year's interim dividend was 20.5¢.

The improved result was driven by increased sales volumes in Orica's core market of Australia, Indonesia and the Pacific, where the company said miners were gradually starting to move waste at historically normal rates.

Ammonium nitrate volumes were 4 per cent higher at 1.78 million tonnes, with Australia's coal and gold sectors showing strong demand.

Like rival explosives maker Incitec Pivot, Orica pointed to improved demand from the quarrying and construction sector in the US.

"Activity in the quarry and construction segment, particularly in North America was up due to increased activity on infrastructure projects," the company said.

The cost reduction and efficiency program launched by chief executive Alberto Calderon also delivered a $53 million benefit in the half.

sentiment_pool.headline: It's official: the Coalition is now a principle-free zone
sentiment_pool.text:
As well as dropping the pretence of any fiscal discipline, the Liberals seem to have now abandoned all their other core beliefs as well.

Are there any principles that the Liberal Party still stands for?

Core Liberal convictions used to include: the importance of sound public finances; the need for honesty in budget forecasts; distrust of "government spending" as a solution to problems; and a preference for low taxes, to reward hard work and let individuals keep more of the income they earn.

Liberals used to subscribe fervently to all of these values - and conservatives still do. But after this week's budget, it's unclear if the parliamentary Liberal Party still subscribes to any of them.

Consider them in turn.

After wavering during the Fraser years, the Howard government recommitted the Liberals to balanced budgets as a bedrock virtue. And it delivered, achieving 10 surpluses from 12 budgets and fully paying off the Commonwealth's net debt, despite inheriting large deficits and record debt from Labor. This success reaffirmed budget discipline as a central Liberal tenet, and was the firm anchor to which the politically successful Howard government was tethered.

Indeed, so effective was the Coalition in promoting budget discipline that, although the Rudd and Gillard governments failed to get the budget back to surplus post-global financial crisis, both felt compelled to repeatedly commit to that goal.

sentiment_pool.headline: Super's thin edge of the wedge
sentiment_pool.text:
The government should be careful before it treads much further down the path of allowing first-home buyers to use voluntary superannuation contributions to place a deposit on a house or apartment.

While the scheme will certainly help would-be home owners to save money faster because the savings will be housed in a tax-friendly environment, $30,000 will not make much of a dent in a deposit, particularly for properties in Melbourne and Sydney. Given that the scheme is designed to reduce pressure on housing affordability, presumably it is largely aimed at individuals living in the two major cities where house price inflation has been rampant.

The measure is expected to cost the federal government $250 million over the next four years and will allow first-home buyers to withdraw any voluntary contributions up to a maximum of $30,000, plus an assumed rate of earnings generated from those savings. Under the proposal, withdrawals can take place from July 1, 2018. Contributions can be made from July 1 this year.

Advisers argue one of the benefits of the scheme is that it will enable super funds to lift engagement, particularly among young members. Super will no longer be seen as a pot of money that can't be touched for 30 or 40 years, but a honey pot for something useful.

But super fund bosses are more sceptical. Too many of their young members are not in a position to save for a house, or are put off from doing it, whether inside or outside super.

sentiment_pool.headline: Forget the surplus, China will fund a Band-Aid fix
sentiment_pool.text:
Once again a temporary surge in revenue has been locked into more permanent spending by an over- optimistic government.

The hopes and dreams of treasurers and prime ministers have taken a battering since China entered a slowdown in 2011.

From 2012 onwards, budget nights have seen Treasury regularly write down revenue forecasts, and treasurers gamely try to make the best of it.

Yet "making the best of it" has been pretty painful to watch, with the soaring rhetoric of budget speeches somehow not quite glossing over the gritted teeth as the nation's chief financial officers kept putting off the expected date of any return to surplus, all the while remaining determinedly optimistic that the good news would eventually become evident.

These budget-night performances would have been even more painful if those treasurers had known there were further revenue write-downs down the track.

It's been a grind, and a bunch of careers have come to an untimely end along the way - amazingly, there have been four treasurers and four prime ministers since 2012.

But will tonight finally see that tide turn? And is good news for the economy going to spill over into good news for the budget, thereby generating the first genuine tailwind for a sitting government in six years?

There's no doubting that Scott Morrison will be able to announce the best set of economic numbers in many a year.

sentiment_pool.headline: CONFESSION AND CONTRITION
sentiment_pool.text:
Crown staff go on trial in China on Monday. Humility will be expected of them, write Shanghai correspondents Lisa Murray and Angus Grigg.

As James Packer waited anxiously on his yacht in the waters off Tahiti for news on his bid to build a Sydney casino, the Chinese offices of British pharmaceutical giant GlaxoSmithKline were being raided.

It was June 27, 2013, and the Chinese police questioned dozens of GSK employees, confiscated laptops and files and detained four senior executives over two days of raids.

In hindsight, perhaps Packer should have been taking note. Just over three years later Crown staff would be the target of similar raids by Chinese police, throwing the company into turmoil, triggering a dramatic retreat from Asia and setting the stage for Monday's trial in Shanghai of 19 current and former employees.

But sitting on his boat, the Arctic P, at the end of June, 2013, the then Crown chairman was focused on just one thing, finally breaking into the Sydney casino market.

In his pitch letter to the NSW government, Packer wrote the Crown resort at Barangaroo would "almost treble the volume of VIP business coming to Sydney from Asia, and in particular, China". The pitch worked and on July 4, a week after the GSK raids in China, Packer was given the green light, ahead of rival casino operator Echo Entertainment.

It was a milestone for the company and the lure of more big-spending Chinese tourists and gamblers was key to its success.

sentiment_pool.headline: NSW sets up $15b future fund
sentiment_pool.text:
NSW has set up a $15 billion investment fund to hold the cash from its privatisation sales for the medium term rather than spend it quickly and risk overheating the state's booming economy.

Treasurer Dominic Perrottet handed down a budget yesterday he said made NSW the "envy of the Western world". The NSW government now has negative "net debt", that is cash in the bank, worth $7.8 billion or 1.4 per cent of gross state product compared to a crushing debt of as much 30 per cent of GSP in WA. Unemployment is about 1 percentage point below the other states.

The government is expecting operational surpluses of around $2 billion over the next four years after an incredible $4.5 billion surplus this year thanks largely to a 9.5 per cent jump in residential stamp duty caused by Sydney's housing boom and windfalls from privatisation sales.

It is understood concerns around overheating are one of the factors behind a decision in the budget to delay spending $15 billion from the sale of stakes in the state's electricity networks and other assets and set up a fund called the NSW Infrastructure Future Fund.

The NIFF will be managed by NSW TCorp with a new mandate to invest for the medium-term into equities and other assets rather than the current strategy of keeping the assets in cash.

sentiment_pool.headline: Amazon's 'round the world' warning shot
sentiment_pool.text:
Investors in Wesfarmers and Woolworths may begin the week a little more wary than expected as Amazon moves to deepen its disruption of the global retail sector with an $18 billion deal to buy US grocery store operator Whole Foods with a plan to aggressively compete with lower prices.

News of the transaction hammered a range of retailer stocks in Europe as well as on Wall Street at the weekend and could have a similar impact in Australia.

In New York, shares in Wal-Mart dropped 4.7 per cent, leading the losers on the Dow Jones Industrial Average. A rebound in the price of oil lifted shares in Chevron and Exxon Mobil, and helped edge the Dow up 0.1 per cent on the day and 0.5 per cent on the week. BHP Billiton was 0.5 per cent higher; Rio Tinto dipped 0.1 per cent.

Apple resumed its retreat, losing 1.4 per cent. The iPhone maker has shed more than 8 per cent since Goldman Sachs turned cautious on Apple as well as Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Facebook primarily because the market values of each company had surged and become overbought.

The S&P 500 ended little changed at the weekend and for the week, even amid the rotation out of some of the biggest US technology companies. The S&P 500 consumer staples sub-index, however, shed 1 per cent, even though it has Whole Foods as a member. Shares in Whole Foods surged 29 per cent.

sentiment_pool.headline: Oil risks doomsday scenario
sentiment_pool.text:
The chance of crude oil prices slumping to $US30-$US35 a barrel for several years, sending the global economy into crisis and multiple producers into bankruptcy, has emerged as a real threat, according to one of the world's leading forecasters.

Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman of respected energy consultancy FGE, said much higher US production growth was combining with a recovery in production in Libya and Nigeria, and the start-up of a massive field in Kazakhstan, to cancel out the effects of production cutbacks by the rest of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That sets up a bearish scenario for prices, which have already slid about 10 per cent in the past three weeks. Brent crude was trading around $US48.30 a barrel in Asia on Wednesday morning.

"Today the market move is very negative," Dr Fesharaki said in an interview while in Sydney for the Credit Suisse Australia Energy Conference.

"It takes very little for the prices to just drop to $US40. And then the Saudis have to intervene by cutting back by themselves, and I think they are ready to do it."

FGE's "base case" forecast is still for an initial drop in crude prices in the next weeks and then a recovery as Saudi Arabia is prompted to take unilateral action to further cut back output to address oversupply. Demand is still increasing relatively strongly, by about 1.5 million barrels a day this year.

sentiment_pool.headline: Wesfarmers slide keeps ASX in red
sentiment_pool.text:
Shares were buoyed by slightly better-than-expected economic growth numbers, but a slide in Wesfarmers kept the market in the red, while sentiment remained fragile ahead of a number of global risk events this week.

The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index slipped by the slimmest of margins, 0.005 per cent, to 5667.2, its third close in the red this week.

Gross domestic product growth came in at a paltry 0.3 per cent in the first quarter and 1.7 per cent over the year. But that was still higher than many in the market were fearing, sparking some rises in both shares and the Australian dollar.

"The first-quarter national accounts add to the string of data on the activity side showing that the economy is below trend and will not be reducing excess capacity soon," said JPMorgan economist Ben Jarman. "With the household sector subject to further headwinds from rising interest servicing costs, the pressure on the RBA's 3 per cent and above GDP forecast continues to mount."

Globally, worries about the outcome of the UK elections, a potentially dovish stance by the European Central Bank at its policy meeting and former FBI director James Comey's Senate testimony kept investors on their toes.

"Comey's testimony is likely to be the highlight," said AMP Capital Investors head of dynamic markets Nader Naeimi. "Investors have turned too pessimistic on growth, so the Fed and ECB can lead to large bond-market volatility."

sentiment_pool.headline: Slowdown is not a meltdown
sentiment_pool.text:
Faltering economic growth is likely to keep local investors on their toes this week, but fears of an impending sharp correction in the sharemarket seem overdone.

The market's concern around the economy has risen in recent weeks as more data points to a sharp and unexpected slowdown in economic growth.

Wednesday's first quarter gross domestic product numbers are expected to show anaemic growth of just 0.3 per cent in the first three months of the year, from 1 per cent in the previous quarter, leading to annual growth of 1.6 per cent, from 2.4 per cent.

Some like NAB or Morgan Stanley are even predicting a slight contraction in first-quarter GDP, sparking additional worry in a market that had until recently been betting on stable if unremarkable growth that could even trigger a rate hike by the end of the year.

But the 50-50 chance of monetary tightening seen just two months ago has completely reversed to markets now pricing in a 20 per cent chance of another cut by the end of the year.

The ASX was one of the developed world's underperformers in May, slipping 2.7 per cent over the month, while peers such as Wall Street's S&P500 or Japan's Nikkei rose 1.4 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively.

"In contrast to the RBA's recent upgrade to growth forecasts and the federal budget's seemingly optimistic growth assumptions, we sense investor concern around the economy has risen in May," UBS equity strategist David Cassidy said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Mega-trends shine as The Star rises
sentiment_pool.text:
As The Star morphs into a tourism stock, a casino challenge looms, writes John Stensholt.

Matt Bekier can literally see the big challenge he has in front of him.

All The Star Entertainment Group chief executive has to do is look directly out his office window from his desk in Sydney's Pyrmont and he can see rival Crown Resorts' Barangaroo six-star hotel and casino project being built across the water.

Bekier has helped execute an impressive turnaround in The Star's fortunes since his promotion from director of finance to CEO in April 2014, with the casino and resort group improving operational profits and winning key deals to expand its Brisbane, Gold Coast and Sydney properties in a huge capital works program.

But the not insignificant Crown project is an ever-looming issue, given The Star's casino licence exclusivity in Sydney will end when Barangaroo finally opens its doors in 2022. James Packer's Crown won the right to build in Sydney in November 2013, after a bitter "casino war" between Crown and The Star, which also played a part in Bekier being catapulted into the top job six months later.

"It is in my view line," Bekier says of the Crown project, while looking out his office window in an interview with AFR Weekend to reflect on his three-and-a-half years in the job.

sentiment_pool.headline: Workers fear AI and automation
sentiment_pool.text:
A quarter of Australians fear redundancy due to increased use of artificial intelligence and automation as businesses increasingly investigate options, according to a new report into business use of emerging technologies.

The study from research firm Telsyte looks broadly across Australian businesses and the rapid adoption of new technologies under way, including artificial intelligence and automation, wearable technology, augmented and virtual reality and drones.

It finds that nearly two-thirds of businesses are already dabbling with machine learning or deep learning to improve operations or influence business decision making, with so-called artificial intelligence and automation technology use growing for things ranging from physical robots to digital assistants and chatbots.

Telsyte managing director Foad Fadaghi said there was a distinct difference in the enthusiasm for intelligent automation among company executives from the general population. Despite regular statements that automation will augment rather than replace jobs, workers are not buying it.

The study found that financial processes are considered ripe for early automation, with 65 per cent of chief information officers questioned saying they saw opportunities to deploy machine learning in financial modelling and fraud detection.

sentiment_pool.headline: Water business hots up as Elders poaches four brokers
sentiment_pool.text:
Rural specialist Elders has poached four water brokers from leading player Waterfind as it aims to grow its presence in the $24 billion water market.

Anthony Bent, Kevin Rochow, Matthew Moar and Peter Gale will be based at Elder's head office in Adelaide.

Securing water entitlements has become crucial for farmers as they try to secure their irrigation needs amid changing weather patterns and growth in water-intensive crops such as almonds, and a lucrative market for those selling excess water.

At the same time, the record prices paid for water rights in some regions has raised the stakes for water brokers.

In October, Australia's largest listed agricultural property fund, Rural Funds Group, paid $34 million to buy a 9549-megalitre water entitlement in one of the biggest water deals in the Murrumbidgee River irrigation area.

In 2015, listed Walnut producer Webster Ltd bought listed land and water company Tandou, completing one of the biggest listed agricultural land and water plays in Australia's history.

The signing on of the four grows the Elders team to 17 active brokers, and will give it added clout in the Australian water market, where Waterfind - which calls itself "Australia's leading water exchange" - and Ruralco have large market shares.

It is hard to imagine an Australian prime minister delivering a better speech for today than the one Malcolm Turnbull delivered in London on receiving the Disraeli prize. It was a speech of which all Australian Liberals could be proud.

Reading the press about it, one could be forgiven for thinking that it was unwisely divisive, setting conservatives and progressives in the party against each other. While discordant voices were raised, the speech has justifiably received broad praise across the "broad church" of the party.

The fundamental liberal values of Menzies about the importance of individuals rather than mass identity groups were stated clearly, and applied to trade, immigration and the prevention of terrorist attacks.

Turnbull was absolutely correct to say that from its formation the Liberal Party has stood for "freedom": the right of individual people to set their own course in life, to work to achieve their goals under law, to engage in enterprise, and not to surrender this freedom to politicians, governments, or to interfering and disrespectful authoritarians.

In the 11 years he was chief financial officer of Commonwealth Bank of Australia, David Craig steered clear of politics and focused on delivering successive record profit results.

While he was CFO, the bank's total shareholder return rose 233 per cent and profit per share grew 76 per cent. CBA jumped 18 places up the league table of the world's most valuable banks measured by market capitalisation from 28 in 2006 to 10 in 2017.

But in his first interview since leaving CBA in June, Craig has opened up about the lack of national leadership, the damage caused by the federal bank tax and the potential harm to the Australian financial system from a royal commission into the banks.

"The reality is that we are not as a country performing and learning the lessons of the way good businesses work towards a shared vision," he says.

Craig is particularly scathing about the bank taxes imposed by the federal and South Australian governments.

Neither tax, he says, has been received well by international investors. "No international investor has bought a share in an Australian bank for the last month or two as far as I understand," he says. "Basically the sovereign risk - the fear of what is happening here - has them all spooked."

He believes the South Australian bank tax has compounded the damage caused to Australia's image overseas.

sentiment_pool.headline: Seek considers Open Universities deal
sentiment_pool.text:
Education might be one of Australia's great exports, but after disasters such as ABC Learning and Vocation, it is no surprise that investors are a little cautious about the sector.

But Street Talk understands online course provider Open Universities Australia is having no trouble attracting the attention of potential buyers.

Sources said any deal was at least a month off, but Street Talk can reveal listed online education giant Seek Limited and a number of private equity firms are running the ruler over it.

While Open Universities has been going through a difficult time, Seek may believe it has the potential to breathe life back into the private distance and online education organisation by combining its expertise in technology with experience in education.

The Andrew Bassat-led company already has Seek Learning, which connects job seekers with nationally recognised courses. It has form elsewhere in the sector, too, having bought half of IDP from a consortium of 38 Australian universities for $36 million in 2006.

Seek's purchase followed the near collapse of IDP in 2005, which required an injection of capital from its university owners.

Bassat declined comment yesterday.

Open Universities was established with a grant from the federal government in 1993. The intent was to increase access to online learning materials by students, and cater to the time-poor, adult worker market. sentiment_pool.headline: Top new CEOs hit with 25pc pay cut
sentiment_pool.text:
The 25 new chief executives appointed to top 200 companies over the past 18 months received an average 25 per cent pay cut from their predecessors, according to new research by consultants Egan Associates.

The research reveals that the new batch of CEOs, which included Wesfarmers' Rob Scott, Origin Energy CEO Frank Calabria and Carsales CEO Cameron McIntyre, received an average $4.19 million pay packet compared to over $5 million for the outgoing CEOs.

CEO pay increased by 120 per cent for Australian CEOs between 2001 and 2008, culminating in a 12.5 per cent bump in 2012-13.

However, boards and investors are taking a harder line on CEO pay amid soft wages growth and a preference for internal, lower paid successors over higher paid external appointments.

Reserve Bank of Australia governor Philip Lowe issued an extraordinary challenge to workers last month to be "prepared to ask for larger wage rises", as Australia grinds through more than four years of declining wages growth, the lowest rate in data going back to the late 1990s.

However, workers are likely to continue to face downward pressure as long as their bosses are scrutinised over pay.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull slammed the "cult of excessive executive CEO remuneration" this year which sparked the resignation of outgoing Australia Post CEO Ahmed Fahour over his $5.6 million package, followed by public outrage over CPA Australia's recently resigned CEO Alex Malley's $1.8 million pay.

sentiment_pool.headline: NAB issues tougher ID, credit checks to counter identity theft
sentiment_pool.text:
National Australia Bank is rolling out a new round of identification and income checks for property borrowers in response to increased security and regulatory pressures.

Borrowers, including those applying online, will have to provide photo ID and supporting documents to be verified by the mortgage broker arranging the deal. Other lenders are introducing similar policies.

Interest-only borrowers will have to answer more comprehensive questions about whether that type of loan is suitable for their needs, or if a principal and interest loan may be better.

Lenders are responding to regulatory pressure to improve scrutiny of borrowers' capacity to service loans, particularly interest-only borrowers.

Questions range from if they are borrowing as owner-occupiers or investors, through to how they can cope with temporary income reduction, or a large expense item, such as school fees or renovations.

Interest-only borrowers will also need to disclose if they will require additional bridging finance.

"It will ensure customers take out interest-only lending in the right circumstances, which is suitable for their needs," a bank memo says.

NAB is also tightening credit policies, such as verification of bonus income, and more closely scrutinising any regular deductions from PAYG income, such as superannuation salary sacrifice.

sentiment_pool.headline: Sydney prices set to flat-line, even fall, but no sign of a bust
sentiment_pool.text:
Sydney house prices are expected to flat-line in August, property research group Corelogic says, ahead of the release of a monthly hedonic house price index next week.

Head of research Tim Lawless says Sydney house prices may even fall at the close of the month, but Melbourne house prices will post a rise.

While Sydney's prices may fall over the month, it is not a precursor for a guaranteed downward price correction for the most unaffordable city in Australia.

"If you look back at any past cycle, you will find that prices do not fall off the cliff," Mr Lawless said.

"Sydney has been gradually cooling since November last year, auction clearance rates have starting slowing ... all signs the market is cooling.

"There will be an absolutely flat-line result, even a small decline.

"Six months down the track, you will see a consistent decline in the housing market. The question is what will be the difference between the peak and trough."

While there would be ups and downs in Sydney house prices under cooling measures by the regulators, history has shown price corrections in Sydney have never exceeded 10 per cent, Mr Lawless said.

Melbourne, however, will post a rise in house prices, driven by an increase in prices of houses rather than apartments.

While some steam is coming out of the Melbourne market, it is rising stronger than Sydney because it doesn't have the same large withdrawal in investors [as Sydney] following the banks' curbs on investor loans, Mr Lawless said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Tech giants reject 'voluntary' tax code
sentiment_pool.text:
A voluntary code of conduct for company tax disclosures has been criticised as impotent after it was revealed that none of the global technology companies has signed up.

Google, Apple Facebook, Microsoft, IBM and Apple have rejected the code, which encourages companies to compare their effective company tax rate in Australia to their global operations, detail related-party dealings and explain tax strategies.

Microsoft's corporate vice-president of worldwide tax, Daniel Goff, told the Senate committee inquiring into corporate tax avoidance that company executives had "talked about" signing up but decided not to.

IBM Australia and New Zealand managing director Kerry Purcell said he would not sign because he was worried about his competitors knowing too much and wanted to protect clients.

Labor MP Jenny McAllister, who sits on the committee, said the government's approach to tax transparency was flawed. "The voluntary tax code is a piecemeal policy attracting a piecemeal response," she said. "The government should adopt Labor's mandatory tax transparency measures including public country-by-country reporting [and] a publicly accessible register of beneficial ownership for legal entities including trusts."

Dan F. Stapleton thought such pampering was for women - until he tried one.

I consider myself an enlightened individual and, as someone who suffered his share of acne as a teenager, I accept the power of effective facial cleansers, exfoliants and moisturisers. I visit spas regularly, too, usually for a massage or a therapeutic bath while on assignments overseas. And I find it difficult to resist an expert pedicure.

Rightly or wrongly, the facial has historically been considered an indulgence meant solely for women.

Paul Anderson, who operates spas in Sydney and Melbourne under the Mankind banner, says many men feel intimidated by the idea of facials, despite wanting to take care of their skin.

"Before we opened the first store in 2004, what I was hearing from men was that they wanted to come into a space they felt was their own," he says.

In other words, being in a manly space seemed important for many prospective customers.

Mankind is one of a slew of spas opened in Australia in recent years with the aim of making men feel more comfortable about seeking aesthetic treatments.

Investors' attention was dragged offshore on Friday as growing unease in global financial markets lifted following further political turmoil in Washington and after terrorists struck a crowded Barcelona street.

After a week driven strongly by local company earnings, with the likes of Telstra dragging the bourse down and Cochlear pushing it up, the ASX finished the week marginally higher.

Telstra managed to find only marginal buying support on Friday after a sell-off on Thursday following its announcement it was cutting its dividend. sentiment_pool.headline: Trade war threats warn off investors
sentiment_pool.text:
Years of experience have taught investors that it's smart not to panic whenever geopolitical tensions flare up. After all, the US sharemarket quickly regained its footing after its 7 per cent drop during the 1962 Cuban missile crisis, and although the Standard & Poor's 500 index sold off after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, it was trading more than 15 per cent higher a year later.

So it came as little surprise that the US sharemarket largely shrugged off the increasingly inflammatory rhetoric between US President Donald Trump and North Korea's Kim Jong Un, with the S&P 500 finishing the week only 1.4 per cent lower.

But some analysts are warning that global sharemarkets could suffer greater damage this time around as geopolitical tensions push the world closer to a highly damaging trade war. That's because Trump is ratcheting up his threats to introduce punitive - and economically damaging - trade sanctions against China unless Beijing does more to rein in Pyongyang. This is a departure from the practice of previous US administrations, which tried to keep a strict divide between strategic and economic issues.

Trump is set to begin the week by ordering his top trade negotiator to undertake a broad investigation into alleged Chinese theft of US intellectual property. sentiment_pool.headline: China's Wanda eyes $2b Australia exit
sentiment_pool.text:
China's Dalian Wanda Group, which is under pressure to crimp its overseas expansion and is facing a freeze on bank lending at home, is fielding offers for its two giant development projects in Australia.

The move could be the first of many by mainland companies pulling back from Australia as Beijing tightens its control over outbound investment, potentially putting downward pressure on prices for property, infrastructure and agricultural assets.

A spokesman for Wanda, which also owns the Hoyts Cinema chain in Australia, did not respond by deadline on Monday. Wanda, controlled by one of China's richest men, Wang Jianlin, has had its wings clipped by Beijing in recent weeks as concerns mount that it, and other private companies, overpaid for foreign assets and these now posed a systemic risk to the Chinese banking system. sentiment_pool.headline: The sequel to the GFC is already with us

Rocket-scientist financiers buy up billions of dollars of risky loans and repackage them into complex investments with multiple layers of debt.

Credit rating agencies classify the top layers as AAA. Institutional investors, including pension funds and charitable organisations, flock to buy these apparently risk-free yet high-yielding investments. Tension builds.

sentiment_pool.headline: Equinix, ST Telemedia select banks for Metronode sale

Street Talk understands $US35 billion global data storage heavyweight Equinix has drafted in JPMorgan's team for advice, while Singapore's ST Telemedia, owned by sovereign wealth fund Temasak Holdings, has turned to Australia's own Macquarie Capital.

Higher savings ratios and careful spending are not only occurring against a subdued outlook for the Australian economy - they are two of the causes. A reluctance to spend has an obvious impact on retailers and their share prices. Is it time to buy?

According to the latest retail sales data, the retail environment remains constrained. July sales were expected to increase by around 0.2 per cent. Instead they were flat. The reading is particularly disappointing in light of the improvement in the second quarter of the year, when annualised growth in retail sales was 1.5 per cent. Not great, but a significant lift on the first quarter's 0.2 per cent and the 0.5 per cent average for 2016.

Wages and inflation are inextricably linked by consumer behaviour. Wage increases lift consumer spending, putting upward pressure on prices and inflation. Increasing prices induce business expansion, increasing demand for labour and then wages. This process feeds on itself. The problem for the economy in general and central bankers in particular is how to kick start this virtuous circle.

Business investment is picking up as the drag from the mining boom drops off. The key to economic recovery is therefore in the hands of the consumer. However, the lowest wages growth in decades is weighing on sentiment.

sentiment_pool.headline: NRL's sale of Gold Coast Titans to begin this week
sentiment_pool.text:
While the NRL is in the middle of an exciting finals series on the field, rugby league's governing body will have some crucial meetings off it - starting on Tuesday.

Officials will meet with about half a dozen prospective buyers of the Gold Coast Titans, with a view to selling the franchise back into private hands by October 31.

While the history of rugby league on the Gold Coast is at best vexed - before the Titans came the Giants, Seagulls, Chargers and even, for a very short time, the Gladiators - the league has been pleasantly surprised by how much interest there has been for a franchise that has had a tumultuous time of things and lost plenty of money for various owners.

It either means there are plenty of entrepreneurs who want to burn good money owning a sports club - though there is always that cachet that comes with being at the helm of a team - or there is some value in holding one of only 16 licences in a closed competition.

While the league would love to get a competitive bidding process under way and get a big $5 million to $10 million cheque from the eventual buyer, NRL officials have been telling people they are more worried about finding owners committed for the long term and will prioritise close links to the local community as part of their business plans.

The club certainly has plenty of potential, with more than 600,000 people living within a 30-minute drive of its stadium at Robina and the local Gold Coast economy growing ahead of next year's Commonw

sentiment_pool.headline: Woolies ups solar as costs soar
sentiment_pool.text:
Woolworths has quadrupled capital investment since last year in cutting energy use and improving energy efficiency and will increase installation of solar PV panels at supermarkets as it seeks to rein in soaring energy costs.

Investments are being made to switch all lighting in stores to LED, improve efficiency in refrigeration and airconditioning, as well as in a new energy management centre, Tony Louka, head of the energy transformation project, told an energy users forum in Sydney.

Mr Louka wouldn't reveal the investment involved but described it as "significant".

Brad Banducci, the chief executive of Woolworths, which consumes about 1 per cent of the total electricity generated in Australia, warned of the impact of rising energy costs this year, saying the company is "trying to outrun a bear" amid soaring electricity and gas prices. The company is also investigating direct purchase contracts for renewable energy, through corporate power purchase agreements, and is looking at opportunities for battery storage, Michael Shelley, manager energy and services, told the forum.

Energy users nationwide are taking steps to tackle soaring bills but they need to realise that direct purchasing of power and investing in renewables involve higher risks, said Gilles Walgenwitz at energy procurement adviser Energetics.

But he said there was a range of options users could consider to counter supply contracts now typically costing more than $100 a megawatt-hour and that are unlikely to

sentiment_pool.headline: Chanticleer’s CHOOK ROAST
sentiment_pool.text:
Manufacturing guru Jens Goennemann says Australia is still in the game.

Nothing frustrates manufacturing guru Jens Goennemann more than to hear the false claims that manufacturing in this country is dead or dying.

The popular myth is that the closure of several large foreign-owned car-making plants in Victoria and South Australia will leave a permanent gaping hole in Australia’s manufacturing sector.

It is claimed, in some quarters, that this hole will never be filled and the loss of skills and capabilities will harm our ability to build our industrial competitiveness. The worst-case scenario is that we won’t be able to participate fully in global manufacturing value chains.

This line of argument usually morphs into dire warnings about the lack of readiness among Australian companies to participate in the Defence Department’s $50 billion submarine construction program over the next 15 to 20 years.

Goennemann, who is managing director of the Advanced Manufacturing Growth Centre, responds to this typical pessimism and self-doubt with smiles of the literal and figurative kind: he uses a stylised smiley curve to show why the pessimists and doomsayers have got it wrong about Australian manufacturing.

On the left and right sides of the upward smiley curve are the highest value-added parts of manufacturing. The highest values are attached to the pre-production intangibles such as research and development, design and to the post-production intangibles such as sales and services

sentiment_pool.headline: Globe spared full Lew rage
sentiment_pool.text:
Skateboard and streetwear company Globe International was spared the full barrage of angst from billionaire shareholder Solomon Lew at its annual meeting on Thursday, although his entities are still making their presence felt by voting against the remuneration report.

The Lew family's unusually named corporate vehicle Poly Town is the fourth-largest shareholder in Globe, which held a largely uneventful meeting at Port Melbourne, as elsewhere Mr Lew's Premier Investments again stepped up pressure on the Myer board.

Premier Investments has been increasingly hostile towards Myer and on Thursday repeated its calls for the Myer board to divulge clear details about its first-quarter profits and sales figures, to back up claims by incoming chairman Garry Hounsell that Myer was showing "green shoots".

Poly Town has sat on the share register of Globe International for 13 years and a few years ago was a much more aggressive pot-stirrer at Globe annual meetings. Poly Town was among those that lodged proxy votes that resulted in a 57.9 per cent vote against the remuneration report. It regularly opposes the remuneration report.

Globe notched an improved full-year result in August and lifted its dividend, and on Thursday chief executive Matt Hill told shareholders that profits were "up moderately".

sentiment_pool.headline: Revealed: Quintis founder's margin lending nightmare
sentiment_pool.text:
Quintis founder Frank Wilson was in a legal dispute with his margin lender last year, leading him to make the allegation to a US court that a parcel of his shares was wrongly seized in a "sham" deal.

The case, which was dismissed in June with no findings of fault against any party, shows that at one point Mr Wilson did not know where his shares were, who the custodial provider was, and whether they were sold or loaned out.

Claims made by Mr Wilson in the proceedings also suggest how dogged the former boss was in its pursuit of a float of its Santalis business in the US, and potentially securing a secondary listing for the former TFS on the Nasdaq exchange. It has previously attached a price tag of of up to $US500 million ($635 million) to Santalis.

Today, Quintis is still fighting for a recapitalisation and it has not traded since May. Mr Wilson resigned as its CEO in March after a US short seller, Glaucus, authored a damning research report about the company's business model and the sandalwood market.

The dispute was apparently triggered when loan documents to extend Mr Wilson's 2015 borrowings to $53 million via a second and entirely revised margin lending facility were prepared and returned to the defendants, which are Emerging Markets Intrinsic Cayman and its affiliates.

Mr Wilson and his adviser say they did this only as a goodwill gesture when talks over new terms broke down, as Mr Wilson was insisting on conditions, including that the collateral be voted as per hi

sentiment_pool.headline: Signs of stability seen in construction costs
sentiment_pool.text:
A likely slowdown in the east coast housing construction market is ushering in a period of stable price growth in the industry that home builders are welcoming.

The latest construction pricing forecasts from quantity surveying firm RLB show that cost escalation on the east coast will be steady over the next four years, while Perth will pick up to more normal levels after years of slump.

RLB's latest tender price index predicts cost growth in Sydney will ease from 4.2 per cent this year to 3.5 per cent by 2020, growth in Melbourne will be steady at 3 per cent and Brisbane, after dropping from 7.2 per cent last year, will be steady at 4 per cent growth for the next four years.

"For the next two to three years it seems stable," said Robert Lynch, the executive chairman of Queensland and NSW home builder Tamawood. "Bricklaying prices go up significantly every time there's a boom and they have gone up this time, but it's not significant. I see them ticking back a little bit over the next year or so, but I don't think it's material."

As Australia's white-hot housing market cools - dwelling commencements of new apartments, townhouses and semi-detached dwellings fell to their lowest level in more than two years in the June quarter - it's not only easing demand for materials and labour, but is narrowing the disparity between construction pricing in the country's highly regionalised market.

"Is it the Goldilocks zone?" said RLB head of research and development Stephen Ballesty.

sentiment_pool.headline: Ex-CBA executive joins procurement start-up think as it goes for growth
sentiment_pool.text:
Procurement software start-up think has recruited former Asciano chief financial officer and Commonwealth Bank institutional banking managing director Peter McGregor as its chief executive, as it looks to enter a new high-growth phase and win major enterprise clients.

The start-up, which was founded by one of the original leaders at SEEK, Adam Ryan, has also raised $7.5 million in capital.

Mr McGregor, who is also on the board of the AFL team the Brisbane Lions, comes to the role having spent 20 years in investment banking, before taking on the leadership roles at Asciano and CBA.

Speaking to The Australian Financial Review, Mr McGregor said he had taken on the role in February and was convinced to join the small company thanks to the passion of Mr Ryan and the power of the platform to solve problems he'd experienced first hand while managing procurement at Asciano.

"I've gone from working in the largest organisation in the country to one with only 35 employees when I started," he said.

"At CBA, no matter who you were, you were a small cog in a large machine. At think, every decision you make has an impact on the business. It's been incredibly invigorating and it's got an amazing team of people."

The $7.5 million raised comes from a range of wealthy investors and institutional funds who did not want to be named. It follows a smaller $5 million round in 2016.

Mr Ryan remains the largest shareholder with about 40 per cent.

sentiment_pool.headline: Folkestone buys into hospitality boom at $76.4m
sentiment_pool.text:
Led by property veteran Greg Paramor, fund manager Folkestone is buying into the hospitality boom, snapping up a Sydney Airport hotel for $76.4 million.

The acquisition of the Mercure Sydney International Airport Hotel is the largest single deal yet for Folkestone, which has launched a new fund to hold the asset.

Over his time leading a series of well-known property platforms - Paladin, James Fielding, Mirvac - Mr Paramor has had plenty of exposure to the hotels sector.

Folkestone's move into the sector is more recent. The platform is planning to develop a 142-room hotel in a joint venture at Green Square, a short distance from Sydney Airport.

Mr Paramor has timed it well, increasing Folkestone's exposure to the sector as inbound tourism numbers surge.

Turbo-charging that boom is the rise of an Asian middle-class. Airlines are tapping into it as new technology allows them to launch hundreds of new flights and re-map the traditional aviation hubs linking the country with the rest of the world. Visitors from China, in particular, are expected to surge from 1 million in 2016 to 3.3 million by 2026, according to an Australia China Business Council report this week.

Mr Paramor said Folkestone likes "the thematic" - the investment thesis for hotels - especially in the gateway cities of Sydney and Melbourne.

"Business travel is on the up and up. And just look at the latest figures talking about Chinese inbound going from 1 million to 3 million by 2026," he told The Australian

sentiment_pool.headline: Trojan horse of state tax reform
sentiment_pool.text:
A new PC report into tax distribution could mark the beginning of the end of states being penalised for their own economic success.

Australia's five premiers and two chief ministers could wake up to a new dawn with this morning's release of the eagerly anticipated draft report of the Productivity Commission's inquiry into horizontal fiscal equalisation (HFE).

The principle of HFE has been the foundation stone on which Commonwealth-state financial relations have been built since Federation. It is the mechanism for the distribution of Commonwealth financial support to states and territories in a manner that allows each state the capacity to provide comparable levels of government services.

When the inquiry was announced in May by federal Treasurer Scott Morrison, it was born of a desire to test the credibility of claims by some states, chiefly Western Australia, that the GST distribution arrangements undermine national economic reform and were no longer fit for purpose for a modern, competitive and export-orientated nation like ours.

For West Australians, the issue is acute. In March this year, the Commonwealth Grants Commission (CGC) announced the 2017-18 GST relativity for each state and territory. It allocated WA 34¢ in every GST dollar raised in the state. In the year previous it had allocated WA a dismal 30¢.

The lowest relativity previously determined by the CGC was 84¢ allocated to Victoria in 1994-95.

sentiment_pool.headline: Questions over QBE's plan for $1b buyback
sentiment_pool.text:
Analysts say QBE's $1 billion share buyback is in doubt after the global insurer downgraded its 2017 earnings due to a surge in claims from a catastrophic run of natural disasters.

On Tuesday, the $14 billion global insurer told the market it would raise the amount of money it sets aside for natural disasters for the year to $US1.75 billion ($2.24 billion), taking a $US600 million hit to its pre-tax earnings for this financial year.

At the same time, expectations for the insurer's profitability also took a dive, with the company downgrading its combined operating ratio guidance to 100-102 per cent, which indicates there will be no profit or the potential for losses for the year.

After the announcement, shares in QBE fell as much as 5.2 per cent, their lowest level since November 2016. They recovered to close down 3.5 per cent at $9.82.

Cyclone Debbie in Australia this year, hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria, which affected the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean and Florida, as well as the earthquakes in Mexico have had an impact on QBE's businesses.

It has left QBE grappling with what is tipped to be the worst loss year on record for the global insurance sector and investor discontent over an earlier downgrade in its emerging markets unit.

Shaw and Partners analyst David Spotswood said it was now unlikely the company had the capital to complete the buyback it announced in 2017.

sentiment_pool.headline: Sales total $27m on east coast
sentiment_pool.text:
Village Building Company has snapped up a residential development site approved for 60 units, six villa homes and 118 car parking spaces north of Wollongong for about $9 million.

Hospitality business Aster Group sold the 9093-square-metre site at 54-62 Railway Street in Corrimal.

The property is zoned medium density and comprises a two-storey commercial building and a bitumen car park at the rear. These will be demolished to make way for two four-storey residential buildings with basement parking.

Savills' Rob Lowe brokered the deal.

Private developer Ekko Point Properties has scooped up a 3.14 hectare amalgamated development site at 310 and 314 Albany Creek Road in Bridgeman Downs, Brisbane, for $9.1 million. Ekko has also obtained approval for 50 housing lots on the site.

Two private landowners sold their adjoining sites together in an expressions-of-interest sale handled by Ray White's Matthew Fritzsche.

Parkville land

The Victorian Department of Treasury and Finance has offloaded a vacant 585-square-metre Parkville site in Melbourne for $1.46 million.

A local developer has purchased the site at 81 Manningham Street for a luxury townhouse project.

Savills Australia's Julian Heatherich, Nick Peden and Mark Stafford acted on the transaction.

Epping sale

A private developer splashed out $3.05 million for a vacant 4046-square-metre development site at 72 Cooper Street, Epping, in Melbourne before auction.

sentiment_pool.headline: Plenty of life in Propel Funeral debut
sentiment_pool.text:
It's gone from an idea on a whiteboard five years ago to a company now worth more than $300 million after a stellar debut on the ASX.

But the managing director of newly listed Propel Funeral Partners, Albin Kurti, said on Thursday that "there's still a lot to do" as the firm looks to expand from its 4.1 per cent market share in Australia's $1.1 billion death care industry.

Propel, which runs 80 funeral homes mainly in regional Australia, delivered big stag profits to investors in its initial public offering when it burst on to the ASX with opening trades at $3.50, almost 30 per cent higher than its issue price of $2.70. The stock settled a little lower in mid-afternoon trading to close at $3.30, which still represented a handsome premium of 22 per cent.

"It started life as an idea on a whiteboard five years ago," said Mr Kurti, who has a personal stake of just over 10 per cent in Propel.

He said the strong opening was partly to do with the pent-up demand for stock in an IPO that had been handled by Bell Potter and well supported by institutions. But the long-term fundamentals of the business in an industry where consolidation was occurring, and the upside for the No.2 player with only a small market share compared with industry giant InvoCare, were also important drivers.

"It's obviously still early days," Mr Kurti said late on Thursday morning. "There was strong demand in the IPO and the early trading reflects a bit of that too."
