sentiment_pool.headline: AusNet 'will not fail' on cost targets
sentiment_pool.text:
Victorian energy grid owner AusNet Services has revealed it has slashed 500 jobs since April last year, as it ramps up focus on cost reductions to try to improve efficiency and rein in price increases for customers.

Chief executive Nino Ficca said the job cuts comprise about 18 per cent of AusNet's staff numbers and include about 75 jobs in gas meter reading, which have been transferred to a contractor as the Melbourne-based company outsources that activity.

"Our cost-efficiency program is a top priority; we cannot and will not fail," Mr Ficca said after AusNet reported a 14.1 per cent increase in first-half net profit to $203.7 million.

"It's critical that we deliver in this time of change," he said, pointing to the heightened policy debate and regulatory changes in energy as governments, policymakers and regulators seek to keep surging electricity and gas bills in check.

AusNet reported $8 million of operational cost savings in the first half, on top of $9 million last financial year. Capital investment savings in the first half were $20 million, on top of $38 million last year.

Mr Ficca said AusNet is aiming to operate all three of its core networks' business in the "top quartile" in terms of efficiency, but only electricity transmission and gas distribution were already in that position, with more work to be done in the electricity distribution business.

He wouldn't give targets for further reductions, but suggested the run rate of cost improvements would be similar

sentiment_pool.headline: Quadrant buys into Timezone
sentiment_pool.text:
The team at Quadrant Private Equity will get the chance to relive their teenage dreams of spending the whole day playing arcade games after the firm invested in the iconic Timezone Group.

As first reported by Street Talk on Monday, Quadrant has formed a new holding company, The Entertainment and Education Group [TEEG], to make acquisitions in the rapidly-growing family and children entertainment and early education markets in Australia and across Asia.

Timezone is understood to be the first step in Quadrant's roll-up plan and also marks the final transaction out of its last fund.

The business, which runs 200 Timezone and Timezone Play & Learn stores across Australia and Asia, was founded by the Steinberg family in 1978.

Malcolm and Adam Steinberg are expected to remain with TEEG as it pushes into the Asian market, where spending on education, entertainment and leisure is rising.

TEEG will be led by current Timezone managing director Scott Blume, who ran ASX-listed Wotif before it was sold to Expedia. Adam Steinberg has also been appointed as non-executive director of TEEG.

Private consumption growth across South-east Asia is forecast to be over 30 per cent across the next five years and largely focused on education, entertainment and leisure, according to the Economist Intelligence Unit.

Quadrant was advised by Record Point, EY and Gilbert +Tobin. Timezone took its counsel from Allens and Deloitte.

The deal also comes as Quadrant targets a first and final close for it

sentiment_pool.headline: K. Wah gets in at sub 4 per cent
sentiment_pool.text:
More records are set to be broken in the commercial property market with multinational conglomerate K. Wah Group finalising its first property deal in Australia, buying US financial services giant TIAA's TH Real Estate office building in Sydney on a sub 4 per cent yield.

A deal to buy the 16-level, A-grade office tower at 20 Hunter Street is understood to have exchanged at a price of more than $190 million, well ahead of initial expectations of about $170 million.

The deal comes fresh off the back of Hong Kong-based Early Light International Group, backed by billionaire toy maker Francis Choi, entering a deal to buy Blackstone's 1 Castlereagh Street tower in Sydney for about $220 million which would also break a record of more than $19,000 per square metre.

The frenzy of deals involving the big Chinese-backed buyers supports market participants' forecast earlier this year of a wave of offshore money that would boost values for commercial property, especially Sydney office towers that are receiving rental growth in a tight market.

Sub 5 per cent yields were anticipated this year with talk of increased demand from offshore investors and the market has responded with several massive deals. Local group Dexus bought a half share in the MLC Centre in June on a yield of 4.5 per cent while Early Light purchased the ASX headquarters at 20 Bridge Street for $335 million on a 4.5 per cent fully leased yield. sentiment_pool.headline: Could late-year talks see 2018 IPO plans Unlockd?
sentiment_pool.text:
It's that time of year when equity capital markets teams are looking to restock deal pipelines and unlisted initial public offering targets can demand plenty of attention.

With that in mind, Street Talk understands Australian mobile advertising start-up Unlockd is making the most of its status as a promising Australian technology success story, reaching out to a number of investment banks to discuss a number of matters, including the pros and cons of an initial public offering.

Sources said Unlockd, which has attracted a raft of big name backers during its rapid rise over the past two years, is keen to at least consider its options, with a number of stakeholders believed to be pulling the company in different directions.

It would appear an aggressive move to pursue an initial public offering worth hundreds of millions of dollars only two years after inception. But there is no doubt it is the sort of company bankers would like to get to know better given its potential to help bulk up the Australian listed technology sector and the names involved with the company.

"After raising over $60 million of capital, we continue to look at every opportunity to grow the business for shareholders and our customers, whether that's public, private or domestic," Unlockd co-founder and CEO Matt Berriman told Street Talk yesterday.

"The Australian stock exchange has a lot of appetite for tech stocks with global growth aspirations."

sentiment_pool.headline: Cotton weaves a mining Base in Africa
sentiment_pool.subhead: Resources Supporting local communities can be good for business, writes Peter Ker.
sentiment_pool.text:
When you run a mining operation in Africa, it can be hard to avoid the stigma from scandals affecting big companies like Rio Tinto, Shell and Glencore in nations like Guinea, Mozambique, Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

"My kids particularly notice it among their peers and their peers' parents," says Tim Carstens, the managing director of ASX-listed Base Resources, which produces mineral sands in Kenya.

"Unfortunately the relatively isolated incidents of things not going the way they should taint the rest of us, that is part of the reason we are trying to set a new standard in successful mineral development in Africa."

Extractive industries have the potential to generate enormous wealth for host communities, but even the longest-running mines are temporary enterprises.

When Base was building its mine in Kenya's Kwale County in 2013, the project had an expected life of 13 years, and so Carstens' team knew they had to do something different if they were going to impact local communities in a way that was both positive and permanent.

To deliver on that goal, Carstens brought in Melbourne-based firm Business For Development (B4D), which had previously designed and co-ordinated social programs in developing nations for big businesses like Oil Search.

sentiment_pool.headline: Oracle's $1.6b takeover of Aconex exposes timid Aussie tech investors
sentiment_pool.text:
Mike Cannon-Brookes has warned Australian fund managers to ignore local tech firms at their peril, after construction software company Aconex announced a $1.6 billion acquisition offer from Oracle yesterday and sparked a brutal rout of short sellers who had attacked the stock.

The deal heralds a significant payday for the company's founders, Scotch College Melbourne friends Leigh Jasper, 43, and Robert Phillpot, 44, who are set to bank more than $95 million each on the back of the deal.

Mr Cannon-Brookes, the founder of $11 billion tech giant Atlassian, congratulated the pair on the deal, calling it a big win for Aussie tech.

"To local fundies who don't believe in tech, 47 per cent premium will hurt a lot?," he said on Twitter. The deal sent Aconex's share price soaring more than 44 per cent to $7.63, just below the $7.80-a-share bid from Oracle.

While the offer came at a significant premium to its last trading price, it was below the stock's peak of $8.38, achieved in July 2016.

Aconex sells a cloud-based system to allow collaboration across the thousands of documents involved in a construction project and has more than 5.5 million users. Mr Jasper and Mr Phillpot retain almost 12 per cent of the business between them, making them the second-largest shareholders behind Oracle, which increased its stake through Vantive Australia to 13.53 per cent yesterday.

But while Christmas came early for Aconex's founders, it was an end-of-year nightmare for the short sellers that h

sentiment_pool.headline: Ivory price crashes ahead of China ban
sentiment_pool.text:
Li Chunke began carving ivory after leaving school as a 15-year-old boy.

Today, at 68, this master craftsman is working until the early hours of every morning, trying to finish a 50-centimetre statuette of Buddha on an unforgiving deadline - before China implements a total ban on ivory sales at the end of this month. The art of ivory carving survived even the tumult of China's Cultural Revolution, but he's worried it may soon die out.

"What makes China great is that its traditional culture still exists," he said. "If it disappears in China, it will be a loss for the whole world."

Yet China's commitment to put craftsmen like Li out of business and close down its ivory industry has thrown a lifeline to African elephants, and brought new hope in the battle to end the poaching of tens of thousands of animals every year for their tusks.

The Chinese government shut down 67 ivory carving workshops and retail outlets in March, and will have closed the remaining 105 by the end of this year, honouring a commitment President Xi Jinping first made alongside then US president Barack Obama back in 2015.

"China's ban is one of the most important things that has happened to elephants in the last 10 years," said Iain Douglas-Hamilton, one of the world's leading elephant conservationists and founder of Save The Elephants.

sentiment_pool.headline: Why economics is still a man's game
sentiment_pool.text:
A couple of weeks ago, I was strolling through the marble corridors of the mighty Federal Reserve in Washington when I spotted a gaggle of students from different colleges. They were taking part in a Fed competition meant to inspire would-be economists to get excited about monetary policy.

So far, so encouraging; after all, the world needs a new generation of economists with public service ideals. But there was a catch: although the team that won the challenge (from Pace University) included women, most of the runners-up who were milling in the corridors were male.

If there were more male entrants to the competition, that is certainly not the fault of the Fed; on the contrary, like most Western central banks and other public and private financial institutions, the Fed tries to celebrate female economists. It took care, for example, to post a picture of the smiling Pace team on the website. And it has a particular reason to bang the drum about female financial power: Janet Yellen, the Fed chair, is the first woman to hold this position.

Despite Yellen's seniority, the fact remains that economics and economic policymaking is mostly a man's domain. Yes, there are some women at the top: the Fed board includes Esther George, the no-nonsense head of the Kansas Fed. Then there is Christine Lagarde, head of the IMF.

But barely a 10th of tenured economic professors in the US are women and only one woman has ever won a Nobel prize for economics (Elinor Ostrom). Across the world, on

sentiment_pool.headline: Decade-long glut forecast for LNG called into question
sentiment_pool.text:
An ultra-bearish forecast by Macquarie of a decade-long glut in LNG and rock-bottom prices has been questioned by Woodside Petroleum and industry consultants, who say demand growth is robust and a shortfall may emerge sooner than many anticipate.

The bank predicts global oversupply lasting until 2022, or even as long as 2027 if the US, Russia and Qatar push forward with more new projects and fight it out for market share, ignoring economic drivers.

The rise of renewables and outperformance by production plants could extend the glut even further, it said in a bleak assessment that drove a downgrade on Santos and a negative call on Woodside Petroleum.

Macquarie cast doubt on Woodside's circa $US23 billion ($30 billion) Browse LNG project making the grade on costs, and said the producer would face price cuts as sales contracts came up for renegotiation in the next few years.

It envisages "difficult" negotiations between Woodside and its Pluto LNG customers, Tokyo Gas and Kansai Electric. "With the commencement of ~40Mtpa of new volumes by 2019 from the US alone, we do not see Woodside having much leverage in the negotiations," Macquarie said.

Woodside would not comment on Pluto but a spokeswoman pointed to the robust demand for LNG this year, which has driven up spot prices.

"The strength of global LNG demand growth has surprised in 2017, and that could happen again in 2018," she said.

"That indicates that both LNG suppliers and LNG buyers are going to have to get to work

sentiment_pool.headline: Markets are neverong wrong, until a crash
sentiment_pool.text:
There's an old saying that dictates the market is never wrong, that the price of any asset is in line with the basic fundamentals that are there for everyone to see.

There is always a reason for a good old-fashioned price surge, up or down, even when nobody can find it, but it's fair to say the "efficient market hypothesis" has been tested in 2017 with bubbles all over the place.

For example, there's bitcoin, the property markets in Sydney and Melbourne, Wall Street, which has been in a bull market since early 2009, and even the art world where Leonardo da Vinci's Saviour of the World was bought for $US450 million in November.

That sale created a record, but it changed hands for just £45 in the 1950s when there were doubts over its authenticity that still linger today.

Even the debt markets have had their moments this year when $US9 trillion of bonds were still trading with a negative yield as the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates, a move that should send bond yields higher.

Then Austria sold €3.5 billion of 100-year debt, the largest ever century bond to hit the market, while Argentina, a year after emerging from its latest default, also sold bonds that don't mature for another 100 years.

Is lending money to anyone for 100 years the right move?

The Austrian bonds delivered investors a yield of just 2.1 per cent and maybe shows there is just too much money floating around or that prices can indeed be unpredictable and wrong, it just takes time.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fundies kick in at Healthia
sentiment_pool.text:
Ask a small cap fund manager about the roll-ups they've studied since the initial public offering window opened in 2013, and they will be able to rattle off a long list.

There were funeral homes (Propel Funeral Partners), veterinary services (National Veterinary Care), accounting firms (Kelly Partners), rubbish removal (Bingo Industries), aged care (Estia Health), child care (Affinity Education, Evolve), in-home care (Zenitas Healthcare), packaging (Pact Group), and plenty of others.

One industry they haven't had to think about too much is podiatry.

Until now.

Fundies are expecting to be asked to take a look at Brisbane-based podiatry roll-up Healthia in coming weeks, as part of its run at the ASX boards.

Healthia has grown to about 50 podiatry clinics under the My FootDr and other brands, following chunky acquisitions in the past two years. Its most recent accounts show $20.1 million annual revenue, up 362.8 per cent in the 2016-17 financial year.

Healthia's pitch is expected to revolve around consolidating Australia's fragmented podiatry services market, which IBISWorld estimates is worth $900 million a year.

Much of the revenue comes from private health insurance providers, with IBISWorld estimating more than 2.7 million podiatry sessions will be covered by private health insurance companies in the year to June 30.

Healthia was set up by podiatrists Darren Stewart and Greg Downer in 2004.

sentiment_pool.headline: Euphoria turns around in no time
sentiment_pool.text:
The latest cryptocurrency price collapse is a reminder of the terrifying speed with which paper profits can be completely wiped out.

On Wednesday investors watched in horror as growing anxiety about a regulatory crackdown sent prices for bitcoin, Ripple and Ethereum plunging.

But that's not the only market where alarm bells are sounding. Wall Street's abrupt turnaround on Tuesday provides a timely demonstration of just how quickly air pockets can open up in markets trading at perilously high valuations.

In euphoric trading on Tuesday morning, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 283 points, or 1.1 per cent, to hit a fresh record high.

But then the mood on Wall Street suddenly soured, with the DJIA finishing the day 10 points, or 0.04 per cent lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 0.35 per cent.

This left analysts in an embarrassing predicament, because they had no convincing explanation either for Wall Street's early rally, or for the subsequent sell-off.

Most argued that the US share market was extremely overbought - just before the sell-off, the DJIA's 14-day Relative Strength Index (which measures the speed and size of share price movements) hit its highest level in more than 60 years - which meant that a correction was both overdue and healthy.

Some analysts, however, said the sell-off reflected investor anxiety over growing tensions with China, as US President Donald Trump pushes his America First Agenda.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fed member relaxed on inflation risk
sentiment_pool.text:
The Federal Reserve should raise interest rates three times this year given the already strong economy will get a boost from tax cuts, and can tighten more or less aggressively if needed, a key US rate-setter said on Saturday.

San Francisco Fed president John Williams painted a benign picture of the world's largest economy operating at or near its full capacity over the next few years. While his colleagues at the US central bank see unemployment dipping only slightly from 4.1 per cent currently, Williams predicted it would fall to 3.7 per cent this year without any risk of a worrisome jump in inflation.

The comments from Williams, a veteran policymaker at a time of an unprecedented leadership overhaul at the Fed, suggest the central bank remains confident in its approach after a year of gradual tightening even in the face of the $US1.5-trillion tax-cut bill passed last month.

"We're in a pretty good situation: the economy is doing great, everyone expects us to raise rates gradually ... and if the data change we can respond to that," said Williams, who has a vote on policy this year under a rotation.

"I'm not worried about inflation suddenly taking off," he told Reuters over lunch during an American Economic Association conference in Philadelphia. "Something like three rate hikes makes sense to me" this year, he added.

sentiment_pool.headline: Alpha and beta of a defensive portfolio
sentiment_pool.text:
It goes without saying: the sharemarket is risky. But investors seem to have lost sight of this as the market marches higher each day with little or no volatility. The market hasn't fallen by more than 5 per cent in more than two years, which is unhealthy.

While there is much talk of animal spirits, how can we have them without the attendant risk of loss?

This false comfort will be shattered one day as the embedded risk of inflated prices is laid bare. The principal risk in holding any asset is in the price; if you overpay you stand to lose. The chart below reveals a sharemarket that is expensive on historic valuation measures.

Another way to consider risk is to think about where we are in the business cycle. You can see in the chart this cycle is shaping up as one of the longest on record.

As shares become more expensive and the business cycle approaches its inevitable conclusion, investors should contemplate how they can avoid these mounting risks. While you may miss out on the final blow-off in shares, by avoiding the next inevitable drawdown you will be miles ahead in the long run.

Consider where the market is today. The All Ordinaries index is still trading below its previous high, reached more than 10 years ago. Most investors are yet to recover these losses. The key message at this late stage of the cycle is clear: protect your capital and avoid the next drawdown.

sentiment_pool.headline: EnergyAustralia buoyed by power prices
sentiment_pool.text:
Higher electricity and gas prices helped propel EnergyAustralia's operating earnings up 48 per cent last year and the foreign-owned retailer is expecting to benefit from another year of high tariffs before a softening in 2019.

The improvement to $HK2.738 billion of operating profit in 2017 made Australia the most improved business for Hong Kong-listed CLP Group, which also operates in mainland China, India, south-east Asia as well as in its home market.

EA managing director Catherine Tanna defended the improved performance, noting that the company has often made no returns in previous years, and has suffered $1.9 billion of asset write-downs since 2006.

"Now, with the tailwind of a once-in-a-decade tightening in supply, our business is financially stable, and we have an opportunity to help modernise the country's energy system," Ms Tanna said. She pointed to an investment of almost $150 million in power plants in the past year, and a commitment to underpin 500 megawatts of new wind and solar projects.

CLP said power plant reliability would be a key focus for EA this year as it seeks to run its assets efficiently and help ease pressure from higher wholesale prices. Generation fell at both EA's Yallourn coal plant in Victoria and its Mount Piper plant in NSW last year.

The parent company, it added, expected no reduction in pressures in the "extremely competitive" retail market in Australia where customer churn rose in the December half.

sentiment_pool.text:
ING, Macquarie Bank and Virgin Money are reducing rates on interest-only investment loans despite regulatory efforts to curb these loans due to concerns about growing household debt.

As a Reserve Bank of Australia executive noted in a speech on Tuesday, interest rates for investors on interest-only loans have jumped 60 basis points since late 2016 after pressure from regulators to encourage borrowers to pay down debt.

But lenders claim they are responding to strong demand for investment borrowing, particularly borrowers wanting to make the most of lucrative tax breaks.

Major banks including ANZ and Commonwealth Bank have reported in recent weeks that their home loan books continue to grow.

The niche lenders are targeting investment property buyers by reducing rates by up to 24 basis points for borrowers with loan-to-value ratios typically of between 20 and 30 per cent.

There is also closer scrutiny of their ability to service the loan for the full term.

For example, ING, which has about 2.6 per cent of the mortgage market, is reducing variable interest rates on investment loans by about 5 basis points to 4.64 per cent for loans of at least $150,000 with loan-to-value ratios of at least 80 per cent.

It is raising fixed rates on principal-and-interest, interest-only loans by between eight basis points for a one-year loan and 41 basis points for a five-year fix.

sentiment_pool.headline: Europe looks to get smarter about modern defence
sentiment_pool.text:
Military The latest attempt to increase ties has a broader purpose.

Between them, members of the European Union produce 17 different battle tanks - compared to one in the United States, 29 destroyers and frigates - compared to four in the US and 20 different types of fighter planes, compared to six.

EU countries also have 178 different sorts of weapons systems, compared to 30 in the United States.

The duplication of effort is a powerful symbol of the dilemma facing Europe's defence and strategic environment in the post-Brexit, post-Trump age.

While much of the coverage of the EU in the past 18 months has been dominated by Brexit, the more profound change occurring in Europe concerns defence, and the decision of the remaining 27 countries in Europe to step up their defence links.

This weekend will see some of the most powerful people in the world converge at the annual Munich Security Conference with the expectation of a number of major statements.

The Europeans - and many others - are anxious to hear US Defence Secretary Jim Mattis explain the evolving USW position on the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, given US President Donald Trump has at times questioned the value of the alliance.

British Prime Minister Theresa May will also be in town and is supposed to be (finally) laying down clear guidelines about Britain's path to a European exit - something that also has significant implications for strategic policy .

sentiment_pool.text:
Elon Musk did it, and now a group of Australian entrepreneurs have started a primary school aimed at making kids better problem solvers.

The Luminaria Group, led by Susan Wu - an early team member of tech unicorns Stripe and Twitter - has implemented its new education model at Melbourne's Sandridge School, now known as The Lumineer Academy, and wants its homework-free, child co-created system to go global.

"Most educators are iterating off a model that's 150 years old, designed to produce factory workers for the first industrial age," Ms Wu told The Australian Financial Review.

"We've taken it back to first principles, and asked what kids need to think independently and sort fact from fiction, in a world where 65 per cent of the jobs they will do haven't been invented yet."

Luminaria's model, which began running at its Williamstown pilot location last year and is open for new enrolments, sees students move rooms throughout the day and work primarily via collaborative projects, rather than worksheets.

It claims not to silo so-called STEM subjects (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) but treat them as a foundation of all learning, making and emotional intelligence.

"For example, when we teach robotics we integrate the overall context of computational data, design, engineering, human rights, ethics, civics and algorithm design," Ms Wu said.

"What it is? I don't know," Flatt assessed. "As far as we can tell, it has no intrinsic value. There isn't anything in it. There is nothing it will do to create wealth. Therefore it is not an asset for us. Whether some others think it is an asset, I don't know. It is just not, not for us. And I would say good luck to all the people that do invest in it. We wouldn't."

In Flatt's February newsletter to Brookfield shareholders, the contrarian investor listed "bitcoin mania" and the recent $US500 million sale of an Italian renaissance painting as two topical triggers for a new investment prudence.

"Our definition of an asset is something that generates cash or has the ability to generate cash. Bitcoin does not generate cash and it has no ability to ever generate cash. Therefore it isn't an asset.

"As to the technical things that go into bitcoin mining, I just don't have an answer for it."

Flatt also offered to shareholders two other twinned clarions that announced the need for circumspection, global equity and bond markets.

sentiment_pool.headline: DBI Design goes to China in slow Australian market
sentiment_pool.text:
Gold Coast-based DBI Design has offset a slowing Australian market with a contract to design and project manage a $3 billion masterplanned new financial district in Shantou, north-east of Hong Kong.

The 70-person high-rise residential specialist returned to mainland China in late 2016 after a 15-year gap, opening an office and employing a business development manager in an effort to find work when it was clear Australia's biggest-ever housing construction boom was going to end.

"We could see things were slowing down and needed to look at other markets," DBI Design director Raith Anderson said.

"We've always done international work but traditionally we've waited for people to come to us. This is the first time we've really actively spent time and money in China marketing our brand."

It worked. The Shantou Overseas Financial Centre being developed by Guangdong-based JinFeng Group is centred around two 380-metre-high towers - one hotel and one office - and comprises 10 commercial buildings, 16 apartment and residential towers, two hotels, a shopping centre, cultural precinct and marina.

Setting up in China was no harder than expanding to new Australian markets, said Mr Anderson.

"It takes a while to get established in cities like Sydney or Melbourne," he said. "To become a local you really need to set up a full practice for people to accept you. You're seen as an outsider, whereas if you go to China they actually want your brand."

sentiment_pool.headline: Banks, miners drag ASX into the red
sentiment_pool.text:
Worries about the future tax treatment of dividends, a probe into bank behaviour and a sharp drop in iron ore prices combined to push Australian shares lower yesterday.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index moved down 21 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 5974, while the All Ordinaries lost 24 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 6077.

The Australian dollar traded at US78.70¢ as traders also parsed data on housing finance and a survey of business conditions ahead of US inflation data due overnight.

Investors appeared troubled by the news that franking credits may not be available to retirees if Labor is elected next year.

"Lots of retirees have been focusing on high-dividend shares to boost income levels," noted AMP Capital's head of investment Shane Oliver.

Dr Oliver estimated franking credits currently add about 1.5 percentage points to Australian sharemarket returns. If the dividend franking plan is introduced "at the margin you're getting less of a kicker on Australian shares. You may look overseas or you may look at property, or high-yielding global shares," he said. "Markets are trying to get to grips with that."

Companies such as Telstra are vulnerable to changes in the treatment of franking credits because the bulk of their earnings are in Australia, Mr Oliver noted. Telstra shares fell 0.9 per cent to $3.41.

Property Chief executives pitch their wares on global stage.

Will the $32 billion Unibail-Rodamco takeover of Westfield go ahead? How much more pop is left in Sydney's office markets? And who's still shopping in the malls Down Under?

These were among the burning questions for the world's property heavyweights - insofar as they turned their mind to the Australian market - at Citi's global property conference in Florida.

It's an annual event and this past week more than 1200 chief executives, analysts and investors - a record number - gathered at the Diplomat Beach Resort on Hollywood Beach, just north of Miami.

The weather is balmy but it's a serious event for Australian's own listed property barons, giving them a chance to pitch their stock.

For Peter Allen, who heads the $21 billion Scentre that owns and manages Westfield malls in Australia, it's an opportunity to meet his US-based investors.

About 45 per cent of Scentre is held by global investors and more than half of them are in the US.

Scentre, like other shopping centre landlords, was hit by negative sentiment toward retail last year that dragged the whole listed property sector into negative territory in the 2017 financial year. The impact of e-commerce - as a headwind for retail and a tailwind for logistics -was a pressing issue for many of those at this year's meet-up.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fair Work slams Caltex franchise model
sentiment_pool.text:
Petrol giant Caltex Australia has been blasted by the Fair Work Ombudsman for widespread and systemic underpayment of wages and an unsustainable operating model across its franchise network.

The report, the culmination of a lengthy investigation into one of the country's biggest franchise operators, comes days after Caltex shocked the market with a decision to exit franchising.

The FWO has found 76 per cent of Caltex stores audited were exploiting workers, including breaching workplace laws and "significantly" under paying award wages to young foreign workers on visas.

In a statement to The Australian Financial Review, Caltex confirmed it had completed 293 audits - which represents half its franchise network. It said for the period from October 2016 to mid-2017 its audit results were in line with the work place regulator.

The regulator found evidence of wage underpayment, non-payment of overtime and penalty rates, poor record keeping and pay slip breaches.

It said the lack of records "suggests serious and systemic non-compliance". In some cases there was deliberate falsification of payroll records.

It said Caltex's failure to put effective systems in place to ensure its system complied with work laws contributed to the underpayment of workers.

sentiment_pool.headline: Bega braces for impact of milk wars
sentiment_pool.text:
Bega Cheese is bracing itself for the impact of a bidding war for Australian milk supply at a time when global farm gate prices are expected to fall.

Bega was able to increase its milk supply by 25 per cent in the first half of fiscal 2018 when it processed 465 million litres, but executive director Barry Irvin knows the honeymoon is over.

Canadian dairy company Saputo has flagged increasing milk intake by 600 million litres a year once it has finalised the $1.3 billion acquisition of Murray Goulburn.

Saputo's target of 2.5 billion litres is based on boosting capacity at Murray Goulburn's seven processing facilities, but subject to change depending on the findings of an Australian Competition and Consumer Commission review of the deal, which is due tomorrow..

Mr Irvin said now the Murray Goulburn deal was reasonably well understood, less milk was moving among the big players in processing. "It has become highly competitive with some of smaller players looking to acquire milk wherever they can," he said.

"The environment has quickly changed from one where we have had the luxury of being able to acquire milk rather smoothly to one where we are back to something we have been very used to over recent years, where it is highly competitive."

Bega revealed on Wednesday its first-half net profit jumped by more than 30 per cent to $20.6 million as the additional milk supply increased manufacturing efficiencies.

sentiment_pool.headline: Solution to retirement? Spend bit more money
sentiment_pool.text:
Want more income in retirement but scared to withdraw too much in case your superannuation runs out? Financial consultant Rice Warner argues there's a way to enjoy a bit more income without hitting your balance too hard.

The context to its research is the continuing need for products that manage the competing priorities of managing longevity risk (you lasting longer than your savings) while providing enough income in retirement.

This was highlighted in the Financial System Inquiry (FSI), which recommended the government set up a suite of products to provide a minimal additional level of income or a guaranteed level of income, with the expectation that it stays constant (in real terms) for life. Dubbed Comprehensive Income Products in Retirement (CIPRs) or MyRetirement, the process is continuing with much consulting between government and providers.

In the meantime, says Rice Warner, a practical strategy is for retirees to stop being so frugal and live it up a little.

Martin Stevenson, a consultant at Rice Warner, explains: "Our position is that if you simply bump up the minimum drawdown rates, it will leave a slightly smaller bequest but will increase income over retirement."

The stock fell from $1 to 32.5¢ in morning trade before closing Monday's session down 55.5 per cent to a record low of 44.5¢.

The company said fewer users comparing products in the health insurance, energy and telecommunications channels contributed to a downgrading of expected earnings before interest and tax for the year from a range of $26 million-$29 million to just $8 million-$12 million. sentiment_pool.text:
The Turnbull government has fallen short by a whisker of meeting the goal of creating 1 million jobs in five years as last year's record employment growth comes off the boil.

The milestone will have to wait for another month after the release of the employment figures for March, which showed the economy added a seasonally adjusted 4900 jobs.

The jobless rate was steady for the third-straight month at 5.5 per cent after the February figure was revised down, while the participation rate came in at 65.5 per cent.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected 20,000 jobs to be added to the economy in March.

The Australian dollar dropped to US77.69¢, from 77.96¢ immediately before the data, but recovered to finish at 78.07¢.

"Jobs growth has remained somewhat soggy after last year's spectacular performance," BIS Oxford Economics' head of macroeconomic research Sarah Hunter said. "In part this was inevitable [the economy can't sustain growth of 400,000-plus pa], but it also highlights that the labour market has run ahead of output growth in recent months."

The economy needs almost 20,000 jobs to be added each month to bring down the unemployment rate.

"We are cautious about reading too much into a single-month figure given most leading labour market indicators remain consistent with decent rates of employment growth ahead," said Paul Dales at Capital Economics.

sentiment_pool.headline: Afterpay, a growing concern
sentiment_pool.text:
Afterpay, which has been a magnet for Millennial shoppers, continued its slide on the sharemarket yesterday, after Goldman Sachs downgraded its price target and sliced earnings forecasts citing doubts about whether the rapid growth could continue.

In an exclusive interview in BOSS Magazine, in today's The Australian Financial Review, Afterpay's co-founders say they're confident they can maintain momentum while also overcoming growing concerns around responsible lending, which have made investors in the one-time ASX high-flyer nervous.

"The board and the team feel like we have the ability to be an enduring player in the global retail scene and what is absolutely imperative is that we don't cut corners, and keep focused on the customer," says Anthony Eisen, the former Guinness Peat Group executive who started Afterpay with youngster Nick Molnar after noticing him selling jewellery on eBay.

Sydney-based Afterpay, founded in mid-2015 and listed on the ASX in 2016, allows shoppers to pay in four instalments but has fiercely divided analysts and brokers. This week it said its customer numbers had surged to 1.8 million.

A whopping 25 per cent of all online retail apparel transaction volumes in Australia - and 8 per cent of all online retail - is now being paid for using the platform.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASIC hauls Spaceship back to earth

It's the sort of marketing guff you've read on a thousand websites.

"We will fight to get you the very best assets in your portfolio," the Millennial-focused superannuation fund Spaceship said on its website.

"We will measure companies in our portfolio based on their ability to provide defensibility of profits and high levels of product differentiation."

Sounds great. Who doesn't want their super fund to fight for them? Who doesn't want to invest in companies that can defend their profits and demonstrate their products are different to everyone else's?

But the corporate regulator has found - relatively quickly for an institution that has often been accused of moving at a horse-and-cart pace - that Spaceship was actually fighting with one hand tied behind its back.

Almost 80 per cent of its assets were in index-tracking funds. It's ability to fight to get the best assets in your portfolio, or hand-pick companies based on their profits or their products, was therefore limited.

Spaceship, which counts tech titans Mike Cannon-Brookes and Peter Thiel among its backers, has been fined $12,600 for false and misleading conduct. The fund's trustee company has been fined the same amount. There is no suggestion that Cannon-Brookes or Thiel were involved in the false and misleading conduct.

sentiment_pool.headline: Twin deals signal healthy week for Riverside Company
sentiment_pool.text:
There's no complaints about the exit environment at global growth private investor The Riverside Company, with the firm finding offshore buyers for two of its five local portfolio companies in the past week.

Street Talk understands Riverside has agreed to sell its occupational rehabilitation, employment services and disability support services provider Work Health Group to United States-based Exam Works, which is backed by large US buyout fund Leonard Green.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX in the red on Westpac, Treasury
sentiment_pool.text:
Australian shares fell for a second session this week led lower by Westpac, CSL and Treasury Wine stocks.

The S&P/ASX fell 12.6 points, or 0.2 per cent, to 6094.3, as Westpac wiped 14.1 points from the index alone.

Westpac traded ex-dividend , sending its shares down 3.7 per cent to $29.10. The bank will pay a fully franked dividend of 94¢ a share on July 4.

Treasury Wine shares fell 6.2 per cent to $16.90 after The Australian Financial Review reported the company was facing a supply glut in China. The company also revealed sales in China were being hurt by new import verification requirements. Treasury said it was "seeking greater understanding of new and additional verification requirements" from the Chinese government.

Shares in Santos closed at $6.20, down 1.9 per cent following news that US private firm Harbour Energy has submitted a binding proposal for the takeover of the gas producer.

Coca-Cola Amatil shares fell 3.2 per cent to $8.68. At its AGM on Tuesday, the soft-drink maker warned earnings at its Australian beverages unit would be hit by the lauch of a container deposit scheme.

Kidman Resources shares rose 2.8 per cent to $2.22 after it struck a three-year deal with electric car marker Tesla to supply the US giant with lithium hydroxide from a refinery south of Perth.

Other lithium miners followed Kidman's advance.

The electricity industry attracts an unusual level of policy-based evidence making these days. A prime example is last week's support from ACCC chairman Rod Sims for the National Energy Guarantee (NEG). This is on the grounds that the agreement will force the vertically integrated retailers to have explicit and "transparent" hedging arrangements between their wholesale and retail arms ( "AGL Energy's NEG complaint shot down", AFR May 11).

Sims argues that forcing the vertically integrated businesses into having explicit and transparent hedging contracts will improve competition and, hence, prices for customers.

But there is no logic in this claim. Each time Sims has ended in court fighting against vertical integration, he loses. This is because he cannot mount a coherent argument to convince an impartial judge that vertical integration is bad and should be stopped. Indeed, judges have repeatedly found that the vertical integration cases that have been brought before them would do no harm to competition.

Now, instead of trying to make a cogent argument, Sims has taken to appealing to politicians, who prefer quick fixes to the mess they have made of the National Electricity Market.

sentiment_pool.headline: Passengers face new airport body scanners
sentiment_pool.text:
Screening at airports and international mail and cargo centres will be dramatically beefed up after last year's failed terrorist plot to blow up a flight from Sydney exposed worrying gaps in aviation security.

The government has announced a $293.6 million package over four years to roll out international airport-style body scanners for passengers and improved X-ray equipment for baggage screening at major domestic and regional airports, as well as new and upgraded equipment to enhance screening of inbound international mail and cargo.

The police presence at airports will also be increased, with the deployment of an extra 140 counter-terrorism officers who can rapidly respond to attacks, and a further 50 officers to provide tactical intelligence.

Security guards who perform screening at airports will also be required to undergo additional training and accreditation.

In conjunction with the new measures, new laws will be introduced giving the Federal Police broader powers to perform identity checks at airports and move on suspicious people. However the government has stopped short of introducing requirements for domestic passengers to present photo identification before boarding a flight.

sentiment_pool.headline: Stockland keeps guidance amid 'positive' housing
sentiment_pool.text:
Stockland is counting on a strong residential market to meet its earnings targets, even as retirement living earnings weaken and retail earnings growth across suburban Sydney slows.

The country's largest-listed developer said in a third-quarter update yesterday it was on track to expand in funds from operations - its preferred profit measure - 5 per cent to 6.5 per cent for the year to June, with a pipeline of 6367 residential contracts exchanged that would help meet its target of about 6500 residential settlements for the year.

"Residential trading conditions remain generally positive, particularly in Melbourne and Queensland," Stockland chief executive Mark Steinert said. "In line with expectations, Sydney has seen a slight moderation in demand from its peak."

The company said it was still targeting a distribution per security of 26.5¢, representing 4 per cent growth on last year, provided there was no material change in market conditions.

While the Sydney-led national residential housing market is slowing, the update was a reminder of the persistent strength of the housing market - despite what the company called "flat" price growth in NSW and WA - and that even if sales and activity have come off their recent peaks, they remain buoyant.

Macquarie analyst Paul Checchin said the company's number of contracts on hand was a record.

sentiment_pool.headline: Yuan hits five-month low against greenback
sentiment_pool.text:
China's yuan weakened to a more than five-month low against the dollar on Thursday, as corporate greenback demand picked up and higher US bond yields pushed the US currency higher against most of its peers.

Prior to market opening, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) set the midpoint rate at 6.4706 per US dollar, the weakest level since January 12.

Thursday's official guidance rate largely matched market expectations, unlike the central bank's firmer-than-expected fixing seen a day earlier.

In the spot market, the onshore yuan opened at 6.4793 per dollar and fell to a low of 6.4941 at one point, the weakest level since January 11.

Traders also noted that some companies picked up their dollar buying for their seasonal needs given the greenback's continued rising trend.

June and July are traditionally the peak season for dollar demand as foreign companies repatriate profits and Chinese companies pay dividends to overseas investors.

sentiment_pool.headline: WA ruling gives Atlas berth pain
sentiment_pool.text:
The battle for Atlas Iron has taken another twist with the West Australian government notifying the company it does not have a priority right to develop new berths with export capacity of 50 million tonnes a year at Port Hedland.

The notice affects Atlas' prized North West Infrastructure (NWI) port project and has ramifications for the three Rich Listers jostling over the junior iron ore miner.

Atlas maintains it does hold priority rights to the long-stalled project and the government's stance represents a significant change in policy.

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti told WA Parliament that NWI had been stripped of exclusivity by the previous government after it failed to advance the project.

Ms Saffioti said Atlas sought clarification on the government position last week and her advice confirmed NWI no longer had exclusive rights.

The rights to develop two berths at Stanley Point in addition to access to government-owned export infrastructure at Utah Point are central to the three-way tussle for Atlas involving Chris Ellison's Mineral Resources, Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals and Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting.

Atlas came out of a trading halt on Thursday and announced that correspondence from Ms Saffioti suggested NWI did not have a priority right to develop Stanley Point.

sentiment_pool.headline: Spurned Goldfields suitor looks to sell stake over 'dumb' Finsure deal
sentiment_pool.text:
Firstmac, the largest shareholder of Goldfields Money, is considering selling out of the challenger bank and is seeking its own banking licence after failing to snare Goldfields last year.

Kim Cannon, chief executive and owner of non-bank lender Firstmac, said he had lost confidence in the Goldfields board, which is pursuing a merger with the fast-growing mortgage aggregator Finsure.

Firstmac owns about 13 per cent in the ASX-listed Goldfields and Mr Cannon has claimed the board and management is overvaluing Finsure, has provided it with a loan not disclosed to shareholders, and is pursuing the deal in the face of uncertainty as the Hayne royal commission investigates the mortgage broking model. He also reckons Finsure is undercapitalised and expects Goldfields shareholders will continue to be diluted in the coming years as more regulatory capital is required to support loan growth.

"If you get banking, this is a dumb deal," Mr Cannon said of the merger, which is expected to go to a shareholder vote next month. "We are Australia's largest online lender and now we will do our own thing."

For most of its six years as a listed company, the Kalgoorlie-based Goldfields, with a market cap of $35 million, has been a "thinly traded, sub-scale regional banking operation", according to a recent report by stockbroker Hartleys. sentiment_pool.headline: Narrower $1b surplus keeps optimism up
sentiment_pool.text:
The robust health of the external sector has been underscored by a 16th trade surplus in 18 months, picking up where better-than-expected first-quarter growth left off.

Australia's economy recorded a $977 million surplus in April, close to the $1 billion result the market was looking for. The trade report also showed an upwardly revised surplus for March of $1.7 billion from $1.5 billion. On Wednesday, the national accounts revealed that GDP accelerated the most in seven quarters, rising 1 per cent in the March quarter for an annual growth rate of 3.1 per cent.

Exports fell 2.2 per cent in value, trimming the increase during the past year to 11.3 per cent, according to ANZ. Excluding the more-volatile non-monetary gold component, this largely reflects some weakness in the price of metals and thermal coal about this time because volumes were up throughout the resources category.

ANZ senior economist Joanne Masters said that, despite the narrowing of the surplus, it was still a favourable result at almost $1 billion, and with the benefit of two upward revisions during the past two months.

"Volume growth still looks to be very strong, and LNG exports were up in both price and volume," flattering the external picture, she said. "Momentum in the global economy is rolling over, that's been evident in the PMI surveys, but it's rolling over from what's been a strong period of synchronised global growth." sentiment_pool.headline: Coles board conflict dogs Wesfarmers
sentiment_pool.text:
Pressure is mounting on Wesfarmers over its appointment of James Graham as chairman of Coles after the veteran banker revealed an interest in almost 800,000 shares in Wesfarmers worth $39 million.

Mr Graham stepped down as a non-executive director of Wesfarmers last week, after more than 20 years on the board, after being named chairman-elect of Coles post the $20 billion demerger.

However, according to a final directors interest notice lodged on Monday, Mr Graham retains a direct interest in 10,802 Wesfarmers shares worth $535,747 and a relevant interest in another 774,353 shares worth $38.3 million, including 582,729 shares owned through investment bank Gresham Partners.

Mr Graham is chairman of Gresham and owns about 25 per cent of the shares, making him the second-largest shareholder after Wesfarmers, which owns 50 per cent. Gresham is one of four firms advising Wesfarmers on the Coles demerger and has received more than $88 million in fees from Wesfarmers in 10 years.

Analysts expect Gresham to generate more fee income from Wesfarmers as chief executive Rob Scott sells assets and makes acquisitions to further diversify the conglomerate's portfolio.

Mr Graham declined to comment, saying it was best to let Wesfarmers run the demerger process. His large stake in Wesfarmers means he will emerge with a similar-sized stake in Coles post the in-specie distribution.

sentiment_pool.headline: Slowdown in east coast housing gathers speed
sentiment_pool.text:
Sydney house prices fell 4.5 per cent in the year to June, their fastest rate in a decade, and Melbourne houses grew at their weakest pace in almost six years as the unwinding of the housing boom gained pace.

Tighter credit and weaker investor activity continued to slow the housing market on Australia's eastern seaboard in the June quarter, with the national median house price falling 1 per cent - its first annual fall since 2012 - to $802,077, Domain Group figures showed. "On a national level we're seeing a softening of conditions which is being driven by Sydney and Melbourne," Domain analyst Nicola Powell said. "All capital cities are showing softer conditions compared with last year, with the exception of Hobart and Perth."

Domain, majority owned by Fairfax Media - publisher of The Australian Financial Review - measures median prices to determine price movements, while rival data provider CoreLogic uses a hedonic index to track home values. Despite having different methodologies, the two paint a similar picture of downturn. Earlier this month, CoreLogic also showed a 4.5 per cent year-on-year decline for Sydney home values, the weakest decline since March 2009 on its records.

The extent of the duration of property price falls is unknown - and subject to further possible tightening in credit and interest rate rises - but comes after a six-year boom in growth and is unlikely to roll back all of the gains made. sentiment_pool.headline: Hilton owner could double its money
sentiment_pool.text:
The five-star Hilton Hotel in Surfers Paradise is for sale - with a price tag of about $80 million - after its Chinese based investors decided to sell out.

Privately owned Ji Feng bought the hotel from Brookfield in 2011 for about $37 million and has now appointed specialist McVay Real Estate Australia to sell the property. The owner has no other commercial property interests in Australia but could be looking at new investments in Sydney.

The hotel, once part of the failed Raptis company, comprises 169 guest rooms, four food and beverage outlets, conference facilities, pool deck, two gyms, a day spa and 89 undercover car parks.

There has been a strong rebound in Gold Coast tourism.

McVay Real Estate's Sam McVay said the Gold Coast market recorded revenue growth per available room in the year to date up 15.6 per cent on the same comparative period last year, placing it among the best performing destinations in Australia.

"We see the continued growth across the entire Gold Coast market over the coming years on the back of unprecedented infrastructure investment into the Airport, rail and roads," he said.

Mr McVay said the new owners had a major opportunity to replace Hilton as the manager and make significant improvements to the hotel.

The pricing of about $80 million would still be substantially below replacement cost, allowing the new owners to make further capital investments, with more upside to be gained.

sentiment_pool.headline: Seven promises 13 'mega-days' of cricket this summer
sentiment_pool.text:
When Seven West Media chief executive Tim Worner sealed his network as the new free-to-air home of cricket, one of the first people he texted was the then Network Ten cricket-mad head of sport, Dave Barham.

Cricket Australia's $1.2 billion deal, revealed by The Australian Financial Review in April, shocked the media landscape as the sport switched to Seven and pay television provider Foxtel from Nine Entertainment, which had already turned its focus to tennis, and Ten.

Mr Barham, who had been part of Ten's negotiating team, had played a pivotal role at the network for the sport, helping build the Big Bash League from a $20 million property nobody wanted into Cricket Australia's crown jewel.

"He was one of the first people I texted to say, 'I'm sorry and I greatly respect what you've done with the game'," Mr Worner told the Financial Review. "I felt for him because I knew how much he loved doing what he did."

In less than two weeks, Mr Worner hired Mr Barham as Seven's new head of cricket. "It was pretty quick. It had to be that way," Mr Barham said.

"Channel Ten were really good. [Ten chief executive] Paul Anderson let me out of my contract, which was good of him. I was really keen to keep going. I love the Big Bash, I feel really connected to the Big Bash, I feel like I understand it really well and have a good grasp of the game, and Test cricket, I've always thought it would be a great challenge."

sentiment_pool.headline: How the US experience will guide European rates
sentiment_pool.text:
When looking at the outlook for rates in Europe, which is pivotal to forming a view on Australia, it's instructive to look to the US experience. It provides a rare and concrete reference point that investors can draw upon.

So if we consider the state of incomes today, and the sequence of monetary stimulus, the US has a three-year head start on Europe.

The peak in US unemployment occurred in late 2009, at 10 per cent. Middle-class incomes, a key driver of business capital expenditure and platform for shifting an economy into higher gear, started lifting in mid-2011.

By 2016, middle-class incomes had returned to pre-GFC levels in real terms, after a two-year period when economic growth transitioned from patchy, to a more consistent and virtuous growth cycle.

The US Federal Reserve ceased quantitative easing (QE) in October 2014, three years after incomes started growing again. It lifted the cash rate for the first time 13 months later.

European unemployment did not peak until mid-2013, and Australia in mid-2014. Middle-class incomes in Europe - particularly southern Europe - started lifting in 2015, suggesting the starting point of the European recovery was three years after the US, and placing Europe now in the equivalent of the US circa 2014.

sentiment_pool.headline: South32 a climate change winner
sentiment_pool.text:
New Energy Minister Angus Taylor should pick up the phone and talk to South32 chief executive Graham Kerr about the significant climate change issues driving his strategic thinking.

Kerr is selling out of energy coal in South Africa partly to invest in higher growth assets, but mainly because it will help attract a cohort of climate change-sensitive investors to the South32 share register.

"We've made the absolute strategic call last year that we're exiting that business and that's driven by a number of reasons," he tells Chanticleer.

"One being that you know we have from day one not been huge fans of thermal coal and it is becoming more and more of a discussion point when you see investors.

"You know, 10 years ago no one really talked about it, five years ago you had maybe one investor talking about it, and now we have a couple of investors probably at every roadshow every day talking about how they can't invest in you because we've got energy coal exposure. So that is becoming more of a reality."

Kerr said the base of investors who cannot invest in coal is growing and becoming more powerful.

Another climate change issue driving investment decision making at South32 is the move by China to clean up its environment by closing down high polluting factories and shifting to less carbon intensive production methods.

"China is obviously making steps on pollution reduction and it has a big impact on our business, especially around the blue sky policy," he says.

sentiment_pool.headline: Lenders launch spring campaigns to grab market share
sentiment_pool.text:
Property lenders are rolling out spring campaigns in a bid to revive sluggish markets and attract investors and home buyers during the peak selling season, offering lower rates, improved conditions and cash incentives for switching existing loans from competitors.

But they are also protecting their net interest margins against rising wholesale funding costs by targeting new borrowers rather than their existing customers, particularly for standard variable lending.

They are also imposing tougher conditions on high-rise, high-density apartments, including minimum sizes for studio and one and two-bedroom apartments.

Smaller lenders - and subsidiaries of the big four banks - are launching their campaigns in a bid to grab market share before the majors announce their new rates and conditions over coming weeks.

Some lenders, such as Teachers Mutual Bank and associated banks, are launching aggressive strategies targeting investors after the regulator lifted restrictions on their interest-only products.

AMP Bank, a division of the nation's largest financial conglomerate, is offering owner-occupied variable rates for loans of $750,000 and above of 3.69 per cent.

Others, including Newcastle Permanent, the nation's largest building society, are offering borrowers $1500 cash for switching their loans from competitors.

sentiment_pool.text:

"This notion that television is dead is really a pretty poor analysis of our market, you've really got to understand how television is changing to operate a business. It's content," Mr Marks said.

Nine's audience accesses its content on free-to-air television, digital publishing assets, streaming service 9Now and Stan, its 50-50 joint-venture subscription video on-demand service with Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review.

"We're in relevant television categories and certainly our shows are resonating with audiences and working across all those platforms. We have the opportunity to continue to grow."

The metropolitan network, home of The Voice and The Block, is forecasting earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation to grow in the range of 9 per cent and 17 per cent to between $280 million and $300 million. The earnings target comes despite the company forecasting the metro free-to-air advertising market will grow just 1 per cent in 2018-19.

Politics Malcolm Turnbull's position is under threat over energy policy - but would the conservative wing's leading light Peter Dutton make a difference, asks Andrew Tillett.

Malcolm Turnbull, a student of history, may not appreciate the analogy. When the Tet offensive was launched by Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces in January 1968, militarily it was a disaster for them. After being surprised by the offensive, the Americans and allies counter-attacked and inflicted huge casualties on the Communists.

But it was the US that suffered the greater longer-term damage, as the tide of public opinion turned sharply against the war and prompted the opening of lengthy peace talks and the eventual US withdrawal.

Now the Prime Minister faces his own Tet offensive over energy policy. He and the indefatigable Energy Minister Josh Frydenberg have won a series of battles with the National Energy Guarantee - getting the states to keep it alive last week, steering it through the party room this week - but the Prime Minister risks losing the war as dissident MPs use it to threaten his leadership.

Some of the guerillas in his midst Turnbull will never convince - Exhibit A Tony Abbott - but the PM is fighting a rearguard effort among waverers promising to take a "big stick" to energy companies to bring down power prices.

sentiment_pool.headline: Macquarie Street strata owners sell in one line
sentiment_pool.text:
Seventeen owners of 21 strata office suites at the Sydney CBD office building 195 Macquarie Street have banded together to sell their office units in one line with a price expectation of $21 million to $22 million.

The portfolio represents 64.3 per cent of the total units in the building and the successful buyer will need to acquire another 10.7 per cent in unit entitlements to have a majority 75 per cent ownership before they can force the collective sale of the remaining 25 per cent of the offices.

The building has the potential to be redeveloped into a luxury residential development, subject to approval.

The 21 office suites in 195 Macquarie Street have a total net lettable area of 873 square metres.

CBRE's Nicholas Heaton, who is selling the properties with Danny Shi and Tao Shi, said the immediate purchaser focus would be to capitalise on the strength of the Sydney CBD office sector, which is suffering a low vacancy rate and a rise in rents of 2.8 per cent to 4.5 per cent over the June quarter.

"This growth had led to a concurrent uplift in office capital values underpinned by substantial stock withdrawals, particularly compulsory acquisitions for state government infrastructure and a series of residential and hotel conversions, which had resulted in an undersupplied market," Mr Heaton said.

The building is opposite NSW Parliament and the Sydney Hospital.

sentiment_pool.headline: Digital tennis rights were crucial for Nine
sentiment_pool.text:
Nine Entertainment chief executive Hugh Marks says securing both Tennis Australia's digital and broadcast rights was crucial for being able to build new audiences and explore a range of new opportunities to boost earnings from the Australian Open.

Nine, which is progressing its takeover of Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, originally swooped on Tennis Australia's broadcast rights for 2020 to 2024 for $60 million annually in March, wresting the rights from incumbent Seven West Media.

Nine and Seven later cut a $48.5 million deal for Tennis Australia's 2019 broadcast rights after the latter secured Cricket Australia's broadcast rights, along with Foxtel in April, bringing forward Nine's tennis coverage by a year.

"We wanted all live rights and near live, so that if you want to see those games, in that environment, you have to come through a Nine platform," Mr Marks told the Financial Review.

"I think that's the way you ideally can position yourself in modern broadcasting. I think that was a big part of our decision to team up with Tennis Australia, it was that opportunity in the way we're running our business now."

This is in contrast to Cricket Australia's broadcast rights, which Nine previously held. Foxtel holds exclusive digital rights and broadcast rights to every ball bowled, while Seven has free-to-air rights and no digital rights.

sentiment_pool.headline: Big turnout at Diggers and Dealers plants seed for M&A
sentiment_pool.text:
The biggest Diggers and Dealers event since the last mining boom has wound down with a pregnant pause in big transactions, but they are on the way.

That's the message from Diggers and Dealers co-owner Myles Ertzen as about 2297 delegates depart Kalgoorlie after three days of presentations, private meetings and partying.

"It is never as simple as doing a deal on the back of a serviette," he said.

"It is about getting people in a room and starting off a dialogue. A lot of deals get done because of Diggers, because of the meetings at Diggers and people catching up."

One prominent chief executive in the gold industry said an atmosphere of anticipation surrounded this year's event. "In past years, there have been one or two booths with a line five deep waiting to talk to them because they are doing a deal or have made a discovery," he said.

"It has been a bit different this year, but no doubt the mood is very positive."

Argonaut director of mining and metals research Matthew Keane said deals were in the wind based on discussions at Diggers, and some would likely involve a repositioning of assets around the goldfields.

Mr Keane said the mood was buoyant, but not as buoyant as in the past two years when the industry was on the upswing. "The mood has plateaued, but the good news is that it has plateaued at a high level," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: China tariffs on US LNG may boost Australians
sentiment_pool.text:
China's threatened tariffs on US liquefied natural gas imports could help Woodside Petroleum, Santos and Oil Search get more than $US25 billion ($34 billion) of LNG projects over the line as the world's fastest growing importer looks elsewhere for supplies to meet surging demand for cleaner fuel.

All three companies are targeting final investment decisions by the end of next year on their respective projects: Woodside's $US11 billion Scarborough project in Western Australia, Santos' circa $US4 billion Barossa venture off the north coast, and Oil Search's circa $US12 billion expansion in Papua New Guinea.

All are expected to target long-term customers in China, where the government on Friday flagged its intention to impose a 25 per cent tariff on LNG imports from the US.

"The 25 per cent import tariff on US LNG would make new non-US LNG supply more appealing," said Wood Mackenzie upstream analyst David Low. "In Australia, this bodes particularly well for the Scarborough and Caldita-Barossa projects, which would be looking to market gas to China, amongst other destinations, in the next year or so."

Both Woodside's Scarborough and Browse projects could benefit if the tariffs go ahead, said EnergyQuest consultant Graeme Bethune. The first stage of the $US20.5 billion Browse venture, in which PetroChina owns a stake, is targeted for a go-ahead in 2021.

Neither Woodside nor Santos would comment on the tariffs on Monday.

sentiment_pool.headline: Home Consortium sells two assets in Perth for $18m
sentiment_pool.text:
Leading large-format retail landlord Home Consortium has offloaded two former Masters properties in Perth for just over $18 million.

The group, which amassed a 700,000-square-metre portfolio of large-format retail properties after a $725 million acquisition of 61 Masters properties in 2016, sold down two former Masters hardware assets in the south of the Perth CBD because they were in more-industrial areas and did not suit the Home Consortium lifestyle and convenience retail profile of assets.

In Bibra Lake, Home Consortium sold the office and airconditioned warehouses at 7 Sobek Pass for $10 million to a private high-net-worth group.

The 13,197 sq m office and airconditioned warehouse sits on a 3.3-hectare site and can be used as an entertainment precinct, food or product storage, a hardware nursery or another large-format retail property.

In Forrestdale, Home Consortium also offloaded a similar property at 600 Ranford Road to a development company, Property Development (WA) Pty Ltd, for $8.1 million in an unconditional cash offer.

The 13,440sq m office and airconditioned warehouse also sits on a large site of 3.5 hectares. Both sales closed after 12 months on the market.

Savills' James Condon and Lachlan Webster brokered the deals.
