sentiment_pool.headline: Rising pay of chairmen sparks angst
sentiment_pool.text:
Leading fund managers have taken aim at the growing ranks of chairmen of ASX-listed companies collecting annual pay packets above $500,000 even though they acknowledge the complexities of overseeing businesses with increasingly large amounts of their operations offshore.

While high chairman salaries have traditionally been the preserve of the big banks and heavyweight miners, the list of companies paying well over half a million dollars has swollen to include companies like Treasury Wine Estates and hearing device pioneer Cochlear.

Geoff Wilson, chairman and portfolio manager of Wilson Asset Management, said the remuneration of chairmen in many cases was "excessive" among Australian companies.

"They are big numbers. The amount chairmen are being paid seems excessive," Mr Wilson said. "I would prefer a fee structure where they get a very small base and the rest is tied to long-term performance of the company".

Dean Paatsch, a founder of proxy advisory firm, Ownership Matters, said the non-executive director market didn't appear to be based on a clinical assessment of skills and demand, with pay rates often set on the basis of what other companies were paying.

"There is a market for non-executive labour that doesn't seem to be particularly functional," Mr Paatsch said.

Paul Rayner, the chairman of Penfolds owner Treasury Wine Estates made it past $500,000 in 2017-18. His pay packet rose to $508,900 from $466,605 a year earlier. He became chairman in 2012. The Treasury sha

sentiment_pool.headline: Court probes Westpac's $35m deal
sentiment_pool.text:
The legal foundation for Westpac Banking Corp's settlement with the corporate regulator over "irresponsible lending" is up in the air, with the Federal Court yet to appoint a senior barrister to probe whether their $35 million deal is appropriate given that no facts about unsuitable loans were presented to the court.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission and Westpac support the $35 million payment offered to resolve the case on September 4.

But in an unusual legal move, Justice Nye Perram said last week he must play "devil's advocate" and would appoint an "amicus", or court-appointed "contradictor", to test whether the amount of the settlement - and its legal basis - is justified. The extra judicial scrutiny on the settlement comes as ASIC's soft corporate penalties and excessive use of agreed settlements and enforceable undertakings have been exposed by the financial services royal commission.

Lawyers expect it will take at least another month before Justice Perram makes a decision and suggest the outcome is uncertain.

Depending on the strength of the arguments made by its independent counsel, the court may wave through the deal, increase or decrease the penalty, or possibly throw out the whole case on the basis that there was no breach of the law.

At a hearing last Friday, Justice Perram suggested he was uncertain about the legal foundation for the deal.

"So I'm asked here to impose a penalty for failing to comply with the procedures required by the sta

sentiment_pool.headline: Show ratings halve under Wilkinson
sentiment_pool.text:
Ratings for Network Ten's weekend current affairs show, The Sunday Project, have almost halved since the station's star recruit, Lisa Wilkinson, took over as host.

Viewers over the hour-long show in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth fell from 543,000 in January to 281,500 last Sunday, a fall of 48 per cent, according to industry figures.

The decline is a blow for American television giant CBS, which bought Ten this year and hailed the recruitment of the highly paid celebrity from Nine as a sign of its determination to turn around the perennially third-ranked commercial broadcaster.

"Having an incredible talent like Lisa Wilkinson coming over to join Ten ... was another indication of our investment in this market," the head of CBS's international division, Armando Nunez, said in April.

In her late 50s, Wilkinson appears to be struggling to appeal to the younger audience on Ten than Nine, where she co-hosted the Today show for 10 years. She quit Nine last year after complaining she wasn't paid enough, triggering a debate over gender-pay equality in commercial TV.

At the time, Nine chief executive Hugh Marks said he personally structured a $1.8 million pay package for Wilkinson to convince her to stay. But she wanted $2.3 million, according to Mr Marks, because she believed it would give her pay parity with co-host Karl Stefanovic.

A powerhouse on morning TV, Wilkinson's ratings on Ten's Sunday evening show have never come near the almost 600,000 for her Janu

sentiment_pool.headline: US dollar's dominance unimpaired for now
sentiment_pool.text:
While the US dollar has eased from a one-year peak in August, signs are pointing to a renewal of its year-to-date bull run.

The greenback continues to benefit from an expectation that US interest rates will rise further, including later this month, and the ongoing strength of the US economic expansion, with still relatively muted inflation. On Friday, the US 10-year yield topped 3 per cent for the first time in six weeks. "We remain in a strong dollar environment," PIMCO portfolio manager Russ Koesterich said in a new blog post.

While the US dollar has been flat since June, it is more than 5 per cent higher than its May low. And as the dollar has retained its strength, assets priced in them have stumbled including gold and industrial metals such as copper. The red metal has tumbled into a bear market.

Also bolstering bets on the US currency has been a rise in US Treasury yields during the past month; the US 10-year yield is 10 basis points higher.

"We expect that the upward pressure on US yields will tend to support the US dollar, potentially driving it to new highs in coming months, notwithstanding increasing political risk in a polarised US electorate, approaching November midterm elections and an ongoing [Robert] Mueller investigation," Amplifying Global FX Capital's Greg Gibbs said.

Oliver Jones at Capital Economics sees the 10-year yield climbing towards 3.25 per cent by the end of the calendar year. The latest retail sales, industrial production and consumer sentim

sentiment_pool.headline: A good economy can trump bad politics
sentiment_pool.text:
The business community and the broader public may be ever more frustrated by the chaos of Canberra leadership brawls. The good news is extreme political dysfunction doesn't always translate into a bad economy.

A surging US economy, about 18 months into an erratic Trump presidency proving even more contradictory than expected, is the most obvious example of this phenomenon.

A decade after the global financial crisis and a few years after the eruption of populist politics, with complaints about "fairness" and the failures of capitalism gaining global momentum, the US economy is in remarkably rude health.

That's despite Washington DC being in continuous uproar over the aggressive behaviour, White House witch-hunts and tweeted thought bubbles of a US president who ignores then sacks most of his advisers.

The latest furore over Bob Woodward's aptly titled book, Fear, and his lurid tales of one policy debacle after another, puts the surprise advent of a Morrison government, and even Peter Dutton's vicious brawl with his former head of the Australian Border Force, into bizarre perspective.

The Trump tax cuts may have accelerated the rise in the US sharemarket but the economic improvement is being reflected in Main Street almost as much as Wall Street.

A US unemployment rate below 4 per cent and lay-offs at a 50-year low hardly accord with Donald Trump's bitter complaints the US is being ripped off by China's trade policies - with an unacceptably large trade deficit to show for

sentiment_pool.headline: What economists are thinking about the next wave of reform
sentiment_pool.text:
Regulation | Attention is being shifted to a German-style model.

Breaking up the banks, circling them with industry superannuation fund-backed banks or "people's banks" offering "no frills" retail banking out of Australia Post or the Reserve Bank, letting the Future Fund manage super, taxing "economic rents" instead of company profits.

In short, ditching our Anglo-Saxon model of capitalism for a "German-style" version.

These are just a few of the ideas some of Australia's finest economic and financial minds - including some of the engine drivers of the last great reform wave of the 1980s and 1990s - are mulling over as they contemplate an economy that 10 years after the global financial crisis still isn't delivering for all Australians.

It's a bracing menu, and a sign that the problems below the surface of Australia's solid economy - misconduct by banks, rent-seeking across the business landscape, weak wages growth and angry voters - are reinvigorating debate about economic reform.

"Economic rents are becoming a larger and larger part of the Australian economy, and if we want improved economic performance ... and improved distribution of income then we are going to have to do something about that," top economist Ross Garnaut told the Melbourne Economic Forum on banking last week.

The staunchest industry super fund advocate could not have imagined in his or her wildest dreams the mugging commercial banks would receive at the royal commission. They emerged "riddled with c

sentiment_pool.headline: Powerhouse developer capitalises on big trends
sentiment_pool.text:
Just over two years ago Australia's global construction and development giant Lendlease presented to its investors a series of far-reaching shifts that were under way across its business.

The changes - the product of sustained in-house research - were both a response to broad global trends such as urbanisation and ageing demographics as well as an effort to ride through the profoundly cyclical nature of property markets.

However, with almost three-quarters of Lendlease's register dominated by institutional and index style investors, there is little room for sudden lurches.

Lendlease chief financial officer Tarun Gupta describes the big changes as "pivots".

"What we've been doing for the past few years is making certain pivots in our business model that respond to the key trends that are driving our strategy and also they reinforce the direction we are going in," Gupta says.

The first of those shifts is geographic. Until recently typically 80 per cent of Lendlease's capital was deployed in Australia.

Now that weighting is changing. The target is for between 50 per cent and 70 per cent of capital in the local market, with the rest abroad. The mix is currently about 60 per cent locally. The pivot, as Gupta explains, is well under way and it's all about diversification.

"We've had a very good run in Australia," he says.

"We foresaw this many years ago when we looked out into the future: that residential markets would come off their cyclical peaks, which is what is current

sentiment_pool.headline: Claimant ranks grow in NAB UK class action
sentiment_pool.text:
London | Lawyers behind the British class action against National Australia Bank and its former subsidiary Clydesdale & Yorkshire Bank have announced the recruitment of up to 550 new claimants to the lawsuit, in a bid to inject fresh momentum into the long-running wrangle.

RGL Management, the London claims management firm run by Australian lawyer James Hayward, has been marshalling claimants for about 18 months to challenge the two banks in court over about 8300 fixed-rate business loans that Clydesdale issued to British customers from 2001 to 2012.

On Tuesday, RGL announced it had teamed up with All Square Finance Limited, which, like RGL has been rounding up businesses and individuals with potential claims arising from the so-called "Tailored Business Loans" (TBLs) affair. AllSquare has up to 550 claimants on its books and RGL already has almost 500 potential litigants of its own, so the alliance could perhaps double the number of parties to the action.

"Clydesdale and NAB now have a bigger, stronger and more-determined group to face. Our case is strong and we will issue proceedings in due course," Mr Hayward said.

NAB is on the hook in this case because it owned the regional British bank until 2016, before spinning it off in a demerger after years of underperformance and big compensation bills for mis-selling complex financial products. sentiment_pool.headline: Data sharing law overhaul set for 2019
sentiment_pool.text:
The Coalition will overhaul cumbersome and outdated data sharing laws in 2019, part of efforts to close an entrenched trust deficit with the public and improve service delivery.

Digital Transformation Minister Michael Keenan wants to win back public confidence about privacy and security, to harness the power of big data through government digital transformation.

Aiming for Australia to remain among the top three nations for digital delivery through to 2025, Mr Keenan says the appointments of former deputy Australian statistician Randall Brugeaud to head the government's Digital Transformation Agency and former IP Australia chief operating officer Deborah Anton as interim National Data Commissioner will help deliver progress and reform.

"We have to do what we can to make accessing government services an easy seamless experience, but also to ensure people trust us to make sure any information we have about them is treated appropriately, and that we do respect their privacy," he told AFR Weekend.

"We have incredibly strong protections in place and individuals' data is safe with us."

The Digital Transformation Agency is preparing a whole-of-government digital strategy, coming as the government progresses controversial digital ID programs including GovPass and myGovID.

The opt-in myGovID pilot run by the Tax Office will enable 100,000 participants to apply for a tax file number online, replacing the need for paper-based proof of identity.

sentiment_pool.headline: PM Morrison must cut through on economy
sentiment_pool.text:
Short of a postal vote surprise, independent Kerryn Phelps looks set to overturn the huge Liberal margin in Wentworth, taking a federal seat that has been in the fold for more than a century. The extraordinary result humiliates the government in its own heartland in one of the nation's wealthiest and most enterprising electorates. Scott Morrison must use the jolt to pull his destabilised government together and reset its focus on delivering the prosperity that voters want most of all.

The Turnbull factor is very big. In August, Liberal MPs turned on a prime minister who personified this cosmopolitan seat, wealthy but socially diverse and liberal-minded. There are other urban electorates like it, and more may emerge as ageing tree and sea changers move into city fringe and coastal seats - a factor in another female independent, Rebekha Sharkie, holding SA's once-safe Liberal seat of Mayo in July. The Liberals must learn to win them back, as well as working-class electorates such as Longman that equally eluded them on Super Saturday.

In Wentworth, Dr Phelps made the suitable liberal-progressive noises on climate and refugees - along with supporting small business tax cuts and opposing Labor's promised attack on property investors. And then Mr Morrison panicked days before the poll, springing a potentially serious shift in Australia's Middle East policy in a ploy to shore up the Liberals' Jewish vote in Wentworth. sentiment_pool.headline: $567m set for Kidman sale deal went to Brazil
sentiment_pool.text:
Shanghai-based conglomerate Pengxin redirected the $US400 million ($567 million) it was prepared to pay for Australia's largest private land holding, S. Kidman & Co, into investments in Brazil after it was snubbed by then treasurer Scott Morrison in 2016, a move that "discouraged the conglomerate from looking for further deals in Australia".

A former senior executive of Pengxin who was close to the deal said there was a "bitter aftertaste" when its $371 million bid for S. Kidman, which owns almost 11 million hectares of cattle stations including the world's largest, Anna Creek, was blocked in 2016. The bid was made through Pengxin's subsidiary Hunan Dakang Farming Pasture.

Pengxin moved on and took the $US400 million as well as another $US200 million and invested it in agricultural deals in Brazil.

Information from the new Chinese Investment in Australia (CHIIA) Database created by Australian National University in collaboration with Treasury shows that Chinese investments in Australia slumped 40 per cent last year, twice the drop worldwide.

While concerns the decline in Chinese interests in Australia was caused by poor China-Australia political relations worsened by xenophobic tensions, Chinese deal intermediaries such as lawyers and agents say economic reasons precede political ones.

sentiment_pool.headline: Centuria Industrial repels $755m takeover move
sentiment_pool.text:
Propertylink chief executive Stuart Dawes has failed to gain support for his $755 million bid for Centuria Industrial REIT after it was rejected by an independent board on Tuesday.

Centuria Industrial REIT's board, advised by UBS, rejected the $755 million bid from listed fund manager Propertylink, citing Propertylink's own risk of being taken over as a reason not to accept.

Last month Asian logistics platform ESR Real Estate, controlled by US private equity giant Warburg Pincus, joined the flurry of corporate action by launching a $693 million cash takeover bid for Propertylink.

It is this takeover that has influenced Centuria to reject the offer from Propertylink but also other factors such as increased gearing in Propertylink following any takeover.

"Propertylink announced the receipt of a non-binding, indicative proposal from ESR Real Estate (Australia) to acquire all of the stapled securities of Propertylink ... which is subject to a number of conditions including a condition that Propertylink not proceed with the proposal to acquire Centuria Industrial REIT."

Centuria said there was now "material uncertainty" around the proposal.

Mr Dawes has declined to comment on Centuria's decision but people close to him suggest the decision to refuse Propertylink access to due diligence based on the prospect of Propertylink being taken over is not fair for shareholders, who should be more focused on the premium being offered for their shares.

sentiment_pool.headline: Start again with wealth sector
sentiment_pool.text:
If the interim report from Royal Commissioner Kenneth Hayne provided one ray of hope for the Commonwealth Bank, ANZ Banking Group and National Australia Bank it was this: The decision to get rid of their wealth businesses has been completely and utterly justified.

If the report describes the entire banking sector as riven by greed, then the financial advice sector is the lowest of the low.

This is an industry where the interests of the client conflict so badly with those advising them that mums and dads seem more likely to have their interests trod on than not.

But it's important to remember that while the banks may soon be rid of these wealth businesses, investors won't be.

CBA and NAB look certain to spin their wealth businesses off to their investors at some stage over the next 12 to 18 months - goodness knows it's highly unlikely they'll find anyone to buy them. And it is IOOF's investors that will soon own the ANZ wealth division.

So it is crucial that investors - and the current and potential clients of these financial advice businesses - understand exactly why Hayne's interim report raises such huge questions about how the financial advice sector can continue in anything like its current form.

sentiment_pool.headline: WeWork losses mount amid rapid rollout
sentiment_pool.text:
Co-working hub provider WeWork deepened its losses last year, due largely to an "intercompany expense" of nearly $3.4 million that shows how it uses transfer pricing to send some of its profits abroad.

Lodged for the first time in the Australian market, the financial statements also reveal how the global co-working giant has racked up more than $250 million in lease commitments as it accelerates its rollout through the Australian market.

Those commitments represent the grand tally of all the rent it has agreed to pay across its Australian portfolio over the next decade or so.

At the same time, the results register the surge in custom filling WeWork desks since its launch in late 2016 in Sydney. Membership and service revenue rose to $22.9 million over the 2017 calendar year, up from $1.4 million in its truncated 2016 year. But WeWork's expenses rose faster, taking it deeper into the red, with a $2.9 million loss recorded in 2017 compared with a $2.6 million loss in previous year.

Among those items was an "intercompany expense" of almost $3.4 million, up from zero the previous year, also described as a "management expense fee" paid to a related party. "Related party management fees are typically charged by multinational companies to share global management costs," PwC's tax partner Ellen Thomas told The Australian Financial Review. sentiment_pool.headline: SolGold now boasts 'tier one' copper discovery: expert
sentiment_pool.text:
The Ecuadorian copper prospect pursued by BHP and Newcrest Mining now deserves to be considered alongside elite copper discoveries such as Chile's Escondida, Australia's Olympic Dam and Indonesia's Grasberg, according to an analysis of the latest drilling results by one of Australia's top mineral exploration consultants.

Minex Consulting managing director Richard Schodde said the updated mineral resource estimate published by Ecuador-focused SolGold on Tuesday night had confirmed its Alpala prospect within the Cascabel tenement was a "tier one" copper and gold asset.

SolGold told the London Stock Exchange on Tuesday that the Alpala resource was now estimated to contain 13.1 million tonnes of copper equivalent metal; a 77 per cent increase on the previous estimate published in December 2017. Perhaps more importantly Alpala's high-grade core is now estimated to be 99 per cent larger than the previous estimate with a copper equivalent resource of 6.1 million tonnes, and that could prove pivotal as many copper mines are now built small with a focus on a high-grade core leaving potential expansions for later when commodity prices make them viable.

Mr Schodde said Alpala, located in northern Ecuador, easily met his criteria for "tier one" status.

"As part of my job I maintain a database of over 58,000 mineral deposits of all types around the world and 304 of these are classified as being 'tier one' so they are very rare and special by definition," he told The Australian Financi

sentiment_pool.headline: Dar cards close to its chest as $1.1b Worley book set to close
sentiment_pool.text:
There will be some nervous bankers at UBS and Macquarie Capital sitting by the phones after market on Wednesday.

The two banks and their equities clients are on the hook for $1.1 billion, thanks to corporate client WorleyParsons' rights issue.

The raising's $1.1 billion retail portion will close at 5pm on Wednesday and with the shares trading well under the offer price, expectations are for a big shortfall.

Sources said the offer was fully underwritten, which means a bunch of funds are likely to be asked to take up the shares.

The big swing factor, though, is Worley's largest shareholder and one-time suitor Dar Group, which has rights to $490 million of the $1.1 billion offered to Worley's retail shareholders.

And true to form, it is understood the Dubai-based construction company is making Worley and its brokers sweat.

Heading into Tuesday afternoon's close, sources said the investor was yet to notify Worley one way or the other. And it is expected to wait until late Wednesday before making the call.

Dar is believed to have funding lined up for the play, should it wish to pull the trigger, after talking widely to banks about its options including a margin loan.

How good the funding is though, and whether it is still affordable with Worley shares trading not much above $14, remains to be seen.

sentiment_pool.headline: Behind the decoupling of US, Aussie rates
sentiment_pool.text:
Australian and US markets have enjoyed such a close relationship, it has been easy to view Australia as the 51st state.

Of course, that's an oversimplification. But with that in mind, it's worth investigating why that no longer seems to be the case. Why are Australian yields so far below the US?

Is the US economy growing faster than Australia? Actually, no. The most recent real GDP reading has Australia's year-on-year growth at 3.4 per cent, versus 3 per cent for the US. Both nations have falling and historically low levels of unemployment. But there are a number of key differences.

That Australia's jobless rate has recently fallen to about 5 per cent is a remarkably good outcome, when you consider Australia's population has grown by about 16 per cent over the last decade. Although Australia has absorbed the uplift in the labour force, part of the answer lies in underemployment.

In the aftermath of the GFC, US underemployment, as measured by U6, peaked at around 17 per cent. At the same time, Australia's underemployment was about 7.8 per cent. US underemployment has fallen to 20-year lows. It is now 7.8 per cent, while Australia's has actually increased, to 8.2 per cent. In that time, the retirement of the Baby Boomers has been a phenomenon shared by both economies, naturally tightening the labour market. After adjusting for inflation, median household incomes show Australia largely at the same level as it was in 2014.

sentiment_pool.headline: Developer considers build-to-rent apartments
sentiment_pool.text:
Developer and investor Poly Australia has joined the build-to-rent bandwagon, and could soon kick off a rental apartment project in Sydney.

While plans have not been finalised, Poly is contemplating the conversion of its residential site at Stanley Street, Kogarah, in south Sydney - originally earmarked for standard build-to-sell apartments - into 100 build-to-rent units with a rooftop garden and outdoor amenities.

"The project is well under consideration mainly because the build-to-rent industry is growing in Australia and because of the engagement of our competitors in it," Poly sales and marketing director Jay Carter said.

"Kogarah is a solid middle market where you have a major hospital close by, really solid infrastructure that anchors employment and activity to handle rental apartments."

The advent of build-to-rent or rental apartments leased by a single corporate landlord in Australia is a result of the worsening home ownership affordability with many other developers such as Mirvac and Clean Energy Finance Corporation and UBS Asset Management, Grocon and JLL set to replicate the same multifamily style of apartment renting popular in the US and Europe.

But Poly is no stranger to the build-to-rent or multifamily industry. Its 208-apartment project in Los Angeles is a multifamily property that also offers dining and retail.

In Australia, Poly will join the movement but is also likely to sell build-to-rent units after holding onto them for about six to 10 years.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fort Street fund buys retail asset
sentiment_pool.text:
Real estate fund manager Fort Street has bought Keilor Central, a sub-regional shopping centre in Melbourne for $113 million from ASX-listed Vicinity Centres as investor capital continues to pour into convenience-based retail assets.

The 19,700-square-metre mall and car park on a 9.1-hectare site on Taylors Road in Keilor Downs in the city's north-western suburbs was acquired on an initial yield of 6.3 per cent and is almost fully occupied.

Alongside anchor tenants Coles, Aldi and Kmart, there are 59 primarily convenience-based specialty tenants including Commonwealth Bank, Australia Post, The Reject Shop, Vodafone, Specsavers, Hungry Jacks and KFC.

The shopping centre is the first asset acquired for a new fund called Fort Street Real Estate Capital Fund IV, which launched in June with gross assets of $76 million and about $150 million to invest initially in retail, commercial and industrial assets.

The deal negotiated by Lachlan MacGillivray of Colliers International.

sentiment_pool.headline: Aspen closer to Discovery rights deal
sentiment_pool.text:
Accommodation parks owner Aspen is inching closer to a deal with Discovery Holiday Parks, which has revised the terms of its offer to manage Aspen's property portfolio.

Aspen's board said it was now seeking to enter into "a deed of confidentiality" with Discovery, allowing the two parties to exchange further information and paving the way for a binding proposal.

The mooted deal does not involve a change of ownership but would generate management fees for Discovery, which operates the country's largest network of parks.

Aspen was already engaging with an offer to appoint Mill Hill Capital - its major investor - as its investment manager.

Discovery lobbed in its initial management offer in late November, just as Aspen investors were preparing to vote on the Mill Hill offer at a meeting on December 14.

Led by Grant Wilckens, Discovery has revised its initial offer with fresh terms, prompting Aspen to postpone the shareholder meeting for a second time, to January 11.

The management proposal would cover the day-to-day management of Aspen and its property portfolio.

In return, Discovery would collect a base management fee of 2 per cent annually of Aspen's total book equity up to the first $115 million and 1.15 per cent in excess of $115 million.

Under its revised offer, Discovery is offering an up-front incentive payment of $250,000.

sentiment_pool.headline: 'We'll see how good I have been'
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian Financial Review's Business Person of the Year, Nicholas Moore, says it will be years before the market can make a realistic assessment of his performance.

"We'll see in years to come what changes I have made and how good I have been," he says.

"Obviously, as I sit here today it feels fine, but it's a long-term business."

Mr Moore retired as chief executive of Macquarie Group on November 30 after 10½ years in the top job and 32 years in the banking, asset management and global securities business.

He will become the second Macquarie bank person, after David Clarke, on the Financial Review's list of those leaders, builders, pioneers and stirrers who have most shaped Australia's business landscape since 1963, when the Financial Review became a daily publication.

Other bankers and financiers on the list include Sir Ian Potter, Gail Kelly, Bob Joss, Bill Ferris and Don Argus. Since 2014, the Financial Review has added a business person of the year to the 50 list including Boral CEO Mike Kane, Commonwealth Bank chairman Catherine Livingstone, the Atlassian founders Mike Cannon Brookes and Scott Farquhar, and Qantas CEO Alan Joyce.

"I am very flattered to have been considered as one of Australia's leading business people, although I am mindful of being singled out given my experience in dealing with truly outstanding business leaders every day," Mr Moore said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Victorian Premier turns guns on PM
sentiment_pool.text:
Victoria Premier Daniel Andrews has turned his sights on what Labor calls the Morrison government's short-changing of his state on federal transport funding, in a refrain likely to be repeated regularly in the lead-up to next year's federal election.

As the federal government reeled from nearly losing a vote on the floor of the House of Representatives on Thursday, Mr Andrews wrote to Mr Morrison in advance of Wednesday's Council of Australian Governments meeting on population, saying there was no point to the discussion if the Commonwealth wasn't prepared to fund Victoria's $90 billion infrastructure pipeline fairly.

The Andrews government's huge pipeline of road, rail, hospital and school building was a key reason for its thumping defeat of the Liberal-National Coalition in the November 24 state election, and the Premier seems intent on not letting the fragile Morrison government off the hook in the lead-up to a federal election that could be held in March or May.

Mr Andrews' "Dear Scott" letter reminds the Prime Minister that one of his predecessors - Tony Abbott - had stowed $3 billion originally destined for the former Coalition state government's East West Link in a "locked box", and that Canberra has agreed to fund only $1.75 billion of the $16 billion cost of the North East Link road and tunnel project.

He says the East West Link has now been rejected by Victorians at two elections, yet the federal government continues to withhold the $3 billion, which "would part

sentiment_pool.headline: App empowers landlords
sentiment_pool.text:
In the lead-up to Christmas, shopping centre landlords across Australia and as far off as Norway have started using a little known app designed by Brisbane business Norbit as their first line of defence in the battle against the rising power of online retailing.

The threat of Amazon and online retailing has taken a while to change traditional mall owners' appreciation of shoppers, but with the Lowy family selling out of Westfield earlier this year, landlords are taking the threat more seriously and are scrambling to adapt the latest technologies to ensure they keep hold of their retail customers.

Norbit managing director Gerry Mezzina has created an app that tracks shoppers' spending habits in a way that tips the power back into landlords hands.

"There is a lot of talk about Amazon. Everyone says Amazon has done so well because they are online, but really, they win because they know their customer - they have been tracking their customers since 1996 and the big landlords haven't," he said. "I think the market - the shopping centre landlords - are a bit behind in terms of where the customers want to spend money."

And tracking customers is exactly what the Norbit app does for landlords.

The shopping centre landlord pays to rent the white-label app at a low cost and then gives the app its own name - such as that of the shopping centre. It then encourages shoppers to download it with the incentive of discounts and points. As the shoppers use the discounts and chase the point

sentiment_pool.headline: NSW, Victoria vie with Venezuela as worst places for gas investors
sentiment_pool.text:
Unscientific onshore gas restrictions in NSW, Victoria and Tasmania have left the three states battling it out with Venezuela and Yemen for the bottom spots in a closely watched annual international ranking of attractiveness for oil and gas investment in a further deterioration from last year's poor showing.

The three have sunk to number among the 10 worst laggards on the Canadian-based Fraser Institute's 80-strong overall list, alongside Libya and Iraq. They also occupy the last three places in the specific ranking on environmental regulations, lower even than New Zealand which has banned the award of new offshore exploration permits.

While US states grabbed nine of the top 10 spots in the ranking for the most attractive perceived destinations for oil and gas investment, all Australian jurisdictions slid. South Australia, the top-ranked Australian jurisdiction, dropped 10 places from last year to 20th due to increased concerns over regulatory enforcement, protected areas, labour regulations and employment agreements.

The Fraser Institute cited comments from investors in the region, one of which referred to Victoria's ban on onshore unconventional gas exploration and development as "a major deterrent to investment" while a NSW investor said: "Regulatory processes are unpredictable and subject to uncertainties surrounding the term 'social licence'."

NSW and Victoria have substantial onshore gas resources that are being kept in the ground by unworkable restrictions in NSW,

sentiment_pool.headline: Spikes in prices spark fears for power retailers
sentiment_pool.text:
Last week's once-in-a decade prolonged surge in wholesale electricity prices on the National Electricity Market has fuelled worries that some junior energy retailers may be at risk of collapse, mirroring the fate that has befallen at least 10 small players in Britain since the beginning of last year.

Retailers that do not own any power-generation capacity or without adequate hedging in place, or simply those without the cash flow to tide them over the period until their hedge contracts pay out, are most vulnerable to problems, according to industry sources.

Wholesale electricity prices reached the maximum $14,500 a megawatt-hour for several hours in Victoria and South Australia on Thursday, and again briefly on Friday before the maximum threshold for the rolling seven-day total was reached, causing the market operator to step in to impose a cap on prices.

It was the first time in 10 years that the so-called Cumulative Price Threshold of $216,900 for one MWh over seven days was reached, signalling the weight of the financial burden on any retailers exposed to market prices. Wholesale prices remain capped at $300/MWh in both Victoria and South Australia.

This comes as retailers are under intense pressure from federal Energy Minister Angus Taylor to cut electricity tariffs for homes and small businesses and face the proposed introduction on July 1 of a "default" tariff that they fear will act as a price cap and force smaller competitors out of business.

sentiment_pool.headline: US investors more bearish than bullish
sentiment_pool.text:
The S&P 500 is up 6.5 per cent this year, yet the advance has so far failed to offset lingering bearishness among US investors.

The latest weekly survey of investor sentiment by the American Association of Individual Investors showed that pessimism about the short-term direction of the sharemarket has risen and is now higher than its historical average for the 17th time in 19 weeks.

Bearish sentiment leapt 6.9 percentage points to 36.3 per cent in the week ended January 16; bullish sentiment slid 4.9 percentage points to 33.5 per cent. Neutral sentiment dipped 2 percentage points to 30.2 per cent.

Bearish sentiment reached 50.3 per cent in the week ending December 26. The last time bullish sentiment topped 50 per cent was a year ago; it has held below 40 per cent for three months now.

Tematica Research chief macro strategist Lenore Hawkins said she sees what's happened so far this month on Wall Street as "a reversal of the heavily oversold conditions" from the end of 2018: "Those stocks that were hit the hardest in 2018 are materially outperforming the broader market in 2019."

Ms Hawkins, however, is sceptical of reading too much into the rebound.

"The fundamentals both domestically and internationally are not giving us reason to think that this bounce is the start of another major bull run. With all the uncertainty out there, despite the market's recent 'feel good' attitude, we expect to see rising volatility in the months to come as these problems are not going to be

sentiment_pool.headline: Carsales' drive for overseas earnings
sentiment_pool.text:
Carsales chief executive Cameron McIntyre believes the company's international business has the chance to contribute more than half of overall earnings, but he is conscious of the challenges of taking the digital automotive classifieds business overseas.

Mr McIntyre was a key part of developing Carsales' international strategy, which began in 2012, after he spent nine years at the business under co-founder Greg Roebuck.

Carsales now has businesses in Mexico, Chile, Argentina, Brazil and South Korea and international business contributes 20 per cent of the company's revenue. It has also opened offices for its vehicle-inspection and report business Redbook in China, Thailand, Malaysia and New Zealand.

Mr McIntyre says a major challenge is that each market is at a different stage of development and presents a host of country-specific issues, including politics and economic outlook, which means Carsales cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach.

Like online job marketplace SEEK, investors have put their money into Carsales on the basis of future earnings growth. But, also like SEEK, Carsales shares have dropped - down 16 per cent in the past year - and investors are waiting to see whether Carsales can deliver on its overseas potential.

SEEK was particularly punished in August by investors when it warned profits would remain flat, despite continued revenue growth, because of its reinvestment plans in international and early-stage ventures. Morningstar analysts believe Carsales

sentiment_pool.headline: ANZ Bank buys into online mortgage broker Lendi
sentiment_pool.text:
ANZ Banking Group has taken a strategic stake in online home loans platform Lendi.

Street Talk understands ANZ paid close to $40 million for a minority stake, to become Lendi's second-largest strategic shareholder behind fellow Australian financial services giant Macquarie Group.

Importantly for Lendi, which has 37 banks and lenders on its open home loans platform, the business will continue to be run independently and at arm's length to its strategic investors.

ANZ will not be given a board seat, as consistent with Lendi's treatment of Macquarie and other strategic investors including Pepper.

It is understood ANZ agreed to write the cheque after spending much of last year talking to Lendi about products and process innovations. Some of those innovations are expected to play out this year.

Lendi is an online home loans broker, which has directly settled loans worth close to $8 billion. It's a small part of Australia's $400 billion-a-year mortgage market, although has grown quickly and has grand plans to dramatically increase its footprint.

ANZ needs little introduction in Australia's mortgage marketplace. It had $341 billion in home lending on its books in Australia and New Zealand as at September 31, and writes more than half of its home loans through mortgage brokers.

ANZ's investment comes amid much investigation and scrutiny of Australia's mortgage broking market and the role of the big four banks. It has recently taken steps to try to tighten up its lending practi

sentiment_pool.headline: Jangho's Liu seeks medical help to revive building empire
sentiment_pool.text:
Shanghai | Liu Zaiwang's rags-to-riches story is shared by many of China's new generation of billionaires.

The young entrepreneur dropped out of university to start his own business in the 1990s as China's economy was taking off. He rode the wave of the country's construction boom after winning his first major contract on a high-rise government building not far from the ski resorts in the north-western province of Jilin in 1997.

Liu's company Jangho - which is now seeking to diversify into Australian healthcare with the $2 billion acquisition of Healius - became a symbol of China's extraordinary building boom. It has manufactured the so-called "curtain wall" or outer steel and glass cladding for some of the country's most prominent high-rises and airport terminals as well as casinos in the former Portuguese colony of Macau.

The 2008 Beijing Olympics also underpinned the company's growth after spurring a string of building work. Jangho had already won major contracts in Beijing, including the city's new airport terminal, China World Trade Centre and the headquarters for broadcaster CCTV. Liu expanded into the country's south and further afield to the Middle East, south-east Asia and Australia.

But as China's construction market slowed, Jangho struggled to maintain the lucrative profit margins that underpinned its early growth.

At 46, Liu slipped more than 200 places on China's rich list to 787 last year, although his fortune remains considerable. Shanghai-based research h

sentiment_pool.headline: Zip Pay supports some lending checks
sentiment_pool.text:
Westpac-backed credit card disrupter Zip Pay is ready to embrace responsible lending checks and caps on late fees, as the buy-now, pay-later sector faces increasing scrutiny from the regulator and a Labor-led Senate committee.

Zip Pay, a buy-now, pay-later service owned by ASX-listed Zip Co, is the major rival to Afterpay and has more than 10,600 retail partners including Bunnings, Officeworks, Target and Virgin. The companies offer a lay-by service that allows consumers to pay for goods via direct debit instalments.

Under responsible lending laws, credit card providers have to make reasonable inquiries about consumers' finances and verify their situation before extending credit. In practice providers ask for identity, income and expense information.

Zip's co-founder and chief operating officer Peter Gray said Zip Pay would be open to a more limited regime. This would include verifying income and identity, and checking credit history, but would not extend to expense checks.

This position is in contrast to Afterpay, which said it supported the corporate regulator exercising its soon-to-be-granted product intervention powers but has been resistant to the idea of responsible lending checks.

"At the bare minimum we would support income verification, ID checks and credit checks. Ideally, that would be the best outcome for the industry," Mr Gray said.

The company would support caps on product fees and charges, he said. "Particularly late fees, which make out a considerable po

sentiment_pool.headline: Rinehart bids $591m for Riversdale Resources
sentiment_pool.text:
Gina Rinehart's Hancock Corporation has moved to take full ownership of the nascent coal miner Riversdale Resources, offering $591 million for the remaining shares in the company.

Hancock offered to acquire all remaining shares in Riversdale in an all-cash offer at $2.50 a share, a 47 per cent increase on the $1.70 Hancock paid for a 19.8 per cent of Riversdale shares in August and September last year. Riversdale's main asset is a coking coal mine to be developed in Alberta, Canada. Known as Grassy Mountain Project, the mine has 195 million tonnes of high-quality coking coal and expects first coal production in 2021, according to the company's 2018 annual report.

Riversdale considered a sharemarket listing last year but abandoned the plan after "feedback" from the market suggested it was too far out from production. The founding shareholders - Steve Mallyon, chairman Michael O'Keeffe and chief financial officer Anthony Martin - provided statements of intent to accept the offer, Hancock announced on Wednesday.

"The directors of Hancock consider that its premium pricing and low conditionality make it a compelling opportunity for Riversdale shareholders," Hancock director Jay Newby said in a statement.

sentiment_pool.headline: New-look Nine group predicts double-digit earnings growth
sentiment_pool.text:
Nine chief executive Hugh Marks says the merger with Fairfax Media has created a diverse media business with increasing digital earnings and less reliance on television and print advertising.

Following the merger, which was completed on December 7, the combined firm has businesses across digital, publishing, streaming, radio, TV and real estate classifieds.

Despite the challenging television advertising market and a downturn in the property market, Nine increased pro-forma profits in the first half and expects earnings to rise by 10 per cent-plus in the full year, thanks to the radical change in where the company earns its money.

"With the headwinds we've had - Domain has headwinds, the free-to-air market has had headwinds - to still be able to lift pro-forma profitability and to be confident we can do that over the full year and see that momentum go into [2019-20], I think for me that's what we set out to do, diversify the business so that we could trade through cycles, and we're seeing that play out in the numbers. That's the most pleasing thing," Mr Marks said.

"People ask 'how's the merger gone and did it play out as you expected?' I think, for me, it's gone very well, relatively low noise, the businesses are operating well together and we're starting to see not only the cost benefits, but also the revenue benefits of being one business."

In the first half, 54 per cent of Nine's revenue came from its broadcasting division - which includes the Nine Network and its 54.

sentiment_pool.headline: RBA on alert, but not yet alarmed on risks
sentiment_pool.text:
Philip Lowe has been forced to concede economic risks have intensified in the wake of falling house prices and China's slowdown, even though he wants to keep believing low unemployment will generate wage inflation.

The Reserve Bank of Australia governor's dovish shift to an "evenly balanced" stance on next moving interest rates up or down, away from his earlier tightening bias, was perhaps inevitable given the disappointing run of weak economic data over summer.

Retail sales are weak, house prices falling, new car sales declining, manufacturing and services activity slumping, building approvals tanking and business conditions deteriorating.

Lowe is maintaining the RBA's traditional dismissal of "high- frequency" data and hopes a strong labour market will be a positive counterweight in 2019.

Yet there is no denying the RBA is now more alert, though not yet alarmed, about lurking dangers.

"Against this generally positive picture, the major domestic uncertainty is the strength of consumption and the housing market," Lowe said.

What falling house prices and continuing subdued wages mean for consumer spending, which has softened of late, will be vital for the economy this year.

Lowe has set a high bar for cutting the record-low 1.5 per cent overnight cash rate, flagging an easing would require a "sustained increase" in the jobless rate and continued undershooting of the 2-3 per cent inflation target. After the speech, financial markets priced in a rate cut in the next 12 mo

sentiment_pool.headline: Cladding blamed for fire's spread
sentiment_pool.text:
Combustible cladding on the recessed balconies was the "main contributor" to the spread of fire in a Melbourne residential tower yesterday morning, the city's Metropolitan Fire Brigade said.

The fire, which started on a level 22 balcony just before 5am and spread to level 29 before it was extinguished, travelled quickly because of polyethylene-core aluminium panels running up the length of the 43-storey building, MFB deputy chief officer Adam Dalrymple said.

"A number of balconies had a fair bit of clutter on them, which would contribute to the spread of fire, but the main contributor to the spread was the amount of cladding in each particular balcony which allowed the fire to [spread upwards]," Mr Dalrymple told The Australian Financial Review.

Residents of the 372-apartment building were evacuated. Flames from the balconies penetrated some apartments but were contained by fire sprinklers, Mr Dalrymple said. Firefighters had to extinguish the blaze from inside the building as it was so high.

The building's fire-prevention engineering plus a quick fire brigade response prevented casualties in the building at the corner of Spencer Street and Little Bourke Street. However, the fire showed that the nightmare combustible cladding remains a liability for Australia's commercial and residential building stock. In contrast to claims made in tweets in 2017, the building did not comply with building regulations, Mr Dalrymple said.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASIC does not want to be banks' friend
sentiment_pool.text:
Don't even think of calling James Shipton "mate". He really doesn't want to be your friend.

The ASIC chair says sternly there is a simple solution for financial institutions digesting the lessons from the Hayne royal commission and the greater willingness by the regulators to go to court: "Don't break the law."

Yet there's rarely anything simple about the law, including the definition of what constitutes Shipton's other stated imperative of "fairness". And with ASIC's new mantra being "Why not litigate?" this is proving a confronting combination for banks.

That is just as Shipton wants and needs it to be. Stung by Hayne's criticisms of ASIC's past passivity, the regulator is clearly determined to sound and act tough, bolstered, of course, by considerable additional funding for enforcement.

So even as bank executives make fulsome apologies for past behaviour and earnest promises of radical change, Shipton sounds unimpressed with the level of sincerity on show.

"Financial institutions must respond responsibly to the challenge and not, as we have seen in some segments, with resistance and reluctance to the job we as a conduct regulator are expected to do," he told The Australian Financial Review Banking and Wealth Summit.

That means he is not impressed with emerging criticism of ASIC's greater enthusiasm for litigation, saying "it shows a resistance to a meaningful mindset change as well as a fundamental misunderstanding of our broader fairness mandate and statutory mandat

sentiment_pool.headline: Big telcos slam NBN Co's push on marketing
sentiment_pool.text:
Major Australian telcos are demanding NBN Co stop aggressively targeting their business customers, a move they claim is breaching the government-owned infrastructure provider's strict remit as a wholesaler.

TPG Telecom executive director David Teoh said NBN Co had been directly contacting his company's business customers, promoting its high-speed fibre optic broadband.

"They approached some of our customers," Mr Teoh said. "We complained multiple times, but it's what they did. [We complained] to the government and also to them." But he said the complaints did no good.

The issue has been raised privately by other large telcos, but few have been willing to air their complaints. The basis of their objection is that NBN Co is strictly a wholesaler, and should not be dealing directly with end customers.

NBN is pumping more resources into its enterprise business in an effort to meet the ambitious revenue targets required to remain a commercial operation.

The telcos worry that customers will be persuaded to switch to an NBN plan provided by another retailer. Or that, by switching to NBN's network, the telcos will lose the higher margins they could have reaped from serving business customers on their own networks.

TPG's chief operating officer Craig Levy said: "They [NBN Co] have the responsibility of rolling out the infrastructure into the customer's premises and they have to co-operate and do the delivery of the actual fibre infrastructure. But I'm told customers have actuall

sentiment_pool.headline: Atlassian customer issues drive deal for AgileCraft
sentiment_pool.text:
Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar says growing pains for customers using its issue-tracking application, Jira, have driven the tech firm's $US166 million ($234 million) acquisition of planning software provider AgileCraft.

Customers using Jira software in independent teams within businesses had complained that, as their enterprise grew, it was cumbersome to oversee projects, Mr Farquhar wrote in a blog post on Atlassian's website on Tuesday.

"We know loads of time is wasted collecting status updates across hundreds of agile teams, getting unstructured snapshots of capacity, and trying to measure value generation. These challenges require a different set of tools - ones that give leaders critical visibility and allow them to adapt in a timely way," Mr Farquhar wrote.

These difficulties drove the decision to acquire AgileCraft, which he said gave solutions to those customers.

Jira offers issue-tracking software for bug tracking and "agile" project management. The "agile" methodology is an incremental project management theory developed by tech companies now widely adopted across other industries.

The AgileCraft deal, expected to close next month, comprises a $US154 million cash payment with the rest in Atlassian restricted shares.

Atlassian said many of its customers, including communication companies AT&T and Nielsen, already used AgileCraft alongside Jira in their engineering and IT teams.

sentiment_pool.headline: A NEVER-ENDING NIGHTMARE
sentiment_pool.text:
Brexit Britain has long prided itself on its ability to keep calm and carry on but its bewildering failure to negotiate a way out of the EU has changed that, writes Hans van Leeuwen in London.

Brexit has divided Britain as almost nothing else. Living here, you can't even visit your dentist without risking a pro or anti-Europe diatribe. Families, political parties, buck's nights and book clubs are all factionalised. Even the internationally myopic Donald Trump can see it's "tearing the country apart", as he said this week. But amid all the loggerheads, one thing unites the nation: nobody is happy with the dire state of British politics.

"I'm dancing up and down in my front room like Pinocchio, my arms are going all over the place," east London car dealer Frankie yelled at talkback radio host Nick Ferrari earlier this week, the morning after Prime Minister Theresa May's Brexit deal went down to a second massive parliamentary defeat.

"The democracy side of things in this country is well and truly finished. Last night I was embarrassed by watching those MPs ... The solution [to Brexit] is, get a big skip outside the Houses of Parliament and get the lot of them loaded into it!"

Months of Brexit paralysis have culminated in a desperate scramble to reach a resolution by March 29, after a series of crunch votes in Parliament this past week yet again failed to resolve the mother of all political deadlocks. sentiment_pool.headline: Another site for Potter George in Melbourne
sentiment_pool.text:
Property developer Potter George has acquired another Melbourne development site, a 12.68-hectare parcel in the north-west suburb of Fraser Rise, for $19 million.

The group will subdivide the site into 196 lots for a new housing community Kerani Heights, which will also include 2.5 hectares of parkland.

Construction at the Kerani Heights project at 937 Melton Highway is set to begin this year.

"We are confident in the fundamentals of the Victorian market and see our new development, which is adjacent to Caroline Springs and Taylors Hill, as a logical progression to the suburban growth corridor," Potter George director Phillip George said.

"The area is well supported with infrastructure, schools and all of the amenities that are expected in fresh new communities."

The site falls within the Plumpton Precinct Structure Plan, which was drawn up in early 2018 outlining urban development plans for the then Plumpton and now Fraser Rise. A new residential community of around 29,900 people across nearly 11,000 dwellings is on the cards.

Mr George is a Sydney businessman who previously owned Mrs Crocket's Food Group. His partner at Potter George is former residential group Villa World CEO John Potter.

Together, their company - set up in 2012 - has put out both residential and commercial property projects worth between $40 million and $350 million nationally.

One of the most notable is the $50 million redevelopment of the heritage-listed office block at 66 King Street in Sydney'

sentiment_pool.headline: Australia set to seal FTA with Indonesia
sentiment_pool.text:
A long-anticipated free trade agreement with Indonesia will be signed in Jakarta on Monday, ending more than eight years of negotiations and offering new economic opportunities for industries including the country's citrus farmers.

Trade Minister Simon Birmingham will sign the deal with his Indonesia counterpart Enggartiasto Lukita, ending delays caused by the Morrison government's proposal to formally recognise Jerusalem as the capital of Israel.

Known as the Indonesian-Australian Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, Senator Birmingham said the deal would take months to be ratified by federal Parliament, but he called on both sides of politics in both countries to support the final step.

Under the agreement, 99 per cent of Australian goods exports by value will enter Indonesia duty free or under significantly improved preferential arrangements by 2020, with Indonesia guaranteeing automatic import permits for live cattle, frozen beef, sheep meat, feed grains, rolled steel coil, carrots and potatoes.

"It's an important agreement, not just in terms of trade between Australia and Indonesia, but one that will strengthen all aspects of our strategic relationship in the years to come," Senator Birmingham said on Sunday.

"We would absolutely expect to see an uptick in trade to Indonesia and indeed an uptick in trade from Indonesia. We would hope that we definitely do see from that growth in jobs and more opportunities for Australian business to more readily base themse

sentiment_pool.headline: Helium play eyes ASX listing
sentiment_pool.text:
An emerging South African helium and LNG producer is set to kick off its run at the ASX boards.

Renergen is a South African-listed microcap that is pitched as the country's first and only holder of an onshore petroleum production right with a licence valid for another 23 years.

Renergen has a 90 per cent stake in Tetra4 Proprietary Ltd, which holds the production right for its Virginia Gas Project. It wants to expand the project to produce liquid helium and liquid natural gas.

The company is seeking to raise up to $10 million via a secondary listing on the ASX boards.

Funds raised would primarily be used to drill production wells at Tetra4 and help pay for a feasibility study looking at commercialisation of the project's helium reserves.

Renergen is due to open the offer and start pitching Australian investors this week. If successful, its ASX-listed CDIs would commence trading on May 31.

The Eights Group is listed as lead manager and Gleneagle Securities as broker to the offer. Norton Rose Fulbright is doing the Australian legal work.

sentiment_pool.headline: Property buyers may be better off renting
sentiment_pool.text:
More than 60 per cent of Sydneysiders who bought properties in the past 25 years would have been financially better off renting and investing their money in the sharemarket instead.

An analysis by EY of the sharemarket and Sydney property prices across 43 local government areas between 1994 and now found that in 62 per cent of like-for-like cases it was financially advantageous for buyers to invest their 20 per cent deposit in an ASX 200 fund.

"A lot of people assume you're better off owning your own home and that renting, saving and investing in other ways is always a less attractive option," said EY's Sydney managing partner, Andrew Price.

sentiment_pool.headline: Telstra reveals replacement for Tesla-bound Denholm
sentiment_pool.text:
Telstra has named Vicki Brady as its new chief financial officer, replacing Robyn Denholm who leaves the company to become chairwoman of US electric-car maker Tesla.

Ms Brady is an internal appointment and begins on July 1. She was previously group executive of consumer and small business, having joined Telstra in 2016.

Michael Ackland, who filled in for Ms Brady while she was on extended leave last year, will become her permanent replacement in the consumer and small business segment.

Telstra chief executive Andy Penn said: "It is testament to the strength of our internal talent that we were able to appoint Vicki as CFO and head of strategy, and have Michael continuing permanently as group executive, consumer and small business, a role he has being acting in since September last year."

Ms Denholm announced she was leaving Telstra last November, after just a few months in the role.

She was appointed as Tesla chairwoman after founder and chief executive Elon Musk, who was the previous chairman, was forced to step down after agreeing to a $US40 million settlement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

The regulator had alleged Mr Musk misled investors with statements on Twitter declaring he had secured finance for a buyout of Tesla. Mr Musk remains chief executive.

Ms Denholm said of the appointment: "I believe in this company, I believe in its mission and I look forward to helping Elon and the Tesla team achieve sustainable profitability."

sentiment_pool.headline: Boomtown set to sell regional markets
sentiment_pool.text:
Advertising Marketers too often ignore non-metro areas.

Woolworths, Coles and McDonald's get something many Australian brand owners don't: regional economies are bustling and regional communities are spending up.

Most marketing professionals and their marketing advisers see non-metro areas as a wasteland - drought or flood-ravaged and a population with lower spending power and propensity.

But just as state and federal politicians have been forced to turn their attention beyond capital cities in the current election cycle, a once impossible alliance of rival regional media groups officially launched an unlikely offensive this week to arrest metropolitan marketing bias against regional economies.

Called "Boomtown", the consortium's killer statistic is that just 10 per cent of national media budgets are spent in regional markets while those markets account for 36 per cent of Australia's population, or 8.8 million people.

Fixing the investment "imbalance" is a priority of the Boomtown alliance which includes Southern Cross Austereo, Win, Prime, Grant Broadcasters, Imparja and Australian Community Media (ACM is owned by Nine, publisher of The Australian Financial Review).

"This initiative is 50 years later than it could have been," said Brian Gallagher, chairman of the Boomtown consortium and chief sales officer at Southern Cross Austereo.

sentiment_pool.headline: Huawei calls for end to technology 'warfare'
sentiment_pool.text:
Huawei Australia chairman John Lord has accused the federal government of pursuing a path of "technology warfare" in its ban on the Chinese telecommunications firm from providing equipment for 5G networks, and urged a shift to what he called "cyber diplomacy".

Such diplomacy would include a detailed agreement between Australia and China covering "all aspects" of cyber warfare and espionage, along with a "globally acceptable law for cyberspace" overseen by the United Nations.

Speaking at RMIT University's ICEGOV conference in Melbourne on Wednesday, Mr Lord said the ban on his company's equipment - grounded in a fear that the Chinese government might compel Huawei to spy on Australia - was a "nationalistic" move based on exaggerated security concerns. He claimed the ban, which was imposed in August and prevents Huawei from providing any equipment to 5G network operators such as Telstra and Optus, had been implemented without dialogue with the industry, and warned it would have "highly detrimental" consequences.

"By banning a global leading player, in Australia's case Huawei, from participating in its 5G future, Australia has accepted the dual penalties of delays in its digital future and substantially more cost, and furthermore is eroding global trade norms for overseas investment and trade."

sentiment_pool.headline: Perth 'as good as it's likely to get' for rental affordability
sentiment_pool.text:
Falling dwelling prices and rents have have pushed rental affordability in Perth to as good a level as it is likely to see, but a lack of new housing stock - particularly for lower-income households - means the city will suffer a severe affordability crisis when the market picks up, new research from Bankwest Curtin Economics Centre shows.

The Getting our house in order? BCEC Housing Affordability Survey 2019 shows that rental affordability for households on median incomes had benefited from the weaker housing market, with the majority of households spending 30 per cent or less of their income on rental payments.

But the same survey shows that the 125,000-odd households in the lowest income quartile are are already highly stretched, with rent-income ratios for lower-income families well above 30 per cent in suburbs such as Gosnells, Armadale, Fremantle and Hamilton Hill. Lower-income households are spending over 35 per cent in Cockburn Central and Jandakot to the south of the city, in Rockingham and Cooloongup. Households are generally regarded as being in housing stress if they are spending more than 30 per cent of their income on keeping a roof over their heads.

The post-mining boom slowdown that has hit WA's housing market, pushing prices down more than 18 per cent over the past five years and halving the annual total of new dwelling approvals to just over 16,000, has resulted in little new stock at the affordable end - particularly given the vast majority of new approv

sentiment_pool.headline: Hold your horses: house prices are not about to take off yet
sentiment_pool.text:
There's reason to be more optimistic around the prospects for housing prices, but don't believe all the headlines: we are not back to boom times - yet.

I say this in the wake of some excitement around the weekend's auction rates in Sydney and Melbourne, which, in the case of the former, reportedly jumped as high as 69.9 per cent - a level consistent with the go-go days of a few years back.

There is, however, an issue, says Louis Christopher, managing director of SQM Research: "That figure of 70 per cent is nowhere near correct."

"It doesn't reflect where the auction market is now," he says.

High auction clearance rates are typically associated with a strong housing market. They show vendors are having little trouble selling their properties for an acceptable price. And while house price moves are measured monthly, auction rates take a "real-time" pulse of the property market.

But preliminary weekend clearance rates are, as the name suggests, only an estimate. In the case of Sydney, they are typically downgraded through the week - by around 5-6 per cent, Westpac economist Matthew Hassan reckons.

In this case, Christopher reckons the number is more likely to settle around 58 per cent. This is above a clearance rate in the "high 40s" ahead of the election, but "70 per cent suggests a boom and there's not a boom out there right now. There's a lot of stock the market needs to absorb first before we see a tightening of supply," he says. "I'm not surprised there's more confide

sentiment_pool.headline: 'Quiet Australians' a divided bunch
sentiment_pool.text:
Trends Education, class and religion are splitting the nation.

It was meant to be a victory for the "quiet Australians" - a wholesome, aspirational, and unassuming majority who had finally stood up.

This was the unifying message of Scott Morrison as he claimed the Coalition's shock win in the federal election: "Tonight is about every single Australian who depends on their government to put them first."

But away from the jubilation at the Liberals' victory party at the Wentworth Sofitel in Sydney, a disaffected country was divided along new and shifting fissures of class, education, and religion, according to experts who have studied the data from this and past elections.

They say now that the LNP has won re-election, its next challenge is to govern across these dividing lines. The emerging data on voters reveal two trends that influenced the result.

First, the Australian public is increasingly disaffected with the political system and turning away from the major parties.

The Australian Election Study (AES), a survey conducted by a multi-university working group, found that levels of voter dissatisfaction in 2016 were among the highest in 20 years.

Only 26 per cent of 2818 respondents said "people in government can be trusted"; overall satisfaction with democracy had dipped to 60 per cent. Each figure was the lowest recorded since 1993.

sentiment_pool.headline: Buyers up for 42pc of income on mortgages
sentiment_pool.text:
A fall in house prices and sustained low interest rates have made property purchases more palatable for buyers, but sluggish wage growth means the average Sydney household buying in the current market will initially have to fork out more than 40 per cent of their pay packet a month towards a loan.

The proportion of household earnings in Sydney spent on initial mortgage repayments fell from a record 50.9 per cent - $5344 per month - at the peak of the market in June 2017 to 42.1 per cent - $4654 per month - over the recent March quarter, as a result of house prices falling 14.3 per cent, according to Domain Group data.

In Melbourne the proportion of household income spent on mortgage repayments peaked in December 2017 at 39.2 per cent - $4039 per month - but has since fallen to 34.4 per cent, or $3664 per month.

Perth, where average incomes are pushed higher by well-paid mining jobs and where property prices have fallen 14 per cent since 2014, has the smallest mortgage burden, with just one-fifth of household income put towards mortgage repayments.

The analysis, by Domain Group economist Trent Wiltshire, took into account the RBA's discounted mortgage rate, median house prices and average household wages across each capital city. Domain is majority-owned by Nine, publisher of The Australian Financial Review.

sentiment_pool.headline: Power company CEOs set Coalition a post-election energy challenge
sentiment_pool.text:
Power company chief executives called on the Morrison government to use its surprise election win to reach out to others in Parliament and forge a bipartisan energy and climate policy to unlock private investment in new capacity.

In contrast to Labor, the government campaigned with no renewable energy target and no explicit emissions target for the power industry or new policies for reducing carbon emissions in industry and transport, which have increased sharply since the Coalition abolished Labor's carbon tax in 2014.

Jon Stretch, chief executive of ERM Power, said the result hadn't changed the policy challenge, and the government should not be frightened to use the clear post-victory air to revisit previously abandoned policies such as an emissions intensity scheme, Chief Scientist Alan Finkel's Clean Energy Target or the National Energy Guarantee.

"We still need enduring national energy policy that delivers increased reliability and lower price and emissions. The transition to renewables remains inevitable and absolutely requires supporting policy," Mr Stretch said.

"The Morrison government has been given a mandate and it should do what's required to get a bipartisan and sustainable solution. We have seen some really valuable work in the past few years - some of which was ruled out by the prevailing political climate.

"We clearly have the components of a solution, and now the opportunity exists to build broad bipartisan consensus."

sentiment_pool.headline: Hydrogen power could get a runout at the biggest stage
sentiment_pool.text:
CSIRO and EnergyAustralia have presented a plan to the trustees of the Melbourne Cricket Club to trial hydrogen fuel cell technology on the nation's biggest stage - the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

The plan - yet to be accepted by the trustees - would include a small, 35-kilowatt fuel cell fuelled by hydrogen produced from methanol as part of a hybrid clean energy system for the MCG, including lithium ion batteries, solar panels and renewable energy from the grid.

CSIRO chief executive Larry Marshall said work could begin on the project as early as next year if the trustees and MCG supplier EnergyAustralia decide to go ahead, and CSIRO expects hydrogen fuel cell technology to be viable for transport and remote, off-grid sites by about 2025.

"We believe hydrogen will compete on an economic basis in transport and remote area power by 2025 - for remote mines and towns," Dr Marshall told The Australian Financial Review.

The MCG's main energy needs are for lighting, heating and airconditioning. Each light tower used for night matches and during daytime matches when the light is poor uses about 1.8 megawatt of power at high beam.

The groundkeepers also use LED lights to speed the growth and post-match recovery of the turf on the northern wing - which the winter sun rarely reaches above the three-tiered grandstand.

sentiment_pool.headline: Webjet CEO avoids Google search for building brand
sentiment_pool.text:
Marketing Going old school with a long game can pay off.

John Guscic, the CEO of listed online travel group Webjet, says his company has a "high motivation" not to pay Google escalating prices for paid search clicks and his secret sauce for success lies in years of investment in longer-term brand building.

It's a rare, strategic marketing approach from the boss of a $2.2 billion digital company but increasing industry and academic evidence the world over is backing Mr Guscic's multi-year focus on building Webjet's brand.

Most of the $8 billion pouring annually into the Australian digital advertising sector is based on what the industry calls performance marketing, the online equivalent of direct marketing, direct mail, catalogues, telemarketing and direct response TV.

"We were zigging when everyone else was zagging," Mr Guscic told CMO Brief after a recent UBS Tech Investor forum. "Everyone else was interested in last-click [attribution]. Everyone else was interested in search optimisation and pay-per-click. All of those transactional tools are what drove the vast majority of our competitors both here in Australia and internationally and we spent very little on that We built a brand. We built an old-fashioned brand through mediums like TV, billboards and sports sponsorships."

sentiment_pool.headline: FlexiGroup signs swag of deals
sentiment_pool.text:
FlexiGroup's new Afterpay challenger Humm will be available in Myer, Ikea and even a chain of IVF clinics under a set of deals announced on Wednesday.

Other sellers that will begin offering the buy-now, pay-later provider's service include JB Hi-Fi New Zealand, Solomon Carpets and trans-Tasman leather goods retailer Strandbags, which has 300 stores.

Humm, which is targeting the health sector as well as retail and home improvement, has also reached agreements with 300-store audiology chain National Hearing, dental software group National Dental Plan and, in an Australian first, City IVF, which has 16 clinics around the country.

FlexiGroup, which is rebuilding under new chief executive Rebecca James, has been operating in the buy-now, pay-later space for two decades and has a 17 per cent market share in terms of transaction volumes and 40 per cent share of receivables.

But its previous brands in the category, Certegy Ezi-Pay and Oxipay, were largely unknown and the Humm brand, which was revealed in February, at the same time FlexiGroup revealed an investment by veteran investor John Wylie, is critical to Ms James's plans. Its key point of difference is it can be used for purchases from $1 to $30,000, in contrast to rivals such as Afterpay, which has an average transaction of about $150.
