sentiment_pool.headline: Dexus seals record $1.5b Collins Street deal
sentiment_pool.text:
Dexus has undertaken the biggest capital raising in the property sector since the global financial crisis to back its $1.476 billion acquisition of the 80 Collins Street mixed-use precinct in Melbourne's CBD from Queensland funds giant QIC.

Dexus will split the ownership of the precinct - 105,000 square metres of net lettable area at the Paris end of Collins Street - with its balance sheet taking 75 per cent and its wholesale property fund taking the remaining 25 per cent stake.

The acquisition boosts Dexus's office portfolio weighting to the Melbourne CBD office market to 17 per cent from 9 per cent. Chief executive Darren Steinberg said the deal, following Dexus' purchase of 52 and 60 Collins Street last year, further enhanced the landlord's scale and presence at the city's east end.

"Importantly, vacancy in the Melbourne CBD office market is nearing an all-time low, supported by strong population growth and significant pre-commitments across the upcoming supply pipeline," Mr Steinberg said.

To fund the stake held on balance sheet, Dexus launched a fully underwritten $900 million placement to institutional investors at $12.10 per share.

The 25 per cent share held by the Dexus Wholesale Property Fund will initially be debt-funded.

The precinct includes an existing 47-storey A-grade office tower, as well as a 35-storey premium office building under construction - with 63 per cent of tenancy pre-committed - and a new 255-room boutique hotel and retail complex. JLL's Rob

sentiment_pool.headline: Lowe leery of market's confusion
sentiment_pool.text:
A rather bemused-sounding Philip Lowe calls it a "strange world". His puzzlement is due to the combination of investors expecting "central banks will ride to the rescue" with a reduction in interest rates globally while remaining somehow unconcerned about corporate profits or credit risk.

He also points to the limits of what further monetary easing can achieve anyway. That includes the fact that with so many central banks expected to cut rates almost simultaneously over the course of the year, the usual stimulatory benefit of a decline in the exchange rate for any one country effectively disappears.

Lowe hardly counts as a pessimist, referring to recent IMF predictions global growth will still be higher next year - at 3.6 per cent - than this year's expectation of 3.3 per cent. Nor does he think another global financial crisis likely given the increased resilience of the world's financial system.

But the biggest global risk he sees is the uncertainty over whether the technology-trade dispute between the US and China can be resolved. According to Lowe, such uncertainty is causing businesses worldwide to "sit on their hands" rather than invest. That's even though they remain happy to hire people - at least for now - with unemployment rates in the US, UK, Germany and Japan at their lowest in decades.

sentiment_pool.headline: Wattle Health tests patience with ambitious plans
sentiment_pool.text:
A combination of negative cash flow and heavy capital spending on production facilities in Victoria have triggered a tumble in the share price of Wattle Health as the broader sharemarket approaches record highs.

The infant formula group was a sharemarket darling trading at $2.70 in February 2018 but has since sunk to about 54¢, with investors increasingly nervous about its ambitious plans, and an organic formula brand, Uganic, central to its aspirations in consumer markets.

The arrival to the scene last month of US-based emerging markets fund manager Gramercy is also intriguing.

Gramercy signed a $US75 million ($109 million) debt facility term sheet to help Wattle fund the acquisition of 75 per cent of the Blend & Pack processing and packaging business in outer Melbourne.

Gramercy has a team of 60 people scouring the globe for deals and has been increasing its focus on Latin America from its headquarters in Greenwich, Connecticut. It has a private equity arm and also runs a "special situations" fund, as well as generating returns from distressed debt.

The debt facility has a term of four years, with a coupon rate of 9 per cent per annum. Gramercy is also being granted 14.5 million ordinary shares to be held in escrow.

Wattle executive chairman Lazarus Karasavvidis said the debt facility was embarked upon to prevent the need for another equity raising, which would have been "unnecessarily dilutive".

sentiment_pool.headline: Diversification and calm approach key to coping with low rates
sentiment_pool.text:
With the interest rate reality that investors face in the foreseeable future - one of continuing low rates - the key question you need to ask is how much capital security you want from your investments.

Do you want a decent income flow where you are not worried about changes in the capital value of your investments, or is absolute capital security your most important consideration?

If the latter is your priority, then unfortunately with the latest reduction in the official cash rate to 1.25 per cent, bank deposits paying less than 1 per cent and term deposits paying below 2 per cent will increasingly be the best you can get. For many this will be a dismal prospect.

But if you can tolerate fluctuations in the capital value of your assets, identifying investments that offer income such as share dividends that can pay income of 4 to 5 per cent and distributions from managed funds, including exchange traded funds (ETFs), are available alternatives.

Further, many of these investments since the federal election continue to be enhanced with dividend imputation franking credits that pay cash refunds to investors on marginal tax rates below 30 per cent. Investors most relieved by this are self-managed superannuation funds that pay investment-tax-exempt pensions.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fair Work upholds Qantas sacking for 'encouraging' strike
sentiment_pool.text:
The Fair Work Commission has backed Qantas' sacking of a veteran employee for supporting an unprotected strike against the airline that disrupted dozens of flights and thousands of customers.

Senior deputy president Jonathan Hamberger held former Q Catering cabin service attendant Loata Petrunic's actions were "fundamentally inconsistent with the obligations she owed to her employer" and her 22-year history with the airline did not result in making her dismissal harsh.

He held Ms Petrunic was an active participant in a four-hour stoppage at Sydney airport last year and Qantas was justified in firing her and not other workers who were "more or less herded" into the action by union delegates. "It is clear ... that [Ms Petrunic] had prior knowledge of the unprotected industrial action, and still decided to participate. Her actions were deliberate and premeditated."

Ms Petrunic and four Transport Workers Union delegates were fired for their alleged role in the stoppage in June 2018 that disrupted 50 domestic and international flights and more than 7500 customers.

More than 40 Q Catering employees walked off the job in solidarity with a sacked union delegate and in protest over the uncertainty of their conditions from Q Catering's pending sale to airline service provider dnata.

During the stoppage, cars belonging to two TWU delegates were illegally parked at exit gates to block trucks from delivering meals to aircraft.

sentiment_pool.headline: Sirtex settlement leaves growth mystery
sentiment_pool.text:
No doubt we should all be pleased that the shareholder class action brought against biotechnology company Sirtex over a 2016 profit downgrade has been settled.

Justice is done and the costs associated with running the final two weeks of the four-week Federal Court trial will not be foisted on the poor old taxpayer. But Chanticleer can't help feeling a twinge of disappointment.

This was the case with some very unique elements and, had the trial run its course to a full judgment, it could have set some important precedents about how guidance is set - and then maintained - by ASX-listed companies.

The settlement, which arrived two weeks into the trial before Justice Bernard Murphy, was officially confirmed on Friday, after being reported by The Australian Financial Review on Thursday evening. The parties will need to finalise the settlement agreement before it is approved by the court. The next hearing is scheduled for June 24.

The maximum liability in the case was $280 million, but it is understood the settlement was $40 million, which will include the costs of the class action lawyers and funders.

Central to the case was Sirtex's earnings guidance for the 2017 financial year, which was given on August 24, 2016 (at the company's annual results) and confirmed on October 25, 2016 (at the company's annual general meeting).

sentiment_pool.headline: Former Octaviar CFO facing fraud charge
sentiment_pool.text:
The former chief financial officer of Gold Coast investment group Octaviar Limited (MFS), which collapsed in 2008 owing $2.5 billion, has been charged with fraud totalling $4.61 million.

David Mark Anderson appeared in Southport Magistrates Court on Monday charged with 26 counts of fraud following an investigation by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

ASIC alleges that between June 18, 2012 and September 21, 2015, Mr Anderson, while a director of Octaviar Investment Holdings No.3 Pty Ltd (OIH3) - a subsidiary of Octaviar - "dishonestly applied $4,611,571.86 of OIH3 money for his own use". At the time of the alleged conduct, Mr Anderson was the sole director of OIH3.

Octaviar Ltd, previously called MFS, was a publicly listed company with interests in financial services, travel and leisure and childcare businesses, based on the Gold Coast. Its collapse in 2008 wiped out thousands of mum-and-dad investors, who had put their life savings into MFS investment vehicle, the Premium Income Fund.

Mr Anderson was released on bail on condition and the matter adjourned to September 2.

In May 2017, Mr Anderson was disqualified from managing corporations for 25 years and ordered to pay penalties of $500,000 and almost $206 million in compensation to PIF.

sentiment_pool.text:
Gambling Lawrence Ho has been integral to many of James Packer's biggest casino wins. He's now paying Packer out again, but this time it's different, writes James Thomson.

Could Lawrence Ho become James Packer's $9 billion man?

During a lucrative joint venture that lasted for 11 years, Packer's Crown Resorts and Ho's group Melco Resorts built a casino business in Macau and Manilla that earned Crown about $4.5 billion, at a stunning return of almost six times his investment.

On Thursday night, Ho lined Packer's pockets again, paying $1.8 billion for a 19.99 per cent stake in Crown, in a deal that again redefines Packer's relationship with both Australia and the gaming sector.

With Ho ready and willing to increase that stake - and perhaps even take Crown private - it's not hard to think that Packer could sell his remaining 26 per cent stake in Crown for well above the $2.3 billion it is valued at by Melco's $13.00-a-share entry price.

Kerry Packer only got one Alan Bond. James Packer will surely only get one Lawrence Ho.

Of course, this has always been a relationship that both parties say is about more than just business. It is a bond that Ho describes as "brotherly".

When Ho came to Sydney in August 2004, he was looking for a business partner who could help him start the next phase of his life. He wanted backing for a casino development in Macau that would let him sever ties with his father, the legendary Asian gambling billionaire Stanley Ho.

sentiment_pool.headline: RBA could cut cash rate as soon as August
sentiment_pool.text:
Futures markets are suggesting the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut the cash rate twice more in the next 12 months, with the next cut potentially coming as soon as next week.

Economists say while a third cut in as many months is unlikely, a disappointing inflation print on Wednesday could mean August becomes a "live" meeting.

NAB economist Tapas Strickland said the RBA could cut next Tuesday "if core inflation were to print substantially weaker".

The Australian Bureau of Statistics releases its inflation report on Wednesday at 11.30am AEST and the market is expecting the consumer price index to print at 1.5 per cent, below the RBA's forecast of 1.6 per cent. CPI is expected to edge up 0.5 per cent on the previous three months.

A cash rate cut in August would require a much weaker result, Mr Strickland said. The RBA has eased a quarter of a percentage point at each of its last two meetings, taking the cash rate to a historic low of 1 per cent.

"I think in order to get that outcome, you might need to get something near 1.3 per cent or 1.4 per cent," he said.

The Australian dollar dipped to US69.09¢ on Monday, down from US70.42¢ a week ago, as markets price in a higher chance the board cuts rates more than once this year.

Futures markets are implying just a 20 per cent chance the RBA board cuts for a third time in August although the bank is widely expected to cut at least once more before the end of the year.

sentiment_pool.headline: Nine to keep Stuff as sale bid goes on
sentiment_pool.text:
New Zealand publisher Stuff will come under the umbrella of Nine managing director of publishing Chris Janz as the Australian media company continues to look for a buyer but prepares to run the business itself.

The sale process for Stuff is still under way and there are conversations with a number of parties. However, Nine, which owns The Australian Financial Review, has failed to get an acceptable offer and is preparing to run Stuff itself if it does not.

Formerly known as Fairfax New Zealand, Stuff became part of Nine following a merger with Fairfax Media, which was completed in December.

Nine chief executive Hugh Marks and Stuff chief executive Sinead Boucher addressed Stuff staff in Auckland and nationally via teleconference on Tuesday to update them on the process and give the business a new reporting line into Mr Janz.

"As we get into this next six months, obviously there are still discussions afoot, but if we aren't able to bring those to any satisfactory conclusion I think we will move on at that point. What's important for the business is to effectively start moving on anyway," Mr Marks said.

Stuff owns various digital businesses and New Zealand's most popular domestic website, news site Stuff.co.nz. In recent times, Stuff has launched retail broadband provider Stuff Fibre and acquired 100 per cent of Neighbourly, a website that allows communities to have a private "neighbourhood" website to share information about the local area.

sentiment_pool.headline: MCN explores rebranding to Foxtel Media
sentiment_pool.text:
Foxtel advertising sales business Multi-Channel Network is exploring a rebrand to more closely align itself with the pay television provider.

Sources told The Australian Financial Review the business is working through new names, with Foxtel Media Group and Foxtel Media believed to be at the top of the list. MCN is at the beginning of the process.

The rebranding of MCN comes after multiple years of discussions and with the exit of Network 10 in January this year, a change to reflect the business' closer ties with Foxtel made sense.

Sources said a rebrand will also put a line in the sand, showing the business will stay outside the News Corp portfolio and be tied to Foxtel, rather than the long-rumoured News Corp advertising super group.

It has long been speculated News Corp would combine its own ad sales with Foxtel and potentially Nova's. The move would combine print, digital, pay TV and radio ad sales. A rebrand tied to the Foxtel name would make it clear that move is not on the table at this time, sources said.

Nova is 100 per cent owned by News Corp co-chairman Lachlan Murdoch. It is a privately held business under Mr Murdoch's investment vehicle Illyria.

News Corp owns 65 per cent of Foxtel, while Telstra owns the remaining 35 per cent. Foxtel chief executive Patrick Delany is MCN chairman.

In a statement, MCN chief executive Mark Frain confirmed the brand name was under review.

sentiment_pool.headline: Estia Health served with class action
sentiment_pool.text:
Residential aged care provider Estia Health has been served with a class action proceeding by law firm Phi Finney McDonald over alleged breaches of market disclosure obligations in 2015 and 2016.

The class action alleged Estia failed to disclose serious difficulties the business was experiencing in the lead-up to the publication of its 2016 financial year results.

The class action was filed in the Federal Court on Monday and served to Estia yesterday morning.

On August 29, 2016, the company published its full-year results and it is alleged it gave misleading guidance for the 2017 financial year that it subsequently slashed on October 6, 2016.

The company told the market yesterday that it would fight the charges. "Estia will vigorously defend the proceeding," a company statement said.

It said it could not state what the financial impact of the class action would be. "Estia is not in a position to state whether the proceeding is likely to have a material impact on its financial position or performance," the statement said.

The share price fell 5.78 per cent on the news, closing at $2.61.

The next stage in the legal process is for the case to be allocated a Docket Judge, who will be responsible to conduct the trial of the proceedings. This normally takes a couple of days.

sentiment_pool.headline: Entrepreneur visa fails to attract offshore talent
sentiment_pool.text:
The federal government's entrepreneurship visa has attracted almost no company founders from overseas in almost three years, despite high hopes it would help draw the world's brightest minds to start businesses here.

A freedom of information request by The Australian Financial Review to the Department of Home Affairs showed the visa class has been such a failure the number of entrepreneurs settling in Australia fell underneath a threshold of just five people required to record arrivals from different countries.

The Department said the underperforming visa could be replaced with an alternate scheme, on trial in South Australia, with less stringent funding requirements to qualify.

The entrepreneur stream within the Business Innovation and Investment visa was introduced in September 2016 as a National Innovation and Science Agenda initiative, but has been criticised by potential users for being too hard to access.

Australia has received a small number of applications from China, Hong Kong, Russia, Ukraine, Britain and Vietnam-based entrepreneurs, but none of those countries had more than five people applying or relocating to Australia.

James Taylor, the British founder of e-commerce start-up Particular Audience, is one of the few to have received an entrepreneurship visa, and said he was not surprised there had been such a low uptake, given the illogical vetting rules.

sentiment_pool.headline: Local investors lose in Deutsche drama
sentiment_pool.text:
It will likely take some weeks before the full local ramifications of Deutsche Bank's global restructure are clear, but it's fair to say the initial (and emotional) reaction is that the Australian business has been cruelled by its shaky German parent.

Deutsche will slash 18,000 jobs - just under a fifth of its workforce - in a €7.4 billion ($11.9 billion) restructure that will see it push $US300 billion ($429 billion) of assets into a so-called "bad bank" and then retreat from the global equities business.

Chief executive Christian Sewing's grand reset is designed to focus the bank on more stable sources of income, particularly commercial and private banking. Deutsche Bank's grand plan to challenge the titans of Wall Street investment banking looks all but over.

As The Australian Financial Review's Street Talk column reported at the weekend, Deutsche's local equities business will be basically wiped out, with equities research, sales trading, derivatives and equity capital markets likely to be shuttered.

The investment banking team is bracing for cuts, as life without an equities function will mean big changes to the sort of service Deutsche will be able to offer.

The overwhelming sense in the Australian market is that a profitable local business, with some really good people in it, has been steamrolled in what Sewing described as "the most fundamental transformation of Deutsche Bank in decades".

sentiment_pool.headline: 'We have to discriminate to hire a man'
sentiment_pool.text:
One of Australia's most female-friendly law firms says it has to practise "positive discrimination" to employ male law graduates, because of the superiority of female candidates.

Lander & Rogers chief executive partner Genevieve Collins told the July edition of The Australian Financial Review Law Partnership Survey the main reason was that young women presented so much better at interviews.

The firm has the highest ratio of female senior associates (76 per cent) in the survey and ranks fourth on the list of female partners (37 per cent).

The only other firm with more than 50 partners that had similar figures was Maddocks, which is also headed by a female CEO in Michelle Dixon.

There was only one woman among Lander's four new partners in 2019, but in the previous four years the average was 66 per cent.

When it comes to hiring graduates, she says the firm has "to practise positive discrimination to have any boys at all". "Have you ever interviewed kids coming out of uni in their early 20s? The women interview so much better. If we didn't practise positive affirmative action for males, we wouldn't have any males," Ms Collins said.

"It's stark. They [women] just mature earlier; they are more nuanced and emotionally intelligent at that age."

sentiment_pool.headline: Morrison can lead repair of trade Humpty Dumpty
sentiment_pool.text:
Prime Minister Scott Morrison is one of the few world leaders on unqualified good terms with President Donald Trump. After extended time with the US leader at the G7 in France, he should have more insight than most on the trade mayhem that escalated in the past week.

The Prime Minister matter-of-factly explained to The Australian Financial Review's Europe correspondent Hans van Leeuwen that the trade war is not about Mr Trump's personality, nor clashes of civilisations and the like, but is a transition to be expected. China has outgrown the trade rules under which it soared to become the world's second biggest economy, he suggests, and now we need new ones. It is inevitable that the US will be affected the most by this. "It's totally structural. It's a history issue. We are finding ourselves in a new phase. And we don't have to place or characterise people's motives in any of this, it's just the juncture we are at and we have to deal with it". Australian economist Adrian Blundell-Wignall makes a similar argument on these pages today. It's not about Mr Trump per se. While the trade war is bad, not confronting China's mercantilist economic development path would lead to a potentially more damaging financial crisis, says the former senior OECD economist.

sentiment_pool.headline: Bottomline ratings kill Worner as Seven CEO
sentiment_pool.text:
Kerry Stokes has installed James Warburton as chief executive of Seven West Media to lead a "change in direction", help find new revenue streams and reduce its reliance on the under-pressure, free-to-air advertising market.

Mr Warburton spent eight years in a number of senior roles at Seven, including chief digital and sales officer, before leaving in 2011 to become chief executive of Network Ten.

His appointment comes after the sudden resignation of Tim Worner on Thursday night, who had been Seven chief executive since 2013. There had been speculation about Mr Worner's future for some time. Mr Warburton is Seven's new boss effective immediately.

Seven shares have been languishing at their lowest point since the merger of Seven Network and West Australia Newspapers in 2011, around 38¢. On Friday, Seven shares closed 6.7 per cent higher at 40¢ and the volume of shares traded was about 10 times the average turnover of the past 20 days.

"We needed to have a change in direction," Seven chairman Kerry Stokes told The Australian Financial Review.

"The industry is going through an issue where traditional media and revenue are getting more difficult, we thought that if we're going to change the company and pursue the next phase of some growth we had to change the way we do business."

sentiment_pool.headline: De Maistre connection set to yield a bonanza at D&H

A feast of Australian 1920s and 30s art dominated by outstanding pictures by Roy de Maistre and Margaret Preston is a highlight of Deutscher and Hackett's Sydney art sale on August 28.

They married in 1946, soon after Sydney-born Ken joined the CSIRO, where he became a principal research scientist and ultimately did pioneering work on wood composites and adhesives.

An early interest in art and books led them to art dealers such as Dr Joseph Brown and Joan McLelland. Ken's family link to de Maistre (they were distant cousins) led to the acquisition of what was ultimately described as one of the largest collections of the artist's work in the country. The couple were also keen fans of Australian print makers.

Among the top offerings from the collection is de Maistre's The Meeting in the Garden. This large work dates from circa 1929, when the artist had returned from Europe and occupied the upper floor of Burdekin House, a grand mansion opposite Parliament House in Sydney's Macquarie Street, in collaboration with photographer Harold Cazneaux.

sentiment_pool.headline: Rich feel richer as the working households fret
sentiment_pool.text:
Australians are feeling worse about their wealth as worries about falling home prices and a weaker job market take their toll, says a new report.

Financial comfort across most of the 11 drivers that make up the index fell over the past six months, led by net wealth which recorded a 3 per cent drop to 5.54 out of 10.

"The dramatic drop in residential property prices was a big drag," said ME Bank consulting economist Jeff Oughton. "Comfort with wealth would have fallen much more if it wasn't for record bond prices and a rebound in sharemarkets as well as the government's retention of negative gearing on investment properties and cash refunds for franking credits."

Working households recorded a significant deterioration in financial comfort weighed down by the lack of job security and income growth, claimed the ME Household Financial Comfort Report.

Full-time workers reported a 3 per cent drop while part-time and casual workers fell by 4 per cent and 1 per cent respectively.

The high costs of necessities and the lack of savings to deal with emergencies topped the worries of most Australians, according to the report.

Two in five households continued to spend all their monthly income while one in five households said they didn't think they could raise $3000 in an emergency.

This has been the case for homeowners Rosy Lone and partner Alexander Habilay of Tamworth, NSW.

sentiment_pool.headline: Rare earths miner hopeful about signing a Korean funding deal
sentiment_pool.text:
High-tech metals hopeful Alkane Resources believes a South Korean conglomerate offers the best chance of getting its $1.3 billion project into production, as manufacturers outside China increasingly worry about Beijing's threat to ban the export of rare earths.

Nic Earner, the managing director of Alkane, is confident of getting the company's Dubbo Project funded in the next 12 months as geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing show few signs of moderating.

"I do see the Koreans as the most prospective as they want to establish supply independence and they are prepared to mobilise government money to support their industry," he told The Australian Financial Review.

"Having said that, I have spent the last six years thinking I was 12 months away from a deal."

South Korea, with its reliance on large manufacturers such as LG, Samsung and Hyundai for jobs and export earnings, is highly exposed to any move by China to restrict the trade in rare earths, which are crucial components in everything from headphones, to wind turbines, electric vehicles and smartphones.

As an ally of Washington, Seoul has had a difficult relationship with Beijing in recent years and has been punished with trade and investment restrictions for agreeing to host US missile defence facilities.

sentiment_pool.headline: Investors gain despite Rio's output pain
sentiment_pool.text:
Surging iron ore prices and beneficent swings in exchange rates have fully insulated Rio Tinto shareholders from Pilbara production shortfalls triggered by fierce weather, port fires and humiliating cracks in mine planning.

Despite a June half blighted by upset and operational fragility enough to make Rio Tinto miss iron ore production guidance, the dual-listed Anglo-Australian has lifted interim dividend by 19 per cent and thrown an additional $US1 billion at its owners in the form of a special dividend.

For a third successive reporting period Rio Tinto is likely to draw on the strength of its balance sheet and use debt to fund shareholder returns. This strategy is made sensible by the fact that as recently as December 2018 Rio Tinto was net debt free and by the fundamentals of an iron ore market that was so gruesomely undermined in January when Vale's Brumadinho tailings dam collapsed.

It is variously estimated that the iron ore market is short 50 million-70 million tonnes as a result of temporary mine closures forced by governments in Brazil and by operational issues at both the Rio Tinto and BHP operated mines in the Pilbara.

While BHP's issues have proved passing, Rio will endure for another 18 months while material reductions in Brazilian supply could extend until 2022 and beyond.

sentiment_pool.headline: Teachers Mutual says CSR helped it top NPS ranking
sentiment_pool.text:
The chief executive of Teachers Mutual Bank - which has the highest 'net promoter score' of any bank in Australia - says surging customer satisfaction has been driven by the creation of "ethical" banking products, as more customers pay attention to the industries their deposits are lent to.

With Teachers Mutual driving customer numbers above 200,000 for the first time, Steve James, who has been CEO since 2005, said "we are starting to see a pick-up of membership and are well placed as more people recognise good corporate social responsibility and ethical investments ... People looking for housing loans have been seeking out our brands".

In the latest Roy Morgan Net Promoter Score (NPS) rankings, published last month, Teachers Mutual pipped ING on the leaderboard with an NPS of 52.6; Commonwealth Bank is the only major bank with a positive NPS score.

All of Teachers Mutual's deposit and savings products have been certified as "responsible investments" by the Responsible Investment Association Australasia (RIAA) and it is the only bank in the country to have its entire wholesale debt issuance program certified.

It refuses to fund companies involved in alcohol, armaments, correctional facilities, cryptocurrency, deforestation, fossil fuels, gambling, military or political activities, pornography, slavery, tobacco or uranium.

"Social responsibility has always been a cornerstone of our philosophy as a business," Mr James said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Cashed-up buyers target luxury homes in regions
sentiment_pool.text:
Top end City dwellers escape to the country as urban prices rise.

The regional luxury markets are feeling the ripple effect of the rising city markets with cashed-up Sydney and Melbourne buyers targeting prestige homes in popular areas, agents say.

In the past three months, a number of premium properties in the Southern Highlands of NSW were snapped up by Sydney buyers with deep pockets, including Widgee Waa, a 155-hectare property in Kangaloon, sold for $14.5 million to tech billionaire Mike Cannon-Brookes.

And the four-hectare Bellbrook Park estate in Bowral sold for $4.2 million to a Sydney family in July by Ben Olofsen, selling agent with The Agency.

"This property was snapped up by a wealthy executive coming out of Sydney," he said.

Another Sydney family recently splurged $6.8 million to buy 30-hectare Pepper Tree Creek Estate in Kangaloon, one of the highest deals in the area this year.

"We're seeing a number of families move here because they can send their children to good schools and still enjoy the rural lifestyle," said Southern Highlands selling agent Sarah Burke of DiJones.

Mr Olofsen said demand from Sydney buyers, who account for 85 per cent of their sales, had surged in the past three months.

"We're experiencing strong activity at the luxury end of the market particularly for farm properties around the 100-acre mark (40 hectares)."

sentiment_pool.headline: The $10m men reap benefits of high returns
sentiment_pool.text:
The 10 top-paid CEOs took home more than $10 million each last year on the back of strong shareholder returns, and only one CEO in the top 100 missed out on a bonus.

Australian Council of Superannuation Investors analysis showed Qantas boss Alan Joyce topped ASX 100 CEOs with $23.87 million in realised pay in the 2018 financial year, narrowly beating Macquarie Group chief executive Nicholas Moore by $20,000.

ASX 100 CEOs' median realised pay - which includes the actual value of equity vested during the year - hit its second successive record at $4.5 million, up from $4.36 million.

Only one eligible ASX 100 CEO did not receive their bonus for the year, Domino's Don Meij, compared with six in 2017. The new figure was the lowest ever recorded. However, the companies on the top-10 list also saw an average total shareholder return of 432.7 per cent over the past five years.

ACSI CEO Louise Davidson said the payments were made in the wake of soaring "first strike" votes against remuneration reports and while the banking royal commission was "in full swing", revealing executives not being held to account for poor conduct.

"The way bonuses are being handed out suggests there is a culture of entitlement whereby supposedly 'at risk' pay is not very risky at all," she said. sentiment_pool.headline: Draghi's warning will resonate Down Under
sentiment_pool.text:
Paris | European Central Bank president Mario Draghi isn't leaving office quietly. The question is whether any politicians are listening.

At his second-last monetary policy meeting, after eight hard-scrabble years at the helm, he fired off every monetary policy weapon in his arsenal, riding roughshod over the naysayers on his governing council.

He's desperate to kickstart the 19-member eurozone's sputtering economies and to punt the pallid inflation rate somewhere even close to the 2 per cent ballpark. But he didn't leave it there. He also took the fight to the governments of Germany, the Netherlands and other fiscal disciplinarians, with a few simple words that should reverberate in Australia.

"Now it is high time for the fiscal policy to take charge," he declared. "Fiscal policy should become the main policy instrument."

He's done his bit, delivering negative interest rates, cheap lines of credit to banks and quantitative easing (QE) - to little effect. The market certainly doesn't think his latest salvo will fare much better. So Draghi is calling on Germany, in particular, to start spending its budget surplus on pro-growth policies, and even to borrow more dough at these impossibly low rates of interest.

sentiment_pool.headline: Saxo backs ASIC plan to slash leverage on CFDs
sentiment_pool.text:
Saxo Capital Markets, one of the nation's leading online trading and investment platforms, has broken ranks to back ASIC's plans to drastically cut leverage on derivative products being flogged to small investors.

Adam Smith, chief executive of the fintech specialist offering platforms for multi-asset trading and investing, has also challenged claims by other providers that ASIC's move would push contracts for difference (CFD) investors offshore into less-well-regulated markets, such as the Seychelles or Vanuatu.

"I am sure common sense would make them aware of the inherent risk of that strategy," said Mr Smith.

The regulator is attempting to ban binary options and reduce leverage on CFDs to about 10 times, which is in line with best international practice, particularly in Asian markets.

About 65 Australian derivative licensees last year traded about $22 trillion worth of the products. The top seven are believed to account for about 70 per cent of the sector's turnover.

Last year Saxo's parent, Saxo Bank, one of Denmark's biggest banks, took a hard line against its peers in the UK when its equivalent of ASIC, the Financial Conduct Authority, moved to restrict the amount of leverage, which is borrowed money that increases a client's stake. Saxo came out in favour of caps that set back the sector's attempt to present a united front.

ASIC is concerned about sophisticated CFDs that are leveraged by 200 to 500 times and targeted at investors earning less than $37,000 a year.

It is fair to say that the past couple of years have not been kind to the brand trust of some financial institutions - but not all players in the sector have seen theirs eroded.

Many of the customer-owned banks have net promoter scores (a score ranging from -100 to +100 that measures the willingness of customers to recommend a company's products or services to others) over 90, says Steve James, chief executive of Sydney-based Teachers Mutual Bank. sentiment_pool.headline: Inquiry can restrict auditors' conflicts of interest
sentiment_pool.text:
The risk to independence that arises when an auditor also provides non-audit services to a client is high on the agenda of Parliament's broad-ranging investigation into assurance quality.

The inquiry is responding to, among other things, the erosion of public trust in the integrity of the work of professional service firms, especially the big four audit firms Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC.

There have been calls for several decades to prohibit or severely curtail the ability of auditors to also do non-audit work for audit clients that compromises, or seems to compromise, independence.

Last month's revelations about NAB's alleged influence in the preparation of a prudential report by EY clearly demonstrate the risks to independence in such circumstances. (NAB and EY deny any wrongdoing.)

While EY might be in the firing line now, none of the big four is immune.

Looking back across a decade, financial companies such as St George Bank, QBE and Perpetual Trustees were commonly spending more than 70 per cent of their payments to their auditors on work other than the audit.

Going back as far as 2006, EY's bill to NAB of $26 million included work other than audit of about $7 million.

The Hayne royal commission demonstrated that other professional firms also could have their independence compromised by existing relationships.

sentiment_pool.headline: Wagners to expand in US after $40m raising
sentiment_pool.text:
Construction group Wagners will build manufacturing plants for its composite fibre business in either Texas or Wyoming after a $40 million equity raising, co-founder Denis Wagner says.

The Queensland construction company on Tuesday confirmed a report in The Australian Financial Review's Street Talk column that it would issue new shares to pay down debt and strengthen its balance sheet so it could expand internationally.

Mr Wagner, the non-executive chairman, said the group wanted to produce composites in the US early next year. "We've got machinery ordered and being delivered in the US," he said.

The US market now makes only "minimal" contributions to Wagners' revenues but this could grow to as much as 50 per cent, he said.

"There is a huge opportunity over there."

Wagners expects to spend between $5 million and $10 million building the new plants over the next two years to manufacture composite material that can be used to repair bridges. A decision on the location of the US plants is expected in the next six weeks.

Wagners currently manufactures the composite fibre - used to build bridges, boardwalks, wharves and light poles - in Australia, and exports it around the world.

The renounceable offer, priced at $1.55 a share, will be fully underwritten by stockbroker Morgans. The Wagners family, which owns 55 per cent of the company, is taking up their full allocation of shares.

sentiment_pool.headline: Key university player is relaxed on China research collaboration
sentiment_pool.text:
Australia cannot afford to cross some countries off the list for research collaboration because of changing geopolitical alliances, and, if anything, the bigger issue is how to keep control of intellectual property in the commercialisation process with other countries, Paul Wellings says.

He was commenting on concerns that universities were jeopardising national security in joint research projects with China.

In an interview with The Australian Financial Review, the Wollongong University vice-chancellor and chairman of the Education Minister's university reference committee agreed he was sanguine on the subject of research collaboration.

"We have to do things in Australia's interest, but to do that we have to have partnerships and links with major research labs where ever they are.

"If you just cross out whole countries on the basis their political system is different, that narrows the scale of the collaboration."

Education Minister Dan Tehan appointed the university reference committee to produce the Wellings performance review but it was extended to advise him on the relationship between universities and business.

Australia's information and communications technology (ICT) industry is flatlining and it has been for 28 years, give or take.

This is the unfortunate truth when you look at the data released by Harvard University's Kennedy School's Center for International Development.

The data plots what the university calls the Atlas of Economic Complexity, which is essentially an index showing the value added to the exports of 133 economies, measured by the complexity of what they export. Exports can boom, but there's a difference between exporting raw materials or foodstuffs for example, and complex products such as gas turbines, computer systems or software.

The Australian Financial Review's Aaron Patrick aptly described the findings for Australia as: we're rich, dumb, and getting dumber. Our Economic Complexity Index ranking has dropped from 19th to 32nd, even as our GDP per capita has grown by 182 per cent between 1995 and 2017.

sentiment_pool.text:
Oil and gas group Santos will gain control of the Darwin LNG plant after buying a range of northern Australian assets for $2.2 billion from United States giant ConocoPhillips, as chief executive Kevin Gallagher shifts further into growth mode three years after rescuing the company.

ConocoPhillips becomes the second big US player to sell down assets in the volatile Australian gas market, after ExxonMobil said last month it would seek a buyer for all its Bass Strait oil and gas operations, in a move that could trigger a multibillion-dollar shake-up of the east coast industry.

Tensions are rising between manufacturers and gas producers over the structure of the Australian market. It has become much more export-focused since late 2015 after $80 billion was invested in three large LNG plants near Gladstone in Queensland, leading to accusations that domestic users are second in line, prices are higher than they should be and a raft of closures threatens the industry.

Santos announced yesterday it would pay $US1.39 billion ($2.05 billion) to buy the ConocoPhillips assets in northern Australia, along with an extra payment of $U$75 million contingent on a final investment decision being made on the $7 billion-plus Barossa natural gas project, about 300km north of Darwin.

Labor is ready to pass legislation ratifying free trade agreements with Indonesia and Hong Kong that will make it harder for foreigners to take legal action against the Australian government over domestic policy decisions that affect them.

The ALP also expressed concerns about the potential for the importation of foreign labour and will seek to make changes in Parliament.

The ACTU, which met Labor leader Anthony Albanese and senior members of his shadow cabinet on Friday to discuss the deals, remained opposed to the agreements.

In the case of the Hong Kong deal, the committee accepted concerns about doing a deal while the territory was mired in political turmoil.

sentiment_pool.text:
Qube Holdings has made novel use of the reforms to competition law in bringing a misuse of market power claim against the increasingly aggressive private equity-owned operators of the Port of Newcastle.

Qube's legal action represents a relatively rapid escalation of a seven-month dispute over who should own and operate the quay-side cranes needed to unload ships at one of the two dry bulk berths at the Port of Newcastle (PoN).

Qube's law suit, filed last week, marks the second time since the PoN's privatisation in 2014 that a key customer relationship has been pushed to the point of legal stand-off by claims that the port's new operators were being excessive in the exercise of their monopoly market power.

Two months before Qube trooped off to the Federal Court, a lapse in judgment by federal Treasurer Josh Frydenberg handed PoN final victory in a dispute of more than four years with Glencore over increases in shipping channel access fees just after privatisation.

sentiment_pool.headline: Seven merger a 'matter of survival' for Prime

Prime chairman John Hartigan has urged the regional broadcaster's shareholders to vote in favour of a merger with Seven West Media as a matter of survival for both the company and journalism outside metropolitan cities.

Last month, Seven made a move on Prime with an all-scrip merger proposal which was unanimously recommended by Prime's board.

sentiment_pool.headline: Climate needs reason not rhetoric
sentiment_pool.text:
Energy transition Solving climate change needs calm consensus, not hysterical headlines. The doomsayers of the past got it wrong too.

Climate change is a serious and difficult challenge. It deserves a response which is sober and analytical. So it was disappointing to see a group of scientists - usually a bastion of reason and empiricism - demanding we declare a "climate emergency" and warning of "untold suffering".

This might make for good headlines. But it does little to advance the cause of science or the level-headed and purposeful debate we need to have - around trade-offs, global co-operation and behavioural shifts - on this issue.

Too often this issue is hijacked by emotion and appeals to passion. If we really wish to see effective action on climate change then what is needed is cool-headed reason and the building of consensus, not apocalypticism and the demonisation of large swathes of human culture.

The evidence for human-induced climate change grows more compelling by the day, as does the seriousness of purpose needed to comprehensively address it. But though there is no scope for complacency, some optimism and belief in the ingenuity of humans is called for.

New technology, market forces and human behaviour are shifting our emissions curve in the right direction, as a recent report from the Australian National University makes clear.

sentiment_pool.headline: Latest Fed move could make Australian dollar stronger
sentiment_pool.text:
The US Federal Reserve's "insurance" interest rate cut is much more likely to boost the resilience of the Australian dollar next year than genuine easing, historical analysis shows.

When the Fed cut rates in the deliberate easing cycles of 1984-86, 1989-92, 2000-03 and 2007-11, the Australian dollar lost ground, but when it made insurance rate cuts in 1995 and 1998, the Aussie climbed, Westpac analysis shows.

Genuine easing cycles by the Fed result in the Australian dollar falling about 7 per cent in the first year while insurance rate cut cycles tend to cause a rise in the Aussie of about 8 per cent over the following 12 months.

Westpac's head of foreign exchange strategy Richard Franulovich said the evidence showed the Australian dollar tended to be far more resilient during a cycle of Fed insurance rate cuts.

"If the Fed only delivers insurance, by definition the global picture is OK keeping the Australian dollar supported. If a true Fed easing cycle emerges, the global picture is by definition weak and the Australian dollar tends to be weaker," Mr Franulovich said.

"We only looked at the first year after Fed cuts, but if I was a betting person I'd say that into the second and third year of Fed cuts, such is the loss of US dollar support that it actually helps the Australian dollar."

The question now is whether the Fed's rate cuts are of the "insurance" type or are part of genuine easing to avoid a recession.

sentiment_pool.headline: Extreme heat and flames to close out 2019
sentiment_pool.text:
A severe to extreme heatwave is expected to worsen bushfire conditions in Australia's south-east in the last days of 2019, while officials debate disaster policy and national preparedness.

The weather bureau said extreme heat, which smashed record high temperatures earlier in December, would re-emerge in South Australia on Friday, and travel across to NSW and Victoria at the weekend. "Some areas are forecast to reach extreme heatwave conditions," a Bureau of Meteorology spokeswoman said, adding that "severe" heatwaves could reach southern NSW first. "With the increasing heat and winds, the fire danger will worsen into the new week, with Monday and Tuesday most likely to be the most significant fire weather days."

The deteriorating conditions were expected to further strain firefighters, 2500 of whom were out in the field in NSW over Christmas, and keep the spotlight on the Prime Minister, who spent this week touring fire-affected areas. On Boxing Day, 1400 firefighters were battling 72 fires across the state, 30 of them uncontained, including the blaze at Gospers Mountain that has burnt almost 500,000 hectares.

More than 829 homes have been destroyed and another 333 damaged in NSW since September, the latest statistics show. Sixty-two non-residential structures (such as car yards) and 1925 outbuildings were destroyed, as more than 3.4 million hectares have burnt.

sentiment_pool.headline: Melbourne on the rise in 2020
sentiment_pool.text:
Melbourne's housing market is set to eclipse Sydney's in 2020 fuelled by a stronger economy and higher population growth, although the rapid pace is expected to lose steam as listings rise and affordability worsens.

CoreLogic is expecting Melbourne home values to rise by up to 14 per cent in the next 12 months, while Sydney is forecast to grow by up to 12 per cent.

"Considering the strong economy and demographic fundamentals, we could see the Melbourne housing market outperform Sydney's in 2020," said CoreLogic head of research Tim Lawless.

"Although we don't expect the rapid price growth evident during the past few months to be sustained, the high rate of population growth, low rate of unemployment and lower housing prices relative to Sydney should help support further gains in home values next year."

Since bottoming out in May, Melbourne's housing values had surged by 8.6 per cent, while unit values jumped by 8.1 per cent.

At this rate, CoreLogic expects Melbourne home values to hit a new record as early as January next year.

Sydney house values have rebounded by 8.8 per cent and a smaller 6.8 per cent for units since bottoming out in May.

Mr Lawless expects Sydney home values to reach a new high by March next year, however worsening affordability, slowing population growth and higher stock levels could slow the current growth momentum.

"It's hard to imagine such a rapid rebound in housing values being sustained far into 2020," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Kina shareholder cashes out
sentiment_pool.text:
Kina Securities' biggest shareholder has cashed out of the Papua New Guinea diversified financial services provider.

Nambawan Super Limited divested 24.05 million shares, representing 14.67 per cent of securities on issue, in a block trade which got under way after-market yesterday, according to terms sent to fundies.

Morgans Financial oversaw the $32.7 million trade.

It is understood the shares were picked up by new and existing investors.

Nambawan Super is the biggest superannuation fund in PNG and was one of the cornerstone investors in Kina's initial public offering in 2015.

The offer price was pegged at $1.36 a security, which reflected a 9.93 per cent discount to the last close and an 8.86 per cent discount to the five-day volume weighted average price. Bids were to be submitted by 5.30pm Sydney time, the term sheet said.

On a stormy night in October, a handful of students met for the first time at the Manhattan's Columbia University. It was 11pm, cold and raining, but the group trekked here after being summoned by text messages and flyers pasted to dormitory doors and in the library. They were here to, in the words of one student at the meeting, "become TikTok famous".

This was the inaugural meeting of Columbia University's first club devoted to TikTok, the latest social media app to capture the attention of teenagers. It's a short-form video app that offers users sophisticated editing tools and visual effects; lip-syncing, comedy sketches and "challenge" dance videos dominate TikTok, which is free to use.

The app is owned by ByteDance, a Beijing-based tech company valued by SoftBank last year at $US75 billion ($110 billion) - making it one of the world's most valuable start-ups. It says it has more than 1 billion active users, which would have it trailing Facebook, but more popular than Twitter and Snapchat combined.

Many of those billion users are young people hoping to parlay the app's burgeoning popularity into their own.

Isaac Quiles is one of them. At Columbia, he has set out to turn his hobby - filming silly videos in the hopes of going viral - into a campus-wide organisation and charity fundraiser.

sentiment_pool.headline: Montem eyes $100m listing
sentiment_pool.text:
Two years is a long time in the fast-moving world of initial public offerings.

And it's long enough for coking coal outfit Montem Resources to get set for another charge at the ASX boards.

Street Talk can reveal the Peter Doyle-led company has appointed stockbroker Morgans Financial to manage an IPO that could see Montem list with a market capitalisation of as much as $100 million.

Montem got set for a sharemarket float in 2018 but it didn't get off the ground.

However, 18 months later and it has invested more money into its two Canada-based coking coal projects, which it hopes will be a compelling proposition for potential investors.

Doyle and his advisers will no doubt point out that one of Montem's projects - named the Chinook Properties - is next to the Grassy Mountain coking coal project owned by Riversdale Resources, which was bought by Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting last year.

And while ESG concerns have seen some investors turn away from coal companies, Montem is sure to emphasise the metallurgical coal it produces is used to make the steel that underpins the world's infrastructure, and not electricity.

Regal Funds Management and Rich Lister Brian Flannery are already on Montem's register.

sentiment_pool.headline: UK splits from Australia, US on Huawei
sentiment_pool.text:
The global struggle over Huawei's future in 5G isn't following the script.

Australia's decision to ban the Chinese telco giant from all involvement in the rollout of the new mobile network was seen as the precursor to other allies in the Five Eyes intelligence network taking a similar approach.

Instead, a conservative British government led by Boris Johnson is poised to ignore concerted US pressure and announce this week that Huawei will be permitted a role in its 5G network after all.

It also means the Australian and British security agencies have come to very different views on the ability to manage the security risks of having such a powerful Chinese telco equipment supplier. That is going to complicate the usual exchange of intelligence between the Five Eyes partners of the US, Britain, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. The US has been threatening to limit intelligence briefings to Britain if it proceeds with what Secretary of State Mike Pompeo has labelled a "momentous decision".

Yet despite objections from some of his ministers, including the defence minister, Boris Johnson is believed to have been persuaded the economic and technology costs of blocking Huawei's participation are too high - and unnecessary.

sentiment_pool.headline: LAW GRADS IN THE RAT RACE
sentiment_pool.text:
Disruption Something is going on in legal circles, and it's a bottom-up change, write Hannah Wootton and David Marin-Guzman.

In September last year, management at top-tier law firm Ashurst received a letter unlike any they had seen before.

Nineteen of the young lawyers who had just completed the firm's prestigious graduate program had banded together to ask for more money.

The $80,000-plus salaries they had been on as grads, and which were going up now they had finished the program, might have seemed hefty but compared to the riches being offered by similar firms, the sums were less impressive.

An internal meeting followed. The 19 junior lawyers received explanations about their pay and the status quo was maintained.

But a few months later, some started receiving backpay for the long hours they had pulled as grads.

It was one of several unprecedented events in the legal industry in the past 18 months.

SafeWork investigations into lawyer fatigue and overwork, new industrial rules on hours and pay and an extraordinary push to re-regulate the sector have shaken up a decades-old culture.

All three of the events culminated in the revelation this month of widespread firm reviews into whether graduate lawyers have been underpaid due to excessive hours.

While many firms are yet to uncover issues, the revelation some grads at Ashurst were underpaid between $10,000 and $15,000 raises questions about how far underpayments will spread.

sentiment_pool.headline: Neuberger Berman kick-starts raisings
sentiment_pool.text:
Global asset manager Neuberger Berman is leading the charge of listed debt funds as it seeks to raise $750 million from yield-hungry investors.

The NBI Global Corporate Income Trust, which invests in global high- yield bonds, has already raised more than $900 million, and the follow-on offer comes ahead of an expected rush of prospective fixed-income listed investment trusts.

The fund's second follow-on offer since it listed in August 2018 is to meet demand among investors, said Vivek Bommi, the listed fund's senior portfolio manager.

"Since the IPO, [the units] have almost been at a premium the entire time, so it shows there is latent demand for income based products," Mr Bommi told The Australian Financial Review.

"This is one where we have thousands of shareholders and the theme from them is they would like to add more, but they don't want to pay a premium."

The listed investment trust invests in around 300 global sub-investment grade corporate bonds and targets a distribution to investors of 5.25 per cent.

It was among the first global corporate debt funds to raise money from Australian individual investors via the listed investment trust, or LIT, format.

Since the Neuberger Berman raising, private equity funds KKR and Partners Group have issued listed private debt funds on the ASX, while global bond giant PIMCO has made clear its intentions to raise money via a LIT.

sentiment_pool.headline: APRA risks 'wasting time' with super review
sentiment_pool.text:
The prudential regulator should abandon plans to assess the performance of 40,000 superannuation options on the market because the task will be a "time-consuming distraction", a leading academic says.

Scott Donald, the director of the Centre for Law, Markets and Regulation at the University of NSW, said the mammoth undertaking was unnecessary because ratings agencies already performed such analysis.

"The resource commitment required for this task will distract APRA doing a good job in the all-important MySuper sector," he told The Australian Financial Review.

In early December the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority published analysis of the performance of no-frills MySuper options, including investment returns and fees.

The options are required by law to be simple and low cost, and most big funds offer at least one MySuper product.

APRA deputy chairman Helen Rowell has said the regulator's next task will be to publish analysis for the 40,000 or so other products that super funds offer.

An article on the MySuper heatmap written by Dr Donald will appear in the January edition of the Australian Superannuation Law Bulletin.

It will be one of the first independent academic assessments of the heatmap initiative, which comes as APRA is under pressure to be seen to be cracking down on under-performance.

"The last thing we need is for APRA to get swamped and for its findings to be diluted, by the generation of heatmaps on such an ambitious scale," Dr Donald writes.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX could hit 7000, but don't get too excited
sentiment_pool.text:
This year Australian shares will topple the record of 2019 and break through 7000 points for the first time according to leading market strategists, who warn the historic feat won't be enough to match last year's double-digit returns.

A gradual improvement in global growth was identified as driver for the year ahead, where resources and energy stocks stand out as a potential source of gains.

But the mounting tensions between the US and Iran highlight the risk to global trade and could develop into a flashpoint for equity markets, which may boost oil and gas producers but would weigh on resources stocks.

Morgan Stanley's Australian equity strategist, Chris Nicol, expects earnings growth to remain subdued this year, despite being on an improving path. "We do see a turn in the earnings cycle later in 2020 but this is more relevant for [2021 financial year] earnings forecasts," he said.

"[This] will be a year when companies will have to try hard to keep their investors happy, as they'll be missing the tailwinds of easier central bank policy and lower starting valuations as they enjoyed in 2019," MST Marquee senior analyst Hasan Tevfik said.

Along with other market observers, Mr Tevfik cites company earnings growth as a hurdle for shares in the year ahead.

sentiment_pool.headline: Ola, Didi tipped to face uphill battle
sentiment_pool.text:
The chief executive of the company that operates the 13cabs taxi network says new ride-sharing entrants like Ola and Didi will find it very hard to make inroads into the powerful position established by Uber because they are only competing on price.

Andrew Skelton, the boss of A2B, which runs 13cabs and a fleet of 9800 taxis, says in contrast his firm has been investing heavily in lifting driver standards and the quality of vehicles, and that will deliver a long-term pay-off.

Mr Skelton says there won't be room in the end for all of the new ride-sharing firms in the market, with Ola and Didi effectively trying to claw away customers from Uber with price-driven strategies.

"I think Uber starts a long way in front and has a big advantage. It is all price-driven. There is nothing really that differentiates them," he said.

A2B has undertaken a large modernisation program and invested in technology programs and a rebranding to give 13cabs a more contemporary look and feel, while also forcing taxi owners to retire old vehicles under age restrictions that began in January 2019.

Net profit after tax slipped 37 per cent to $3.5 million in the first half of 2019-20, even though revenue was up 4 per cent to $105 million as it stepped up capital spending. The company kept the interim dividend steady at 4¢ per share. A2B had spent $6.6 million on in-car equipment in the first half, including $4.3 million on safety cameras.

sentiment_pool.text:
Exclusive | The federal government will review tax barriers deterring businesses from paying workers employee shares, to lift participation in equity compensation schemes used by some of America's most successful technology start-ups.

Committee chairman and Liberal MP Jason Falinski said the alignment of incentives of workers and owners encouraged them to share in the risk and success of a new venture. Employee shares had been crucial to "some of the most successful and innovative companies in the world - Google, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon".

sentiment_pool.headline: Xero hour: ASX tech index ready to take off
sentiment_pool.text:
Accounting technology giant Xero will head the Australian Securities Exchange's new technology index to be unveiled today, giving investors the chance to invest in the fastest-growing segment of the market in one trade.

The ASX will launch the S&P/ASX All Technology Index or the S&P/ASX All Tech for short, at a ceremony at the exchange in Sydney, with technology minister Karen Andrews and executives from each of the WAAAX stocks (Wisetech, Afterpay, Altium, Appen and Xero) there for the ribbon cutting.

The index will go live from Monday morning and will be a smaller, localised version of the US's Nasdaq composite index.

The executive general manager of listings and issuer services at the ASX, Max Cunningham, said returns from investing in tech had exceeded the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 Index in recent years, and this new index would be seen as highly investable.

"There are 20 tech companies with market caps over $1 billion, and the index is a barometer of the general health and performance of that part of the market," he said.

After Xero, the top five of the inaugural list comprises Computershare, Afterpay, REA Group and Altium.

Mr Cunningham has spearheaded a push for the ASX to be seen as a junior Nasdaq board, and as a well regarded home for tech companies which are large, but not necessarily the equivalents of Alphabet or Atlassian in terms of market capitalisation and profile.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX charges higher despite outbreak toll
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian sharemarket rose to its highest level in more than two weeks yesterday, as investors disregarded the growing number of coronavirus deaths amid strong earnings results.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index advanced 42.8 points, or 0.6 per cent, to 7055.3, its highest level since January 24.

Stocks across Asia moved higher yesterday as investors continued to shrug off concerns over the economic impact of the widening coronavirus, with the number of deaths rising above 1000.

Investors on the local market turned their attention to earnings season, positioning themselves ahead of a flurry of results in the second half of the week.

"A pick-up in equity market volatility in recent weeks is starting to result in the emergence of meaningful bottom-up investment opportunities, both on the long and short side, as investors are shying away from uncertainty," said Tribeca Investment Partners lead portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu.

"Particularly as we head into the interim reporting season, we retain a key focus on stock fundamentals."

Transurban was among the market leaders yesterday after reporting an 11 per cent increase in its interim net profit, with traffic increasing 2.3 per cent across its toll roads. The profit rise drove an increase in the company's interim dividend, up to 31¢ from 29¢ a year earlier. Transurban's shares closed 0.9 per cent higher at $16.25.

sentiment_pool.headline: WA health giant looks east for young dollars
sentiment_pool.text:
Western Australia's biggest health insurer HBF will begin a major marketing push in the eastern states this month in an effort to add more young people to its ageing pool of members.

The not-for-profit fund will join major players such as Medibank and NIB in the scramble to persuade the highly valuable but increasingly coy younger market that it needs private health insurance.

Unlike some players, HBF will not try to win them over with budget products. The fund's chief executive John Van Der Wielen says he believes customers in their 20s and 30s can be persuaded to buy premium grade policies.

The campaign, which has been led by advertising agency Leo Burnett with input from ad guru and TV personality Russel Howcroft of PWC, will favour digital channels like Facebook and YouTube over television, newspapers and billboards. It will feature charismatic West Australian marsupial the quokka in an attempt to leverage the fund's west coast roots.

HBF will not use broker channels such as comparethemarket.com and iSelect, of which Mr Van Der Wielen is a fierce critic.

"We were the first big insurer to come off broker sites, because the cost of broker commissions is nearly 30 per cent. The industry is shrinking in size and we're spending twice as much on commissions," he said.

"I'm absolutely and categorically not supportive of the current broker regime in health insurance.

sentiment_pool.headline: Next Capital inks third deal from $300m fund IV
sentiment_pool.text:
They say good things come in threes.

And mid-market private equity firm Next Capital has done its bit to make sure that holds true, closing a third deal for its $300 million-odd fourth fund last week.

Street Talk understands Next Capital has purchased a 51 per cent stake in supply chain, property and project management services business TM Insight, as the company's founders Travis Erridge and Milan Andjelkovic sold down their holdings.

TMI has 50 staff across four offices in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Singapore and works with clients such as BMW, Kathmandu, Woolworths, Asahi and Bunnings to streamline their supply chains.

The Next Capital deal gave TMI an implied enterprise value of about $60 million, which was five times its earnings. The founders plan to use the new equity to expand TMI's offering into Asia, from a Singaporean launchpad.

Next Capital worked with KPMG and Talbot Sayer on the purchase, while TMI tapped Equity Advisory.

The stake will sit in Next Capital's fourth fund, which is on track for a final close at just above the $300 million mark in coming weeks.

The John White and Patrick Elliott-led firm has already tucked away two other deals into the new fund, acquiring a majority stake in health roll-up InterHealthcare for $100 million last December and purchasing Silver Chef's hospitality business three months before that.

sentiment_pool.headline: Copper miner looks to life after DeGrussa
sentiment_pool.text:
Sandfire Resources is grappling with the reality that all good things must come to an end.

With its flagship DeGrussa mine in Western Australia reaching the last years of its remarkable life, the copper producer needs to find replacement tonnes - and soon.

The good news is Sandfire has options but they involve the Perth-headquartered miner making a big leap offshore where it has development projects in Botswana and Montana.

The big question for investors is where does Sandfire land in making the jump. Is it on two feet or is there a stumble?

Right now, DeGrussa continues to deliver for Sandfire, which is well on track to meet its 2019-20 production guidance of 70,000-72,000 tonnes of copper and 38,000-40,000 ounces of gold. But there are just two years and change to run on the mine's life.

Meanwhile, Sandfire is stepping up activity on the big parcel of land it picked up in Botswana through the acquisition of MOD Resources, including the T3 project.

Sandfire expects to make a decision on mining at T3, a copper-silver project in the Kalahari copper belt, after releasing an updated feasibility study and ore reserve in the June quarter.

It is understood Sandfire is talking to banks about the funding package as it prepares for a final investment decision.

The company is also encouraged by drilling results from a target known as A4 Dome about 8 kilometres west of T3 in its 11,700 square kilometre package.

The worst-kept secret in Canberra for months has been Treasury trying to convince the government to embrace stimulus. Australia's success or failure in public health will determine the effectiveness of the economic measures. People won't deploy much stimulus until they feel safe.

The central task now for government is threefold: lock the country down (with comprehensive testing and contact tracing); support incomes until after the virus peaks; and "triage" firms financially to avoid insolvency and mass joblessness.

sentiment_pool.headline: Deflation spiral risks a rerun of Depression
sentiment_pool.text:
The coronavirus recession and oil price crash could push inflation below zero for the first time since the Great Depression, causing a dangerous deflation spiral that will require a huge government spending stimulus after the virus passes, a former top Treasury economist has warned.

Canberra-based Outlook Economics director Peter Downes said that because the Reserve Bank of Australia would not cut the cash rate below the current 0.25 per cent, real interest rates - which are adjusted for inflation - would rise and hurt the economic recovery.

The government would ultimately need to step in and inject another huge fiscal stimulus on top of the $84 billion announced so far, he said.

Rising unemployment, weak wage growth and the oil price collapse to below $US30 a barrel after negotiations broke down between Russia and the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries would push inflation to or below zero by the middle of next year, according to his preliminary economic modelling.

That is despite a likely short-term price spike in some grocery items because of panic buying.

"Once you throw in the low oil prices with unemployment rising you get a disinflation dynamic developing," said Mr Downes, a former top forecaster at Treasury and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

sentiment_pool.headline: Scape offers student digs to boost coronavirus fight

The country's largest provider of student accommodation, Scape, could free up building space across its east coast portfolio to accommodate COVID-19 cases as its own occupancy tightens.

Under the plan, Scape could consolidate student residents into some buildings in order to leave entire facilities vacant and available in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.

Those buildings could then be devoted to housing coronavirus self-isolation cases, executive chairman Craig Carracher said.

A key hurdle was amending existing state-based tenancy laws, which prevented landlords from unilaterally moving residents.

"I can't as a landlord tell my student 'you've got to terminate your tenancy and take up an alternative tenancy'," Mr Carracher told The Australian Financial Review.

Scape has about 7000 beds in its portfolio and has its foot on another 7000 acquired through the $2 billion purchase of the Urbanest portfolio, the largest single deal in the commercial property sector last year.

The Foreign Investment Review Board had not yet approved that acquisition but the green light was expected within days.

With a large exposure to the overseas student market, Scape moved early in its response to the looming threat of COVID-19, putting returning students into voluntary isolation in its facilities from January 24.

Most rooms in Scape facilities were self-contained studios with individual ventilation systems and non-opening windows.

sentiment_pool.headline: Clearance rate to be hammered
sentiment_pool.text:
Auctions Fear appears to be winning as buyers and sellers reconsider real-estate plans.

Auction clearance rates are poised to fall as more buyers delay their purchase and shun public gatherings for fear of contracting the fast-spreading coronavirus.

Property search activity - a leading indicator of the health of the property market - has already fallen during the past two weeks.

"All search activity on realestate.com.au has slowed over the past week," said Nerida Conisbee, chief economist with the property listing site.

Queensland recorded the biggest drop in searches, while Victoria has had the lowest decline in activity.

"There is no doubt that the coronavirus is impacting buyer confidence, despite the interest rate cut last week," said Ms Conisbee.

"We are likely to see clearance rates decline this weekend.

" But at the same time, listings may be impacted as people hold off selling until there is greater certainty around the spread of the virus and ultimately what happens to the economy."

Property portal Domain said the number of people attending open homes had also dropped.

The data gleaned from its Homepass app that agents use to check people in at open homes showed that the number had fallen in all capital cities over the past two weeks compared to early February.

sentiment_pool.headline: Young Rich tip: don't be afraid to let yourself fail
sentiment_pool.text:
You don't have to be a pioneer like Elon Musk or Steve Jobs to start a multimillion-dollar business, according to Financial Review Young Rich List members Nick Bell and Josh Fegan.

Mr Bell, 39, and Mr Fegan, 35, were valued at $217 million and $56 million respectively by 2019's Financial Review Young Rich List, which ranks Australia's wealthiest self-made people aged 40 and under.

However, both of them jumped on bandwagons to get there, they readily admitted at The Australian Financial Review Business Summit on Wednesday, which extracted from them their lessons on building businesses and creating wealth.

"Being first to market means you're taking all the risks. I don't want to be Elon Musk," said Mr Bell, who catapulted into the Young Rich List in 2017 when Melbourne IT bought the Australian arm of his digital advertising agency WME for $39 million.

"I'd rather take an existing business model that you can see works, and do it better."

WME began when Mr Bell, at the time running a failing skincare start-up, started a side hustle in promising businesses that appeared on the second page of a Google keyword search that he could elevate them to the first page.

"I didn't know anything about digital marketing at the time, but I thought that I could sell it - and then get in a third party to actually do the work," Mr Bell said.

sentiment_pool.headline: PM's crisis call to big business
sentiment_pool.text:
Scott Morrison says the "time is now" to sacrifice the forecast budget surplus for economic stimulus, while also demanding big business help pull Australia through a downturn which, he says, is "potentially greater" than the global financial crisis.
