"We now have one goal in 2020 - to protect the health, wellbeing and livelihoods of Australians through this global crisis, and to ensure that when the recovery comes, and it will, we are well positioned to bounce back strongly on the other side."

With the government to release later this week a multibillion-dollar coronavirus stimulus package in a bid to avoid recession, the Prime Minister will say that big business has "a huge role to play', including providing paid leave to workers, including casuals, who need time off due to the virus.

Warning companies that they will be forever judged on how they respond over the next six months to "one of those national interest moments", Mr Morrison, whose package will focus on small and medium enterprises, will call on large businesses to do what they must to keep their workers employed.

"Hold onto your people, you will need them on the other side. Wherever possible, support them - whether full-time, part-time, or casual - including with paid leave if they need to take time off due to the virus," he will say.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX edges lower on renewed uncertainty
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian sharemarket edged lower yesterday, with a rally in material and energy stocks not enough to avoid a fourth day of losses for local shares.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index dipped 4.2 points, or 0.1 per cent, to 5217.1, with the market now sitting at a two-week low.

A rally on Wall Street on Wednesday was driven partly by a recovery in oil prices, although sentiment remains fragile, particularly as US companies report their quarterly earnings and Australian banks prepare to report interim results next week.

"While improving news on both the policy and the coronavirus fronts propelled markets out of the deep gloom of mid-March, we believe that the next major battle for market sentiment will be fought over the outlook for the world economy in the second half of the year," said Janus Henderson Investors head of multi-asset team Paul O'Connor.

"One cautious view that must be respected here is that investors have very little visibility on this outlook right now, given the uncertainty surrounding the coronavirus and the economic restrictions associated with it.

During the digital platforms inquiry, competition tsar Rod Sims spoke about the idea of creative destruction: innovation and technological change creating a more effective and efficient product. It's something that has occurred countless times through humanity's existence.

But Facebook and Google don't create any journalism, and the world is worse for it. Their response to the digital platforms inquiry sought to misdirect government and hide their power.

As recently as March last year, Google argued it didn't have market power, saying it faces fierce competition from little-known rival DuckDuckGo.

Farmers are banging down the door of a federal government agency tasked with doling out $4 billion in loans amid fears a finance squeeze will limit agricultural production just when Australia needs it most.

The Regional Investment Corporation (RIC) has been overwhelmed by loan applications from farmers wanting to restock and plant crops after what is seen as drought-breaking rain.

Farmer frustration has forced the federal government and Bendigo and Adelaide Bank, which is contracted to support RIC, to hire more staff after loan approvals blew out to more than six months.

Farm lobby groups are already fighting against a drought in finance linked to falls in equity that traditionally follows prolonged dry weather.

In the case of grain growers, the window to secure funding for this year's crop is closing fast, while the low Australian dollar is pushing up the cost of farm inputs.

The National Farmers' Federation has been in urgent talks with the federal government, RIC and banks to make sure farmers are adequately financed.

NFF president Fiona Simson said she could understand why some farmers were disgruntled with RIC, dubbed Barnaby's Bank after former deputy prime minister Barnaby Joyce.

"There have been some resourcing issues there. I don't think there is any doubt that it [RIC] is far from what it was envisioned to be," she said. "We have worked very hard to make sure it can step up and deliver the products that it needs to."

sentiment_pool.text:
Backstop Super funds should be allowed to borrow emergency cash from the RBA, but must cop a haircut to avoid moral hazard.

Australia faces the risk of a run on its super funds. While we are accustomed to thinking about the potential of a run on banks, the idea of a run on super is novel.

Banks face the risk of runs because their depositors can withdraw their funds at any time. It would be possible for each bank to retain its own very high level of liquid reserves to manage this risk - as the very first banks did before the emergence of central banks. However, prudential regulation and a backstop offered by the central banks have made that unnecessary. Socially, we have judged this as better because it allows the banks to take more risk and to lend more freely, thereby helping grow our economies.

Now, in the midst of these extraordinary circumstances, it would have been better for Australians if the superannuation sector had faced a similar set of constraints to the banks - minimum liquidity requirements coupled by access to central bank liquidity in extreme situations, but subject to significant haircuts in return for emergency liquidity. As with the banks, this would have allowed super funds - especially the industry funds that have tended to chase higher returns and hold less liquid assets - to better optimise their portfolios in full knowledge of how they would manage liquidity risk. The 135 Smiggle stores in Britain will stay closed until at least June 1 and in Ireland a handful of stores will remain shut until June 29 in line with government restrictions.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX heading for worst year since GFC
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian sharemarket is on track to record its worst performance in a fiscal year since the global financial crisis after local shares tumbled to a two-week low yesterday.

The local market is down more than 12 per cent over the past 12 months with the end of today's session set to mark the first negative financial year since 2015-16 and the biggest fall since 2008-09.

The poor year comes despite the market hitting a record high in February before the COVID-19 pandemic. The worst sell-off in a decade then saw the market fall 36.5 per cent before rallying on record fiscal stimulus and central bank action.

Yesterday, the S&P/ASX 200 Index fell 89.1 points, or 1.5 per cent, to 5815, its lowest since June 15 as pandemic fears once again gripped the market and pushed investors towards safer havens.

US shares ended last week firmly lower after a spike in new COVID-19 cases across the nation fanned concerns about a slowdown in the economic recovery as states introduced new restrictions to curtail the virus' spread.

Yesterday, Victoria reported 75 new cases of COVID-19, its fourth-highest single-day increase since the start of the pandemic and the 13th consecutive day of double-digit increases.

The US is also facing a record surge in new cases, with some states scaling back their reopening plans, delaying longer any economic recovery.

Maybe. But even if that's true - albeit far from satisfactory - there's one area where progress in the gender equality battle has stalled, and even gone backwards: the home front.

The gap between the amount of tedious housework done by men and women in Western societies is rising. In a world where women want to have it all, as it were - that healthy career and that happy family - they're having to put in a double shift to get it.

Men are certainly doing more housework than they used to: an average of 18 hours a week in 2016 in Britain, compared with just 80 minutes a week in 1971. But women are clocking up twice that, at 36 hours a week.

In Australia, women report averaging 15 hours of housework a week, men just five hours. And the difference isn't narrowing. In fact, British and American men in their 30s and 40s now do one to two hours less housework than their counterparts did in the mid-1990s. Self-funded retirees in self-managed superannuation funds fear an income crisis because of falling returns, lower dividends and interest rates, and uncertainty over rental returns.

More than two dozen PwC partners have left or are planning to leave the firm as new chief executive Tom Seymour slashes costs, cuts staff and restructures the firm to adapt to the evolving advisory market and offset the COVID-19 downturn in business. Some of the partners heading for the exit of the 700-partner strong firm were senior leaders under former CEO Luke Sayers.

They include Sammy Kumar, a member of PwC's executive for the past 10 years and the former national consulting leader and head of the firm's ventures business; Peter Mastos, a current member of the global deals leadership team; Richard Shackcloth, the digital platforms leader; and Tony Peake, former global leader for government and public sector. sentiment_pool.headline: 'Don't buy into theory office space is dead'
sentiment_pool.text:
Non-bank lender Merricks Capital has backed a recovery in demand for office space post-COVID-19, after providing $150 million of construction finance to ensure developer Alfasi Group can complete a speculative office development in Cremorne on Melbourne's city fringe.

Alfasi, which also operates big construction and equipment hire businesses, had used its own funds to kick off construction of its 20,000sq m, A-Grade office tower at 510 Church Street last year.

However, when potential financiers pulled back from the project in the wake of the pandemic, Merricks - which is backed by the ultra-wealthy Liberman family - stepped in to provide finance through its Partners Fund, which lends capital raised from institutional and high-net-worth investors.

It is the second speculative office development in Melbourne that Merricks has agreed to finance. In November, developer Goldfields secured funding from the non-bank lender for a $300 million office tower in South Yarra.

"We don't buy into the theory that office space is dead," said Andrew Torrington, managing director of investments at Merricks Capital.

"Post-COVID, it's up in the air what the office market will look like. We don't really know. We know it will change.

"But our research suggests there is still demand out there for large-scale tenancies. Corporates may not take 10 floors, but they won't retreat out of the office market entirely."

sentiment_pool.headline: Gaslighting just weakens our fight against the virus
sentiment_pool.text:
Pandemic Shaming the Andrews government is futile when it is decades of free-market utopianism that has hurt our capacity to deal with COVID-19.

After a period of relative harmony, Australia's navigation of COVID-19 has entered stormy waters. Finger pointing, point scoring and recriminations are the order of the day, even as this deadly virus pays no heed to its prey's ideological tastes.

Parochialism is in vogue. Victoria is the federation's statum non grata. Divisive voices target multicultural communities, notably residents of Melbourne's public housing towers subject to strict lockdown and economically precarious suburban working-class communities. Australians of Chinese and Asian heritage continue to endure racist attacks. Inadequately trained private security guards supervising returned travellers held in quarantine are the object of public opprobrium.

Most of the tumult and shouting transpires on social media platforms, a toxic sewer of incivility and clashing egos, licensed by anonymity. Yet bilious memes and character assassinations have seeped into mainstream public debates, courtesy of right-wing libertarians attached to the Institute of Public Affairs think tank, a smattering of journalists and fringe politicians, most prominently Tim Smith, a Liberal member of the Victorian Parliament.

sentiment_pool.headline: Will Hong Kong collapse or thrive? We'll have to wait and see
sentiment_pool.text:
The last 12 months have not been kind to Hong Kong.

Even before the damage to the economy from the COVID-19 restrictions, it suffered from months of school and business closures and a collapse in tourism and hospitality thanks to almost six months of protests, initially over a proposed extradition treaty. They morphed into a more violent and widely televised "freedom and democracy" protests towards the end of the year.

It is in the aftermath of these protests that we now see the new security law, imposed at the beginning of this month. The reaction in the West has been near-universal condemnation mixed with projections of the end of times for Hong Kong, and yet the financial markets have risen.

So who is right? Is Hong Kong going to collapse or thrive?

As with all seemingly black-and-white issues, the background is more nuanced and cannot be separated from the new cold war between the US and China, and the fact that an anti-China stance is a bipartisan issue in the upcoming US election.

Fifteen years ago, the US economy was 15 times the size of China's. Now, on a purchasing power parity basis, China has overtaken the US - and it has done so without adopting the preferred US-centric model for emerging markets.

sentiment_pool.headline: Forrests outbid Indigenous group for WA cattle station
sentiment_pool.text:
Mining billionaire Andrew Forrest says conservation and heritage considerations must be balanced against the need for farming and job creation after confirming his purchase of a vast land holding nestled on Western Australia's Fitzroy River.

Dr Forrest's private holding company, Tattarang, outbid an Indigenous group for Jubilee Downs. He joins Gina Rinehart and Kerry Stokes as owners of big cattle stations in the Fitzroy Valley.

The $30 million purchase from American billionaire and environmentalist Edward Bass, and minority shareholders Keith and Karen Anderson, was revealed by The Australian Financial Review on Wednesday.

In a joint statement, Dr Forrest and his wife, Nicola, said they looked forward to working "with and for" the Yi-Martuwarra people, who came up short with a $25 million bid for Jubilee Downs and the incorporated Quanbun Downs station, which cover 220,000 hectares and have about 90 kilometres of Fitzroy River frontage.

"We recognise the Yi-Martuwarra have been the guardians of this sacred country for tens of thousands of years," the Forrests said. "We very much look forward to working with their local elders and communities to ensure access, and to preserve and protect significant and sacred sites."

The Forrests said the need to protect WA's Kimberley region and the river shouldn't rule out sustainable agriculture and jobs for local communities. They intend to commission a baseline native fauna study at Jubilee Downs and build on the work of the Anders

sentiment_pool.headline: Never say never on zero brokerage in Australia: fintechs
sentiment_pool.text:
The prospect of Robinhood-style free trades for individual investors in this country is still a fair way off, despite the lockdown spawning record numbers of new retail traders on the Australian sharemarket.

This week, budget trading platform SelfWealth said it added just under 25,000 active new retail traders in the six months to June 30 from a total of 46,455. It also posted six consecutive record months of trade volumes to June.

The ballooning number of novice traders is coming from younger generations attracted by the market-leading $9.50 flat brokerage rate per trade: 60 per cent of new clients in 2020 are aged 20 to 34. That means mum and dad investors are being usurped by their working-age children.

SelfWealth managing director Rob Edgley said a generation of savers was being transformed into a generation of traders.

"You can't watch your term deposit on an app, can you? It's very boring," he said. "But if you're in that Gen Y or Millennial age group, you live your life online, you're not likely to ring a financial planner, you're likely to find info yourself, and you operate in a world of social media."

The broker just posted its maiden quarterly positive operating cash flow of $809,000 on revenue of $4.18 million. Its share price has nearly quadrupled from 17¢ to 66¢ in 2020. About 70 per cent of its revenue is from brokerage fees. The balance is income on clients' cash balances, which totalled $366 million as at June 30.

sentiment_pool.headline: QSuper quits financial advice, leading to job losses
sentiment_pool.text:
The $110 billion industry fund QSuper is the latest financial institution to exit the comprehensive financial advice, resulting in at least 20 redundancies and deploying its planners to call-centre advice.

The Queensland-based superannuation giant will cease providing holistic advice to new members from Monday, opting instead for so-called intra-fund advice, limited to members' superannuation and not their broader financial affairs.

The decision will result in 23 jobs made redundant in August, primarily support staff providing paraplanning services to licensed advisers. Another 32 employees potentially face redundancy if they can't be rehoused within the QSuper group.

QSuper now has 75 individuals listed on ASIC's register of financial advisers as licensed by its QInvest subsidiary, of which 61 are understood to be practising advisers. Sources said the fund had no plans to cull its workforce of licensed advisers, though the services they provide to new members are being restricted.

A review of the super fund's advice operations found the comprehensive financial planning services had been used by less than 1 per cent of its 585,000 members across the state, with many opting instead to use third-party advisers or the limited intra-fund and phone-based service.

sentiment_pool.headline: Bega to replace China's Mengniu
sentiment_pool.text:
Bega Cheese is firming as a strong Australian alternative to acquire Lion's dairy and drinks business after Treasurer Josh Frydenberg blocked a Chinese takeover of the company on national interest grounds.

A domestic contender would fit neatly into the Morrison government's post-COVID-19 focus on trying to encourage more local manufacturing in areas where Australia has a natural advantage - such as making greater use of its plentiful, high-quality food and dairy supplies. Some Australian super funds are also believed to be interested in investment prospects while other private equity or corporate bidders are also possible.

China Mengniu Dairy Co withdrew from its $600 million bid for Lion Dairy & Drinks yesterday because the Treasurer was not going to allow it to proceed - as revealed last week by The Australian Financial Review.

This was despite recommendations of support from the Foreign Investment Review Board and Treasury, and approval from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

The likelihood of a range of potential alternative buyers, particularly including Australian bidders like Bega Cheese, would have made such a sensitive decision somewhat easier for the Treasurer. It is still a big personal call for Frydenberg, given Australia's official policy of welcoming foreign investment.

sentiment_pool.headline: NIB commits to riding travel insurance storm
sentiment_pool.text:
NIB boss Mark Fitzgibbon says he has not given up on travel insurance despite losing $20 million as the pandemic shut down the industry virtually overnight.

NIB, which is primarily a health insurer, reported an overall 40 per cent fall in full-year profit as the expected boost from a halt to elective surgery during the first round of COVID-19 lockdowns failed to materialise.

But it was the travel insurance business that really suffered from the coronavirus fallout, as revenue plummeted in line with international travel bans, domestic lockdowns and state border closures.

Things did not look much better in the first six weeks of the 2021 fiscal year, when NIB sold fewer than 7000 policies. In the same period last year it sold nearly 160,000. The result was worse than expected and the share price fell more than 7 per cent by mid-afternoon.

But Mr Fitzgibbon said he was "committed to riding the storm".

"We'll see what the world looks like when, hopefully, COVID-19 is behind us. We're not a distressed seller. People will travel again. And there's a nice symbiosis between selling health insurance and travel insurance," he said.

While the health fund managed to grow its customer numbers by 1.9 per cent in its core insurance business, its claims bill continued to run far ahead of its revenue, growing at 6.7 per cent compared with total revenue growth of 3.4 per cent.

That dynamic saw gross profit margin squeezed to $506.2 million, from $529.4 million in fiscal 2019.

sentiment_pool.headline: Investors putting capital gains ahead of dividends
sentiment_pool.text:
Investors using some of the bigger online trading platforms are pursuing capital gains after the heavy sharemarket sell-off rather than fretting too much about big cuts in dividends as ASX companies preserve cash in tough times.

Gemma Dale, director of investor behaviour at nabtrade, said there had been some big shifts in strategy among customers, with many piling into the market in late March and early April after the hefty falls.

Blue-chip companies that had been sold off aggressively were heavily pursued in the chase for a rebound in price. Dividends seemed to be a secondary thought.

"We saw a huge uplift in buying over March and April as the market bottomed; cash was at record highs in February as the market peaked, so investors had cash available to invest," Dale said. "Investors appear to have been looking for companies with price upside rather than yield. It feels like they haven't felt the impact of lower dividends yet".

Many ASX companies have either reducing or cut out dividends.

Penfolds owner Treasury Wine Estates chopped back its final dividend by 60 per cent to just 8¢ per share when it announced its profits last Thursday.

Contractor Downer EDI scrapped its final dividend in a scene commonplace across the stockmarket but expects to restore them this financial year.

sentiment_pool.headline: He's one in a million seeking work
sentiment_pool.text:
The COVID-19 recession hasn't just thrown young hospitality and retail employees out of work. Steve Rowe was an executive director of a technology company that sold photocopiers when he lost his job in July.

But the 57-year-old now also joins 1 million people out of work, available to work and seeking it.

"I am actively trying to get work but it's pretty tough out there. Not scorched earth though - there are still opportunities around if you look hard," said Mr Rowe, who has also worked in the pharmaceuticals, construction and insurance and financial services industry.

"I have been through a recession before so I know what it's like to have to adjust the household spending, but I do need a job - I have three kids still at home including one with special needs. I am lucky that I have at least paid off my mortgage."

He has since signed up to five job search agencies, and refreshed his network, creating a list of "all the names of everyone I knew who could help".

He says it is hard because director level jobs don't come up all that much.

Stephen Moir, director of recruitment firm Moir Group, has been helping Mr Rowe find a new job.

"There are a lot of people in Steve's situation - the senior white-collar level finding it quite difficult," Mr Moir said.

"I see a lot of commentary around people in the hospitality and tourism sector but there are also a lot of people in that senior executive level that are out of work.

sentiment_pool.headline: Alcoa deal to kick-start onshore field
sentiment_pool.text:
Western Australia's biggest gas buyer, Alcoa of Australia, signed a large 10-year gas purchase deal that looks set to kick-start a fresh phase of development of onshore gas in the state.

The binding deal with junior Warrego Energy for 155 petajoules of gas was enough to commit to develop the West Erregulla field in the Perth Basin, a decision targeted for the June half of 2021, Warrego said yesterday.

The major West Erregulla discovery was made only last year by Warrego and partner Strike Energy about 300kilometres north of Perth. The large, low-cost resource was immediately seen as a significant new source of supply for WA.

Warrego managing director Dennis Donald said the deal "will send a positive signal to other potential gas buyers" but noted that no other customer deals were needed to proceed with development of the first phase.

Strike has already agreed to sell 100PJ of gas from its 50 per cent share of the field to Wesfarmers' CSBP business under an 11-year deal starting in the June half of 2022 at 25 terajoules a day.

The investment required for the project for Warrego and Strike will be reduced by the use of processing infrastructure built and owned by a third party. That would likely limit up-front capex for the first phase to about $30million-$40 million, Warrego executive director and CEO Australia David Biggs said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Cluey zooms towards ASX
sentiment_pool.text:
Online tutoring business Cluey is stepping up its initial public offering plans in a bid to make the most of exploding demand for its services.

The education technology business has hired Bell Potter and Canaccord Genuity to sell it to listed equities investors and will make its maiden pitch to fund managers today.

Cluey is expected to tell funds that it has quickly become the leading online tutoring and test prep business for primary and secondary students.

An explosion in online tutoring thanks to the COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdowns and restrictions, is turning parents and students online for extra tuition.

Cluey will tell funds it is delivering 20,000 tutoring sessions on its platform a month - up from 8000 only six months ago - and is adding more than 1000 new students a month, to have 5000 active students on its books.

While the structural change is happening quickly, Cluey reckons it has a big market to go after. There are about 4 million primary and secondary students in Australia, of which they believe about 50 per cent have paid or intend to pay for help outside school.

Cluey's also adding products - such as NAPLAN test preparations, small group learning and the like - and reckons there is nothing stopping it from attacking adjacent industries such as pre university courses, universities and TAFE, and offshore markets with its platform.

sentiment_pool.headline: Markets live afr.com Breaking news and analysis for what's moving the market, online daily and in The Australian Financial Review
Reserve Bank and markets are out of tune
sentiment_pool.text:
Investors are not picking up what the Reserve Bank of Australia is putting down.

A super-sized $120 billion easing in monetary policy this month, through an expanded term funding facility for super-cheap 0.25 per cent, three-year loans to commercial banks, generated barely a reaction in financial markets.

Perhaps frustrating officials at Martin Place, investors don't really understand why the RBA expanded the TFF and don't view it as a meaningful loosening of monetary policy.

More communication in coming RBA board meeting minutes and speeches will be required.

The Australian dollar remains stubbornly high during a recession, with currency traders largely unpersuaded by the bank's easing actions. The Aussie has jumped from US55¢ when the virus struck in March to recently hover in the low US70¢ range.

To be sure, there are reasons why the currency is relatively strong in this huge recession. The iron ore price is high, the US dollar has weakened against most currencies as the Federal Reserve conducts aggressive asset purchases, Australia's economy has been hit less by the virus and New Zealand's central bank is flirting with negative interest rates.

Moreover, perhaps if the RBA had instead allocated $120 billion to government bond purchases through quantitative easing, the reaction from traders would have been more evident.

The financial easing effect of TFF and QE should be very similar, at least according to economic theory that central bankers are closely attuned to.

sentiment_pool.headline: Road map smashes sellers, buyers
sentiment_pool.text:
Sellers and buyers caught short by the lockdown extension in greater Melbourne face potentially severe financial losses if they can't complete transactions, industry advocates say.

Buyer's agent Miriam Sandkuhler of Property Mavens said those who had bought to upgrade or downsize, but could no longer sell their own home, might lose their deposit or incur hefty bridging finance costs.

"Those who have sold but can't buy, due to low stock levels or because they can't inspect the property in person, are facing the possibility of homelessness, given they can't even inspect property to rent as an interim measure," Ms Sandkuhler said.

"While agents can still list properties for sale, most won't sell due to the inability to hold private inspections. While videos and photos help, they don't show faults, overshadowing from neighbours, or provide spatial awareness when it comes to room size, and so on.

"I think the lockdown extension will likely cause financial ruin for many."

Under Victoria's extended lockdown, public auctions with limited numbers and home inspections by appointment will not be permitted before October 26 at the earliest.

Real Estate Institute of Victoria president Leah Calnan said the move would compound the financial stress on Victorians and the Victorian economy.

sentiment_pool.headline: ANZ sets out its climate course
sentiment_pool.text:
Scott Morrison insists Australia's climate change policies will be determined here rather than in other countries. This is a polite dismissal of Boris Johnson's call for "bold action" during this week's prime ministerial phone chat.

But global capital markets and investors don't necessarily follow national government agendas, especially from a mid-sized economy deemed to be out of sync with international trends. The intense focus on the impact of COVID-19 has not lessened investor appetite for faster progress on combating climate change.

One result is that a 2050 target of net zero emissions has increasingly become the standard rallying cry for big business as well as some of Australia's key customers for coal and gas such as South Korea and Japan.

That means businesses operating in Australia, whether local affiliates of global companies or home grown corporates, are adopting a rather different tone to the messages from Canberra.

That much of this corporate rhetoric is more like a marketing exercise than evidence of dramatic shifts in behaviour is largely irrelevant. It all forms part of the pressure for change and for companies to be seen to be responding and, of course, innovating.

sentiment_pool.headline: Adairs' sales jump 22pc in online shopping boom
sentiment_pool.text:
Homewares group Adairs has survived a protest vote against its remuneration report after awarding big bonuses to executives, as it reported a 22 per cent bump in sales between July and October despite store closures in Victoria.

About 20 per cent of votes were cast against the group's remuneration report at its annual meeting yesterday after chief executive Mark Ronan received his maximum short-term bonus of $420,000, bringing his total pay packet during the pandemic to $1.06 million.

Chief financial officer Ashley Gardner received a $339,500 bonus, lifting his total pay to $1.24 million, including share options after receiving an interest-free loan of $750,000 from the company to buy its stock.

Adairs has been among the companies criticised by politicians for using the money it received from JobKeeper subsidies to boost profits.

Adairs received more than $11 million from JobKeeper, and while almost $6 million was passed directly to staff, the rest was used to slash costs and deliver a 40 per cent increase in annual earnings to just over $60 million.

Chairman Michael Butler said yesterday the JobKeeper benefits had been excluded from executives' "performance considerations".

He was also asked to explain why a company with large numbers of female customers and staff had only two women on its eight-person board, and whether the board could be truly independent given that it includes several former executives.

sentiment_pool.headline: The death of the Reserve Bank overnight cash rate
sentiment_pool.text:
Within two weeks, it's widely expected the Reserve Bank will cut the cash rate to a level lower than it thought was possible. Although this would be historic, the overnight target cash rate reduction has little relevance.

That's because with rates so low, central banks have resorted to pulling on a string, and the target cash rate no longer has any bearing on money market interest rates.

To understand why, just look at how the financial system works at the zero bound.

Consider a typical transaction: you sell your house for $500,000. The bank, say Westpac, lends the buyer money it doesn't have on hand but can borrow from another bank at, you guessed it, the overnight cash rate set by the Reserve Bank

You have just received $500,000 which will land in your bank account, at, say ANZ, in the form of a deposit.

The next day, Westpac has to repay the money it borrowed overnight.

If it doesn't have the funds on hand, it can go into the short-term money market and borrow money for a one-month term by issuing a 30-day bank bill, at a rate typically slightly higher than the cash rate.

A likely provider of the funds is ANZ, which has $500,000 on deposit that it needs to deploy to return some interest.

Over time, Westpac will gradually refinance most of that bank bill with more stable funds such as proceeds from a bond issue, or from household deposits.

With a hectic campaign schedule derailed by a nasty, but ultimately short-lived, bout of COVID-19, the US President's already flagging fortunes - thanks in part to a disastrous first debate - appeared to have been dealt a lethal blow.

Madder-than-usual Twitter volleys, a virus-wracked White House, poor polling and an interminable row with Congress over stimulus funding to help lift the US out of recession made his re-election bid look all but hopeless.

However, after 11 rallies in eight days of frenetic campaigning, a now fighting fit President Trump is managing to nudge the polls in his direction.

Although there is still plenty of ground to cover before he catches Joe Biden, his chances have improved at the margins.

RealClearPolitics' aggregate of Las Vegas betting odds have Biden at a 60.8 per cent chance of winning on November 3, down from 67.5 per cent on October 11, just as Trump was itching to escape Walter Reed hospital after surviving COVID-19.

The President's return to the fray has given his supporters hope the 2020 race is still alive. Even on Monday (yesterday AEDT), as Biden announced he wouldn't be campaigning that day or the next as he prepared for Thursday night's final debate, Trump held his fifth rally in three days.

sentiment_pool.headline: Thinner, smaller, lighter, dearer - iPhone 12
sentiment_pool.text:
Apple has finally brought 5G to its mobile phones, announcing that the entire lineup of its latest generation of iPhones, including a new "mini" iPhone, will support the latest mobile phone networks.

Apple CEO Tim Cook said the move to 5G ushered in a "new era" of iPhones, with faster download and upload speeds than had previously been possible on Apple phones.

The four new models of the iPhone - the iPhone 12, the iPhone 12 Pro, the iPhone 12 Pro Max and the new iPhone 12 mini - will support download speeds of up 3.5 gigabits a second, depending on the network they're attached to, Apple officials said.

Not only would 5G make the phone faster, it would also improve user privacy because iPhone users wouldn't need to use unsafe Wi-Fi hotspots as often, Mr Cook said.

But with 5G networks yet to be rolled out to all locations across Australia, and with the technology having lived up to neither its hype nor its advertised speeds, it's other improvements in the iPhone 12 that could be of more interest to many would-be owners.

The standard iPhone 12 model will be 11 per cent thinner, 15 per cent smaller overall and 16 per cent lighter than the previous model, Apple said. (It will also be 12.5 per cent more expensive in Australia.)

All models of the iPhone 12 will come with a new coating of protective glass, which Apple is calling "Ceramic Shield" and which will make them four times less likely to smash when dropped, Apple said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Adviser who stole from disabled jailed eight years
sentiment_pool.text:
A former financial planner who transferred more than $1 million from his clients' accounts to fund lifestyle purchases including a boat has been sentenced to eight years' imprisonment with a two-year non-parole period.

Anthony Vivian Dick was sentenced in the Townsville District Court after pleading guilty to 11 counts of "dishonestly applying to his own use of property belonging to another" following an investigation by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

The former adviser accessed and transferred about $1.1 million from his clients' superannuation, pension and bank accounts over a decade from March 2006 and December 2017.

The client funds were used to make personal purchases including a $72,000 vessel, and some of his victims were intellectually disabled, ASIC's investigation concluded.

Dick's conduct saw his authorisation to provide advice terminated by his licensee, Synchron, in April 2018, and it then reported the matter to the regulator.

He had previously been licensed by AMP-owned Jigsaw Support Services between 2004 and 2012, and National Australia Bank-owned GWM Adviser Services from 2012 to 2014. GWM is one of the licensees being closed as the bank readies to transfer ownership of its MLC Wealth subsidiary to IOOF.

"Mr Dick has been found to have breached the trust of his clients, who included unsophisticated investors and intellectually disabled consumers whom he deliberately targeted," ASIC deputy chairman Daniel Crennan, QC, said.

sentiment_pool.headline: A November to remember
sentiment_pool.text:
As President Donald Trump prepares to exit the White House in high dudgeon, equity investors might want to contemplate the potential Dickensian qualities of this extraordinary November month.

After the biggest November gain in the local market in a century, are we about to witness the sort of contrasting fortunes described in the first sentence of Charles Dickens' novel A Tale of Two Cities? Will it be the best of times and the worst of times?

Will the apparent wisdom of being "risk-on" be proven to be a folly? Are those who believe they have everything soon to find they have nothing?

Markets love extremes and always overshoot on the upside and the downside, which means Chanticleer cannot rule out a correction of some sort soon.

The idea of going from everything to nothing probably only applies to the cryptocurrency Bitcoin, which is arguably the best-performing asset in the world this year - up 177 per cent. The last time Bitcoin was at these levels it fell 70 per cent in the space of a few days.

Nevertheless, the crypto coin's stellar performance, which is being sheeted home to institutional support, easily nudges out the next four best-performing global assets - Nasdaq equity index, up 34 per cent, S&P 500 growth index (up 25 per cent), MSCI China index (up 24 per cent), and gold (up 18 per cent).

Iron ore outlook firms despite Beijing tension
sentiment_pool.text:
Beijing is applying pressure to overlook Australian products and preference alternative sources of iron ore supply, according to an industry source of leading UBS resources analyst Glyn Lawcock, challenging a startling rally in the commodity price that's defying the risk iron ore becomes a lever in China's stoush with Canberra.

But while business continues to raise concerns about the risk of exporters becoming collateral damage of government posturing, the outlook for iron ore sales to China has firmed amid a rally in prices for Australia's most valuable product.

Spot iron ore prices rose to $US126.34 a tonne on Wednesday, according to the latest data available from Fastmarkets MB, up 8.9 per cent since the end of October, as the steel input is snapped up by buyers in China, which continues to lead the global recovery.

"[The] message that's coming down very, very clearly yesterday on the phone call was one, 'let's reduce our reliance where we can', and two, 'don't buy Australian'," Mr Lawcock said, citing a consultancy in China with coverage of the steel industry.

The reported instruction from Beijing to industry to reduce reliance on concentrated sources of supply is significant to the trade in iron ore, albeit still sheltered by the lack of alternatives, Mr Lawcock explained.

sentiment_pool.headline: Forrest's 'bizarre' green power pacts with slave-tainted nations
sentiment_pool.text:
Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group says the Democratic Republic of Congo will need to free more than 1 million people from modern slavery to keep its end of the bargain under a deed of agreement on hydropower signed by the company and the African nation.

Mr Forrest has either signed deeds of agreement or held talks on deals with heads of government in a string of countries rated among the worst in the world for modern slavery by his family's philanthropic Minderoo Foundation as he seeks to further Fortescue's ambitions to become a global force in renewable energy.

The Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility said Mr Forrest's actions were "simply bizarre" given his public comments on not doing business with countries that tolerate modern slavery and the reality of the situation in nations where he has flagged major investments.

Minderoo's anti-slavery arm, Walk Free, estimates more than 1 million people live in modern slavery in the Democratic Republic of Congo and ranks the government's response as the second-lowest rating available.

Mr Forrest signed similar deeds on renewable energy assets with Afghanistan (rated the fifth-worst country in the world for slavery by Walk Free) and Papua New Guinea (No. 21).

The Fortescue founder and chairman last week committed the company to becoming one of the biggest energy companies in the world on top of its position as one of the biggest iron ore producers.

sentiment_pool.headline: Investors caught in Cold War II crossfire
sentiment_pool.text:
Renowned economic historian Niall Ferguson says China is making an example of Australia to highlight the dangers to other Asian economies of challenging its power, underscoring the need to cement relations with the incoming Biden administration to ensure Canberra is not isolated amid deepening trade tensions.

He warned that what he terms "Cold War II" will not end with the exit of US President Donald Trump from the White House, saying the election of Joe Biden will not lead to a wholesale reversal of the more assertive approach to dealing with China's rise as an economic and military challenger to the US.

"Joe Biden's national security team is not going to try and turn the clock back to 2016," Mr Ferguson told the UBS Australasia conference.

He said likely appointments such as former Obama staffer Michèle Flournoy as defence secretary or Kurt Campbell, who may play a role in China policy, had become "significantly" more hawkish on US China relations.

The coming change in key policymakers will be closely watched not only by the Australian government but also by investors who have witnessed an ever-expanding list of industries targeted by Beijing in a unashamed exercise of economic coercion.

"I think the Chinese are seeking to make an example of Australia to try to show to other Asian countries in particular that if you tangle with China politically, there will be dire economic consequences."

He said the "crucial" issue was for Australia not to be isolated.

sentiment_pool.headline: Big companies switch to flexible working space
sentiment_pool.text:
Large corporate tenants around the globe will seek out a more flexible office footprint and flexible lease contracts will become the norm as a result of COVID-19, according to a new report on the future of the workplace.

Future of Work - A Global Real Estate Player's Point of View, a report published by EY and the Urban Land Institute and based on a survey of investors, developers, real estate services firms, architects and operators of space, said major changes are expected in the office market in the next three to five years.

Of the 555 respondents surveyed, 96 per cent expected large corporate users to look for a more tailored and flexible office footprint, while 66 per cent expected flexible lease contracts to become the new normal.

More than half (53 per cent) of real estate players expected tenants to reduce their office space as a result of changing work patterns, while a quarter of respondents anticipated their office space requirements would decrease by more than 20 per cent.

Mark Tindale, director at Sydney leasing agency Cadigal, said there had been increasing demand for flexibility from corporate tenants over the past few years but the trend would only accelerate as a result of the pandemic.

"One part of flexibility is providing access to third spaces including tenant lounges and larger meeting and event facilities," he said.

Mr Tindale pointed to co-working group Hub Australia recently partnering with landlord Brookfield to lease two floors at Brookfield Pl

sentiment_pool.headline: Banks stake out new battleground
sentiment_pool.text:
The country's big banks are increasingly attempting to lure prospective borrowers with attractively priced fixed-rate home loans, as they vie to increase their share of the mortgage market.

According to Reserve Bank figures, lending for housing was the only area where credit is expanding. Lending for housing rose by 0.4 per cent in September, compared with an 0.8 per cent shrinkage in personal lending, and an 0.3 per cent drop in lending for business.

In response to the Reserve Bank's move to push longer-term interest rates lower, the country's big banks are focusing their competitive energies on the fixed rate end of the market, rather than on the standard variable rate loans.

As the Reserve Bank's Statement on Monetary Policy noted, "since March, the major banks have captured a larger-than-usual share of refinancing by offering very low rates on fixed-rate loans and offers of cash rebates to refinance from another lender".

The statement notes that rates for new fixed-rate housing loans fell by around 70 basis points between the end of February and the end of September, in tandem with the drop in the swap rate (the benchmark for pricing fixed rate loans).

As a result, by the end of September, the interest rates on new fixed-rate loans were around 55 to 65 basis points below new variable rate loans.

sentiment_pool.headline: RBA nails low rates to the floor
sentiment_pool.text:
The Reserve Bank has promised to keep its official cash rate at 0.1 per cent for at least the next three years and will buy $100 billion of bonds in the coming six months to force cheaper bank lending to boost the economy's jobs recovery.

RBA governor Philip Lowe announced a $5 billion per week buying program - worth about 5 per cent of GDP in total - along with a suite of lower rates for bank funding, while also upgrading forecasts for economic growth from 4 per cent to 6 per cent by June next year.

The Australian dollar fell to as low as US70.40¢, while bond yields were also driven lower in expectation of the ramp up in purchases by the bank.

However, the governor said that a slower jobs recovery as well as upward pressure on the Australian dollar from trillions of dollars in bond purchases from other central banks meant the trigger now had to be pulled on the country's first formal quantitative easing program.

"The lower interest rates and our plan to buy $100 billion of government bonds over the next six months will help people get jobs and support the recovery of the Australian economy," Dr Lowe said.

"A sharp bounce-back in jobs is unlikely and it will take time to return to where we were before the pandemic. Even if Victoria had not gone into lockdown we still would have made this decision because the outlook for the labour market required further action."

sentiment_pool.headline: Brighte raises $100m for rooftop solar retail play
sentiment_pool.text:
Rich Lister Mike Cannon-Brookes has doubled down on clean energy retailing, injecting another $78 million into Brighte to transform the buy now, pay later green lender into a clean energy retailer.

Existing investors rounded out the $100 million capital raise to fund Brighte's new retail arm - a one-stop-shop that will offer unsecured loans for rooftop solar and batteries, and enable customers to sell excess rooftop solar and battery power to other customers through the grid.

Brighte is seeking to carve out a slice of the booming rooftop solar market, which added 2.6 gigawatts of solar capacity this year - up from 1.9 gigawatts in 2019 - and generated 9 per cent of National Electricity Market energy last month.

"[This] gentailing model, where our customers own the energy assets and pay Brighte back over time, [means] Brighte will be [an] energy retailer and also help our customers realise revenue from their solar and batteries," said Brighte founder and chief executive officer Katherine McConnell, a former Macquarie Group senior manager.

Traditional "gentailers" such as AGL Energy, Origin Energy and EnergyAustralia generate power from coal, gas, wind and solar assets and sell it to retail and business customers over the grid.

Origin offers a similar service to that proposed by Brighte - it also finances customers' solar panels and lets them pay them off gradually - but has to worry about cannibalising its coal, gas and large-scale renewable energy sales.

The Australian economy appears to be turning a corner after a big year, but not everyone is wholeheartedly celebrating. For bond fund manager Chris Rands at Nikko Asset Management, the improved outlook probably means it's going to be harder to make money.

In the strange world of quantitative easing - which Australia ventured into for the first time in November - central banks are buying up government bonds to keep borrowing costs low and spur an economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has committed to keeping the three-year yield at 0.1 per cent and is also out in the market buying longer-dated bonds as part of its new six-month quantitative easing program.

With the RBA buying five to 10-year government and semi-government bonds, fixed income fund managers are enjoying the support the RBA is bringing to the market. But low yields hide a growing dilemma for bond investors: With the economy improving, is that substantial central bank support going to last much longer?

"When I look at the market at the moment, I feel like there is starting to be a discrepancy between just how much support the central banks are providing and just what the asset markets are telling us," said Mr Rands, part of a team that manages $2.25 billion in fixed income. sentiment_pool.headline: Some China problems just can't be fixed
sentiment_pool.text:
The sharp deterioration in relations between Australia and China is regrettable but also entirely expected.

For the best part of a decade, this column has asserted that China and the Western world are on a collision course for conflict. This was not a fashionable view back in 2013 when the Asian Century paradigm was in full-flight.

The probabilities of economic and military conflict have escalated under the current regime, which cannot be judged according to a rational, profit-maximising Western calculus. Rather, China's actions can only be understood through the prism of President Xi Jinping's Marxist-Leninist framework, which he describes as "socialism with Chinese characteristics".

Xi believes conflict between capitalism and Chinese socialism is inescapable, and he has been preparing for this contingency since he came to power. To properly divine our destiny, one must come to grips with the essence of the man who will exert enormous influence over the distribution of possible outcomes.

Xi is a brilliant yet fatalistic princeling-politician, who was arrested alongside his father, the Communist Party's former vice-chairman and propaganda chief, as a teen during the Cultural Revolution, and whose sister was tragically murdered by revolutionaries at the time.

sentiment_pool.headline: Virus tailwind is set to linger at the checkouts
sentiment_pool.text:
Supermarket sales growth is likely to remain elevated long after coronavirus lockdowns, underpinning another year or two of strong earnings growth at Woolworths, Coles and Metcash, says investment bank Jarden.

Food and grocery sales rose about 10 per cent year-on-year in Western Australia and Queensland in July- December - more than double the historic average - even though there had been no meaningful lockdowns since May and the cafe and restaurant sectors had fully reopened.

Jarden retail analyst Ben Gilbert said channel checks suggested grocery sales rose more than 10 per cent in December and January, buoyed by more Australians holidaying at home, consumers treating themselves to premium products and amid rising food and grocery prices.

Mr Gilbert believes investors have underestimated the duration and size of the COVID-19 benefit to the big food retailers, pointing to how the sector underperformed the S&P/ASX 200 Index by 14 per cent since the start of the pandemic.

Shares in Woolworths, Coles and Metcash are trading at the bottom of their relative price/earnings ranges after P/E multiples spiked at the beginning of the pandemic.

Most analysts expect grocery market sales to fall as much as 1 per cent in the June half as supermarkets cycle double-digit growth from panic hoarding and pantry stuffing in March and April last year and elevated levels of consumption from consumers working from home for much of 2020. Grocery sales are expected to rise by 2 per cent in 2022.

sentiment_pool.headline: Meet the other Goyder who just made $225m

As Richard Goyder frantically worked to shore up the future of Qantas, Woodside and the Australian Football League, around the corner from his Mosman Park home in Perth his cousin, Tim, was hitting the jackpot.

The exploration minnow hit the proverbial pot of gold at its nickel, copper and palladium Julimar project about 70 kilometres north-east of Perth. That lit a fire under its share price that continued to burn as the company kept drilling.

By November it was telling investors its project was emerging as "a globally significant deposit of critical metals in Western Australia".

Mr Goyder starts 2021 with an equity wealth pile of about $225 million compared with roughly $36 million a year ago.

But it is not all from Chalice. Mr Goyder is behind not one but two of the 10 best-performing stocks on the All Ordinaries Index in 2020. Liontown Resources, a lithium play, is up 290 per cent.

"I pinch myself every morning," Mr Goyder told The Australian Financial Review. "I've been at it a long time. I pegged my first tenements when I was 20."

Chalice Mining jumped from 22.5¢ at the start of 2020 to close at $3.90 on December 31, making it the second-best-performing stock on the All Ordinaries Index behind De Grey Mining, while Mr Goyder's lithium explorer Liontown Resources delivered a 290 per cent return, making it the eighth-b

sentiment_pool.text:
Talk about a confidence killer. Just as the first big week of reporting season had shown the corporate sector is emerging from the fog of 2020 with real momentum and a desire to push forward with strategic plans delayed by the pandemic, the country's second-biggest state has been stopped in its tracks again.

Like all Australians, the nation's business community will be praying that Melbourne emerges next week from five days of hard lockdown with its latest outbreak under control. But even if it does, Victoria's battle against the ultra-aggressive British strain of COVID-19 is a stark reminder to the business community that it must bake in a new normal where we are living with - and fighting - this virus for years to come.

No doubt there will be lots of criticism of the use of snap lockdowns in the coming days and serious questions over how we strike the right balance between hotel quarantine and getting stranded Australians home from overseas.

But what we saw on Friday from Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews and his health officials was genuine concern about the way the virus has mutated and what they are now up against.

There are no easy answers or guaranteed solutions in a situation like this. Vaccines loom as an important weapon to control the virus but even they have limitations.

As Magellan's Hamish Douglass said this week, the effectiveness of today's vaccines is no guarantee against tomorrow's mutation of the virus.

sentiment_pool.headline: No longer a believer in the housing Big Short
sentiment_pool.text:
Exactly five years ago a hedge fund manager and an economist posing as a gay couple toured Sydney investigating whether Australia's housing market was a bubble. They decided to short it.

Now the hedge fund manager behind that view, Bronte Capital chief investment officer John Hempton, says there is no case for positioning to benefit from a significant fall in house prices. If anything, he expects prices to rise.

"More responsible lending - at least relative to where Australia was - and lower interest rates have eased concerns," Mr Hempton told The Australian Financial Review. "That said, prices and lending are at levels way above where other economies have had problems."

Mr Hempton had joined economist Jonathan Tepper, now of Prevatt Capital, back in 2016 in their search for mortgage brokers who were willing to help people get bigger loans by distorting their incomes.

"When JT and I went and visited mortgage brokers in western Sydney the official numbers were that banks would lend just under seven times income. However - using brokers - it was easy to obtain eight times income. And when we found aggressive mortgage brokers they could get you loans of 10 times income," he said.

"At the moment, Australian banks will lend about seven times household income, so the lending is clearly more responsible but I'm surprised at how little effect that it has had."

sentiment_pool.headline: Bankers and regulators resist the surging house price alarm
sentiment_pool.text:
Australia's top bankers and their chief regulator are adamant rapidly rising house prices are not seeding financial risks that warrant lending curbs but have signalled borrowers' incomes will be a key indicator for taking future action.

Surging house prices in New Zealand have forced its government to introduce tough curbs through taxation and lending limits. But in Australia, which is set to record house price growth of 2.8 per cent in March alone, regulators are waiting to see the effect on incomes from the wind-up of record government wage subsidies, cash boosts and $10 billion in bank interest payment deferrals.

Australian Prudential Regulation Authority chairman Wayne Byres said that while certain risks were rising, there was no need for intervention yet.

"We are alert to signs that very low interest rates and rising housing prices create a dynamic in which households seek to take on even higher debt levels, and that banks searching for credit growth seek to accommodate that demand through greater risk taking," Mr Byres told The Australian Financial Review Banking Summit.

"Should risks materialise, we have a range of tools we could employ, from interventions similar to that in 2015 and 2017, to the countercyclical capital buffer ... The exact tools we choose will depend on the environment we face, and we are giving careful thought to which tools might work best in different scenarios."

sentiment_pool.headline: Co-operation best for trans-Tasman banking systems
sentiment_pool.text:
Small, isolated and capital-importing economies need to be careful about scaring off global capital, especially during a global pandemic that has shut down one of its biggest export-earning industries. But that may be what New Zealand's central bank has done by demanding that the big four Australian-owned banks that dominate its financial system increase their capital reserves to among the highest in the world, in turn crimping their profits.

That has prompted Westpac to appoint advisers to look at how it might sell off or float its New Zealand operations, which stretch back 160 years. New Zealand's Finance Minister, Grant Robertson, even appeared to welcome the move and foreshadowed taking the government's business away from Westpac. That comes amid a startling spat between the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and Mr Robertson over how to control a bubble that has inflated housing prices by up to 30 per cent in the past year. It hardly looks like an endorsement of the Kiwi central bank's political independence, another potential worrying sign for global capital.

In Australia, healthy capital buffers have been an article of faith since David Murray's 2014 financial system inquiry said that the banking system here must be "unquestionably strong". But New Zealand reckons its risks are higher. The country is unusual in having no big domestic banking player; 85 per cent of its banking is done by subsidiaries of Australia's big four. sentiment_pool.headline: Foster Blake seeks fresh faces with Go-To offer
sentiment_pool.text:
Beauty entrepreneur Zoe Foster Blake is priming her Go-To Skincare business for plump returns, shopping around a stake of up to 45 per cent in her company to fast track its global sales growth.

Street Talk can reveal Go-To has appointed Canterbury Partners to help snare a strategic investor as it moves to pounce on strong momentum that has fuelled a 41 per cent jump in revenue to an estimated $37.5 million.

Driven by a consumer binge on at-home self-care, Go-To is forecasting earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $12.1 million. In 2020 it turned over $26.5 million, up 41 per cent on 2019, when it posted revenue of $18.9 million.

sentiment_pool.headline: Career changers find meaning in teaching
sentiment_pool.text:
A teacher at a tiny Arnhem Land school who embedded a revolutionary "both ways" approach to education that melds culture and knowledge is one of 12 teachers to be recognised with a major teaching award.

Former doctor Daniel Yore has been a teacher at the Yirrkala Bilingual School since 2017. Last year, for the first time, the school had four students who gained an Australian Tertiary Admissions Rank including one who was accepted into medicine. Another four graduated Year 12 without an ATAR.

Mr Yore was drawn to education, from medicine after he spent time in communities like Yirrkala and determined that education might be a more powerful lever to fix disadvantage.

"I got to see what makes people healthy or sick is derived from structures in society that reflect people's socioeconomic status," he said.

"I got really interested in the power of education for changing that."

After teaching in Darwin for four years, Mr Yore moved to Yirrkala where he worked with local educational leaders to integrate the traditional Yolngu language, knowledge and cultural practices with the mainstream Australian curriculum taught in English.

By the end of 2021, a total of 20 students are set to have graduated, with the school producing more Year 12 finishers than the annual average of all remote schools in the Northern Territory.

"The Yolngu elders talk about two waters mixing," said Mr Yore.

sentiment_pool.headline: Pandemic revs up new demand for classic cars
sentiment_pool.text:
British auction platform Collecting Cars will ramp up its presence in the Australian market after it facilitated $1.5 million in rare automobile sales in a soft launch, including a world record for a 1975 Porsche 930 Turbo.

The 18-month-old tech start-up oversaw sales of more than 1300 vehicles worth a collective £46 million ($82.7 million) in calendar 2020, which it said was the highest volume of any UK auction house or online platform.

Richard Fowler, the platform's Australian head, said customer feedback indicated the record was a function of many investors seeking an alternative to wild sharemarkets in the pandemic, including Millennial collectors first gaining exposure to the asset class.

"What we have noticed in the Australian market since launching Collecting Cars is that the ages of buyers have been extremely varied," the former Formula Ford racer told The Australian Financial Review. "Whilst a majority have been aged between 40 and 50, what we are noticing is that there is a fast-growing skew of younger bidders emerging.

"With the stock market so volatile at the moment, what we are hearing is the youth market are looking for safer investment options where they can still enjoy the asset," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Channel 9 returns to WIN as Nine signs new affiliate deal
sentiment_pool.text:
Nine has signed a new affiliate agreement with Bruce Gordon's WIN Corp, returning Channel 9 television content to the regional broadcaster in Tasmania, regional Western Australia, Victoria, Queensland and southern NSW.

The deal marks the end of a five-year agreement with Southern Cross Austereo to broadcast Nine content across regional Australia.

The Southern Cross agreement, which will officially conclude at the end of June, was worth almost $500 million and ended a long-standing relationship with WIN.

In a note to staff, outgoing Nine CEO Hugh Marks said the company had enjoyed its "five-year relationship with Southern Cross Austereo", but the decision was made "strategically on the basis of WIN's larger broadcast footprint".

Under this new seven-year agreement, which will start on July 1, WIN will pay an affiliation fee of around 50 per cent of its regional advertising revenue to Nine and provide airtime to Nine to allow promotion of Nine's assets across WIN's television and radio network.

WIN will also provide a sales representation service for Nine in Northern NSW and Darwin for a period of time. WIN will deliver its local news bulletin in regional areas at 5.30pm before taking the 6pm state bulletin in each state.

The switch in affiliate relationship will affect Nine's regional news services, which it provides on behalf of Southern Cross Austereo.

sentiment_pool.headline: Exploration boom sparks drilling and lab backlogs
sentiment_pool.text:
An "unprecedented" flow of cash into the high-risk mineral exploration sector has sparked a drilling boom that is causing huge backlogs at the laboratories whose assays determine success or failure.

More than $2.2 billion flowed into the 656 pre-revenue explorers on the ASX in the final three months of 2020, in a result that was 72 per cent higher than average and was described by advisory firm BDO as "unprecedented".

The $587 million spent on exploration by those companies was also well above average and 50 per cent higher than the June quarter, echoing the Australian Bureau of Statistics' finding that metres drilled by mineral explorers had surged to a nine-year high.

The statistics fit the mood witnessed on the ground by veteran explorer John Holliday, who was one of the founders of Australia's most lucrative gold mine at Cadia in NSW.

"We are in a boom I would say for exploration at present," he said from his latest drilling project with Kincora Copper near the NSW town of Trundle.

Mr Holliday said the boom conditions were manifesting in many ways, including longer waits for drilling results to come back from laboratories.

"It is stretching out here to two months and normally you might expect three weeks or so," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: AMP Capital sells another fund
sentiment_pool.text:
AMP Capital has carved off another limb as it prepares for a sale to Ares Management, inking a deal to sell its $US500 million ($650 million) Global Companies Fund and its team of four investors to Montreal-based fund manager Fiera Capital.

The move follows a planned pivot for AMP Capital from public markets investing to a focus on its private markets capability in infrastructure and real estate, while looking at other options for its global equities and fixed income businesses.

Fiera Capital paid an immaterial amount for the Global Companies Fund.

The Global Companies Fund, set up in 2017, has more than $US500 million under management and gives investors access to a portfolio of 25 to 35 global companies.

AMP set up the London-headquartered global equity capability in June 2016 and launched the Global Companies Fund, its first global equities product, in March 2017, run by Simon Steele.

The team also includes the Sydney-based Andy Gardner and London-based Neil Mitchell and David Naughtin.

The Global Companies Fund's local institutional offering has achieved an absolute return over the first three years to March 31, 2020, of 92 per cent, net of fees.

Simon Warner, AMP Capital's global head of public markets, said the deal cemented the company's strategy to find the best opportunities for its global equities and fixed income businesses.

The Global Companies Fund had "delivered great returns for our clients and I have no doubt that this will continue under new leadershi

sentiment_pool.headline: Raise the Mastt: Aconex founders back spreadsheet killer
sentiment_pool.text:
Aconex founders Rob Phillpot and Leigh Jasper have been joined by a former Lendlease executive and global investment firms in an early-stage investment round at construction technology start-up Mastt.

The company sells subscriptions to its software platform, which gives capital project owners and project managers a real-time overview across projects to help them analyse their work and avoid cost blowouts.

The start-up has grown notably since it was founded in 2019 by construction industry veteran Doug Vincent and software engineer Jamie Cerexhe, signing on an impressive early roster of clients including the Australian Army, Aurecon, Jacobs Engineering and Mr Vincent's former employer, RPS Group.

Mr Vincent told The Australian Financial Review the company's mission is to kill spreadsheets and digitise the construction industry by providing project owners a portfolio management system that can deliver projects faster and with less risk.

sentiment_pool.headline: ASX rises as growth thumps expectations
sentiment_pool.text:
The Australian sharemarket rebounded from a day-earlier loss yesterday, supported by a stronger-than-expected increase in the country's fourth-quarter economic output.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index climbed 55.7 points, or 0.8 per cent, to 6818, its highest level in four sessions.

Investors on Wall Street pulled back from riskier assets once more amid heightened volatility in both bond and equity markets.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was hit hardest, falling 1.7 per cent, while the S&P 500 declined 0.8 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.5 per cent.

Despite the poor lead from Wall Street, the local sharemarket shot up at the open and remained firmly higher.

Australia's fourth-quarter gross domestic product beat expectations, expanding 3.1 per cent from the previous three months, buoyed by strength from consumer spending despite a drop in income.

"Quarterly GDP continued its strong recovery in the fourth quarter with activity just 1.1 per cent below December 2019 levels," said Morgan Stanley equity strategist Chris Read.

"The growth in spending was very much linked to reopening, with hospitality, recreation and vehicle-related spending the biggest drivers of uplift in the quarter.

"More importantly, the spending growth occurred in conjunction with a 3.1 per cent decline in disposable income - as much of the crisis stimulus that was in place through the middle of 2020 was tapered or removed."

sentiment_pool.headline: Canberra can help bring Myanmar back from brink of chaos
sentiment_pool.text:
Diplomacy Myanmar's military is losing control of the country it has seized. Regional diplomacy is now seeking a face-saving exit for the generals.

In Jakarta at the weekend, the 10-member Association of Southeast Asian States, or ASEAN, passed an important test of relevance and credibility.

In response to the Myanmar military coup of February 1, ASEAN leaders met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, demanded an immediate cessation of violence and appointed a special envoy.

Myanmar has been in the grips of an alarming downward spiral, with a military increasingly brazen in its use of lethal force to suppress peaceful protesters and a civilian death toll approaching 1000.

Already lacking legitimacy, the military appears to be losing control, resorting to growing violence and intimidation to subdue a civilian population whose spirit and resilience it has grossly underestimated.

Only a few months ago Myanmar was hailed as the coming success story of south-east Asia.

It is now on the brink of becoming, as The Economist cover described it, "Asia's next failed state".

In Australia's Parliament this month we heard from a large number of Myanmar community and diaspora representatives about the strength of civilian resistance in Myanmar.

Ousted parliamentary representatives are regrouping and reorganising under the banner of the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw, or CRPH.

sentiment_pool.headline: Food for thought as apartment scrap recycling pays off
sentiment_pool.text:
There is a common misconception that apartment blocks are more sustainable than stand-alone houses because of the economies of shared space.

They're not. The energy consumed by indoor lighting in common areas, lifts, extractor fans to keep air flowing and the fact that water has to be pumped to the top of the block gives high-rises a much larger carbon footprint.

Then there's the air conditioning required to stop those boxes getting too hot as global warming kicks in. Ironic, eh?

With that in mind, some councils with high numbers of apartment blocks have been trying to find ways to offset the carbon cost of the blocks by recycling anything that can be reused - including food scraps.

City of Sydney council, overseeing one of the largest concentrations of apartment blocks in the country, has been at the forefront of this movement, including extending its food scraps collection and recycling service from stand-alone houses to strata schemes.

The CoS trial involves more than 1000 houses and 120 apartment buildings across the city, comprising more than 10,000 households. The plan is to more than double the number of apartment blocks involved from 120 to 250.

OK, but why would non-greenie investors care? Interestingly, studies conducted in the US and UK in the past year or so found that sustainability rates very highly among prospective property purchasers and tenants.

sentiment_pool.headline: Pepper Money eyes Liberty multiple as ASX guide
sentiment_pool.text:
KKR Credit and Seumas Dawes will seek buyers for about a 40 per cent stake in non-bank lender Pepper Money as part of its re-listing on the ASX.

Pepper's adviser Reunion Capital and its three lead managers kicked off the lender's charge at the ASX boards yesterday, dispatching pre-deal analyst reports to explain the business, its industry and outline its earnings prospects.

While the reports stopped short of valuing the business, it should be a pretty straightforward task.

Pepper's newly listed rival Liberty Financial Group is an appropriate benchmark and from there it's just a question of applying an adequate IPO discount.

The only complication is Liberty's tax structure, which means its effective tax rate is about 12 per cent while Pepper's is up near 30 per cent. It means Liberty records a higher profit and pays bigger dividends to investors, but investors are left with a tax bill.

So if you apply Pepper's tax rate to Liberty's pre-tax earnings, the stock would be trading at about 14.5-times profit. Assuming investors won't give up all that ground, the appropriate benchmark is probably about 13-times.

From there, you imagine fundies would want a 10 per cent IPO discount which would mean a $1.4 billion-odd market capitalisation for Pepper Money and a $550 million-odd raising.

If that's the case, it would be the biggest IPO in Australia this year in terms of funds raised.

sentiment_pool.headline: Accountants resist as banks shift risk
sentiment_pool.text:
Accountants have slammed banks for an "explosion" of requests to provide "capacity to repay" letters, as the financial services sector seeks to shift its credit risk amid the post-pandemic recovery and surging property market.

Long-running tension over requests has ramped up in the wake of COVID-19, with landlords and real estate agents requesting the certificates for the first time, which in some cases extend to accountants being asked to certify if a borrower's future earnings will be affected by coronavirus.

Industry associations have been advising members not to sign the certificates because they are "too risky", but pressure from the banks is ramping up because of the pandemic, and surging real estate prices, accountants say.

"People are really pushing the envelope with property prices, so they are having to extend themselves further than they thought - the rental market is white hot at the moment too," said long-time NSW Central Coast accountant Gavin Swan, who has more than 1600 mum-and-dad clients.

"The banking relief is coming to an end at the same time as people are trying to borrow more because property prices have gone through the roof.

"All we need is for interest rates to go up a per cent or two and a lot of people will be in trouble after over-extending."

He said the requests tended to mostly come from the smaller lenders and mortgage brokers and were being made at the last minute in urgent terms for clients to provide within the same day.
