sentiment_pool.headline: Why women are getting more jobs
sentiment_pool.text:
Women are surging back into the workforce with female participation growing at five times that of men in the latest strengthening employment figures.

Women took almost 80 per cent of the 70,700 jobs added to the economy in March, continuing their strong recovery out of the COVID pandemic.

Female participation has now increased to an all-time high of 61.8 per cent and Treasurer Josh Frydenberg expects this will continue.

"It's pleasing to see female participation rate increase as well as these jobs coming back for women," Treasurer Josh Frydenberg said.

"Going into these numbers for the month of March, we had seen 450,000 jobs come back for women, and about 400,000 jobs back for men," he said.

In March, female participation increased by 0.4 percentage points, while male participation went backwards by almost a 0.1 percentage point.

Similar payroll figures produced by the Australian Bureau of Statistics show that since COVID-19 hit in March last year payroll jobs worked by males have decreased by 1 per cent while payroll jobs worked by females have increased by 0.8 per cent.

The total wage bill to females over that same time has increased by 4.7 per cent while the total payments to males have decreased by 0.1 per cent.

ABS head of labour statistics Bjorn Jarvis said part of the surge of women into the workforce was due to the high representation females have in industries that have grown during COVID-19, such as healthcare and social services.

sentiment_pool.text:
Slavery China bans companies that accuse it of maltreatment.

Australia's largest corporations may face a backlash from Beijing if they are critical of China's human rights record when reporting honestly on their supply chain exposure to modern slavery.

Ausbil Investment Management head of environmental, social and corporate governance (ESG) research Mans Carlsson told The Australian Financial Review the issue of human rights in manufacturing in Xinjiang and the Uighur issue was tricky for Australian companies because they might be open to retribution from China if they criticised it in their statements about modern slavery.

"Looking at the average Australian company, their supply chains are very China-centric because it's easier for companies to source from Chinese suppliers, which are quite nimble. They can do short turnaround times, and smaller order volumes," he said.

"[If] Australian companies criticise China openly in a modern slavery statement, that's public information. And that could lead to repercussions."

ESG research weighs environmental and governance factors in company valuations.

Swedish fast-fashion giant H&M felt the wrath of the Chinese Communist Party after refusing to use Xinjiang cotton because of concerns about the region. Its comments were aired last year. sentiment_pool.headline: GFG boss Gupta attacks Greensill Capital creditors
sentiment_pool.text:
GFG Alliance founder and chief executive Sanjeev Gupta has launched a withering attack on Greensill Capital creditors that have taken legal action against him, declaring in an opinion piece for British newspaper The Times they were destroying their own chances of recouping value through "knee-jerk actions".

"Financial institutions with investments connected to Greensill are now trying to bring claims against us," Mr Gupta said in an op-ed on Friday.

"We will of course robustly defend our legal position, including in the courts if necessary."

Credit Suisse, which bought bonds arranged by Greensill that contained invoices from Mr Gupta's companies, is seeking court orders in Australia and the UK to wind up GFG entities, including OneSteel Manufacturing, which operates the Whyalla steelworks, and Liberty Commodities.

If successful, Credit Suisse could sell off GFG assets to repay investors who bought securities in the Swiss group's supply chain finance funds.

Mr Gupta appears prepared to challenge Credit Suisse in the courts, claiming that creditors' "short-term, aggressive tactics" could threaten thousands of jobs in the UK and elsewhere.

Mr Gupta said most of GFG's major businesses were sustainable, but warned that demand for some products in the UK had fallen by up to 60 per cent because of Brexit, the COVID-19 pandemic and Greensill's collapse.

sentiment_pool.headline: Cameron fallout could 'hurt policy process'
sentiment_pool.text:
London | The scandal over former British prime minister David Cameron's lobbying for Greensill Capital last year could potentially deter businesses from getting involved in the policymaking process, Chancellor of the Exchequer Rishi Sunak has warned.

Mr Sunak said businesses' input into policymaking, both formal and informal, was important but executives might be deterred if they thought their contributions could surface publicly.

"If every informal conversation is ostensibly a public interview, people might be more reluctant to share private perspectives or thoughts with ministers which will help inform policy or provide broader context on what is happening," he told the treasury committee on Thursday (Friday AEST).

"The policymaking process would be poorer without it ... Whether it's business, trade unions, trade organisations or civil society, it's important that people feel they can engage with ministers and officials. Policy is better as a result."

Mr Cameron issued a barrage of emails, WhatsApp messages and phone calls to ministers and senior mandarins in mid-2020 as he tried to secure a role for supply-chain finance firm Greensill Capital in support schemes for pandemic-hit businesses.

When details of his lobbying blitz surfaced this year, following the collapse of Greensill Capital in early March, it triggered a major bout of soul-searching in Westminster about the potential for some businesses to get privileged access to politicians and officials.

sentiment_pool.headline: Super rise 'worsens' weak wage growth
sentiment_pool.text:
The scheduled superannuation rise will be a significant contributor to the weak wages growth forecast in the budget that Labor is complaining about.

The federal opposition has criticised the government for negative and flat real (inflation adjusted) wages growth outlined in the budget over the next four years.

The 9.5 per cent superannuation guarantee paid by employers to staff is scheduled to rise by 0.5 of a percentage point each year between July this year and July 2025, to 12 per cent.

The legislated rise has been strongly backed by Labor, trade unions and super funds, and reluctantly supported by the government, which has pointed to the wage-super trade-off.

The government's retirement income review, the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Grattan Institute and Australian National University economists have all estimated that at least 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the scheduled increase would be paid for by lower wage rises.

Grattan Institute household finances program director Brendan Coates said the rise in the super guarantee was a "reasonably significant factor" in why wages growth was forecast in the budget to be so low.

"Super is not the sole driver of low wages growth coming out of a recession, but super is making it worse," Mr Coates said.

The budget notes that the outlook for wage growth is "expected to remain moderate over the forecast period".

sentiment_pool.headline: Oil market braces for the return of Iran supply
sentiment_pool.text:
Oil traders are bracing for the re-entry of Iranian supply into the global crude market, as the Islamic Republic and the Biden administration work towards ending trade sanctions, a move that could stall a rally in prices.

Brent crude dipped 0.9 per cent to $US68.08 a barrel yesterday while West Texas Intermediate fell 1 per cent to $US64.86 amid concerns the crude market could become quickly tipped back into oversupply by Iran's return.

Earlier in the session, Brent crude topped $US70 a barrel for the first time since March.

Washington and Tehran are working on a path back towards the 2015 nuclear deal scrapped under former US president Donald Trump that would pave the way for Iran's oil to once again trade in the open market. Diplomats have speculated publicly about progress on such a deal this week.

"Clearly the headlines will not be great for sentiment, particularly given that OPEC+ countries are gradually increasing output, while there are also demand worries in Asia," said Warren Patterson, ING head of commodities strategy.

Iran's oil exports have been hampered by US sanctions since the nuclear deal was dumped. Its largest customer has been China, but a breakthrough in talks could open the way for the country to pump more crude to a wider customer base.

"If US-Iran talks prove successful, there is a strong likelihood that more Iranian oil supply will make its way to the market," said Vivek Dhar, CBA's mining and energy commodities analyst.

sentiment_pool.headline: File targets financiers of plastics firms
sentiment_pool.text:
Just 20 companies are responsible for producing half of all single-use plastics thrown away around the world every year, and a new report has singled out major banks and asset managers in an attempt to reduce the environmental menace.

The new Plastic Waste-Makers Index ranks ExxonMobile, Dow and China's Sinopec as the biggest producers of polymers for single-use plastics - generating about 16 per cent of plastics waste worldwide.

Despite Scott Morrison's efforts to curb Australia's huge plastics footprint, the country tops nations generating single-use waste on a per capita consumption basis, ahead of the United States, South Korea and Britain.

Worldwide the problem is vast: more than 130 million metric tonnes were thrown away in 2019, almost all of it burned, buried in landfill or discarded directly into the environment.

The report - to be released today by Andrew and Nicola Forrest's Minderoo Foundation - considers single-use, fossil fuel-produced plastics. It finds that 100 companies are behind as much as 90 per cent of global production.

Seeking to maximise pressure to change corporate behaviour, the report names global banks and asset managers funding or profiting from single-use plastics, including Barclays, HSBC, Bank of America, Vanguard and BlackRock.

Australia's ANZ sits at 35 on the ranking of banks financing polymer products, along with global giants Deutsche Bank, Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse and Morgan Stanley.

sentiment_pool.headline: The New Inflation Paradigm
sentiment_pool.text:
Investing Indications in the US in recent days that prices are rising have given markets a foretaste of the risks that could lie ahead, write Colby Smith and Tommy Stubbington.

After three decades as a bond investor, Jim Leaviss has witnessed plenty of false alarms over the return of one of the biggest debt market nemeses: inflation. But as his screen flashed with Wednesday's US consumer price index figures - showing a 4.2 per cent annual rise - he felt the stirrings of a new era in markets.

"It's always been right to be sceptical when someone says 'this is the year that inflation comes back'. But for the first time you can say this time is different," says Leaviss.

"The pandemic might be the systemic earthquake that changes the inflation outlook we have been used to for the past 30 years."

A burst of inflation in the northern hemisphere summer was always inevitable once lockdown measures eased. A year ago the spread of COVID-19 had crushed economies around the world, sending commodity prices plummeting and even pushing the cost of a barrel of oil in the US below zero.

Central bankers - particularly at the US Federal Reserve - have been at pains to insist the current bout of price rises is temporary, and will not push them to an early unwinding of the massive monetary stimulus actions they launched last year to combat the fallout from the pandemic.

Buyers circle Barbeques Galore
sentiment_pool.text:
Trade and private equity suitors are circling specialty barbecue retailer Barbeques Galore after it was put up for sale by Quadrant Private Equity last month.

Quadrant managing partner Jonathon Pearce confirmed the retailer had received interest from trade buyers and private equity firms. But he said Apollo Global Management was not conducting formal due diligence on the chain.

Barbeques Galore chief executive Angus McDonald said all team members who worked at those four stores, not just those working at the time the man visited, were tested and isolated while awaiting their results.

"I'm very relieved and pleased to say all those team members tested negative," said Mr McDonald, wishing the Apollo executive a speedy recovery.

The stores were also professionally deep-cleaned after the company was notified by the NSW Department of Health and resumed trade the following day.

"It's something every business has to be prepared for in this time and it's a situation that could happen to anybody," Mr McDonald said.

Indicative offers for Barbeques Galore are expected to come in over the next few days and Quadrant is likely to draw up a shortlist of bidders by the end of the week.

sentiment_pool.headline: Stockholm syndrome dogs Western firms in China
sentiment_pool.text:
Stockholm syndrome, named after a notorious robbery in the Swedish capital in 1973, is a phenomenon in which the victim of kidnapping or hostage-taking develops feelings of trust, affection or sympathy for their captor. It is a condition that afflicts much of the corporate world and some governments when it comes to their dealings with the Chinese Communist Party.

I was recently invited by a group of Hong Kong-based international business executives to discuss Beijing's moves to crush the last vestiges of democracy and free speech in the territory. Several of these executives from democratic societies said they viewed the free press as their greatest enemy.

To them the problem was not the erosion of rights and freedoms in what was one of the world's most dynamic financial centres. The problem was pesky journalists who dared to report on these developments, thereby convincing head office to stop investing in the city.

It may sound strange to describe successful, moneymaking ventures in China as hostages. But in their daily operations, many of these companies face intellectual property theft, unpredictable and predatory policymaking, intrusive surveillance by secret police and the threat of exit bans or even employee arrest arising from ordinary business disputes.

sentiment_pool.text:
Fast-growing Australian technology company SafetyCulture has blasted through the $2 billion valuation mark with one of the largest venture capital funding rounds of the year, led by New York-based Insight Partners.

The Townsville-founded company achieved the highly prized "unicorn" status of a billion-dollar valuation a year ago, but has grown significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic as enterprises around the world look to its software platform and flagship iAuditor product to ensure offices can comply with the standards required for a return to work.

The funding round was closed at $99 million, with Insight making its second huge investment in an Australian technology company in recent times, after its $221 million investment in Brisbane-based Octopus Deploy.

The SafetyCulture funding will enable the company to expand services available on its platform, further expand internationally and kick the need for an initial public offering further down the road.

Unlike the Octopus Deploy funding round, Insight did not make up the whole investment in SafetyCulture itself; existing international investors Tiger Global and Index Ventures and Australia's Blackbird Ventures also bought in again.

"We continue to invest in building on our product platform," SafetyCulture founder and CEO Luke Anear told The Australian Financial Review in a video call alongside Insight Partners managing director Teddie Wardi.

sentiment_pool.headline: Seafarms rattles tin for tiger prawn project
sentiment_pool.text:
Seafarms Group is seeking to raise $105 million to progress a large-scale prawn project on Australia's far-north coast.

The capital raising will be underpinned by Perth businessman Ian Trahar, who is Seafarms' biggest shareholder and executive chairman. He has been pushing the company's "project sea dragon" for almost a decade and is closing in on a dream of creating a major new industry near Kununurra in Western Australia.

Mr Trahar will subscribe for $20 million in stock under a $90 million placement and has agreed to convert $15.2 million of existing debt into equity. The company is looking to raise a further $15 million through a share purchase plan.

The funds are being sought to begin construction of stage one of the project, with Seafarms aiming for a maiden harvest by the third quarter of 2023.

Seafarms is still trying to nail down another $150 million in finance for the construction work.

The estimated capital cost is $281 million, with stage one intended to produce 18,000 tonnes of black tiger prawns a year once in full flow. The production target for the first 12 months of operation is 6000 tonnes.

AAM Investment Group, the owners of Legune Station on the border of WA and the Northern Territory where the project is based, also intends to take part in the placement, with Bell Potter acting as lead manager.

sentiment_pool.headline: As McCormack bows out, get ready for a wild ride
sentiment_pool.text:
Not since Tim Fischer was applauded after his farewell speech to Parliament has there been such a spontaneous round of applause for an outgoing leader as there was in the House of Representatives yesterday.

As Michael McCormack exited the chamber after his last day in the chair as Deputy Prime Minister, the Liberals, Labor and the Nationals colleagues who voted for him applauded with gusto. Even Barnaby Joyce gave a slow clap.

The applause was more than just respect for a decent person. It smacked of trepidation about what was coming next.

Myriad reasons were cited by Barnaby Joyce and his followers for ousting McCormack. At the heart of it all was a burning desire for Joyce to regain the job he was forced to relinquish in February 2018 when news of an extramarital affair became public and he was subject to sexual harassment allegations.

McCormack was bulleted - ostensibly - because he would not denounce attempts by Scott Morrison to align Australia with much of the rest of the world and commit Australia to net zero emissions by 2050.

To placate the Nationals, Morrison had already pledged that agriculture would be exempt from any sacrifices in reaching net zero.

The party's only involvement would be one of potential profit - that farmers could be paid for sequestering carbon to help achieve the aim. It was a point McCormack and Nationals Minister Darren Chester had tried to make but to no avail.

sentiment_pool.headline: Artists' haven hits the market
sentiment_pool.text:
The Nicholas Building, an 11-level art deco classic on Melbourne's Swanston Street home to a thriving community of artists and artisans, has hit the market as its owners, a group of wealthy Toorak families, move to sell after nearly five decades.

Completed in 1926, the building was commissioned by George and Alfred Nicholas, the founders of the Aspro pharmaceutical business. It was designed by Harry Norris, the architect responsible for a number of significant Melbourne commercial buildings. The property has had just two owners so far and could fetch more than $80 million.

Inside on the ground floor is the Cathedral Arcade with its barrel-vaulted, leadlight ceiling, and a historic postbox set into one wall. Above rise 10 storeys of bustling workshops and galleries populated by a plethora of creative types: jewellers, performance artists, graphic designers, writers and costumer designers.

The CBD building overlooks what will become Town Hall Station, which is being built as part of the Melbourne Metro development. Some of the Nicholas Building's neighbours were compulsorily acquired for the project.

Colliers' Lachlan MacGillivray, Matt Stagg and Oliver Hay are brokering the property along with Joseph Walton, Patrick Barnes and Michael Ryan of Allard Shelton, which also manages the property.

Mr MacGillivray said the Town Hall Train Station project would incorporate a 20,000-square-metre retail and commercial over-station development with commuter entrances from Swanston St

sentiment_pool.headline: Beforepay locks in $45m debt facility
sentiment_pool.text:
Wage pre-payment fintech Beforepay has secured its first major debt facility, locking in $45 million from Longreach Capital to support its next phase of growth.

The business, which is expected to pursue an initial public offering later this year, enables users to access their salaries in advance of being paid by their employer, with the funds able to be spent anywhere, on anything.

It already counts the likes of Airtasker chairman and Vocus founder James Spenceley as an investor, as well as Alium Capital and Pepper Group CEO Patrick Tuttle.

Last month the business brought on former Westpac chief strategy officer Jamie Twiss as CEO, replacing founder Tarek Ayoub, who is now focused on global growth and product innovation.

Yesterday the business was expected to pass the 100,000 active user milestone and Mr Twiss said Beforepay was growing by between 10 per cent and 15 per cent per month.

"We're looking forward with this new debt facility we've signed, which will give us additional financial flexibility," he said.

"We think this will fund the next 12 to 18 months. We don't have a total number of users that will take us to $45 million, but I think it'll be around 400,000."

The Longreach Capital debt facility has a cap of $45 million, but the business will scale up the amount of debt it needs as it grows, rather than accessing it all at once.

sentiment_pool.headline: ResMed swoops on rival's product stumble
sentiment_pool.text:
ResMed aims to capitalise on rival Royal Philips' global device recall but faces supply chain challenges that could affect its ability to respond to increasing demand.

Netherlands-based Philips has a €250 million ($394 million) problem with deterioration of the sound abatement foam used in its first generation DreamStation flow generators for people with obstructive sleep apnoea, which is probably caused by unapproved cleaning methods and higher humidity environments. Its DreamStation 2 is not affected.

ResMed president and chief operating officer Rob Douglas said the company, which makes ventilators, was well positioned to meet patient needs but warned on supply squeezes.

"We can't speak specifically to our competitors' challenges or their ability to deliver product, but we're well positioned to help customers meet the needs of their patients and would look to develop, enhance or expand relationships over the long term, " he told The Australian Financial Review. Mr Douglas would not comment on how ResMed planned to service all these customers, or if smaller orders would be passed over for larger ones.

sentiment_pool.headline: Negative gearing tumbles on lower interest rates
sentiment_pool.text:
The proportion of landlords negatively gearing rental properties has fallen below 60 per cent for the first time on record, reflecting a decline in interest rates.

Of the 2.2 million taxpayers owning at least one rental property, 1.3 million declared a net rental loss in 2018-19, according to new annual data published by the Australian Taxation Office.

Overall, net rental income was negative $3 billion.

Total gross rental income of $47.8 billion received by landlords was less than deductions for their cost of interest, capital works and other rental deductions incurred.

Despite the decline in negative gearing there are still many landlords owning multiple properties who are claiming a tax deduction for earning less rental income than the cost of running investment properties.

The number of landlords negative gearing at least six properties was 11,226 in 2018-19.

Some 10,935 landlords negative geared five properties, 26,719 owners had four properties claiming a net rental loss, 74,955 property investors had three properties negative geared and 250,035 had two properties claiming a loss.

Almost 1 million people - 931,132 - had one property negatively geared.

Landlords who claim a net rental loss are in effect betting on making money from a property investment via house price increases.

There were 19,113 fewer negatively geared landlords than in 2017-18, the first fall in five years, analysis by The Australian Financial Review shows.

sentiment_pool.headline: Victoria public service wages blow out
sentiment_pool.text:
Public service wages in Victoria have grown faster than in any state and territory since the Andrews Labor government took power six years ago, putting more pressure on the state's finances.

Victorian public servants are paid more than their counterparts around the country, except for federal public servants in the Australian Capital Territory, an analysis by The Australian Financial Review of Australian Bureau of Statistics wage data shows.

Full-time adult weekly cash earnings for Victorian public sector workers was $2083 in November 2020, $333 a week higher than the state's private sector workers. The state's public servants earn more than $4800 a year above their counterparts in NSW, which has a higher cost of living due to higher property prices.

Victoria's public sector workforce, including public entity businesses, grew to 322,605 in 2020, according to the Victorian Public Sector Commission. That represents an increase of 44,988 over five years. Public servant numbers have increased 32 per cent to 50,032.

Robert Carling, senior fellow at the Centre for Independent Studies and a former official at the Commonwealth and NSW treasury departments, said the growth in the cost of Victoria's public service had weakened the state's finances and contributed to the loss of its AAA credit rating.

"An increasing proportion of the Victorian workforce is bottled up in inefficient public sector activities," Mr Carling said. "The extremely high growth in the state's public payroll

sentiment_pool.headline: Stokes to chair Boral in board shake-up
sentiment_pool.text:
Seven Group chief executive Ryan Stokes, who became the new chairman of Boral on Friday after his company snagged almost 70 per cent of the building products group, is eyeing the substantial pipeline of infrastructure and construction projects in the eastern states as a major driver of returns.

Mr Stokes is backing CEO Zlatko Todorcevski to further overhaul Boral, and lift its profit margins on a consistent basis towards those of its better-performing US and European peers.

"With a disciplined approach to operational management and capital management, the company can deliver industry-leading margins and returns on invested capital over the medium to long term," Mr Stokes said on Friday.

He succeeds Kathryn Fagg who stepped down as chairman after three years. A board shake-up on Friday happened quickly after Seven Group secured 69.6 per cent of Boral after its takeover offer, launched on May 10, closed late on Thursday.

Richard Richards, Seven Group's chief financial officer, was appointed to the Boral board. He has been CFO since 2013 at Seven Group, which owns the mining-focused heavy machinery business WesTrac, equipment hire company Coates Hire and has a 29 per cent stake in Beach Energy.

Two existing directors, Peter Alexander and Deborah O'Toole, will step down from the Boral board after the October 28 annual general meeting.

sentiment_pool.headline: Japara investors warm to Calvary bid
sentiment_pool.text:
Japara Healthcare shares hit a two-year high as shareholders warmed to a recommended $380 million offer from Little Company of Mary Health Care, also known as Calvary Health Care.

The first of an expected wave of mergers in the beaten-down aged care sector is closer after Deloitte Corporate Finance found the $1.40 per share cash offer fair and reasonable to Japara shareholders and the board backed the offer in the absence of a better one.

The final offer was sweetened twice after Calvary's initial proposal in April of just $1.04 per share, which valued Japara at nearly $278 million. It topped a $326 million bid by rival not-for-profit player Bolton Clarke Group, which declined to comment.

Shares in the aged care operator rose 18.45 per cent to a two-year high of $1.38 yesterday. Calvary is a charitable Catholic organisation with more than 12,000 staff and volunteers, 14 public and private hospitals, 17 retirement and aged care facilities and a national community care centre network.

Shareholders will vote on the offer - proposed as a scheme of arrangement - in October. The $1.40 offer price is 75 per cent above Japara's closing share price of 80¢ on April 29, the day before Calvary's bid was unveiled, and 81 per cent higher than the prior 30-day volume-weighted average price of 77¢.

Japara's shares hit a low of 34¢ less than 12 months ago, and investors seem to see value in Calvary's offer.

sentiment_pool.headline: Morgan Stanley puts Cyara on show ahead of IPO
sentiment_pool.text:
Morgan Stanley bankers will be experiencing Zoom fatigue this week, as they are understood to be kicking off a non-deal roadshow for the latest SaaS play to target an ASX listing - Cyara.

The business, which is expected to go public later this year with a market capitalisation around the $500 million mark, is conducting virtual meetings with potential investors.

An automated customer experience quality assurance platform, Cyara taps into the customer engagement digitisation trend.

It helps businesses not only test their programs (such as call centres and web chat interfaces) for bugs, but ensures they work at scale by flooding them with thousands of calls, emails and SMS to monitor their functionality.

In the year to June 30, 2021, Cyara recorded $US35.3 million ($48 million) in revenue, according to information in front of fund managers.

Of this, $US28.2 million was SaaS-based.

Between 2019 and 2021 the business had a SaaS compound annual revenue growth rate of about 25 per cent.

Cyara has about 200 enterprise customers globally, spanning multiple industries. Some of its customers include eBay, Oracle and Vodafone. It has a customer churn rate of less than 10 per cent per annum.

The business, which is led by Alok Kulkarni who co-founded the business in 2006, raised $US25 million in 2016. Its investors include US venture capital firms PeakSpan Capital and Greenspring Associates. PeakSpan co-founders Phil Dur and Matt Melymuka sit on the company's board, alongside CEO

sentiment_pool.headline: Aldi Australia steps up investment in long-awaited e-commerce foray
sentiment_pool.text:
Discount retailer Aldi plans to spend more than $1.3 billion over the next few years on technology and distribution centres to support growth, keep up with consumer demand for convenience and cut costs to reduce prices.

Aldi Australia chief executive Tom Daunt said the retailer, whose sales last year reached $10.5 billion, would invest all the proceeds of a recent $930 million sale and leaseback of its distribution centres into transforming its supply chain.

It would also spend "hundreds of millions" more on new technology, including digital technology to support its long-awaited foray into e-commerce.

Aldi started selling "online exclusives" such as fridges, freezers and mattresses in May to augment its "special buys" offer in stores, and is assessing whether to sell alcoholic beverages and food and groceries online.

"We've taken the first baby steps in e-commerce ... the response has been fantastic," Mr Daunt said.

Aldi, which entered Australia in 2001 and has about about 580 stores, had been slow to embrace e-commerce until it was convinced it could do so efficiently, he said.

"When we extend our customer offer, either through new formats or e-commerce, we want to make sure we're always doing that in a way that doesn't over-complicate our business or add too much additional cost and compromise our ability to offer the lowest prices in the market," Mr Daunt said.

"We found a way to do that that delivers value for customers and us, so we'll continue with that trial."

sentiment_pool.headline: Behind the scenes of CBA's outage nightmares
sentiment_pool.text:
One of Commonwealth Bank of Australia's most senior executives has laid out the details of a series of tech problems that left customers raging about payment, app and online banking outages, confirming that no cyber attacks were involved and saying each outage was unrelated to the others.

The bank's executive general manager of payments services, Simon Birch, said CBA was well aware of how many problems were caused for its customers and apologised, while saying he was confident the bank had processes in place to prevent regular repeats.

The first outage happened on June 17 when CBA's systems crashed alongside those of numerous other banks after Akamai's Prolexic service, which is a platform used by organisations to protect against distributed denial of service attacks, went down.

This was followed by outages specific to CBA on June 23, when merchant terminals and online banking systems failed, and then last week, when customers again took to social media to complain they were stuck in supermarkets and service stations unable to pay for food and petrol.

"Obviously it has been extraordinarily difficult both for us and particularly for our customers, who rely on availability of our services on digital channels and point of sale to get paid and to pay for things," Mr Birch told The Australian Financial Review.

"The outages are not linked at all, they are unrelated incidents, which does provide a degree of comfort.

sentiment_pool.headline: Companies unleash pandemic war chest
sentiment_pool.text:
Businesses around the world are beginning to spend the vast sums of money borrowed through the pandemic, triggering a surge in takeovers and capital spending that will push corporate indebtedness to record levels, according to fund manager Janus Henderson.

Companies rushed to the capital markets last year to fortify their balance sheets through the downturn, tapping rock-bottom interest rates in a burst of borrowing that pushed total corporate debt to a new peak of $US13.5 trillion ($18.01 trillion) in 2020.

Now, companies are turning from raising money to putting it to work as economies like the US and Australia rebound stronger than expected.

The global spending wave will push net debt - the total amount borrowed, less cash - from $US8.3 trillion last year up to a record $US8.9 trillion by the end of the year, according to the top end of forecasts from the asset manager released yesterday.

"Last year was very much about survival," said Jay Sivapalan, the Melbourne-based head of Australian fixed interest for Janus Henderson.

"The corporate bond market was used by companies to bring forward a lot of borrowing."

Now, against the backdrop of robust global economic growth, companies are looking to spend their pandemic debt "war chest" on mergers and acquisitions, dividends, share repurchases and capital expenditure, known as capex, he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: Fortunes mixed amid virus turmoil
sentiment_pool.text:
COVID-19 is exposing the diverging fortunes of Australia's corporate heavyweights, with $52 billion supermarket giant Woolworths struggling to keep stores fully stocked in Sydney and 10,000 staff facing disruption from rules limiting movement outside of local council areas.

But the retail giant is still delivering healthy profits, reporting a 20.1 per cent increase in net profit to $1.5 billion in 2020-21 from its Australian and New Zealand supermarkets, BIG W chain and digital businesses. The bottom-line net profit before adjusting for the demerger of its Endeavour Group climbed 78 per cent to $2.07 billion, surpassing most market forecasts.

Endeavour Group, which owns the large Dan Murphy's and BWS liquor chains, and 293 pubs with 12,364 poker machines and which split off from Woolworths in June to become an ASX-listed company in its own right, now has 41 per cent of its hotels shut because of lockdowns in Sydney and Melbourne. Hotel sales have slipped by 7.3 per cent in the first eight weeks of the new financial year with 139 venues temporarily closed.

Travel agent Flight Centre yesterday announced a $507 million loss for 2020-21 and estimated it was burning through at least $30 million in cash each month as it waits for the economy to reopen.

sentiment_pool.headline: VGI warns of headwinds after weak start to half
sentiment_pool.text:
A $50 million boost from performance fees earned by VGI Partners in the first half of the year powered its interim profits, but that windfall may be far lower in the second half after poor performance in its portfolios since the end of June.

The investment manager, founded by Robert Luciano, runs an unlisted hedge fund and two listed investment companies. Its first-half performance fees, which are charged as a percentage of excess returns, were the biggest since at least 2018 and compare to just $100,000 earned in the first half of 2020, its results showed yesterday.

Net tangible assets on a per-share basis for VGI Global Investments, the largest of its listed portfolios, are down 8.6 per cent. Assets for its VGI Asian Investments LIC have fallen 12.5 per cent to the lowest level in a year.

Jon Howie, chief executive of VGI Partners, said the two portfolios had faced some headwinds in recent weeks.

"This does mean that our funds are currently below their high-water marks and that we will need to rebuild this performance before VGI begins earning performance fees for the current period," he said.

The declines for the Asia-focused LIC reflected a slide in Chinese tech stocks that sapped big holdings in Alibaba and Tencent since the end of June. Alibaba is down 27.3 per cent and Tencent more than 20 per cent.

The larger, globally focused LIC has suffered a 30 per cent decline in Pinterest shares and a 5 per cent fall for Amazon, two of its largest holdings.

sentiment_pool.headline: Why the best businesses are hiding in plain sight
sentiment_pool.text:
Monday fundie Sam Granger's Equanimity is a fan of big tech.

The megacaps of Wall Street have become market shorthand for why stocks go up and stocks go down, but their ubiquity can mean investors sometimes overlook the qualities that made them the most compelling businesses of our time.

Sam Granger's Equanimity Partners owns Microsoft, Alphabet, Facebook and Amazon in the Equanimity High Conviction Fund, a strategy Granger has newly converted from its previous home at Totus Capital.

"I like studying winners and massive successes. If you want to understand retail, you should study Amazon because they're the leader," the fund manager says. "Jeff Bezos is probably the best business leader of his generation. Is there anyone more capable in the world than him, a combination of ideas and an ability to execute? I don't think there is."

By way of returns, the fund has reported compound annual growth of 20.6 per cent after fees since inception, ahead of the benchmark's 10.2 per cent over its 4½ years. In 2020-21, Equanimity earned 33.3 per cent against the benchmark's 30.2 per cent.

With the majority of his stocks having already reported second-quarter numbers, Granger was impressed by the calibre of earnings.

"Alphabet, Facebook, Microsoft, they're growing their earnings at 40 or 50 per cent each," he says. "It's unbelievably strong."

He finds there's no penalty to staying on top of these businesses from Sydney, where he is based.

sentiment_pool.headline: Nine, News urged to pull Palmer ads
sentiment_pool.text:
Five federal crossbench MPs, including leader of the Australian Greens Adam Bandt, have written a joint letter to Nine Entertainment and News Corp calling on them to stop publishing ads from Clive Palmer that spread misinformation about COVID-19.

The letter, co-signed by Mr Bandt, Helen Haines, Rebekha Sharkie, Zali Steggall and Andrew Wilkie, said Nine and News should acknowledge the harm done by the recent front-page ads in The Age, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Australian Financial Review, and News' The Australian, as well as regional mastheads, including The Mercury, Herald Sun and Adelaide Advertiser, and stop publishing them.

The politicians did acknowledge the newspapers using their reporting to call out the misinformation, which they argue "stands in stark contrast to Nine Entertainment Co and News Corp's subsequent corporate decision to publish front-page anti-lockdown advertisements from Clive Palmer in these same mastheads for profit".

Nine, which owns this masthead, has rejected a number of ads Mr Palmer sought to publish in its newspapers which contravened the health advice or ATAGI guidance on COVID-19 vaccines.

sentiment_pool.headline: Pendula eyes global expansion
sentiment_pool.text:
Pendula, a communications start-up that has created software to enable better conversations between organisations and their customers, has banked a $6.75 million funding round to double down on overseas expansion.

Pendula has clients including Origin Energy, Amaysim, Ramsay HealthCare, TEDX, and the Cancer Council, and plans to use the new funding, which was led by MA Financial Group and existing investor Equity Venture Partners, to build out the product's analysis and insight capability.

"We're in this great stage now where we've got the repeatability, we know how to deploy our software into all kinds of businesses and get them talking with their customers," said CEO Alex Colvin, who founded Pendula in 2017.

The company's technology leverages the Australian preference for SMS to build communication between businesses or organisations and their customers or staff.

This means companies such as telco Amaysim can automatically offer a plan upgrade should a customer run out of data, using a quick automated text message.

Origin Energy has used Pendula to manage power use during busy periods; alerting customers using airconditioners during expensive periods and asking if they wanted to adjust settings.

Using natural language processing, the software can learn and direct a customer's response. Over the last year, Pendula has managed more than 20 million conversations.

sentiment_pool.headline: Crimson Education mulls IPO
sentiment_pool.text:
Kiwi university admissions consultant Crimson Education, whose investors include famed hedge fund manager Julian Robertson and former New Zealand prime minister John Key, is testing the waters for a listing.

Crimson Education introduced the business to Australian fund managers at an Ord Minnett roadshow earlier in the month, which pitched the broker's IPO hopefuls for 2022.

Crimson used the appearance to vet appetite in the local listed markets, and explained its business, which is pinned on helping high school students get into at A-league universities.

It is understood Crimson is weighing up listing venues around the globe, with ASX just one of the stops on the way. It is also understood to be happy to stay unlisted.

The meet and greet with the local listed equities managers comes as it continues to tap the private markets.

Crimson's last capital raising, in August, valued the company at about $US460 ($635 million), and added Sydney's HEAL Partners to its shareholder register.

Its other shareholders include Chase Coleman's Tiger Global Management, Tiger Management founder Julian Roberston, local Perennial Value Management, Korea's Solborn Investment and college rankings player US News.

The business was founded eight years ago in New Zealand, and now works with students in almost 25 countries. It offers university admissions support, including online tutoring and admission essay reviews.

sentiment_pool.headline: More than two in five lie to buy
sentiment_pool.text:
More than two in five homebuyers lied on their mortgage application as they chased the fast-rising property market, according to UBS.

The share of home loans that are not completely factually accurate has jumped by 3 percentage points to a record 41 per cent from a year ago and well above the 27 per cent recorded in 2015.

The poll of around 900 Australians who took out a mortgage in the last year was conducted between June 21 and July 5, at the start of the lockdowns.

The UBS survey also found that among the major banks, ANZ and NAB saw the largest upticks in factual misstatements, climbing by 13 percentage points to 54 per cent and 17 percentage points to 46 per cent respectively.

NAB executive, home ownership, Andy Kerr said: "We are committed to lending responsibly and want to ensure customers are able to appropriately manage their repayments, both today and in the future.

"It is not in customers' interests to borrow money which they cannot afford to repay, which is why NAB will continue to assess a customer's ability to repay their loan by considering their income, expenses and overall indebtedness.

"NAB applies a range of measures to help us verify information to determine a customer's suitability for a loan, and ensure that the information provided is accurate. This is done with the customer directly, as well as verifying the information provided with a number of sources."

sentiment_pool.headline: CBA hit with charges over junk insurance
sentiment_pool.text:
Commonwealth Bank has been hit with 30 criminal charges for its false and misleading conduct in the sale of consumer credit insurance policies between 2011 and 2015.

The action was filed in the Federal Court by the corporate regulator and relates to a prominent case study from the 2018 Hayne royal commission that enveloped its highest-paid executives, past and present.

During the hearings, it emerged up to 64,000 customers had been sold insurance while ineligible to make claims. The bank pulled the products from sale just two weeks before the hearing.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has acknowledged the bank's co-operation in the matter. CBA has said it will plead guilty and has refunded customers a total of $75 million. It is facing a maximum penalty of $51 million under the charges.

The matter of the mis-sold insurance policies was explored in detail by counsel assisting Rowena Orr who accused the bank of minimising the problem by telling "its board one thing" and "ASIC something radically different". Ms Orr questioned CBA's then-general manager of retail, Clive van Horen, about the sequences of events in March and later grilled chief executive Matt Comyn during the final round of hearings in November 2018 in Sydney.

sentiment_pool.headline: Uranium sputters back to life with big buyer, push for clean power

Ten years ago, an earth-shattering magnitude-nine earthquake sent a 15-metre tsunami crashing through the sea wall of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant, disabling the power supply and cooling of three reactors, and triggering a nuclear meltdown.

The chemical explosions that ensued sent radioactive material leaking into the atmosphere and Pacific Ocean, creating what is known as the second-worst nuclear calamity in history, behind the Chernobyl disaster 25 years earlier.

Fukushima's nuclear reactors were fuelled by uranium, which consequently suffered a demand shock and prolonged downturn as mines shut or entered care and maintenance. The spot price traded in a depressed range of $US20 to $US30 a pound - not nearly high enough to encourage production.

But after a decade in the shadows, the sector has been jolted back to life within just a few weeks thanks largely to the Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (SPUT). The vehicle is in the midst of a buying frenzy of physical uranium, taking supply out of the market and boosting the spot price to $US40.40 a pound - its highest level in seven years.

"There's been so much fuel on the floor of the uranium market given it's been such an undersupplied commodity," the portfolio manager of Tribecca's global natural resources fund, Ben Cleary, said. "The match to set this on fire has been Sprott buying spot [uranium]."

sentiment_pool.headline: HOW TO LEAVE THE KIDS 'JUST ENOUGH'
sentiment_pool.text:

Parents who have built large fortunes are increasingly bequeathing their children only part of the estate, with the rest going to favourite charities. This is because they want their offspring to have enough to achieve their goals but not so much that they lack motivation, say Australian inheritance specialists.

Some of the world's richest parents, including Microsoft financier Bill Gates and Berkshire Hathaway founder and chief Warren Buffett, also claim they don't want their children to inherit all of their billions.

Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook's chief executive, has committed to give away 99 per cent of his $US114 billion ($155 billion) fortune to "advance human potential", while 007 star Daniel Craig describes inheritance as "distasteful" and does not want his children to inherit the Bond millions.

Specialist lawyers claim large bequests to charities are increasing among Australian families whose parents have created enough wealth (typically upwards of $10 million) to give their children the option of not working for a living.

Pruning an inheritance can be a sensitive issue for family members and can - if not planned carefully and treated diplomatically - end up in the courts.

sentiment_pool.headline: NSW set to quarantine at home
sentiment_pool.text:
NSW plans to phase out the requirement for Australians returning from overseas to spend two weeks quarantined in hotels and foreshadowed that it will demand all other states end internal travel bans on NSW.

In another sign that NSW has decided to lead the return of regular life in Australia, Premier Gladys Berejiklian said she would end the hotel quarantine system that other states continue to use.

"Once we hit 80 per cent double-dosed, by that stage all internal borders in Australia should not exist," she said yesterday. "By that stage NSW would welcome home thousands of Australians every week."

The NSW vaccination rate has reached 40.8 per cent of the adult population having received two doses, with 73.5 per cent having had one dose.

Ms Berejiklian said it "would make sense" for Australians who receive a "credible" vaccine overseas to be allowed to isolate in their homes.

"We are already considering when we do that and how we do that," she said. "I think the current quarantine system has nearly reached its use-by date in terms of how effective it is."

Esther Rockett, a co-founder of the Stranded Aussies Action Network, said hotel quarantine, which costs individuals $3000 in NSW, could safely end immediately for fully vaccinated Australians.

"When you have such tiny numbers of overseas arrivals testing positive to COVID-19, the risk is just no longer there," she said.

Chief executive Graham Chipchase also warned yesterday about rising inflation as a shortage of timber for making new pallets and rising labour costs lift prices.

"Pallet availability remained challenging in the first quarter, with industry-wide shortages of new pallet supply across the globe as well as lower levels of pallet returns and lower cycle times in our North American business," he said.

They are used to transport food, beverages and dry grocery products into retail stores and large warehouses operated by traditional retailers and e-commerce companies.

Sales revenue in the three months ended September 30 rose 11 per cent to $US1.29 billion ($1.74 billion), Brambles said in a trading update.

Sales in the Asia-Pacific region, which includes Australia where Sydney and Melbourne suffered extended lockdowns, rose 14 per cent. The biggest Brambles business, in the Americas region, reported a 10 per cent rise in sales revenue, as did sales in the European division.

sentiment_pool.headline: US inflation rise fires up talk of earlier rate hike
sentiment_pool.text:
Washington | Economists are pricing in a rate hike as early as next year following higher than expected inflation in the United States, which could start undermining corporate profits in coming months.

The consumer price index rose 0.4 per cent in September, pushing annual inflation back up to 5.4 per cent, the largest annual gain since 2008, according to Labor Department data released on Wednesday (Thursday AEDT).

The pick-up in price growth reflected higher food, energy and housing costs. Rents jumped the most in 20 years.

Though measures of used cars, trucks and airfares cooled, these are expected to rebound. Economists now think inflation data will be "sequentially firm in the months ahead".

"The positive surprise in persistent inflation suggests we remain in a hot economy, which could prompt the Fed to move sooner," Bank of America's Alexander Lin said.

"While transitory factors continue to roll off, stickier, more persistent factors are becoming more prevalent, which the Fed is more likely to respond to."

Following the data, overnight interest rate swaps briefly priced in a September 2022 rate hike before pushing it out to November, with economists such as those at Deustche Bank locking in the first official rate rise in December.

"Deutsche Bank now expects rate liftoff from the Fed in December 2022 from the previous call of the third quarter of 2023," Deustche's Matt Luzzetti said.

sentiment_pool.headline: CBA tops complaint list for third straight year
sentiment_pool.text:
Commonwealth Bank has retained its title as the recipient of the most customer complaints for the third year running, with residents of the outer suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne among the most aggrieved financial services customers.

In the last financial year, consumers lodged 67,613 complaints about financial product providers with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), according to data released by the agency.

It represents a modest fall from the year before, when a record 76,874 complaints were made against financial services providers.

The overwhelming majority of complaints made about the big four were related to payment services, home loans and credits cards. One-quarter of complaints last year were about the big four banks, with consumers making 5815 complaints about CBA. ANZ got the second-highest level of complaints followed by NAB and Westpac.

The big four feature in a large portion of complaints because of their size. CBA, the largest of the major banks, claims to have 15.9 million customers.

A spokesman for CBA said the bank achieved "an industry-leading 11 per cent decrease in the overall number of complaints in the last financial year while we were able to resolve nearly two-thirds of the total without a referral to AFCA".

"Our proportion of resolved complaints was also higher than our major peers," the spokesman said. "That said, we know how important it is to resolve complaints quickly and satisfactorily and we therefore welcome the role t

sentiment_pool.headline: Premier hopeful Perrottet to back euthanasia vote
sentiment_pool.text:
Conservative NSW premier hopeful Dominic Perrottet will support a conscience vote on voluntary assisted dying laws, a move that will placate Liberal moderates and independent MPs ahead of a contested ballot for the leadership.

Mr Perrottet opposed the contentious decriminalisation of abortion in NSW and Premier Gladys Berejiklian has not made her stance on a conscience vote for voluntary assisted dying public.

The Treasurer will face a party room vote for the Liberal leadership today against Planning Minister Rob Stokes, with Mr Perrottet the frontrunner.

NSW State Parliament is in chaos following a series of resignations after Ms Berejiklian announced her own on Friday after becoming the target of an inquiry by the state's anti-corruption watchdog.

Deputy Premier John Barilaro resigned yesterday morning, the day after Transport Minister Andrew Constance announced he would be leaving with hopes of a move to federal politics.

The winner of today's Liberal leadership bout will face a minority government, propped up by the support of independents and former government MPs who quit amid scandal to sit on the crossbench.

Independent MP Alex Greenwich said the crossbenchers would not make any demands of the next premier to guarantee supply.

"The priority for the independents will be to make sure that we are providing stability," he said.

sentiment_pool.headline: AUSTRALIA COUNTS THE COST OF FREE MONEY
sentiment_pool.text:
Monetary policy The wealth gap has been allowed to grow ever wider as the property market has boomed and the sharemarket notches up record highs, writes Richard Henderson.

A year ago, Australia set foot on new terrain, dropping interest rates to near zero as it played its part in a worldwide central bank strike to stabilise the global economy.

The move was a first for Australia. At the height of the global financial crisis more than a decade ago, Australia skirted through the 2008 mayhem largely because of its powerful links with a booming China as other countries slashed rates to fresh lows.

But not this time. The COVID-19 pandemic set the Reserve Bank of Australia on a path to a cash rate of 0.1 per cent, which was reached in November last year. Ultra-low interest rates are a linchpin in the unprecedented monetary support that has reduced borrowing costs across the economy.

That support has come at a cost, however. A runaway property boom and record highs for the sharemarket have widened the wealth gap, refocusing attention on the role central banks play in inequality and prompting the most significant property market intervention by the prudential regulator in almost five years.

sentiment_pool.headline: RBA cuts across PM's rates pitch
sentiment_pool.text:
Prime Minister Scott Morrison's warning that interest rates could be higher without the Coalition in power has been hosed down by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Philip Lowe, who is firm the cash rate is likely to remain at the record low 0.1 per cent until 2024.

Channelling former prime minister John Howard, Mr Morrison this week said the inflation spike seen in the United States should serve as a warning about what could happen in Australia, and local interest rates and the cost of living would be higher than needed under Labor.

But Dr Lowe said global inflationary pressures had been "more muted" in Australia than in other countries, and the cash rate would likely only rise once annual wages growth was above 3 per cent.

The last time annual wages growth was running at that level was March 2013, and Dr Lowe said the "probability" of reversing a decades-long decline in wages growth in just six months was "very, very low".

The RBA has for months sounded a more cautious note on inflation despite financial markets, consumer expectations and now the Prime Minister taking a more bullish outlook, but Dr Lowe's message was blunt.

Markets are pricing in between three and four rate rises by the end of 2022. The RBA governor said the economic data did not warrant that outlook.

"If you think wages are going to go from 2 per cent to 3.5 or something in six months, well, maybe the market's right, and we're wrong," he said in a speech to a group of business economists in Sydney ye

sentiment_pool.headline: Testing biotech Ellume fronts up, seeks $500m-plus valuation
sentiment_pool.text:
Investors are getting up close and personal with rapid diagnostics company Ellume, a Queensland-based biotech with big US government contracts to supply COVID-19 tests and aspirations to list on the ASX.

Ellume has called in stockbrokers Morgans and Ord Minnett to show the business to Australian fund managers this week, in an effort to raise $85 million in a pre-initial public offering funding round.

Sources said the valuation was far from set, but numbers in the $600 million to $800 million range had been thrown around. It's going to take some work for investors to feel comfortable with any valuation thanks to the company's status as a major COVID-19 beneficiary.

It has been on a tear thanks to the pandemic, scoring a $305 million deal with the US Department of Defence to supply 20 million rapid COVID-19 antigen testing kits to the US.

However, it was unable to fulfil all 20 million tests by the end of the first half of 2021 as planned, thanks to supply chain issues.

It also issued a voluntary recall in October of 2.2 million of its home-testing kits thanks to a faulty component affecting 3.3 per cent of its kits. The issue only affected certain batches and has since been rectified and the company continues to send new tests to the US.

The Queensland-based company, which confirmed the pre-IPO raise to Street Talk yesterday, was founded by critical care clinician Dr Sean Parsons in 2010 after seeing the unmet need for rapid diagnostic solutions during the 2009 swine flu

sentiment_pool.headline: US inflation surge fuels bond market hawks
sentiment_pool.text:
Bond yields shot higher globally after the biggest annual gain in US consumer prices in more than three decades fuelled market expectations of an increase in interest rates sooner than the US Federal Reserve's timing.

The US Treasury 10-year yield jumped to 1.57 per cent and the 30-year yield flew to 1.98 per cent before easing to 1.92 per cent. On the shorter end of the curve, which is the most sensitive to Fed rate expectations, the two-year yield powered up to 0.51 per cent and the five-year to 1.22 per cent.

Inflation expectations surged, with the five-year break-even inflation rate reaching a record high 3.113 per cent and the 10-year break-even rate at 2.72 per cent, a level not seen since May 2006.

The US dollar index climbed to a 15-month peak of 94.9 against a basket of currencies. It was last at 94.8.

The US consumer price index increased 0.9 per cent last month for 6.2 per cent annual growth. It was the biggest such rise since November 1990, accelerating from a 5.4 per cent advance in September. The increase was broad-based and led by petrol prices, up 6.1 per cent.

The Fed has long maintained prices will fall once supply bottlenecks start easing, but the data is challenging that interpretation.

Bond futures are now fully pricing a 25 basis point rate increase in the Fed funds rate by July.

Australian bond markets reacted in sympathy, with yields on the three-year government bond about 16 basis points higher to 0.901 per cent.

sentiment_pool.text:
Much has been said and written about the challenges associated with commercialising research from universities and publicly funded research organisations. But little of this has led to step change.

Why? Why is it so difficult to commercialise research, particularly when so many new breakthroughs are discovered at universities? How do we create a system that gives things a chance to succeed?

When it comes to commercialising university technologies, globally less than 5 per cent make it to an actual commercial product that generates revenue for both the inventors and the university.

After 45 years and 10,000 discoveries at Stanford, just three had generated multimillion-dollar licences by 2016.

The reality is that the system to support commercialisation of new technologies, in the broadest sense, is complex, and the roles and responsibilities of each element of the system need to be understood. Universities themselves don't commercialise technologies. Universities work with existing companies, investors, new companies, entrepreneurs, and governments to drive the commercialisation process.

With the economic impact of COVID-19 being felt in higher education more acutely than many other sectors, universities have the opportunity to challenge their business models, which includes prioritising their focus on research commercialisation and partnering effectively with industry.

sentiment_pool.headline: CIMIC chief breaks his silence
sentiment_pool.text:
Skills shortages, cost blowouts, supply chain blockages and the need for greater national co-ordination were the big themes at The Australian Financial Review Infrastructure Summit.

These were all covered by CIMIC executive chairman Juan Santamaria in his first media appearance since taking over in November last year.

Since replacing Marcelino Fernandez Verdes, Santamaria has cleaned up the balance sheet by cutting all ties with Greensill's supply chain finance and moved to spin off the Ventia infrastructure maintenance business through an initial public offering. His contribution was doubly interesting because CIMIC has fingers in more parts of the infrastructure pie than any other company.

To put CIMIC's infrastructure reach in perspective, it has work in hand of $33.3 billion, and it has lodged tenders for projects totalling another $470 billion. These projects include roads, rail, electricity, hospitals and mining projects.

On the first thematic of skills shortages, Santamaria says COVID-19 changed everything because there was no longer the free movement of people across state and international borders.

Before COVID-19 hit the economy, CIMIC relied heavily on fly in, fly out domestic workers from all around Australia. Also, there was free two-way movement of CIMIC staff between Australia and the company's international operations in South East Asia, Hong Kong, India, Canada and Botswana.

sentiment_pool.headline: Luxury goods flying out the door
sentiment_pool.text:
Mary Poulakis cannot keep up with customer demand, particularly when it comes to the shoe of the season (glamour heels from Romanian designer Amina Muaddi).

"There are buying limits placed on us, as retailers, now for those shoes," says the owner and managing director of Harrolds department store, which has boutiques in Sydney and Melbourne.

"We are selling out before the stock even hits the floor. And we're selling them to customers in Hong Kong, Paris, New York ... it's intense."

Other must-have items in the lead-up to Christmas include Jacquemus bags, limited edition Assouline coffee table books and "anything from Bottega Veneta", according to Ms Poulakis.

Luxury retail is set to boom again this year, with pent-up demand from consumers fuelling a shopping spree like no other. Research by the Australian Retailers Association and Roy Morgan predicts that Australians are tipped to spend close to $59 billion before Christmas - a figure similar to last year but up 11.3 per cent on pre-pandemic levels in 2019. After Christmas, sales are predicted to rake in a further $21.1 billion, up 2.1 per cent on 2020 spending and 12.6 per cent on 2019.

"There's a lot at play here," Australian Retailers Association chief executive Paul Zahra says. "Consumers are ready to spend after months in lockdown. Fuel change at a fast and furious pace
sentiment_pool.text:
Two years ago there was little doubt among motoring experts that the big trends were summed up with the acronym CASE. The cars of the very near future were to be increasingly Connected, Autonomous, Shared and Electric.

Since then, the pandemic has slowed — though not halted — interest in the idea of sharing vehicles, while the realisation is landing that full self-driving cars are still some way away, despite anything Elon Musk might say. The first 95 per cent of automotive autonomy was achieved relatively quickly, but the last bit is proving far more complex and expensive than previously thought.

Still, automotive technology is progressing at a pace that is fast and furious. There are step changes in almost every area of the industry, from the way cars are designed, to the way they are built, marketed and sold.

While so-called Level 5 self-driving, which is to say complete autonomy with no pedals or steering wheel inside the vehicle, won't be within the hands of private buyers any time soon, there have been massive improvements in Level 2 and Level 3 systems. Some of today's cars have the capability to drive themselves between cities, hands-off.

This "on-ramp to off-ramp" expressway driving ability, on cars such as the BMW iX, is still waiting for regulatory approval in most places, but the carmakers are confident it's coming.
